docs.title: Age of Sail — Player's Logbook
docs.text:
The Age of Sail is a RoleMaster-based tabletop RPG campaign, set in a fictitious world with technology somewhat akin to the real world of the 1600s to 1800s, but with more of the flavour of the Voyages of Sinbad mixed with classic adventures from the Golden Age of Piracy. Expect exploration, swashbuckling, black powder cannons, scurvy, marooning, pieces of eight, sea monsters, buxom wenches, strapping lads, and the occasional evil sorceress...

This Logbook is the record of everything the crew has done and encountered — session summaries, lore, and handouts, all in one place. Browse by chapter in the sidebar, or check What's New? for the latest additions.

The crew also coordinates on Discord — ask your GM if you'd like to join.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
This session was a character creation workshop, with the GM guiding three of the players through building their characters using the RoleMaster system.

Werner De Rendal, son of Kasimir De Rendal, established himself as a Common Human of the Mariner culture, taking the Labourer profession. The De Rendal family was once a prominent noble house of the North, its wealth built on whaling and later sailing, but their fortune collapsed when the currents changed and swallowed both trades. Werner arrived in the Capitol with little more than a fine suit of clothes, a single silver coin, and the weight of a storied family name — enough to buy himself a good meal and to know which cutlery to eat it with, but little more. He carries no blade, since the family cutlass remains in the North with his elder brother, to be sent south only once Werner actually secures his commission. His grandfather was commissioned as a skilled sailing expert on a royal expedition westward — before Werner was born — and never returned, while his father Kasimir kept to the family's failing whaling trade until debts overwhelmed the estate. With his elder brother holding what remains of the crumbling estate in the North, its debts mounting further with each passing year, Werner has come south to seek his fortune and send back whatever he can, even if he expects to see little of it for himself. He was raised with an education fitting his station: he reads and writes well, speaks and writes the common tongue fluently, and knows the standardised semaphore signals used between ships of a fleet, alongside whatever unofficial signals a given crew might keep to itself. His Boon is his aristocratic status: the De Rendal name still opens the right doors, however threadbare the support behind it, and the manners and bearing of nobility come to him without a thought — though everyone knows a man who falsely claims status and is caught at it pays dearly for the lie, so it is not a card Werner means to play lightly. His ambition aboard ship is practical rather than aristocratic: he pictures himself earning a place as master of sail or senior gunner, taking his share of any prize money, rather than leaning on his name for an authority he could not otherwise back up. He means to build his fighting skill in stages — the harpoon of his family's whaling trade first, the cutlass of a naval officer next, and in time the heavier guns of a warship.

Knick Nab is one-eighth Elf, taken from the Northern Highlands — a country of rough hills and mountain terrain, isolated by the land itself, where people live by herding and whatever farming the ground allows — at a young age and brought to the Capitol to serve as a pickpocket for an underworld contact who runs a group of young thieves. He remains slight and frail, a legacy of some injury or mistreatment he suffered before he ever reached the city; it was that same frailty, together with a recognised talent for thieving, that led his underworld contact to take him in, and he has never fully recovered his strength. He chose the Rogue profession. His partial elven heritage — though he barely understands it himself — shows in a single pointed ear, kept hidden beneath the bandanas and broad hats he always wears, and grants him night vision and a natural quickness of reflex. His Boon is a subtle ability to discern what people truly want at their core, a gift that may prove invaluable in negotiation, leadership, and knowing when to run — though it is no everyday trick, and turning it toward the wrong person could prove as dangerous as it is useful. He imagines working his way up through the crew to a position such as quartermaster or boatswain — respect earned from the men around him, rather than the kind of rank that only ever comes with a title.

Noddy is a Mixed Man of the Harsh culture — a survivor of the city's worst and most desperate corners. He aspires to the Mystic profession, drawn to the realms of Essence and Mentalism, forms of magic entirely unknown to the people of the North and potentially very dangerous to practise there. His abilities, at least in his own experience, have so far manifested as uncanny luck and fortune rather than anything that could be labelled as sorcery. He took the Breath Holding and Elemental Resistance (Cold) talents, practical skills for someone who once dove for pearls to survive. Aboard ship he expects to serve as a Marine, a soldier standing apart from the sailing crew's own chain of command — a role that counts for little at sea but rather more once the ship makes port.

The absent players' characters were also discussed briefly: Mani (Manuel de Barret), a fighter pursuing a Florentine style of swordsmanship with rapier and dagger; Cosimo (Cosimo Cellini Scivio), whose profession had not yet been settled, though the GM mused he might suit a bookish, non-combat role such as a surgeon, given an interest in alchemy and herbs; and Riu (Infurious Montesigna), leaning toward the Dabbler profession as a semi-spell user of Essence — the GM noted his aptitude for machinery might suit him to a role such as carpenter's mate, since a ship is as full of mechanisms, from pumps to block and tackle, as any workshop.

The group are all starting as fourteen-year-olds, not yet of adventuring experience — the GM noted that even a weasel might pose a meaningful challenge to them at this stage.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
The GM shared substantial background on the world:

The Great Change: In the relatively recent past — within the characters' lifetimes — a major and unexplained change in the world's weather systems made ocean travel to the West possible for the first time. Before this, any ship that lost sight of land to the west never returned; the winds simply would not allow it. Now, both the North and South are sending expeditions across the sea. This change is the central premise of the Age of Sail.

The World at War: The North and the South are currently at war, and the characters' story begins against that backdrop.

The Capitol: The main city of the North, built against a great cliff. Power rests with two factions: "the Hill," representing the Divinity of Two and its Temple, and "the House," the seat of Royal authority. These two factions coexist in uneasy equilibrium, with influence shifting between them over time.

The Divinity of Two: The dominant — and effectively only — religion in the North, centred on two gods: the Father and the Mother. All publicly recognised magic in the North is attributed to this religion. Practising any other form of magic is heresy, and heretics disappear without explanation. Among the Divinity's ranks are the Censures, an inquisitor-type order (classed as Paladins in game terms) who enforce religious orthodoxy. The Divinity maintains that two clerics of the Faith must accompany any significant expedition.

Status and Society: The North is rigidly stratified by class and status. Nobles and aristocrats have privileges denied to commoners, including the right to ride horses. The South, by contrast, is far more egalitarian — one of the deep sources of tension between the two powers, and one reason some men choose a life outside both.

Werner's Family History: Werner's grandfather was commissioned as a skilled sailor and sailing expert to join a royal expedition westward at a time when the Great Change had not yet happened. He did not return. The mission was sponsored by the king and included two clerics of the Divinity of Two, one of whom was a Censure. There are rumours in the family that something came back from that voyage — but Werner has never seen his grandfather. His father Kasimir carried on the family's whaling trade until it could no longer support them, leaving the estate deep in debt.

Knick Nab's Background: Knick Nab was taken from the Highlands and brought to the Capitol to work as a pickpocket for an underworld contact who organises a gang of young thieves operating across Low Town and High Town. He is still learning the trade.

Noddy's Background: Noddy comes from the most desperate circumstances in the city — effectively the sewers and lower gutters. He has survived through wit and an uncanny run of luck he attributes, at least loosely, to the favour of the Mother.

Shipboard Roles: The GM outlined the ranks the group might rise to beneath a ship's commissioned officers. The master of sail runs the day-to-day work of sails and rigging; the quartermaster stands the other watch and answers for the ship's stores and material; the boatswain is the senior non-commissioned rank, directing gun crews and work parties. A ship's Marines answer to the captain directly, standing apart from the sailing crew's own chain of command — a position that counts for little at sea, but rather more once the ship makes port. One small compensation: Marines are said to eat rather better than the rest of the crew, even at sea.

Magic in the World: Magic is uncommon and poorly understood by most citizens. The only publicly recognised source of power is the Divinity of Two. Other forms — Essence and Mentalism — are unknown to ordinary people in the North, and practising them openly risks being labelled a heretic. The one other rumour that circulates is of a fire cult somewhere in the South, which the Divinity of Two dismisses as nothing more than flash powder, sleight of hand, and stage trickery — not real magic at all.

The Cost of Magic: The GM indicated that even a spell a character knows how to cast will not come free — many require reagents or components gathered in the world before they can be used. The trade-off cuts both ways: effort spent tracking down the right materials could let a character achieve something more spectacular than their skill would otherwise allow.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
This session continued the character creation process with a fuller group present. The GM took the opportunity to share an overview of the Known World via a map and to expand on several points of world lore.

Mani (Manuel de Barret), played by Scala, was introduced as a Common Human of the Mariner culture. He comes from a family of means — not noble, but wealthy through the fabric trade and, when times are hard, through smuggling. His father's connections run along the coasts and rivers of the North, with fine cloth and other goods flowing through port towns toward the Capitol; the family's home is a harbour town at a river's mouth, well placed for shipyards and river trade alike, though their growing ambitions have lately drawn them toward the Capitol itself. Mani was given a formal education, including tutored lessons in music, history, philosophy, and swordsmanship — but he was never allowed to forget that he lacked the blood of a nobleman. This injustice has become the central fire of his character: he intends to prove that skill, not birth, makes a man great. As a Fighter, he expects to develop breadth across many weapon types, beginning with the blade. He took Prodigy (Blade) as a talent, granting him a natural facility with bladed weapons from the outset, alongside Golden Throat (for charm and persuasion), Pressing Advantage (a bonus to his follow-up attack after landing a solid blow), and Ambidexterity, clearing the way for him to one day fight with a blade in each hand — a rapier paired with a main gauche. His tutoring also left him with an eye for fine materials: he put ranks into Philosophy and into Materials Lore, specialising in fabrics — a fitting complement to a family whose wealth is woven, quite literally, into cloth. Rather than simply killing his opponents, he means to make a habit of disarming them and keeping the hilts of their broken weapons as trophies — a swordsman's reputation is worthless if no one lives to spread it, and he is untroubled by the fact that this approach will make him enemies as readily as it makes him famous. Being feared means little to him; he wants to be known, and intends to make himself a fixture of taverns and gathering-places once his reputation is worth spreading — playing the instrument his tutors taught him and, in time, perhaps setting his own exploits to verse. His Boon was also settled this session: an old coin or medallion, not yet in his possession, that will one day make him strongly resistant to magic — an odd gift for a young man with no facility for or interest in the arcane.

Riu (Infurious Montesigna), played by Alain, was introduced in this session. He comes from a minor noble family on the Plains, known for horses. A younger son with no obligation to carry on the family's core work, he has been free to follow his own obsessive curiosity — books, lore, the mechanisms of things, and the faint scent of magic at the edges of understanding. He is working toward the Dabbler profession, a semi-spell user of Essence, though at this stage he is simply a bookish young man who has come to the Capitol to access libraries and pursue his interests. A dabbler's talents lean roguish as much as arcane, and Riu already sees his own niche clearly: not a housebreaker or a picker of locks, but a pickpocket, light-fingered and quick to vanish into a crowd — and he has an eye for traps as well, both setting and disarming them, a natural extension of his fascination with mechanisms. His most notable talent is an eidetic memory — once he has read something, he does not forget it. True to his magpie approach to knowledge, he spread his language study thin rather than deep, picking up a smattering of several written languages — including fragments of a language claimed to belong to the elves said to live beyond the mountains, and even snippets of a written magical language — rather than mastering one or two. Rather than take the usual Multilingual package of ten ranks in a single language or five ranks apiece in two, he asked for and received the same ten points split three ways across several written-only tongues, which suited a mind more interested in breadth than fluency. His curiosity even brushed against the Divinity of Two's own liturgical writing, of which he now knows a very little — a dangerous thread to pull, since scholars who go looking in that direction draw the authorities' suspicion. He and the GM spent a long stretch of the session trying to define his Boon: Riu wanted something like a knack for improvising working devices out of mundane, scavenged materials, tying into his fascination with machinery and his theoretical dabbling in magic. The GM worried aloud that such an ability could unbalance the game and floated alternatives — an improvising chemist's knack for gunpowder, an intrinsic understanding of unfamiliar peoples and customs, or a spell-like ability to intuit the true nature of an unfamiliar object on sight — but no final form was settled by the end of the session. In the course of the discussion, the GM let slip that some of the world's oldest structures, including the Capitol's own castle, have no known builders or surviving records of their construction. He mused that somewhere in the world there may be a whole class of scholars who keep the old records — a mystery, and a possible source of answers, that struck a chord with Riu's scholarly and mechanical bent.

Werner De Rendal (Allen) confirmed a piece of his background this session: his family are renowned old-school sailors of the North, with particular skill in reading northern waters and navigating by them — a pedigree well suited to a Mariner background, even if the family's fortunes have since faded. Among his weapon skills he chose the harpoon, marking him as something of a whaler as well as a general seaman, a natural extension of that same seafaring pedigree. The GM also noted, without elaborating, that Werner's family has some as-yet-unexplained connection to the great climate shift of a generation ago — a thread Werner himself does not yet understand.

For Knick Nab (Ross), it was confirmed that his 1/8 Elf racial heritage grants him Night Vision and Efficient Sleeper for free. He spent his 18 racial development points on Fast Attack and took the Light-Boned flaw (a genuine fragility, consistent with a childhood of malnourishment), which returned 15 points, giving him 23 remaining to spend on further talents. His Boon was also confirmed this session: through simple conversation he can draw out a person's deepest wants and desires, whether or not they intend to reveal them — a gift he already sees as the foundation of the leadership he hopes to earn one day.

Noddy (Donovan) also continued building his character this session. His race was confirmed as Mixed Man and his profession as Mystic — though at this early stage that manifests as nothing more mystical than remarkable luck: things simply seem to go his way. His background was confirmed as Urchin, the hazardous-environment option, and not merely an ordinary rough upbringing but the worst of it — he was raised in the depths of the city's sewers, and has never known anywhere but the Capitol.

Pat (Cosimo Cellini Scivio) was not present for this session.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
The Known World (Map Overview): The GM presented a map of the Known World as the characters currently understand it. The North and the South are divided by a mountain range with a small number of strategic passes. The Capitol is the largest city in the North and the seat of both Royal and Divinity of Two power. Islands lie off the coast; beyond them, the open ocean has only recently become navigable due to the Great Change. Further afield, rumour holds that a reclusive people with elven blood live beyond the mountains to the east, among ruins resembling pyramids, though no Northerner has ever seen one. Far to the south, past the Sands, lies the domain of the Cult of Fire — a different people again, dismissed by those in the North as charlatans who fake miracles with gunpowder and stage tricks.

The Great Change: Described again for the newer players — this was not a gradual shift but a sudden, cataclysmic change in ocean weather patterns roughly a generation ago. No prophecy warned of it. Before it, ships kept close to the coast and to a scattering of nearby islands, navigating by dead reckoning; no clock yet built is accurate enough for reliable open-ocean navigation, so sailors still find their way by these older methods even as they push further out. The result of the Change is that deep ocean travel to the West is now possible, and both North and South are racing to exploit what lies beyond.

Slavery in the North: The North relies heavily on enslaved labour. People from the Channel Islands and beyond who are brought north are, in most cases, enslaved. Islanders (referred to as "high humans" in game terms) are a distinct race; in the North, a person of Islander descent is presumed to be a slave unless proven otherwise. This is a defining feature of Northern society that separates it from the more egalitarian South. Since the Great Change opened the deep ocean to travel, this supply of enslaved people has widened further still — ships are now returning with captives taken from newly-reached lands far beyond the Islands, feeding the same trade.

The Divinity of Two's Grip on Reproduction: The Divinity of Two holds enormous social power because reproduction in the North requires the Church's blessing. Unions not blessed by the Divinity of Two either fail to produce children or produce children described as "misshapen" — who are killed at birth, along with consequences for the parents. This gives the Church leverage over every family in the North, regardless of rank, and explains their unchallenged religious authority. Knick Nab's misshapen ears are a dangerous secret in this context: by Northern law, he should not have survived infancy.

Magic in the World: Beyond the power of the Divinity of Two — granted, it is said, directly by the Father and Mother above — there is no real magic in Northern society: no wandering wizards, no spells sold in the street. What the Cult of Fire calls a miracle is dismissed in the North as cheap trickery with gunpowder and smoke, and the "witchcraft" attributed to Islanders is written off the same way. Whatever the truth of those claims, the power wielded by the Divinity of Two's own paladins and clergy is real and unmistakably magical — which is part of why their authority goes unquestioned. Anyone found practising magic outside the Church's sanction is branded a heretic and hunted down by the Divinity's own paladins, with predictably final results — a fact that makes the North a dangerous place for anyone harbouring a secret they cannot explain away.

North vs. South: The North's great military strength on land is its cavalry — horses are a major resource and a symbol of status. The South lacks this advantage but has become competitive at sea. With the war now largely a naval conflict, the North's cavalry advantage counts for less than it once did.

Trade and Smuggling: Mountain passes are the primary land routes between North and South. In peacetime, control of these passes generates enormous wealth for those who own them. In wartime — as now — the passes become fortified military positions and trade ceases. The alternative is smuggling, whether through mountain routes or by ship. Mani's family has historically been positioned to exploit both channels.

Languages: There is one common language shared across the North and South. Additionally, Islanders have their own language. A further, more exotic language exists beyond the Sands to the far south, unknown to most Northerners. Mani's background in maritime trade gave him some exposure to this desert tongue, and he took one rank in it.

Weapons and Combat: The group discussed the weapon skill categories in the new rules: melee (blade, chain, halberd, and greater versions; pole arm), ranged (bow, crossbow, sling, thrown, exotic), shield, and unarmed. Black powder weapons — pistols, muskets, and cannons — fall under ranged as separate skills within that category. The GM noted that the physical environment should shape weapon choices, particularly on ships: large weapons are impractical below decks, short blades and pistols dominate in confined spaces. Firearm technology in the world is flintlock — expensive and uncommon among ordinary people, though standard issue for soldiers and an absolute requirement for pirates, who are expected to keep guns and blades ready at all times. Ships remain entirely wood and sail, with no steam power of any kind; the pressures of the Great Change and the ongoing war are pushing shipwrights toward larger vessels capable of longer blue-water voyages, which in turn has made timber one of the most valuable goods moving through the mountain passes. Sloops remain fast, common, and a pirate favourite for short raiding runs, but a poor choice for crossing open ocean. For a sense of scale, the largest single castings anyone in the Known World can presently manage are things like great cathedral bells — true ironclad warships remain a technology generations away.

Shipboard Roles and Hierarchy: The group learned how authority is structured aboard a naval ship. Beneath the captain, the Quarter Master and the Master of Sail each command roughly half the crew's watches: the Master of Sail holds the deep technical knowledge of navigation, sail arrangement, and shipwork, while the Quarter Master oversees the ship's goods and material. On a more piratical vessel, command runs from the captain through lieutenants down to midshipmen — a rank traditionally reserved for the nobly born, since a common sailor promoted to midshipman would be seen as badly out of place. Below the officers, respected specialists such as the bosun, the carpenter and carpenter's mate, and the surgeon (more a knife-handy barber than an educated doctor) each hold real authority within their own domain. Marines, when carried, do no shipwork at all — they are cargo until there is a fight, at which point they fight from the deck or are put ashore.

Talent: Direction Sense: A talent was identified that grants a significant bonus to navigation by detecting the planet's magnetic field. With the campaign's emphasis on sea travel, the group noted this would be highly valuable for at least one party member to possess.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
This session was the final character creation and preparation meeting before play began in earnest, and the GM confirmed early on that all six player characters begin the campaign at the age of fourteen. The GM opened by asking each player to give a "big picture" account of their character, going around the table, after which a number of characters received deeper background treatment. Ross was absent; the GM summarised Knick Nab's concept on his behalf. Donovan was present for the first portion of the session but left early.

Donovan described Noddy as a Mixed Man — Common stock mixed with High, leaving him tall at six feet nine inches but extremely lean. Despite his height, Noddy has cultivated a manner of making himself invisible: he slouches, makes no eye contact, takes up as little space as possible, and is simply not noticed. He grew up in the rubble of Cliff Town after its collapse, surviving entirely through luck and guile, with no knowledge of his parents and no resources beyond what he could scavenge or steal from the detritus that falls from above. His aspiration is the Mystic path, though he does not yet know what that means; the GM was explicit that it should be understood for now through the lens of chance and survival — Noddy's uncanny, near-impossible luck at staying alive is itself the seed of his coming power, and by his own reckoning he is the luckiest man he knows. The GM sketched out how wide that path might eventually run: a Mystic draws on both open and closed Essence and Mentalism, meaning Noddy's future spellcraft could span creation and destruction, discovery and concealment — confusing or frightening a foe, conjuring fog or clearing the air, blurring into shadow, taking on another's shape, even working alteration on solid objects like rope — but whatever form it takes should grow out of Noddy's own survival instincts: his animal handling, his foraging, his hard-earned knack for knowing what scraps of refuse are safe to eat. His Boon is a familiar spirit that currently inhabits a seagull — an entity that can communicate with him across the barrier between its animal vessel and himself, watch over him while he sleeps, and potentially grow in capacity over time.

Allen described Werner De Rendal as a nobleman's son from the far north, at the very threshold of the frozen wastes where only the sea provides any wealth. The De Rendal family was once enormously prosperous from whaling — supplying oil, ivory, and blubber — but the decline began generations ago and accelerated when the Great Change disrupted all the old sea patterns. Werner's grandfather, a renowned sailing expert whose knowledge of harsh northern waters was unmatched, was commissioned by the king to lead an expedition westward before the Great Change — an impossible voyage by all ordinary reckoning. He left, the Great Change followed not long after, and neither he nor confirmation of his fate ever returned. Werner's father Kasimir kept to the whaling trade long past the point of viability and has left the family broke and indebted. Werner has been sent south with letters, papers, and the last of his father's favours to seek a commission in the Navy. His fighting skills will center on harpoon, cutlass, and eventually heavy ship's cannon — a natural continuation of the family's whaling trade, since some of the earliest naval cannon were adapted from harpoon guns, leaving the De Rendals an unusual grounding in naval ordnance even as their fortunes declined. His Boon is the De Rendal name itself — a ducal-level title, still recognised and still capable of opening the right doors, even if the wealth behind it has long since evaporated.

Alain gave the full picture of Infurious Montesigna, known as Riu: the third son of Baron Justinius Mona III, a distinguished family of horse breeders from the Plains. Being a third son, Riu carries no obligations to the family trade and has been free to follow his own passionate curiosity, which runs entirely toward books, lore, languages, and the faint edges of what might be magic. He has recently acquired a small pet squid — Squidly III, the third because the first two suffocated before he resolved the ventilation problem — which he keeps in a purpose-built bottle with an ingenious lid that prevents escape while allowing free gas exchange. His interest in the squid is practical as much as affectionate: he has read that the finest magical inks use squid ink as a base. He is bound for the Capitol to access its libraries. Though he had presented Dabbler as his intended profession in the previous session, he revised his plans during this session, moving away from Essence-based semi-spell use and toward the Lay Healer path instead. He has no practical experience of magic in either direction yet. He arrived at the Capitol recently, having journeyed from the coast where he acquired his squid, and finds the city far more chaotic and militarised than he expected — the whole Capitol is plainly on a war footing.

Pat described Cosimo Cellini Scivio as a young man who grew up in the Capitol working in construction, specialising in the intricate rope work used to build domes, keep walls plumb, and operate cranes — a rigger. His nickname, Scivio, is a truncated Italian word meaning something like slippery or slimy — Pat prefers to render it "silky" — and, like any nickname, it was given to him by others, not chosen for himself. He worked extensively on churches for the Divinity of Two and is genuinely devout, having served as an altar boy and witnessed things in the back rooms of religious services that are not written in any book. He aspires to become an Illusionist, though what that means in practice is not yet clear to anyone; he has floated one concrete idea already, adding a sense of touch to his fantasms so that an illusion of a staircase, say, could actually be climbed, and the GM noted his path may share real synergy with Noddy's, since both trade in concealment, misdirection, and things that are not quite what they seem. He has a weakness for gambling, which led to a serious incident: he incurred a debt to a member of the clergy, who came to the construction site to collect. A very heavy stone fell from Cosimo's crane and killed the man. Whether this was deliberate remains ambiguous even to Cosimo himself. He has been on the run since, wracked with guilt but unable to confess to the same institution that might condemn him. His Boon will be spectacular, but Pat has declined to describe it publicly — it will manifest through roleplay at the appropriate moment.

The GM described Knick Nab in Ross's absence as a young man of one-eighth Elven heritage, taken from the Northern Highlands at a young age and brought to the Capitol to work as a pickpocket for a minor underworld figure who runs a gang of young thieves. He is sharp, flamboyant by nature, and has visions of leadership. His Boon is an ability to perceive what people truly want at their core — not what they say they want, but the real and sometimes unspoken desire beneath the surface — which he intends to use for leadership rather than manipulation.

Scala laid out Manuel de Barret's story — known as Mani — in further detail. His family belongs to the House of Cloth, the merchant guild for fabrics, and while his father is now a respected merchant, he has a past as a smuggler; the family's roots lie in a pair of river towns straddling a waterway that feeds toward the Capitol, a position that has long made them skilled at moving goods between the coast and the interior. As the third child — his elder brother handsome and capable, his sister brilliant and sought-after — Mani was sent to the Ropolos School, a prestigious boarding school in the Capitol that has recently opened its doors to the merchant class, partly for financial reasons and partly because wartime creates demand for capable people regardless of birth. Pushed around by noble classmates at school, he grew large and strong for fourteen and eventually gave as good as he got. The school's fencing master refused to teach anyone who was not noble, which Mani found infuriating. He found an alternative teacher in the school groundskeeper, a former Marine who taught him blade work and brawling as it is actually practised aboard ships, dismissing formal fencing drills as no substitute for a dozen real boarding actions on a swaying deck. The tradition he has set his sights on mastering is Mangos and Rapier. He has a small dueling scar as a result of a fight he picked with someone he should not have. Still stung by being told his birth would always be a barrier, he has come to see the war and a Navy commission as a leveler — a chance to prove that skill counts for more than blood. His Boon is a talisman — an old coin worn around the neck — that will make him substantially resistant to magic. He does not have it yet; it will come to him during the campaign.

The session ended with Scala presenting the substantial collection of hand-painted 3D-printed miniatures he had produced for the game: naval marines, sailors, ruffians, Islander types, civilians, and bartenders, each crew painted in its own distinct colours so that, if two ships' crews ever ended up mixed together in a boarding action, everyone at the table could tell at a glance who belonged to which side. Individual miniatures had been prepared for each PC: Werner in a proper Navy coat reflecting his errand to seek a commission, Cosimo in a brown leather jacket, Mani with a feather in his hat, and Noddy barefoot and hatless but for a plain undyed wool cap, carrying a length of rope instead of a weapon. The GM confirmed that actual play would begin in the next session.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
Cliff Town: The Capitol has a third district beyond High Town and Low Town — or rather, had one. Cliff Town clung to the cliff face itself, below the Hill and the House, home to those who had nothing and no place to belong. For some, it was less a fate than a refuge: predation on the underclass elsewhere in the city — including the risk of being sold into slavery — was severe enough that disappearing into a slum nobody wanted to enter could be the safer choice. A landslide, of uncertain cause, destroyed the entire area not long ago. The rubble remains: navigable but ruinous, with the sewers of the affluent districts above now exposed and draining through it. Guards patrol the old entrances, preventing both entry and departure. No explanation for this has been publicly given. Noddy lives in the ruins.

The Great Change and the De Rendal Expedition: Werner's grandfather was specifically sought out by the king for a westward expedition before the Great Change, because of his unmatched knowledge of harsh northern sailing conditions. He departed, and the Great Change followed within roughly a year. No one has seen him since, and no official account has ever clarified what happened. The Great Change also disrupted the whaling routes the De Rendal family depended upon, changing sea patterns, pushing ice flows into previously clear channels, and scattering the whale populations whose locations had been accumulated over generations of family knowledge.

Gunpowder Technology: The world is fully in the gunpowder age, sitting somewhere between a sword-and-spear army supplemented with guns and a gun army that only occasionally needs sword and spear. Flintlocks are the standard for those who can afford them; matchlocks exist but are becoming outdated, and rifling has not yet arrived. Naval combat at range is conducted with cannon and musket, but a crew that means to capture a ship rather than sink it will sweep the deck with musket fire and chain shot instead of holing the hull; once ships are alongside, cutlass and pistol dominate.

North–South War and Resources: The current war between North and South is primarily naval, driven by competition for resources and territory in the newly accessible West — including, on the North's side, a much larger new source of enslaved Islanders than existed before the Great Change. The South rejects slavery outright and has no interest in the West for that purpose, one of the clearest philosophical divides between the two nations. On land, the North's cavalry advantage is so overwhelming that its armies barely bother to form up before charging in, and that advantage counts for nothing at sea, which is why the South pushed the conflict there. That cavalry is bred and supplied by families like Riu's in the Plains, whose horses are the backbone of the Northern army even though Plains nobility carries less prestige at court than the coastal nobility currently ascendant around the King. The mountain passes between North and South are closed in wartime; legitimate trade ceases, which pushes families like Mani's into smuggling. When the passes are controlled, their owners extract significant revenue from the trade that flows through them; in wartime, that income disappears entirely for whichever side holds them.

Boons: Each player confirmed or clarified their character's Boon in this session. Noddy has a transferable familiar spirit, currently housed in a seagull. Werner's Boon is the weight of the De Rendal name — a ducal-level title that still commands access even without wealth behind it, though Werner himself admitted he doesn't yet have a clear sense of what that will mean in practice beyond invitations to places others wouldn't get; the GM noted it's meant to carry real weight precisely because Riu's family, while also noble, holds only the rank of baron. Knick Nab's Boon is the ability to perceive what people truly want. Mani's Boon is a magical talisman conferring resistance to magic, which he has yet to acquire. Cosimo's Boon will be revealed through play.

Devoutness and the Divinity of Two: The characters vary in their actual belief. Cosimo is genuinely devout, having served in the church from a young age. Riu's family, as Plains nobility, observes the Divinity's requirements as a matter of course. Mani views the Divinity as infallible — it is simply the frame in which he was raised. Noddy has had no formal religious exposure at all. Underlying all of this is a fact everyone in the North accepts as simply true, not mere doctrine: a couple whose union has not been blessed by the Divinity of Two cannot conceive at all, or if they do, the child is malformed and does not survive. Securing that blessing amounts, in practice, to paying the Church, which is why piety alone is never enough — Werner's family, still deep in debt despite their noble name, understand that without money for the blessing, their line itself is at risk. The North's devotion is enforced as much as felt: the Divinity of Two commands the loyalty of the King's Army and Navy, and the Censures — feared enforcers likened to inquisitorial assassins — hunt down those who deny its primacy. Other faiths are not tolerated in the North, and past rebellions against the Church's authority have never lasted. Enforcement is markedly looser in the South, and looser still to the east, though how people manage the matter of children in either place without the same reach of the Divinity is left an open question.

docs.title: First Steps in The Capitol and The Crow's Nest Beckons
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session opened with the party's six members each beginning in different corners of The Capitol, navigating individual crises that would bring them together at a cliffside tavern before nightfall.

Noddy had been surviving in the ruins of Cliff Town for some time, sealed inside by guards who patrolled the old entrances. Watching one particular gate where the two guards had grown slack, he sent Pocket aloft to listen in. The bird overheard the relief pair persuading the outgoing guards to abandon their post for a nearby tavern that, oddly, still had beer to offer; grumbling about the unfairness of it, the two who should have taken up the watch went along anyway, and all four walked off together, leaving the gate unattended. Noddy slipped out behind them and shadowed them down the narrow cliff road, hemmed in on one side by sheer rock and on the other by a steep drop to the sea. He lost them when they rounded a bend and seemed to vanish; searching for a way up, he sent Pocket to scout a balcony carved into the cliff face above a door marked with a rough painting of a masked figure on a platform holding a telescope — through the bird's eyes he glimpsed two finely dressed women talking in a surprisingly comfortable room of wood panelling, chairs, and tables. Below, the doorway turned out to be The Crow's Nest. Noddy scouted further toward the main gate into the city proper, found it heavily guarded, and turned back; on the way, he had to scramble up the cliff face above the tavern door to let a returning pair of guards pass beneath him unseen. When Burlyman came outside to dispose of a basin of slops, Noddy appeared, took the basin from him, emptied it over the cliff edge, and gave it a polish. Burlyman, apparently not surprised, invited him inside.

Cosimo Cellini Scivio had spent the day on the run in High Town after a heavy stone fell from his crane and struck a benefactor of the church who had come to the construction site to collect a gambling debt. He rubbed dirt into his face and worked his way into a group of workers loading carts, trying to pass as one of them, but the crew turned out not to be heading for the gate. Switching plans, he hid in one of the carts driven by a mysterious old woman. She discovered him tucked among the goods but did not raise the alarm; when she pressed him for an explanation, he charmed his way clear by claiming he was fleeing the brothers of a young lady who'd grown too smitten with him. Amused, she drove at a rattling pace along the precarious cliff road and deposited him at The Crow's Nest.

Werner De Rendal arrived by ship from the north — a small sloop carrying whale oil cargo, the larger vessels having all been pressed into other service — with letters of introduction and a handful of silver. The harbor was busier than any he had seen: warships rode at anchor carrying more cannon and swivel guns than he judged normal, a fortress commanded the cliff above a natural, spiral-shaped harbor, and tent encampments spread along the shore beyond the regular dockside. Navigating from the docks toward High Town, he attracted the attention of a small pack of young ruffians in Low Town and picked up a horseshoe from the cobbles as an improvised weapon. He shook the gang by running close to groups of Town Watch and then presented his papers at the High Town gate with as much confidence as he could muster. A guard took the papers away to consult a large ledger and did not return them; instead, a guard seized him, accused his family of owing an unpaid debt to the crown, and warned, ominously, that such debts could be settled in slavery, before threatening him with prison. A commotion caused by a runaway cart crashing into the gate created a moment of chaos, which Werner used to scramble over the gate into High Town, not knowing whether to believe the guard's warning. Once inside, he tried a cheese shop, asking after his father's factor, Lawrence de Rabia; a wealthy servant there — trailed by two silent foreign attendants carrying his purchases, whom Werner suspected might be enslaved — brushed him off with open contempt, mockingly comparing him to visiting royalty and refusing to credit his claim to noble blood. A second shopkeeper reacted little better, growing hostile once it was clear Werner had no papers to back up his name. Soldiers who recognized him from the earlier gate incident arrested him and threw him into a cell.

Knick Nab was working the Low Town marketplace for Nigfa when a cart collision with an apple stall created perfect chaos. He cut two purses from a wealthy merchant and walked away cleanly, for once weighing whether to hand the take over to Nigfa or disappear. The old woman whose cart had caused the commotion was still there sorting out the damage; Knick Nab helped her put things right, and she remarked, not quite joking, that the number of young lads in trouble she seemed to keep running into that evening was extraordinary. She offered him a ride somewhere safe; he showed her a single bronze coin, and she told him he could probably afford it well enough before driving him directly to The Crow's Nest.

Riu arrived in The Capitol and made straight for the docks, where he talked a sailor down to a single silver for a fresh squid — his third, after the previous two failed to survive, and so named Squidly III — then checked her over for damage until satisfied she was whole. At the customs building he asked for directions to High Town and a place to stay for the night. A weathered official told him the city was full to bursting with refugees fleeing up and down the coast and extra sailors besides, and that every inn was full because of the war — but there was an old place on the cliff road, tucked into the rock, that might have space. Riu followed the directions, found the door with the painted sign of the crow's nest, and walked in.

Mani had been attending the Ropolos School in Low Town — the only student there of common birth. Master Gandito had interviewed him personally, seen enough promise to overlook his lack of noble blood, and taken him on, but the other students never let him forget he didn't belong. That friction finally boiled over with a persistent noble classmate, and a duel was arranged on the cliff road near the ruins — away from the school and from Master Gandito, who had forbidden such things, and, as it happened, along the same stretch of cliff road that runs past The Crow's Nest. Mani lost, taking a dueling scar in the process, and his opponent's friends began urging him to finish the job and throw Mani off the cliff before the Town Watch arrived and put a stop to it. The noble students saw to it that all blame fell on Mani; he was arrested and thrown into a cell, where he found Werner — whose fine clothes, Mani noticed, incorporated an odd, non-traditional material that turned out to be sealskin — and struck up an acquaintance. Working a newly posted guard with a fabricated story — that Werner was a fellow student of the noble de Marel family who had simply had too much wine the night before — and a well-turned charm, Mani secured a promise that the man would be on duty when the two of them were brought outside for transfer, in exchange for a reward from the de Marel estate. A search before the transfer turned up one hidden stash of two silver, which the guards confiscated, but missed a second stash Mani had kept separately. As a cart driven by the old woman came racing past, Mani grabbed Werner and they jumped; a guard behind them opened fire with a musket, but the shot went wide. Werner could not get fully into the cart and was dragged on his feet for a stretch, losing the remaining leather from his boots, before Mani pulled him aboard. The cart deposited both of them at The Crow's Nest.

Inside the tavern, the six arrived in a ragged sequence rather than all at once, each striking a private bargain with Burlyman before the others appeared. Cosimo, still shaken, greeted the innkeeper and his wife with a blessing in the manner of the Divinity of Two — "good mother, good father" — and asked not only for a room but for passage out of the city on a ship, in whatever direction one might be found. Werner, having eaten nothing in days, begged for food and drink and spoke half-formed of restoring his family's fortunes. Even before anyone had properly explained themselves, Burlyman could be overheard murmuring to someone unseen, weighing aloud whether one of the newcomers was "small enough" for a task he had in mind. Food — a bowl of gruel — appeared on the counter and then vanished before anyone could reach it, or reappeared elsewhere when someone turned away; Burlyman and his wife seemed to regard none of it as remarkable. A table that had been blocking a doorway seemed to have moved on its own. In exchange for food and lodging — and, for Knick Nab, the promise of a proper meal rather than gruel — Burlyman asked the party to clear a vermin problem in the cellar. He came out from behind the bar with a collection of implements — a large mallet, a butcher's knife, a cleaver, a staff, a giant wooden spoon, and two kitchen knives — and told them to take what they wanted. Torches were lit and the party prepared to descend.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Pocket — Noddy's seagull familiar. Sent aloft to eavesdrop on the guards at the Cliff Town gate, providing Noddy the intelligence he needed to slip out.
  • Squidly III — Riu's squid, purchased fresh off a boat at the docks; his third, the previous two having failed to survive.
  • Burlyman — proprietor of The Crow's Nest; a large former sailor, now running a tavern fallen on hard times. Recruited the party to deal with vermin in the cellar in exchange for food and lodging. Before anyone had spoken to him, he was overheard murmuring to someone unseen, apparently debating whether one of the new arrivals was "small enough" for the job.
  • Burlyman's wife — manages the kitchens. The gruel she brought out kept vanishing before anyone could eat it.
  • The mysterious old woman — drove a horse cart through the city, bringing Cosimo, Knick Nab, and later Mani and Werner to The Crow's Nest. Her appearances at just the right moment for multiple characters in a single evening were not coincidental.
  • Nigfa — Knick Nab's underworld employer; a lean, skeletal man in his fifties who runs a gang of young pickpockets out of Low Town. Mentioned but not encountered directly.
  • Stick Stab — a knife specialist in Nigfa's gang; older than Knick Nab, vicious with a blade, and Nigfa's clear favourite. Mentioned but not encountered directly.
  • Master Gandito — headmaster (or a senior master) of the Ropolos School; personally interviewed and admitted Mani despite his common birth, and forbade dueling among students. Mentioned but not encountered directly.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Capitol — the main city, divided by cliff and class.
  • Cliff Town — the ruined district where Noddy has been surviving; sealed by guards, its collapse still unexplained.
  • Low Town — the lower district, closer to the sea; home to the docks, markets, and Mani's school.
  • High Town — the upper, more affluent district; where Werner was trying to find his father's factor.
  • The Docks — arrival point for Riu and Werner; teeming with wartime activity. The harbor's natural spiral shape forms a well-protected cove overlooked by a fortress on the cliff above; warships anchored there carried more cannon and swivel guns than seemed usual, and tent encampments spread along the shore beyond the regular port facilities.
  • The Ropolos School — Mani's boarding school in Low Town, recently opened to the merchant class.
  • The Crow's Nest — a tavern carved into the cliff face on the road between High Town and the Cliff Town ruins, the same stretch of road where Mani's duel took place earlier that day. Entry through a stout wooden door set directly into the rock face, with a painted sign showing a masked figure on a platform holding a telescope. Above the door, a balcony carved into the rock opens onto a surprisingly comfortable room of wood panelling, chairs, and tables — Noddy, scouting with Pocket, glimpsed two finely dressed women talking there. Once frequented by nobles and sailors alike; now nearly empty. Its common sleeping room holds roughly ten simple cots with straw mattresses — Burlyman said it was once favoured by commoners and nobles alike, though not for years. Strange things happen here: food appears and disappears, objects move without explanation.
  • Cellar — beneath the tavern, inaccessible due to the vermin problem Burlyman wants dealt with.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• Noddy evading guards as he slipped out of Cliff Town.
  • Cosimo escaping arrest after the death at the construction site in High Town.
  • Werner evading Low Town ruffians and later being arrested by soldiers in High Town.
  • Knick Nab's successful double-purse lift in the Low Town marketplace.
  • Mani's duel with the noble classmate — Mani was defeated and received a dueling scar, and his opponent's friends pushed to have him thrown from the cliff before the Town Watch intervened.
  • The prisoner transfer escape — Mani and Werner jumped a moving cart under musket fire from a guard, the shot going wide, with Werner dragged on foot for part of it before getting aboard.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Capitol is at war, which has led to overcrowded conditions, heightened security at every gate, heavy guard presence in High Town, and soldiers in the streets well beyond what peacetime would require. The harbor shows it too: warships riding at anchor carry more cannon than normal, and tent encampments have sprung up along the shore beyond the regular docks.
  • The Northern Navy, long considered superior, is facing unexpected difficulties. Rumours of battles going badly, of spectacular seamanship by the Southern fleet, have put the city on edge.
  • Without papers, Werner's name alone is not enough to open doors — in fact, announcing himself as a noble without documentation attracted suspicion rather than deference.
  • When he was first stopped at the High Town gate, a guard claimed the de Rendal family owes an unpaid debt to the crown and warned that such debts could be settled in slavery. Werner doesn't know whether to believe it.
  • High Town's wealthy keep foreign attendants who may not be free — the servant who brushed off Werner at the cheese shop was trailed by two silent island attendants carrying his goods, lending uncomfortable weight to the gate guard's earlier threat.
  • Mani is the only student of common birth at the Ropolos School, admitted on Master Gandito's personal judgment; the noble students have resented him for it ever since.
  • The Crow's Nest has unusual properties: food appears and disappears, objects move. Burlyman and his wife seem to regard this as unremarkable.
  • The party's first shared task is to clear the cellar vermin, in exchange for which Burlyman is offering better food and rooms.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• A horseshoe, found in the Low Town cobbles (Werner).
  • Three gold pieces in silver and bronze coin across two purses, stolen from a merchant (Knick Nab).
  • Squidly III, a live squid purchased at the docks (Riu).
  • Kitchen implements distributed by Burlyman: a large mallet, a butcher's knife, a cleaver, a staff, a giant wooden spoon, and two kitchen knives (various party members).
  • Torches (various party members).

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text:
• Werner's papers of introduction — taken by the High Town gate guard and never returned.
  • Werner's boots — the soles worn away to nothing during the cart escape.
  • Mani's school books, mandolin, and other personal effects — presumably confiscated or left behind at the Ropolos School following his arrest.
  • Two silver, found in a hidden pocket and confiscated from Mani during a jail search before the prisoner transfer (a second stash of five silver, hidden separately, went undiscovered).

docs.title: Rats in the Cellar, Riddles in the Dark
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session began at The Crow's Nest inn. Noddy followed the inkeeper in off the street after finding him outside emptying a basin of slop, and was invited in. Short of coin, he offered to clean in exchange for food and lodging — the inkeeper instead mentioned a vermin problem in his cellar, and Noddy was tasked with dealing with it. Partway through the conversation two bowls of gruel vanished from the counter without explanation, and moments later a cleaver, a giant knife, and a huge wooden spoon appeared on the counter that had not been there before — offered up, along with a broom and a candle, as tools for the job. The inkeeper also mentioned there ought to have been more torches on hand, though none could be found. When Noddy asked whether the vermin trouble reached the attic as well, the inkeeper's answer was oddly evasive: "no, no vermin upstairs... oh, you'll get into trouble" — one of several small signs that the inn was not behaving quite normally. Other PCs (Riu, Knick Nab, Werner De Rendal, Cosimo Cellini Scivio (Silky), and Manuel de Barret (Mani)), driven by their own reasons or overhearing, also decided to investigate the cellar.

Infurious Montesigna (Riu), having arrived too late in the evening to make it out to the library as he'd planned, settled instead into the common room's one comfortable chair. Before heading down to the cellar, he found it occupied by a mysterious, powerfully built stranger, straddling the chair backwards to keep his ornate-hilted sword clear, dressed in an ornate leather cuirass — rich with filigree and embellishment over finer, flowing clothes beneath — tall boots, a wig worn in the fashion of the well-to-do, and an elaborate hat set on the table before him. A pair of gloves sat tucked, unworn, at his belt, and he had a small book, quill, and inkpot at hand, along with a short stick he tapped and used to flip pages. He identified his profession as a Chronicler — Randolph the Chronicler, as the party would come to know him — and pressed Riu repeatedly on whether he was "interested in the truth," noted the ink stains on Riu's fingers as the mark of a reader, and dismissed Riu more than once as too young to understand such things, even as he wrote down Riu's account of the inn's vanishing gruel and cutlery with obvious interest. At one point he grew suddenly emphatic, thumping the table before catching himself, and sent Riu on his way with the observation that "the answers do not lie here... I would seek the answers elsewhere." Riu also noticed a smaller oddity of his own: the door on the cliff road he had described earlier now had a curtained window beside it that had not been there before.

The PCs descended into the inn's cellar, initially unaware of each other's presence or exact locations, though they all arrived at the bottom of the stairs around the same time.

As they navigated the initial corridors of barrels, crates, and sacks, lighting torches to see by, they became aware of each other. Knick Nab, drawing on a lifetime spent around ships' holds, judged that whatever was down there could gnaw through rope or wood but not stone. He searched for a bowl or dish to hold the rats he meant to bring back, wanting to lay them at the inkeeper's feet as proof of the job done and earn his good favour; failing to find one, he briefly and half-jokingly eyed the sack of rotten fruit for the purpose instead — and took it along regardless.

The group, now loosely formed, was set upon by a first wave of aggressive rats. Noddy set his broom afire to fight with, though his swings kept missing, and he failed twice to scramble up onto a stack of barrels for safety before giving up and retreating to a table. Werner De Rendal's thrown knife scored the party's first solid hit of the night — a deep cut to a rat's hind leg that left it bleeding and hobbled before it died, still pinned by the blade. Silky (Cosimo) followed with a knife-throw of his own that punched clean between the bones of a rat's foreleg and killed it outright, though not before the rats bit through his socks — twice. Knick Nab fought with a wooden spoon and sweeping strikes, earning himself the nickname "the Rat Slinger" from the onlookers, while Mani used a string of powerful kicks, one of which landed so solidly it ruptured something vital, killed the rat instantly, and sent its body flying out of an open window. Riu wedged a barrel between himself and the rats for cover. Several rats were killed, and the party gathered the bodies, along with Werner's now-broken knife, into a sack.

Beyond the corridor, the party found a larger room built around a central pillar, with a second doorway blocked by a flimsy barricade of tables and chairs; Knick Nab pulled it apart with little effort, concluding it was "an inkeeper's idea of a barricade" that would never have stopped a determined rat. Mani paused to say a prayer to the Mother and Father before lighting a pair of torches to see by.

Retrieving a thrown knife from a rat he had already killed, Werner noticed the corpse begin to move on its own, dragging itself across the floor to spell out a message in its own remains — "WHO R U" — witnessed first by Noddy, who alone made out what it said. Werner, with Mani looking on, wrote "WERNER" and "MANI" in blood in reply; the rest of the party was present or nearby to see it happen. After a pause, a response appeared on the floor spelling out "WERNER" and "MANI" back at them. Mani later tried to continue the exchange by carving into a tabletop that had been dragged around during the fighting, without any result. Knick Nab missed the whole episode — he had already carried Riu's jarred squid up to the inkeeper, who had no idea what to make of it ("that's not mine... maybe he'll come back for it") but offered to fetch ale to celebrate once told the rats were dealt with. Returning to the cellar afterward, Knick Nab found the barricade he'd already pulled apart disturbed still further, with no one around who could have done it — despite dark vision keen enough to miss nothing, he had no explanation for it, one more small sign that the place wasn't behaving as it should. A second, smaller ambush of rats near the source of a faint greenish glow further down the corridor gave the party one more round of fighting before they could investigate it in peace: Knick Nab hooked one rat by the leg with a sweep of his spoon and stamped it down, while Silky finished the other with the first open-ended roll of the night, driving his knife clean through its spine. Mid-fight, Riu found an unbidden memory of Randolph surfacing in his mind — his strange insistence, hours earlier, on "the truth" — as he looked down at the rats dead at his feet, though he couldn't have said why the two things connected.

The now-cohesive party investigated the source of the glow: a hole in a wall where a stone had come loose, with glowing water trickling out. One by one or in pairs, with the others waiting their turn (Noddy, then Silky, then Knick Nab, then Werner & Mani together, then Riu), the PCs crawled through the hole into a small, hidden chamber, each finding it in what played out as an almost private, individual moment rather than a shared exploration.

Noddy went first, finding his own Medallion on the remains and opening his box in turn for his Coins of Fate. He checked the little chamber for any way out beyond the bricked archway and found none, and confirmed for himself what the others would each discover in turn — the Medallion could not be seen or taken off once worn, and breaking through the brickwork would need proper tools he didn't have. Silky went next. Examining the remnants of clothing on the skeletal remains inside, he judged them to be many decades old. Studying the chamber's bricked-up archway, he determined it had been sealed from the far side, not the cellar side — the mortar was neat near the floor and sloppier higher up, consistent with someone working from beyond the wall — and that the little chamber itself was of far finer, more deliberate construction than the rough-dug cellar around it. Scratches on the wall, which his knowledge of Divine writing let him read as prayers to the Mother and Father, akin to fragments of a litany, told him that whoever carved them had knowledge of the Divinity beyond his own. Knick Nab followed, squeezing through the narrow gap; he hesitated briefly over the idea of taking a necklace from a corpse — it felt like a small desecration — before deciding it had to be done, and was told, once he opened his box, that the Coins of Fate represented something more, to be explained in a future session. Werner and Mani went in together: before finding the source of the glow, they glimpsed a second storage chamber through a doorway, its chests and crates full of more stores. Werner examined the remains first, learning little beyond that they were adult and skeletal, retrieved his Medallion, and crawled back out to report to Mani — only for the two of them to realize they each already had, or had just found, an identical necklace, and spent a moment trying uselessly to fit the two together, since the gap in each sat in a different place. Neither could remove his own Medallion once it was worn — every attempt left the wearer distracted, doing something else entirely — but Mani was able to remove Werner's for him when asked. Werner, visibly unsettled at carrying a magic item he didn't understand — and privately linking it to whatever had written to them through the dead rat earlier — resolved to keep it hidden and unworn rather than risk drawing attention to it; Mani, trying and failing to remove his own the same way, simply tucked it under his clothes. Riu went last. He found the loose, cracked stone and the trickle of glowing water, judged the gap beneath the brickwork to be rat-sized only, and packed it with sacks of flour — passing over the sugar, which he judged might dissolve — to seal it before crawling through. Inside, he could tell no more of the remains than that they were an adult, found his own Medallion, opened his box for his Coins of Fate, and tried without success to place the Medallion's markings against what he knew of the region's lore.

Towards the end of the session, with the immediate cellar mysteries explored, the party made their way back upstairs.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Inkeeper (Burlyman): Proprietor of The Crow's Nest inn. Distracted and confused throughout — food and cutlery appeared and disappeared around him without comment — and gave an evasive answer when asked about vermin in the attic. Later baffled by the squid jar Knick Nab brought up, and offered to fetch ale to celebrate once told the rats were dealt with.
  • Inkeeper's Wife: Briefly interacted with Noddy, bringing out the bowls of gruel that later vanished and fetching him a broom.
  • Randolph the Chronicler: A well-dressed, inquisitive man found in the common room — powerfully built, wearing an ornate leather cuirass rich with filigree over finer clothes beneath, tall boots, gloves tucked unworn at his belt, a wig, and an elaborate hat, with a sword worn at his back explaining why he sat backwards in his chair. Carried a small book, quill, and inkpot, tapping a short stick he also used to flip pages. Pressed Riu on his interest in "the truth" and the inn's strange happenings, dismissing him more than once as too young to understand, before sending him off to "seek the answers elsewhere."
  • Rats: Aggressive rats encountered in two waves within the cellar. Knick Nab recognized their behaviour from a lifetime spent around ships' holds, and Noddy had encountered similarly vicious rats before in the ruined districts he grew up in; both found this pack notably more aggressive than ordinary vermin.
  • Deceased Individual: Skeletal remains found in the hidden chamber, wearing one of the Medallions. Appeared to have been immured behind a doorway bricked up from the far side.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Crow's Nest Inn: The common room (where Randolph was met), a side room (briefly explored by Riu), and the cellar.
  • Inn Cellar: A series of corridors and storage areas containing barrels, crates, and sacks. Included a larger room built around a central pillar with its own barricaded doorway, and a second storage chamber glimpsed further in, packed with chests, crates, and food stores — before, eventually, the source of a mysterious glow.
  • Hidden Chamber: A small chamber, noticeably finer and more deliberately built than the rough cellar around it, accessed through a narrow, water-carved hole in the cellar wall. Contained skeletal remains, a bricked-up doorway sealed from the far side many decades ago, and evidence of glowing water trickling in. Divine prayers were scratched into the walls.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• Combat with Rats (first wave): A pack of rats in the storage corridor. Werner's thrown knife landed the first critical hit of the campaign, crippling and killing a rat with a deep cut to its hind leg; Silky's knife-throw shortly after punched clean between a rat's leg bones, killing it outright; Mani's kick killed a third rat instantly and sent its body flying out a window. Knick Nab and Noddy fought with a spoon and a flaming broom respectively; rats bit through Silky's socks twice in the process.
  • Combat with Rats (second wave): A smaller ambush of rats near the source of the glow, fought through before the party could investigate further. Knick Nab swept one off its feet and stamped it down; Silky killed the other with the first open-ended roll of the night, driving his knife through its spine.
  • Mysterious Communication: A dead rat's body moved on its own to spell out a message on the floor; Werner wrote their names in reply with Mani looking on, and the unknown presence answered in kind.
  • Tense Dialogue: Riu's conversation with the enigmatic Randolph the Chronicler, who probed him about his interest in "the truth."

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Crow's Nest inn has a rat infestation and a generally strange, possibly illusory, atmosphere: food and cutlery appear and vanish unexplained, the inkeeper's own answers about the place grow evasive when pressed, and even a barricade Knick Nab had already dismantled turned out to have been disturbed further by no hand he could account for.
  • Randolph the Chronicler is a new, significant NPC with an interest in truth and observation, who believes the answers to the inn's strangeness "lie elsewhere" — and grew strangely emphatic on the subject before catching himself. Riu found the memory of that outburst surfacing unbidden while fighting rats near the glow, an association between Randolph's talk of "the truth" and the cellar's strangeness that he couldn't quite explain.
  • A hidden chamber exists beneath the inn, containing ancient remains and a bricked-up passage. Silky's examination showed the chamber itself was of much finer construction than the rough-dug cellar around it, and that the bricked-up doorway was sealed from the far side, many decades ago — divine prayers were scratched into its walls by someone with real knowledge of the Divinity.
  • The Medallions found on the remains (one per PC, from their boxes) become invisible when worn and cannot be removed by the wearer — every attempt leaves them distracted instead — though another person can remove one for someone else, as Mani demonstrated on Werner.
  • The Coins of Fate were acquired by each PC upon opening their boxes after finding their Medallion; the GM confirmed they represent something more significant, to be explained in a future session.
  • An unknown entity or force can communicate through writing on the floor — it first spelled out a message using a dead rat's own body, which only Noddy witnessed happening.
  • Riu tried and failed to place the Medallion's markings against his knowledge of regional lore; their meaning remains unknown.
  • Knick Nab's years around ships' holds and Noddy's experience with vicious rats in his old, ruined neighbourhood both informed the party's read on the vermin they faced.
