docs.title: Westward Through the Maelstrom and Onto Spider Island
Events and Actions
docs.text:
Before departing Newport, the party overheard two locals, Bill and Ted, gossiping in the same tavern where Steel Hand was cared for. The pair traded rumors about giant beasts said to inhabit the western seas, including giant serpents, though they had no real details to offer beyond the sense that few who sailed west ever returned to confirm such tales. The party also revisited writings recovered earlier from Oldport referencing a "Maelstrom" to the west, and debated whether to sail north around it before deciding to press directly west instead. They likewise considered acquiring warmer clothing in case their route pushed them further north, but ultimately chose not to alter their loadout, and set sail from Newport aboard the "Amada," captained by Otto "Cut Close" De Guzman.

After several uneventful weeks at sea, Noddy sighted an unidentified vessel—a three-masted, two-decked ship with numerous cannons, flying an unfamiliar flag bearing a sun and moon motif that none of the party recognized as either Northern or Southern Navy colors—emerging briefly from a fog bank to their south before disappearing back into it. The party decided to pursue, maneuvering along the edge of the fog. When the ship came into view again still holding a westward course, the "Amada" slipped into the fog to follow, with De Guzman deducing the other vessel's bearing by feel and experience. De Guzman repeatedly boasted that no ship could outrun the "Amada," prompting Riu to add the caveat "unless they control the weather"—a pointed nod to rumors of wind witches, which De Guzman dismissed even as he conceded he had once had to outrun a ship crewed by one. When the fog eventually cleared, the pursued ship was sighted some distance ahead; the "Amada" retreated back into the fog cover, and the party resolved to overtake it under cover of night rather than risk being seen. Sailing north of the target's presumed course and crowding on every scrap of sail, they pressed on at full speed—Knick Nab, watching the crew work, recognized tricks he had seen before: extending spars off the yard arms to hang out still more canvas, pushing the jib further forward, and running up an extra spinnaker, all part of what let the "Amada" carry far more sail than her size would suggest. Partway through the night, a bell heard off their port side convinced them they had successfully passed the other ship.

Continuing their westward journey, they soon encountered a vast and violent storm system, identified as the Maelstrom. They sailed directly into it, facing tremendous swells, torrential rain, thunder, and lightning so severe that a wrong move at the wrong moment could have finished them. After a brief period of calm, the storm intensified further. The crew successfully navigated these perilous waters, making five difficult sailing rolls in a row without a single failure. Upon emerging from the far side, Captain De Guzman admitted he had no real idea of their longitude, though he could still fix their latitude and confirmed they had been driven somewhat south. The party debated whether to turn north back to their prior latitude and resume the original bearing, or simply hold their current course; they settled on a compromise, having De Guzman angle the "Amada" northwest in an attempt to recover their presumed lead over the mystery ship, all while acknowledging how much guesswork was involved. The waters on the far side were noticeably and surprisingly warmer.

The "Amada" sailed on for several more weeks in featureless open ocean, with no landmarks beyond the fog, the storm, and a single albatross to mark their progress. Along the way the crew spotted whales for the first time, initially mistaken by some for enormous fish. With the total time since leaving Newport approaching five weeks, supplies grew thin: the ship's chickens had drowned in the storm and been eaten down to a bone stew, leaving the crew on biscuit and salt pork increasingly infested with weevils—made more bearable only by spices the party had thought to bring along—and the cook Batu Batu grew visibly anxious as even the captain's meals converged with the ordinary crew fare. The disciplined crew grew increasingly on edge from weeks with no knowledge of what lay ahead. Finally, keeping watch from the crow's nest, Noddy sighted land on the horizon; the cry of "land!" sent the whole crew rushing on deck in a moment of near-chaos—Mani grabbing his rifle before realizing there was nothing yet to shoot at—until De Guzman restored order and had Noddy call out a bearing to steer by.

As the "Amada" closed on the coast, it became clear the sighting was a large island rather than a mainland coast. Mindful that the mystery ship might still be no more than half a day behind them, and that these unfamiliar waters could be a busier corridor than they assumed, the party had De Guzman look for a spot that would keep the "Amada" out of sight before committing to a landing site. De Guzman proceeded cautiously, taking constant soundings to judge the depth and feel for reefs; the exceptionally clear water let the crew watch the seabed and confirm a clean sandy approach, allowing the ship to come in closer than De Guzman would otherwise have dared. Noddy then spotted a stream running down to the water from the forest, marking a likely source of fresh water, and De Guzman brought the ship in to within roughly 600 yards of shore. The party resupplied for a day ashore—backpacks, ropes, grappling hooks, a shovel, empty water skins, and a pair of torches—and, with the "Amada" carrying only two boats, took the Longboat in with two additional sailors, who would ferry it back to the ship once the beach was confirmed safe, freeing the captain to begin sending parties ashore to gather water and forage.

The landing party—all six PCs plus the two sailors—came ashore on a tropical beach unlike anything they had seen before: lush, unfamiliar vegetation, oversized leaves, and coconut-bearing trees, with no sign that anyone had ever set foot there before. Riu confirmed the nearby stream water was fresh and drinkable. Using Pocket for aerial reconnaissance and a spyglass from the boat, Noddy and Knick Nab spotted what first looked like a fishing net hung in the trees to dry; a closer look by Pocket revealed it was far too dense and organic to be net-work—it was webbing, and whatever had spun it was not sized like an ordinary spider.

On the beach, Werner De Rendal volunteered to lure out whatever was in the web by throwing a crab into it. His first throw went badly: the crab thrashed free of his grip mid-swing, flew back into his own face, and left him dazed for a moment with nothing but a single crab leg to show for it. Undeterred, he grabbed a second crab and threw it cleanly into the webbing, where it stuck and thrashed until a spider roughly the size of a human torso skittered out to investigate. Cosimo cast "Sudden Light," stunning the creature but also catching Werner in the blast and blinding him temporarily. Mani then shot the stunned spider, and the party closed in to finish it off, though the surrounding webbing proved so strong that it had to be cut and pulled apart by hand rather than sliced through cleanly. Nobody in the party carried the specific lore needed to say whether the spider was venomous, so they treated it with caution regardless. Knick Nab, the "Amada's" rigger, recognized at once that the webbing—roughly a tenth the weight of ordinary hemp rope for its strength—could be immensely valuable if harvested and worked into cordage, tempering the party's joking about becoming "spider ranchers" into a genuine plan to gather more once the beach was secure.

Pocket, sent up for aerial reconnaissance, reported that the island was substantial, with dense jungle, inland hills rising toward mountains, and, far to the southwest, a colossal, wall-like structure too distant and hazy to identify further—its unnaturally straight line echoing the strange line the party had puzzled over on their old map fragment, though whether it was a natural formation or something built remained unclear.

The landing party sent the Longboat back to the "Amada" with the dead spider as a warning and orders for the crew to begin gathering fresh water and foraging cautiously, keeping at least two riflemen with the foraging parties. The PCs then organized themselves—Knick Nab and Werner screening ahead to watch for tracks, Mani armed and ready with Riu reloading for him, Cosimo and Noddy toward the rear—and pushed into the jungle to scout, counting paces and notching trees every fifty steps to blaze and track their trail. Along the way they found and sketched coconut trees and spotted a few monkeys, neither of which any of the party had encountered before. They soon encountered more webbing, growing steadily more frequent as they advanced southwest toward the distant hill Noddy and Pocket had marked as a landmark. Werner tested one isolated section by setting it alight; the green webbing resisted burning at first but caught where it had dried, and the small fire was enough to flush two more large spiders, similar in size to the first, which fled rather than attack.

Pressing deeper into an area thick with pervasive webbing, the party was ambushed by several "huge" spiders and one even larger "giant" spider bursting out from all sides at once. A fierce battle ensued: Riu switched from his rifle to his more reliable pistol and delivered a killing shot to one of the huge spiders, Werner repeatedly hit and pinned another with thrown javelins without finishing it off, and Knick Nab knocked one down and staggered it with a solid kick before staggering a second with a follow-up flurry of blows. Cosimo, despite being hit and wounded, kept casting a ranged force-fist spell that struck two more of the spiders, stunning one with a solid hit to the leg, while Noddy fended one off with his club before landing a solid blow on it with his burning torch. Both Cosimo and Mani sustained injuries during the fight, Cosimo taking a serious arm wound. The appearance of a massive "great big [ __ ] spider," presumably the mother of the smaller ones, caused the remaining attackers to retreat and flee back into the jungle rather than press the fight; as they fled, Mani gave chase after one, hoping to rope and hog-tie it, but it escaped into the trees. As the fight ended, Mani felt a strong, dangerous presence somewhere on the island—a sensation he recognized from once before, near the observation post atop Blackstone Peak on Totem Isle.

docs.text:
• The party confirmed the existence of the Maelstrom and successfully navigated it.
  • The lands to the west are significantly warmer and possess unfamiliar flora (e.g., coconuts) and fauna (e.g., monkeys, whales, giant spiders of various sizes).
  • The discovered island has fresh water sources.
  • Giant spider webbing is exceptionally strong and lightweight—roughly a tenth the weight of hemp rope for its strength—and recognized by Knick Nab as a valuable potential resource for rope.
  • The island's giant spiders appear wary of fire and smoke: burning an isolated section of web flushed two large spiders, which fled rather than attack.
  • A colossal, unusually straight-lined wall or barrier—possibly natural, possibly built—exists far inland to the southwest, echoing a straight line previously noted on an old map fragment.
  • As the jungle spider ambush ended, Mani sensed a "powerful and dangerous presence" somewhere on the island—a feeling he recognized from once before, near the observation post atop Blackstone Peak on Totem Isle. He told the party he could "feel something over there," to be discussed further next session.
  • Riu raised the possibility that the mystery ship they pursued was aided by a "wind witch" capable of controlling weather, which would explain both its speed and its apparent indifference to the Maelstrom.
  • The party recalled rumors circulating about westward voyages: many ships never return at all, but among those that do, tales include riches, Islander slaves, and even plague brought back by survivors. Lately it has been southern ships rather than northern ones that return successfully, feeding suspicion that the South holds some advantage—possibly wind witches—that the North lacks.
  • Captain De Guzman remains confident in the "Amada's" speed and capabilities, even as the crew's food stores dwindle.
  • The party discussed the need for resupply (water and food) and the dangers of the island.
  • The party learned that Navy custom counts a man ashore for 28 days as absent—a marker they kept in mind as they pushed further inland from the boats.
  • Initial scouting tactics involved using Pocket for aerial views and cautiously exploring the jungle, with Knick Nab and Werner screening ahead for tracks and Mani providing firepower.

docs.title: The Great Wall and the Gilded Guide
Events and Actions
docs.text:
Following their previous foray, the party discussed their next steps with Captain De Guzman aboard the "Amada," which had been resupplied with fresh water and food. Mani expressed his sense of a significant structure inland, and the party resolved to undertake a longer expedition to investigate it. Noddy's rough estimate put them only about half the distance there on their previous trip, so they prepared to be away at least four days. The Captain reiterated that the anchorage was a fine place to resupply but not to hide, and that if the pursuing enemy ship appeared he would have to flee without them. The party agreed to head south and light a signal fire if separated, and arranged a simpler backup signal with the shore crew: if the ship was forced to flee in their absence, the sailors left behind would drive a hatchet into the inland side of a marked tree, so the returning party would know at a glance why the beach was empty. Before departing, they also had Noddy confirm via Pocket that their current landing point was likely the best available starting place along the coast.

Preparations for the expedition included Riu extracting three vials of venom from the giant spider fang acquired earlier, with Werner coating a harpoon tip with some and the drained fang itself kept as a trophy. Noddy had planned to bring his own fishing line, then realized a thread of spider silk would make a far better one; this prompted the request that rope be made from spider silk instead, and the shore party was tasked with collecting the raw material. By morning the crew had produced twelve feet of it, exceptionally thin yet strong, a discovery the party recognized could be of real value to the ship's sailmaker. The party also packed extra machetes and a boarding axe, oilskins, and a spare length of sailcloth for shelter, while Werner brought along his small keg of gunpowder; they left Salter's swivel gun behind, judging it too cumbersome for the trek. Riu milked his octopus one last time before releasing it back to the sea with a fond farewell, over Batu Batu's mild objection that it seemed a waste of good eating. Batu Batu, the ship's cook, and Salter, a sailor, agreed to accompany the party, Batu Batu going bare-chested with two machetes at his belt and bringing his own sturdy supply crate of camp and cooking gear rather than a simple pack. Batu Batu also delighted the crew with an exceptional fish stew, "Batu Batu" (the dish he is named after), before their departure.

The next morning, the party (PCs, Batu Batu, and Salter) ventured back into the jungle. They retraced their path to where the giant spider had fallen, finding its carcass being scavenged by a wild pig. Nothing else troubled them on the way back to their previous camp, likely because the faster return journey left little opportunity for encounters. Pressing on into uncharted jungle, the party caught a brief flash of yellow off in the trees — a second giant spider of the larger, more dangerous kind — but it kept its distance and nothing came of the sighting. Soon after, Mani sensed he was being watched and glimpsed a person-sized figure in the trees, but it vanished before it could be identified, despite Batu Batu calling out in the Islander tongue.

Later, while scouting ahead, Knick Nab came upon a small stream crossed by a moss-covered, long-fallen log serving as a rough bridge; a small ring of woven vines sat perched at its centre, evidently some kind of snare. As he leapt across, he startled Leela, an Islander woman crouched on the far bank, watching the direction the party had come from. She fled, and Knick Nab gave chase, easily gaining ground until she took refuge up a tree. Noddy attempted to magically put her to sleep, but she resisted despite a strong casting, and continued climbing out of easy reach, where she settled to watch the party below.

The party tried to establish communication through Common and even Elvish and the arcane tongue, none of which drew any response beyond a brief, curious pause at the arcane word. They settled for showing goodwill instead: withdrawing a short distance, building a fire, and setting aside a bowl of food and a cup of rum for her, while Knick Nab sang to ease the tension. Drawn by the smell of Batu Batu's cooking, she eventually climbed down. Batu Batu, though hampered by dialect differences, managed to establish basic communication, confirming for the party — by her sense of smell — that no spiders lurked nearby. She was young, healthy but thin, and adorned with significant gold jewelry — a gold belt, large studded earrings, arm and leg ornaments, and a substantial choker that doubled as a rough breastplate — over clothing carefully worked and stitched from hide rather than simple draped skins, with other metals and beadwork woven in beyond the gold, some of it apparently functional rather than purely ornamental. She carried two fine steel knives. She grew startled at the sight of the party's stacked rifles, then intrigued once Batu Batu conveyed that the party had killed a large spider with them; she repeatedly said "big one" and gestured for the party to follow her in the direction they were already heading — towards the sensed structure. Knick Nab traded one of his plain daggers for one of her ornate, gold-decorated steel knives, a clearly superior blade.

Leela led them at a swift pace, forcing the party to jog to keep up while still notching trees with their machetes to mark a way back. As dusk approached, her anxiety to get out of the jungle grew, and she eventually sped off ahead, leaving the party to continue alone in the dimming light. They pressed on through the night, guided by Cosimo's and Noddy's projected light spells, Knick Nab's innate night vision leading the way, and a torch held in reserve. The going was slow and unnerving; at one point they blundered into a spider web, and the darkness was thick with eerie sounds and unseen movement.

After several arduous hours, Knick Nab crept ahead alone and broke, unseen, from the jungle's edge into a vast, open area of churned, freshly tilled-looking earth. Before them stood a colossal wall of packed dirt, its surface faintly glistening with moisture in the moonlight, rising 80 feet and stretching as far as they could see in either direction, its line meandering rather than running straight.

While gathering firewood, Noddy sent Pocket up for a brief flight along the wall's crest; the gull glimpsed a distant glow and a change in terrain on the far side, feeding Cosimo's overnight theory that the wall might be the product of earth-shaping magic rather than ordinary labor. The party then decided to camp with their backs to the wall for defensibility, working hard to keep a large fire burning through the night despite the dampness of the jungle wood, and standing two-hour watches in pairs. Sleep was fitful for everyone; strange animal sounds, including a violent squeal and tearing sound nearby, kept the camp on edge through the night.

At dawn, the sheer scale of the wall became even more apparent, and Mani confirmed his sensed "thing" still lay beyond it. An inspection of the churned earth near their camp revealed massive, toed footprints — scaling up from a human foot by doubling it twice over suggested a creature perhaps 40 feet tall had passed nearby, alongside broken branches and trampled undergrowth marking its passage. No obvious gates or entrances were visible on the immediate stretch of wall.

The party briefly considered digging hand-holds directly into the packed dirt as a slower, safer way up, but with eighty feet of wall to climb, Riu instead prepared to levitate to the top using a rope and grappling hook for backup. The ascent proved painfully slow, rising at only about a foot per second, and as he climbed the wall's slick, wet surface curved subtly away from him; he used his telekinesis to push off a thrown torch and then a bundle of sticks to stay close against it. The spell's duration gave him barely enough time to reach the top with nothing to spare — had he misjudged the climb, he would have been left stranded partway up the sheer face when it expired — before he finally hooked his rope over the lip at the top and hauled himself over. While Riu ascended, the rest of the party split into two groups to scout along the base of the wall to the left and right. The group heading left discovered a panel-like depression in the wall's surface, about 25-30 feet up and roughly 100 feet from their campsite.

From the top, Riu confirmed a well-worn path along the wall's length, evidence of regular patrol or travel. Looking over the far side, he saw more jungle and clearings, and in the far distance an area where the jungle ceased entirely, with signs of movement — the same distant glow Pocket had spotted the night before. The sea lay only in the direction from which they had come, and the wall did not appear to extend to it in either direction; far off to both sides the land itself seemed to rise, hinting the wall might run all the way to higher ground beyond the range of sight. The island was clearly far larger than they had realized.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Captain Otto "Cut Close" De Guzman: Captain of the "Amada".
  • Batu Batu: Cook on the "Amada", named after his signature fish stew "Batu Batu". Accompanied the party inland. He facilitated basic communication with Leela.
  • Salter: Sailor, accompanied the party inland.
  • Pocket: Noddy's seagull familiar, used for scouting.
  • Giant Spiders: One previously killed, its carcass was being scavenged. A second, larger yellow-morph giant spider was briefly glimpsed at a distance during the day's trek but kept away. Evidence of others in the jungle.
  • Wild Pig: Seen scavenging the giant spider carcass.
  • Leela: A young, dark-skinned Islander woman native to the island, healthy but thin, richly adorned with gold jewelry (belt, earrings, arm and leg ornaments, and a breastplate-like choker) and carrying two fine steel knives. She guided the party towards the Great Wall before speeding ahead and vanishing into the jungle at dusk.
  • Massive Ape-like Creature: Inferred from enormous, toed footprints — scaling to perhaps 40 feet tall — found near the jungle's edge by the Great Wall.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Unnamed Island: The primary setting for the session.
    • Jungle: Dense, spider-infested, difficult terrain.
    • Stream with Log Bridge: A moss-covered fallen log crossing a small stream, with a small woven-vine snare perched at its centre. Site of the first encounter with Leela.
    • Churned Earth Clearing: A large, open area of disturbed, tilled-looking earth before the Great Wall, showing some sparse regrowth and traces of burnt material alongside the fresher disturbance.
    • The Great Wall: An immense, 80-foot-high wall of packed earth, its surface faintly glistening with moisture, meandering rather than running straight and stretching for miles in either direction. It has a well-worn path on top, evidence of regular patrol or travel and broken at intervals by small notches of unclear purpose, and at least one panel-like depression set into its face.
  • The "Amada": The party's cutter ship, anchored offshore for resupply and as a base.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The party experienced a tense night camping at the base of the Great Wall, with unsettling sounds from the jungle, including a pig-like creature apparently being killed nearby.
  • The chase and initial interaction with Leela were tense but did not escalate to violence; the party weighed firing a warning shot into her tree or discharging a weapon to gauge her reaction, but set the idea aside in favor of building trust with food, fire, and song.
  • Riu's levitating climb up the Great Wall was a race against the spell's limited duration: he had just enough time to reach the top and grapple on before it expired, with no margin for a second attempt had he misjudged the ascent.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The "Amada" is resupplied, but Captain De Guzman will flee if the pursuing enemy ship appears, necessitating a rendezvous plan and a hatchet-in-a-tree signal for the shore party.
  • Pocket's earlier reconnaissance found no river delta or shorter inland route along the coast near their camp, confirming their existing landing point was likely as good a starting place as any for the trek toward the sensed structure.
  • The party debated whether carrying part of the dead giant spider might ward off smaller ones by scent — none had bothered them on the carry back with the fang and leg — but couldn't rule out that the shorter return trip alone explained it, and ultimately no one wanted to smear themselves with spider matter to test the theory.
  • Mani's sense of the "wall" or structure was confirmed to be in the direction they traveled.
  • The party is capable of making exceptionally strong and thin rope from giant spider silk, a discovery with potential value to the ship's sailmaker.
  • The island is inhabited by at least one group of people (represented by Leela) who possess gold and steel items, and speak a language distinct from Common or Elvish; only their own tongue and, curiously, a word of the arcane language drew any reaction from her.
  • Leela communicated about a "big one" associated with the direction of the Great Wall.
  • The existence of the Great Wall itself, a massive, ancient-seeming construction of packed earth, possibly magical in origin (Cosimo's theory). Weighing the wall against his own knowledge of earth-shaping magic, Cosimo reasoned that even a powerful caster could raise no more than a small section per day before needing days to recover — meaning a wall stretching for miles represents either an almost unimaginable feat of magical power, or the sustained labour of tens of thousands of people.
  • The wall's smooth, consistently damp, and slick surface seemed deliberately unsuited to climbing, prompting speculation that it was built as much to keep something in as to keep intruders out.
  • Evidence of a colossal, ape-like creature, perhaps 40 feet tall, inhabiting the area near the wall.
  • The top of the Great Wall is patrolled or regularly traversed.
  • There are signs of habitation or significant activity (a distant glow) beyond the Great Wall.
  • A potential point of interest or entry was found on the wall: a panel or depression about 100 feet to the left of their camp, 25-30 feet high.
  • The sheer scale of the wall renewed the party's sense that whatever built it might connect to the very thing they were sent to find: either a civilization capable of moving earth on a massive scale, or a command of power like the kind some of their own number wield.

docs.title: First Steps on a Perilous Isle
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session began with the players exchanging gifts. The party then recapped how weeks of storms at sea had driven the "Amada" well past any hope of turning back before they finally sighted land and made landfall on a mysterious, uncharted island, its strange tropical flora including hard, coconut-like fruit. What had first looked like fishing nets turned out to be giant spider webs, and the party had already had one encounter with a large spider.

Mani reported a strong "feeling" — sensed through his Medallion, and which he likened to the "Big Stone Oolith," a sensation he had previously experienced near the observation post atop Blackstone Peak on Totem Isle — emanating from deeper within the island and compelling the party to investigate. They recounted their initial battle with several medium-sized spiders, three of which lay dead on the ground while a very large yellow spider (nicknamed the "Yellow Bastard") had escaped. Its body alone, once its legs curled up in death, proved startlingly large, and a closer look showed mandibles like knives rather than cutlasses. One of the party wryly compared the ordeal to the "dock spiders" feared back home in the north — real spiders barely bigger than a hand, and nothing compared to the horrors found here.

A debate ensued about whether to press on immediately or return to the "Amada" for reinforcements and to report their findings. The decision was made to return to the beach, carrying all three spider carcasses as proof of the dangers despite the extra weight slowing them down. Someone wondered what Batu Batu, the ship's cook, might make of it all — spider goulash, perhaps — though the joke didn't survive contact with the idea of actually eating one; none of the party, it turned out, had ever eaten a bug in their lives. Riu had been blazing a trail using a distinctive "cracker tree," whose freshly cut wood shone bright white and made for an easy marker to follow. Noddy mentioned his supply of a particular root he chews was dwindling.

On the beach, they met sailors from the "Amada," including Salter, who were collecting fresh water from the stream Knick Nab had set up during the party's initial landing, along with coconuts — some dry and hollow, others full of a pleasant, milky liquid nobody aboard the "Amada" had ever tasted before. One of the sailors present had witnessed the party's earlier spider fight and word of it had already reached the ship, but nothing had prepared the crew for how much bigger this new carcass was; they reacted with visible shock, gripping their muskets tighter. The party reported their encounters and displayed the spider carcasses. They considered bringing Randolph the Chronicler along on a second foray, but decided against it for lack of time, judging him a "nice to have" rather than essential to the mission. Instead, they set out again accompanied by Salter and equipped with additional muskets, to follow Mani's sensed "feeling" and potentially hunt the "Yellow Bastard." Torches were fashioned by wrapping sticks with older, dried spider webbing, which caught readily, unlike fresher webbing that resisted burning.

The second expedition followed Riu's marked trail. The jungle grew denser, requiring Mani, and later Knick Nab with his scimitar, to chop a path. Along the way they passed more webs holding trapped prey — ordinary insects alongside an unusually large flying one, several times the size expected, its wings visible through the wrapping — and a snake and a marmot-like creature, long since caught and desiccated in older webs. They also encountered monkeys, and when they found one freshly trapped in an unusually sticky new web, Cosimo used his Magic Rope spell to unravel it free. It was far from an easy catch: Cosimo lent his leadership to Knick Nab's skill with animals, and between them they calmed the monkey just enough to bag it. It screeched and struggled for a while; when they later tried to placate it with a strange bright-orange fruit found deeper in the jungle — coconut trees being well behind them by then — Cosimo also tried to charm it magically, without success, before it finally wore itself out and settled down for the rest of the trek. The party was adamant they weren't leaving the island without their catch.

The party emerged into a valley of strange, tall, leafless, notched stalks — a kind of giant bamboo unlike anything they'd seen before, growing from damp, firm ground. Cosimo's eyes were exceptionally keen that afternoon: he was first to pick out a giant yellow spider, much like the "Yellow Bastard," spinning a web high in a tree on the valley's far side, sharp-eyed enough to make out that it had eight eyes. Confident it hadn't noticed them, the party held still, scouted for others nearby, and readied a synchronized volley before Mani, Werner, and Salter fired on his mark, Mani calling out reload orders drilled into him from past service alongside Marines. Several shots hit, visibly damaging its legs and causing it to squeal — a sound none of them had ever associated with a spider before. After reloading, they fired again, striking still more legs, until it finally collapsed.

Advancing into the bamboo valley, the party spotted two smaller spiders nearby that showed no aggression, but was then ambushed by an even larger, exceptionally well-camouflaged spider, resembling a colossal "daddy long legs" with limbs indistinguishable from the surrounding bamboo stalks — its actual body, they would realize, was surprisingly small compared to its enormous legs. At first the whipping strikes from its legs were mistaken for nothing more than bamboo swaying underfoot, until it became clear the "bamboo" itself was attacking. In the ensuing fight, Mani fired early while Noddy used a spell to leap back to safety; Werner and Salter also fired their muskets, and Cosimo readied his sword and shield while beginning to summon an illusory apparition of "Handsome Gulliver Gold," an avatar of the gods, though the fight ended before the lengthy working could be completed. Knick Nab and Cosimo were each struck by the creature's legs and stunned. A web-like strand shot from the spider missed Noddy. Salter landed a critical shot on the spider's body, stunning it. Noddy then grabbed the web-strand that had missed him and, using his unique abilities, followed it back into the creature itself, seizing control of its innards from within — and rather than merely choke it senseless, he chose to sever its body outright, killing it instantly.

The massive spider collapsed, partially falling on Werner and Knick Nab, causing them minor injuries. The party debated what trophy to bring back: the head was easily over 100 lbs and the size of a table, promising interesting mandibles, eyes, and a venom sac, but would be awkward to move; a full leg ran some 20 feet long and needed three or four people to carry, but was otherwise the simpler prize. Since none of them had actually been bitten or caught in its webs during the fight, they had no safe way to harvest the venom sac either way. They settled on one giant leg, shared between four of them, along with a single fang. Mani, while hacking off the fang — surprisingly light and almost hollow, as if built more for reach than mass — got its lingering secretions on his hands despite trying to avoid them; he wiped them off on a nearby tree trunk, but spent the rest of the trek feeling foggy-headed and sluggish regardless.

With trophies in hand, Mani argued for pressing on immediately toward the source of his feeling rather than turning back. They pressed on past the first yellow spider's corpse, its half-spun web still fresh in the tree above, and pushed further inland and upward, climbing a steadily rising, thickly overgrown slope. Mani periodically attuned to his Medallion to gauge the distance, growing more convinced with each attempt that they were close, and took the lead, hacking a path and marking trees with fire as they went. As the afternoon wore on and the light began to fail, the rest of the party grew increasingly wary of spending the night in the jungle; with no one among them skilled in jungle survival, they eventually persuaded a reluctant Mani to turn back, marking their farthest point for a return the following day.

The party made their way back to the beach with the fang and the enormous spider leg, arriving as evening approached. The leg proved too long for the longboat and had to be towed alongside through the water instead, though it turned out surprisingly light for its size. Hauling it aboard the "Amada" still required a block and tackle, and the crew reacted with a mixture of alarm and fascination at its size. Randolph the Chronicler examined it alongside the smaller spider bodies already aboard, folding in extra pages to sketch it at true scale, and questioning the party closely about the jungle's flora and fauna.

They reported their expedition to Captain De Guzman and Randolph the Chronicler, describing the giant spiders and explaining that they had been heading for higher ground to get a better vantage point — mentioning a possible wall or line glimpsed through the trees, but withholding both Mani's true sense of the presence and Noddy's earlier aerial sighting through Pocket's eyes. Mani was eager to return to the island's interior immediately, but others advocated for waiting until morning. Captain De Guzman noted that, lacking salt to preserve meat, fresh water remained the expedition's most pressing need — one this bay could supply, alongside fish, oysters, and other shellfish his best swimmers were already gathering from the shallows. A discussion followed regarding contingency plans in case the "Amada" was forced to flee by the anticipated enemy pursuit; they weighed marking a hidden rendezvous point onshore before settling on a simpler arrangement — a fire lit on the beach at noon each day, and a general understanding that the "Amada" would work her way south along the coast if she had to run. Ultimately, it was decided that the "Amada" would remain anchored for the time being, and the party would continue their exploration inland the following day.

docs.text:
• Salter: A sailor from the "Amada" who accompanied the party on their second jungle excursion, armed with a musket. Despite no one having seen him fire before, he proved an excellent shot, landing telling hits on both giant spiders the party engaged — including the blow that finally stunned the massive camouflaged ambush spider just before Noddy delivered the killing blow.
  • Captain Otto "Cut Close" De Guzman: Captain of the "Amada," received the party's report.
  • Randolph the Chronicler: The expedition's chronicler; the party considered bringing him on the second foray but left him behind for lack of time. Examined the spider trophies, folding in extra pages to sketch them at true scale, and questioned the party closely about the island's flora and fauna.
  • Batu Batu: Cook aboard the "Amada"; the party joked about what he might make of the spider meat ("spider goulash"), though none of them could stomach actually eating any.
  • Unnamed Sailors: Crew members of the "Amada" encountered on the beach and manning the longboat; one of them had witnessed the party's earlier spider fight and had already carried word of it back to the ship, though nothing had prepared the crew for how much bigger the second carcass was.
  • Giant Spiders:
    • Small and medium-sized spiders: Encountered previously, three killed; two more small ones were spotted in the bamboo valley but showed no aggression.
    • Large Yellow Spider ("Yellow Bastard"): Escaped a previous encounter; a similarly large yellow spider, with eight visible eyes, was engaged and defeated at a distance in the bamboo valley.
    • Massive Camouflaged Spider ("Daddy Long Legs" type): Ambushed the party in the bamboo valley, its long legs indistinguishable from the surrounding bamboo and its actual body far smaller than its legs suggested; killed by Noddy.
  • Pocket: Noddy's seagull familiar, present but kept safe due to the dense jungle.
  • Monkeys: Observed in the jungle; one was freed from a fresh web, captured, and kept by the party after it wore itself out struggling.
  • Various wildlife: Large insects, a snake, and a marmot-like creature were seen caught in spider webs.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Unnamed Island: A large, tropical island where the session took place.
    • Beach: The landing site, featuring a freshwater stream whose collection point Knick Nab had set up during the party's initial landing. Sailors were gathering water and coconuts here.
    • Jungle/Forest: Dense, with unusual flora. Contained numerous giant spider webs. A "cracker tree" was used by Riu for blazing a trail.
    • Bamboo Valley: An open, wetter depression in the jungle filled with tall, leafless, notched stalks unlike any plant the party had seen before — a kind of giant bamboo — where the party encountered two of the largest spiders.
    • Rising Slope: Beyond the bamboo valley, the jungle climbed a steep, thickly overgrown slope toward higher ground; the party pressed partway up before turning back for the night, marking the spot to resume the climb.
  • The "Amada": The party's ship, anchored offshore in a shallow, sheltered bay. Salter judged from his repeated trips to shore that the ship could edge a little closer in but not by much, given the mid-tide conditions and nearby shoals. They returned here at the end of the session.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• Recounted Spider Battle: The party had previously fought and killed three medium-sized spiders.
  • Engagement with Distant Large Yellow Spider: The party fired upon and defeated a large yellow spider in the bamboo valley from a distance.
  • Ambush by Massive Camouflaged Spider:
    • The party was attacked by a very large, camouflaged spider.
    • Knick Nab: Struck by a spider leg, taking 19 hit points and being stunned. Later, took 7 hit points when the spider's body fell on him.
    • Cosimo: Struck by a spider leg and stunned.
    • Werner De Rendal: The collapsing spider landed on him, grappling him and causing minor injury.
    • Mani: After hacking off a spider fang, he suffered from poison, feeling foggy and slowed.
    • The massive spider was ultimately killed by Noddy.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The island is extremely hostile, populated by giant spiders of varying and enormous sizes: small and medium ones, the very large yellow "Yellow Bastard" type, and now a wholly new, colossal, bamboo-camouflaged variety larger than any previously seen.
  • Mani can sense a powerful energy or presence on the island through his Medallion, similar to a sensation he previously experienced near Blackstone Peak on Totem Isle (which the party jokingly calls the "Big Stone Oolith").
  • Effective trail-blazing methods were developed using "cracker trees."
  • Aged, dried spider webs burn well and can be wrapped around sticks to make functional torches, while fresher webbing resists burning and is far stickier.
  • Coconuts found on the island are a source of food and drink; some are dry and hollow, others full of a pleasant, milky liquid nobody aboard the "Amada" had ever tasted before.
  • The island is home to monkeys.
  • The giant spiders bleed a green ichor, have eight eyes, and can squeal when injured.
  • One type of giant spider is exceptionally well-camouflaged among bamboo-like vegetation, its body much smaller than its long legs would suggest, and its leg-strikes can be mistaken for harmless swaying bamboo until it's too late.
  • The fangs of the giant spiders can be coated in or contain poison; a freshly hacked-off fang proved surprisingly light and almost hollow.
  • None of the party has ever eaten a bug before, and despite some joking about it, none of them could bring themselves to actually try the spider meat.
  • None of the party has any skill in jungle survival, a gap that forced them to turn back short of their goal rather than risk a night in the jungle.
  • The party told Captain De Guzman and Randolph the Chronicler only that they were seeking higher ground for a better vantage, withholding both Mani's sensed presence and Noddy's earlier aerial sighting through Pocket's eyes.
  • Captain De Guzman explained that, lacking salt to preserve meat, fresh water is the expedition's most pressing supply need — one this bay can meet, along with fish, oysters, and other shellfish his best swimmers were already gathering from the shallows.
  • The party discussed and established contingency plans with Captain De Guzman should the "Amada" be forced to flee due to enemy naval presence: a daily fire signal on the beach at noon, and a general plan to head south along the coast to find a rendezvous point, rather than trying to mark a hidden meeting place onshore.

The party considered the head and venom sac too, but had no safe way to harvest the venom sac since none of them had been bitten or webbed during the fight.
  • Giant Spider Fang: Taken by Mani from the massive camouflaged spider; it proved to be poisonous.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session opened with a recap of where things stood: the party was camped at the foot of the Great Wall — the massive 80-foot earthen rampart that stretches across Spider Island's interior — after discovering, the previous morning, enormous footprints pressed into the churned earth near the jungle's edge, belonging to something vast, clawless but toed, and capable of moving through the treetops. Riu had already levitated to the top with the help of a rope and grapple to get the lay of things, and play resumed with him standing on the crest.

There he found the wall's crest walkable — perhaps the width of a table — with a slow trickle of water running in a muddy channel along its length from somewhere to the left. The party split into two pairs to search the crest in opposite directions; one pair found nothing, but the other spotted an irregularity in the wall's face a little further along. Pocket, scouting from height, saw that beyond the wall lay more churned earth, patches of jungle, what might be fields or clearings, and in the distance the glow of firelight the previous night had given way to a more ominous silence. Werner confirmed the sighting from the ground, stepping back to the jungle's edge for a clear look up the outer face: about 30 feet up, set a foot or so into a recessed section of the wall, sat a large metal panel, about half the size of a table.

Before committing to a way in, Noddy floated the idea of using a spell to collapse the wall outright, reasoning it might have been raised by the same magic behind the black monoliths the party had puzzled over before. Werner talked him out of it — the wall belonged to people the party hoped to befriend, and tearing down their defences on a guess was a poor way to start a friendship — and the party agreed they would not damage the wall.

Riu levitated down to the panel and tried a door-opening spell as he leaned into it; the panel lurched a little and thudded to a stop — not open, but the movement was enough to confirm it was a portcullis-style door, barred from the inside and meant to lift upward. He crossed to the interior face by levitating to the top and descending the other side. There, level with the panel, he found an entrance to a short passage through the wall. Inside the passage was darkness, and a wooden box containing a coil of fine spider-silk rope, already attached to a fixed point — clearly pre-rigged for descent on the outer side. Simple metal bars and hooks blocked the door from rising. After clearing the bar, Riu cast a door-opening spell and the heavy metal gate lifted steadily upward. He pegged it open with the six iron pegs set in holes along the gate's track. The portcullis was up.

He tossed the spider-silk rope out over the outer face and it dropped to the ground, just long enough to reach. The party began to climb. It was not a swift process — the rope demanded care, and several members of the party were not strong climbers. Batu Batu and Salter had been waiting nervously at the camp below, keeping their backs to the jungle with weapons ready; now they were called over to make the climb as well.

As people were still on the rope, movement broke at the jungle's edge: a panther, black and lean and 14 feet from nose to tail, closing fast. Noddy, finding a line of sight from the opening, cast a confusion spell on the creature before it could fully commit. Mani, who had already slung his rifle and drawn two pistols, fired both — one shot went wide, but the second connected hard, driving through the panther's forearm and scoring muscle with severe bleeding. Knick Nab, reaching the ground, swept at the animal but barely connected. Werner advanced with his arming sword and the panther turned on him — it snapped, but Werner parried cleanly. Cosimo, watching from the passage above, attempted to find an angle for his flashbang illusion but could not cast without catching his own allies in the burst radius. The panther, confused and bleeding freely, failed to press its attack and was driven off.

The party passed through the gate and descended the inner wall face — a worn streak on the packed earth below the opening suggested something had made this drop many times before, either sliding or climbing. On the other side of the Great Wall, the land opened into more cleared earth and then jungle, with a wide, well-worn path running straight ahead.

Following the same pull Mani had been sensing since deep in the jungle, the party pressed on down the path and soon passed a small cluster of huts, each fronted with a beaten metal door like the one they had just forced. Prying one open confirmed it was a thin sheet of hammered copper fixed to a wooden frame, and a closer look at the surrounding metalwork showed the islanders had access to copper, bronze, and iron alike. Inside one hut stood a curved dais bearing six fist-sized animal figures cast in gold and silver — a spider, an ape, and a parrot in gold; a snake, a panther, and a pig in silver. Reasoning that a people who left such wealth lying in an unlocked, abandoned hut, and who adorned themselves as freely with gold as Leela did, likely set little store by it, the party took three: Noddy claimed the golden spider, in memory of the huge one he had killed back on the coast; Cosimo took the golden ape; and Werner, despite voicing doubts about looting people they hoped to befriend, ended up carrying off the silver panther. The rest were left undisturbed.

The path climbed gradually until it reached the edge of a hundred-foot cliff, which the party followed around a bend where the jungle drew back into a wide, enclosed clearing. A fresh cluster of huts stood on the far side — and movement in the brush betrayed hidden watchers. At least a dozen Islanders armed with long spears were visible, with more concealed nearby. Batu Batu called out that they came in peace, seeking Leela and "the big one." After a tense pause the spearmen fell back and closed ranks quietly behind the party rather than blocking the way, escorting them — watchful but not hostile — deeper into the camp. As they advanced past still more spearmen watching from the grass, Cosimo cautioned against leading with an open display of magic — the gifts he credited to "the mother and father" — reasoning that a people this numerous and this armed might not be as astonished by such tricks as past audiences had been, and that any surprise was better held in reserve than spent carelessly. The party walked on peaceably instead, into a settlement far larger than it had first appeared: hundreds of Islanders, armed only with spears, bows, and clubs, no firearms among them, but heavily adorned with gold, silver, and copper. At its heart, three great cauldrons of grey stew simmered over open fires, tended by a woman who stirred and portioned them out, and nearby a handful of dog-sized dead spiders were mounted on spears — evidence the islanders fought off smaller spiders as a matter of routine. Batu Batu tried what few words the two tongues shared, and the party unravelled the panther's skin to show off their kill before offering a cut of the great spider's meat as tribute, which she accepted, butchered, and added to the pots. Through the exchange the party picked out a recurring word, hintu, for spider, intensified as beeta hintu, and learned that the huge white creature they had killed on the coast — and whatever lay ahead of them now — was beeta beeta beeta hintu to the islanders: the biggest spider. Pointing the way onward past their own homes, the villagers made clear where the party needed to go.

Continuing on, the party reached the point where the two cliff faces drew closest together — a natural gap roughly a hundred feet wide and as many feet high, with a waterfall spilling down one cliff face into a pool that crowded the gap. Here a long column of Islanders worked in relay, passing empty buckets forward and full ones back along two lines that converged on a low, disc-shaped monolith of black stone set flat into the churned earth, the same material the party had puzzled over once before. Two figures knelt atop the disc, working its surface with their hands; each time, the bucket set before them came away filled with fresh earth, with nothing visibly drawn from the stone to account for it. Riu sensed the disc was a conduit for real power, being spent, as best anyone could tell, entirely to conjure ordinary dirt. That earth was being carried off and packed into a new wall rising across the gap, already chest-high on one side though the work looked to have begun no more than a few days earlier, guarded by a line of warriors facing outward into the jungle beyond. It was clear this was a displaced village, racing to seal the chokepoint as a new line of defence.

The party passed through the unfinished gap and its watching warriors without incident, weighing whether to skirt left or right along the cliff faces or push straight through the jungle path ahead. They sent Pocket up to scout before committing to a route.

What the seagull saw was striking. The jungle ahead was only three to four hundred feet deep along the path; beyond it opened a vast Islander settlement. This was no simple village — multi-story buildings, long communal halls, ornamentation, ribbons of decoration hung between structures. A proper town. But every surface was draped in thick ropes of spiderwebs. At the center of the settlement, perched atop a great web that linked the largest buildings, sat an enormous pale-white spider: the same species as the one the party had killed earlier, and by all appearances much larger. Smaller spiders skittered through the web-network throughout the settlement.

Pocket climbed higher still. Far beyond the village and its surrounding fields, at the valley's far end where the cliff faces closed back toward each other, stood another huge wall, built the same way as the one the party had crossed that morning — but with a wide gap on one side where a section had collapsed entirely. Piecing it together, the party concluded this breach was how the great spider had first gotten into the valley, driving the islanders out of the settlement below and back to the chokepoint where they were now racing to raise their new wall.

Given the path was wide and Pocket had confirmed it was navigable, the party settled on the direct route through the jungle rather than skirting the cliffs.

Before they moved, Leela reappeared. Beside her was a man of unmistakable standing among the islanders — a towering headdress of enormous feathers, quantities of gold, gold teeth, a carved staff. Around his neck, tarnished and brass-coloured, was a sextant. He looked hard at the party and pointed, repeating the same phrase the villagers by the wall had used: beeta beeta beeta hintu — the biggest spider — as if the matter of dealing with it were already settled and theirs to handle.

With the day already well along, the party judged there wasn't time to reach the spider village, deal with its occupant, and retreat before dark. Rather than press on into the web-choked settlement at night, they chose to make camp near the new wall and put off the final approach until morning.

  • Feathered Islander leader — A man of obvious authority, elaborately ornamented with a giant-feathered headdress, gold jewellery, gold teeth, and carrying a staff. Most notably wore a sextant around his neck. Pointed at the party and repeated "the biggest spider" as though the task of dealing with it were already theirs.
  • Batu Batu — Present with the party throughout; remained at camp near the wall base during the initial climbing operation, then served as the party's only means of communication with the islanders they met beyond the wall.
  • Salter — Present with the party throughout; alert and nervous, watching the jungle.
  • Giant panther — A 14-foot black panther that charged from the jungle during the rope crossing. Wounded by Mani's pistol fire (severe bleeding wound to the forearm) and driven off by Noddy's confusion spell.
  • Displaced Islander villagers — Hundreds of Islanders encountered at a camp beyond the Great Wall, armed with spears, bows, and clubs but no firearms, and heavily adorned with gold, silver, and copper. A dozen or more spearmen challenged the party's approach before standing down and escorting them through. A woman at the camp's central cooking fires was shown the panther's skin and accepted a cut of spider meat as tribute, and the villagers pointed the way toward "the biggest spider" beyond the cliffs. Batu Batu tried asking where the camp's warriors were, but got no answer beyond more pointing and repeated cries of "the biggest spider." The party noticed the crowd skewed conspicuously young or old, with no one of obvious fighting age in between — raising the question of whether the camp's warriors were away, lost, or already dead.
  • Great white spider — A vast pale-white spider occupying the web-covered Islander settlement, the same apparent species as the one previously killed on the coast. Referred to by the islanders as "the biggest spider."

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Great Wall (Spider Island) — The massive 80-foot earthen wall dividing Spider Island's interior. The party discovered a portcullis gate embedded 30 feet up the outer face, with a short internal passage and a pre-rigged spider-silk rope for descent.
  • Huts beyond the Great Wall — A small cluster of huts just past the Great Wall, each fronted with a hammered-copper door over a wooden frame. One held a dais with six gold and silver animal figures; the party took three (gold spider, gold ape, silver panther) and left the rest.
  • Islander camp near the cliffs — A displaced Islander settlement of hundreds, tucked against a hundred-foot cliff face beyond the huts. Simple dwellings, open cooking fires with three large cauldrons at its center, dog-sized dead spiders mounted on spears nearby, and no visible leader — but heavily armed and heavily gilded.
  • The new wall (under construction) — A partially built earthen wall closing a natural hundred-foot gap between two converging cliff faces, where a waterfall spills down one cliff face into a crowding pool. Raised by islanders using earth conjured from a black, disc-shaped monolith and relayed by bucket brigade. Already chest-high on one side; construction appeared to have begun only days earlier.
  • The Spider Village — A large, well-developed Islander settlement now abandoned and overrun with spiderwebs. Multi-story buildings, communal halls, and ornamentation — a significant town, now occupied by the great spider and its smaller kin.
  • The Second Great Wall — Glimpsed by Pocket far beyond the Spider Village, at the valley's far end where the cliff faces close together again — built the same way as the Great Wall the party crossed, but with a large section collapsed entirely on one side. The party believes this breach is how the great spider first entered the valley.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• Giant panther attack at the wall base: The creature ambushed the party during the rope crossing. Noddy's confusion spell disoriented it; Mani's dual pistol fire tore through the panther's forearm, leaving it bleeding badly. Knick Nab's sweep barely connected. The panther attacked Werner but was parried. It was driven off without injuring any party member.
  • Standoff with Islander spearmen: A dozen or more armed islanders confronted the party at the edge of a clearing beyond the Great Wall. Batu Batu's call of peace and the party's open, unthreatening approach convinced the spearmen to fall back and escort them into the camp rather than fight.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Great Wall contains a portcullis gate 30 feet up its outer face, accessible from both sides via a short internal passage. The interior side had a wooden box with a pre-rigged spider-silk rope for external descent.
  • The huts beyond the Great Wall use hammered copper for their doors, and the surrounding area shows evidence of copper, bronze, and iron working — the islanders are not without metallurgy.
  • Islanders seem to place little value on gold and silver ornamentation given how freely it was left in an unlocked hut and worn openly by everyone the party met.
  • The islanders' word for spider is hintu, and repeating a modifier — as in beeta ("big") — appears to intensify it: beeta hintu is a large spider, and beeta beeta beeta hintu, "the biggest spider," is what both the camp near the cliffs and the feathered leader called the creature the party is hunting.
  • A black, disc-shaped monolith — of the same material the party has puzzled over before — is being used by islander ritualists to conjure earth out of nothing, which is then relayed by bucket brigade to build a new wall sealing a hundred-foot gap between two cliffs. Construction looks to have started only days ago. A sample scooped from a passing bucket confirmed it was ordinary, unremarkable dirt, muddy but nothing more — for all the power evidently being spent to produce it.
  • The interior of Spider Island holds a large and sophisticated Islander settlement — far more developed than a simple tribal camp — now wholly overtaken by a great pale spider and its web.
  • The islanders evacuated that settlement and are racing to build a new defensive wall at a natural chokepoint deeper in the valley. The party suspects they were driven out through a large breach in a second, older wall further beyond the village, of the same construction as the Great Wall — likely torn open by the great spider itself.
  • The great spider in the village is the same pale-white type as the one previously encountered and killed on the coast.
  • The feathered Islander leader carries a sextant — a precision navigation instrument, remarkable in this context.
  • The jungle path to the village is roughly 300–400 feet long and traversable; Pocket could see the village clearly from above the canopy.
  • The party is now roughly three days' hard travel inland from the coast — the sea was no longer visible even from height — with the spider village some five or six kilometres further on, about an hour's walk away.
  • Weighing how to prepare for the fight ahead, Cosimo considered a lengthy ritual to identify the properties of the unattuned trinkets they had gathered, and confirmed he had nothing resembling a fireball ready to call on without a similarly involved ritual. Both ideas were set aside as impractical before nightfall.
  • With daylight running short, the party decided to camp near the new wall for the night and make their approach on the spider village in the morning rather than risk it in the dark.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session opened with the party established at the neck of the hourglass-shaped island interior, having crossed the Great Wall in the previous session. Pocket's aerial reconnaissance had already confirmed the situation ahead: the great pale spider, the same species as the one killed on the coast but vastly larger, had occupied the central building of the islander village, removed its roof, and was periodically lowering its abdomen through the opening to deposit eggs. The building's interior was packed with egg sacs and tiny newly-hatched spiders. The spider had not moved from its perch since the party's arrival.

Before the assault planning began in earnest, Werner examined the feathered islander leader's sextant more closely. The leader, who had appeared alongside Leela at the session's end, allowed Werner to handle the instrument while keeping a hand on its spider-silk lanyard. Werner confirmed it was a proper navigation sextant of northern manufacture — the adjustment knobs were loose, indicating it had been actively used rather than stored. He returned it with a gesture of thanks.

Through pantomime and the handful of islander words accumulated over previous encounters, Werner communicated a need for rope. Leela understood, departed, and returned with three coils of fine spider-silk rope, each approximately fifty feet long. Werner also asked Batu Batu for a suitable pot; the only one Batu Batu had on hand was a small tin pot, plainly too light for the job. Leela caught on and led Werner to a communal cooking hut instead, where the party found a proper iron pot — large, with a hanging loop and a lid, intended to be suspended over fire. Additional islander vocabulary was established through this exchange: molly for small, and approximate forms for yes (ano or I) and no (nayo or nay).

The bomb was assembled from the pot, packed with cannon-grade gunpowder and shrapnel — the party's grenade positioned inside with its fuse exposed through the lid, sharp fragments chipped from a stone Leela intuited was needed and fetched herself, and bits of iron and knives found in the hut. The result was a heavy, thirty-pound improvised bomb. Batu Batu was assigned to carry it during the approach. Riu would decide where it was placed.

The battle plan called for two groups. The first, including Riu, Batu Batu, and Salter, would approach the building through a concealed corridor — Cosimo would cast an illusion making their approach look like undisturbed scenery. The second group, including Mani, Werner, and Knick Nab, would advance openly from the flank to harass and distract the spider with harpoons, blades, and musketry. Werner would throw harpoons attached to the spider-silk ropes, tying them off to buildings to restrict the spider's movement. Noddy would cast confusion on the great spider from range while Pocket maintained surveillance. Cosimo would add a blinding flash and illusory distraction as opportunity permitted. The party also weighed torching the entire web-choked village outright, but held off — everything was interconnected by silk that would carry fire unpredictably, and burning out the islanders' homes risked the goodwill they had been cultivating.

The party moved through the jungle toward the village in mid-afternoon, burning through web barriers as they went. Fresh webs smouldered slowly, while older ones caught more readily; in either case the path was cleared without significant resistance, and small spiders scattered from the flames rather than pressing an attack. At the edge of the field before the village — a stretch of upright poles, formerly used by the islanders for drying, now thick with silk and spider activity — the party built a bonfire at the base of one of the poles as a rally point, piling on dry brush until it would burn for the better part of an hour: a visible, defensible fallback position to retreat to if the assault went badly or the party got turned around in the webs. Pocket confirmed from above that the smaller spiders in the field were occupied catching flying insects rather than watching the approaches. They were not on guard.

Cosimo cast the concealment as a stationary illusory tunnel roughly eighty feet long, its outer surface mimicking the surrounding ground and scenery so that nothing outside could see in — a single casting that needed no ongoing concentration and would hold for about a minute. Before committing to the approach, Noddy swept the nearby buildings with a spyglass; no second great spider was visible anywhere in the village, only the medium and small ones the party already knew about. The bomb-bearing group moved through the illusory tunnel toward the building. The flanking group advanced with torches lit. Leela, who had been following without announcement, suddenly loosed a blood-curdling war cry and charged straight at one of the medium spiders clustered near the approach, drawing its attention and creating an opening at a critical moment. The fight erupted immediately.

Noddy cast confusion on the great spider while maintaining concentration, and the effect was visible and immediate: the creature's legs became unsteady, its enormous white body swaying. Cosimo conjured a brilliant flash of light in the form of the sun descending directly onto the spider's eight-eyed face. The creature's eyes blinked ceaselessly, its legs buckled further, and it swayed without apparent purpose. Cosimo followed this with a fantasm — a twenty-foot rhinoceros beetle, its carapace blue and trimmed in gold, crawling up the building's outer wall, spreading its wing-cases, and rearing toward the confused spider. The great spider gave no sign of registering the apparition at all.

Werner drove a poisoned harpoon into one of the great spider's legs, then moved to tie the trailing rope off inside a nearby building — a metal door with a bar on the inside made it look defensible. The building was already occupied: movement in the dark at the back resolved into the gleam of too many eyes, two more spiders lurking unseen. Werner dropped his torch inside, possibly setting the interior alight, and backed out and barred the door behind him rather than fight blind, continuing the fight with his rifle from outside instead. The great spider fired a web strand toward Noddy, which missed. Mani engaged the medium spiders moving in on the flanking group, trading blows while Leela fought beside him with fierce effectiveness — she drove her hand axe hard into one spider, staggering it and dealing significant damage, before taking a painful slash across the ribs in return; later in the same fight she caught a second medium spider with a crushing blow that shattered one of its legs and sent it flying, killing it outright. Knick Nab brawled with the smaller spiders, taking a sharp bite early and later a hard strike that cracked a bone in the back of his hand and left him bleeding, but landed a solid blow of his own that crumpled one of the medium spiders to the ground. Cosimo, between his illusions, lashed out at the spider harrying Knick Nab with a directed force spell. Salter fired his musket into one of the medium spiders, wounding it, then picked up a second, dropped rifle to keep firing. Batu Batu attacked the spider threatening him with meat cleavers and was nearly bitten in return, but its strike went wide entirely.

Riu opened the nest building's door and stepped inside. The entire ground floor was compromised — egg sacs everywhere, baby spiders crawling in the masses of silk, the staircase to the upper floor buried under it. He briefly considered lifting the cauldron bomb straight up with telekinesis, but it was too heavy for the spell to carry, so he began cutting and hacking his way up through the webs by hand instead, cloaking himself in a shadow spell for concealment as he climbed. Partway up he shifted to levitation, rising the rest of the way to the platform where the great spider hung suspended, and set the cauldron bomb directly beneath its abdomen. He lit the fuse with his torch and leapt clear with a burst of magic, landing fifty feet away.

Werner, at range, fired his musket at the great spider and struck it squarely in the head. The round drove through to the brain. The spider convulsed, its legs shaking under it, and slumped forward — settling directly onto the cauldron below.

As the fuse burned down, the party scattered for cover — Cosimo ducked behind a large tree, Mani pulled Leela clear of the blast radius, and the others put buildings and distance between themselves and the cauldron. The fuse ran to its end. The building erupted. A great fireball lifted the structure apart, debris fanning out in every direction. From within the conflagration came a shriek. Baby spiders blasted outward across the village, many trailing fire. The village fell quiet except for the crackle of burning material and the distant hiss of things landing in the dirt.

Leela, who had never witnessed anything resembling a gunpowder detonation, was completely undone. She screamed, spun around looking at the party with an expression of pure terror, and ran. The party surmised she would recover — the shock appeared to be from the explosion itself rather than any injury — but she was gone.

As the dust settled and small burning shapes rained down through the smoke, the impulse to spread the fire further into the village was there for the taking — but the party caught themselves before committing to it. The great spider, for all its size, did not appear large enough to have punched the eighty-foot breach in the Great Wall on its own, and torching their own vantage point over a threat they couldn't identify seemed unwise. Whatever had made that opening was something else. What that something was remained entirely unknown.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Leela — Assisted in gathering materials for the bomb, fought alongside the party during the assault (downing one medium spider outright with a crushing hand-axe blow), and fled in terror following the explosion.
  • Feathered Islander leader — Present during the planning phase; allowed Werner to examine the sextant before departing.
  • Batu Batu — Carried the cauldron-bomb and fought smaller spiders with his meat cleavers.
  • Salter — Fought with the flanking group and wounded a medium spider with his musket, then picked up a second dropped rifle to keep firing.
  • Great white spider — The enormous pale spider nesting in the central building of the spider village. Disoriented by Noddy's confusion spell, blinded by Cosimo's sun-flash illusion, confronted by Cosimo's beetle fantasm, impaled in one leg by Werner's harpoon, shot through the brain by Werner's musket, and destroyed by the bomb.
  • Medium spiders — Several engaged the party during the assault; at least two were killed in the fighting and more were destroyed in the explosion.
  • Small spiders — Present throughout the jungle approach and village perimeter; scattered from fire rather than attacking directly. Large numbers were ejected from the nest building by the explosion, many burning.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Spider Village — The large islander settlement overtaken by the great spider. Beyond the residential huts, Pocket's earlier reconnaissance had picked out a cluster of larger buildings off to one side, topped with chimney-like stacks and fronted by slag heaps — evidence of some industry distinct from ordinary dwellings, left unexplored this session. The party fought through the village's web-covered streets. The central nest building had a ground-level door and, on its exterior, a ladder leading up to a small platform, ordinary features of island construction now overtaken by web and spider activity. It was destroyed in the explosion.
  • The Jungle Path — The several-hundred-foot stretch of jungle between the island's neck and the village. The party burned through multiple web barriers during the approach.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The assault on the Spider Village: A multi-phase battle involving the whole party against the great white spider and numerous smaller spiders.
  • Knick Nab was bitten by a small spider (minor wound, 5 hits) and struck by a medium spider (cracked bone to the back of the hand, 14 hits, bleeding, at −5 to activity), but felled one of the medium spiders outright with a solid strike of his own.
  • Leela took a slash across the ribs from a spider (7 hits, at −5 to activity), then downed a second medium spider outright with a crushing blow that shattered its leg and sent it flying.
  • A medium spider's bite at Batu Batu went wildly astray, sparing him a hit that round.
  • Cosimo split his attention between the great spider and the smaller ones, striking one of the spiders harrying Knick Nab with a directed force spell.
  • Multiple medium and small spiders were killed in the fighting.
  • The great spider was killed by the combined effects of Noddy's confusion spell, Cosimo's blinding flash and beetle fantasm, Werner's harpoon, Werner's killing musket shot to the head, and Riu's bomb.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The great spider had removed the roof from the central building of the village and was depositing eggs inside. The interior was thick with egg sacs and newly-hatched spiders of wolf-spider size.
  • The feathered islander leader's sextant had its adjustment knobs loosened, indicating it had been recently and actively used rather than carried as an ornament.
  • Additional islander words were established: molly (small); ano or I (yes); nayo or nay (no).
  • A spyglass sweep of the village's buildings before the assault turned up no second great spider — only the medium and small ones the party already knew about.
  • The smaller spiders appear to lighten in colour as they age rather than staying one shade: hatchlings are solid black, maturing through brown and yellow before reaching the great spider's pale white — size and power apparently increasing together with the shift.
  • The great spider showed significant vulnerability to Noddy's confusion spell and Cosimo's blinding flash — both visibly impaired its activity.
  • Riu's telekinesis magic proved unable to lift the finished cauldron bomb — at roughly thirty pounds, it was too heavy for the spell to carry, forcing him to climb and cut his way up through the nest by hand instead.
  • The great spider, despite its scale, does not appear to have been capable of punching the eighty-foot breach in the Great Wall. Whatever created that opening is something larger or differently capable, and remains unidentified.

  • Cannon-grade gunpowder (consumed in the bomb).
