docs.title: Spider Rain, Mangani, and the Road to the River
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session opened immediately after the great explosion that destroyed the enormous spider nesting in the central tower of Spider Island's abandoned village. Riu's improvised bomb — a cooking pot packed with gunpowder, rocks, and assorted sharp implements, thrown down the tower's staircase — had brought the whole structure down, killing the giant spider and scattering its eggs in a rain of fire and debris. Leela had fled in visible terror at the detonation, yelling something none of the party could understand before disappearing back through the wall.

With the centrepiece threat eliminated, Mani led the group in a methodical sweep of the remaining village buildings, working in firing lines of three to deal with the medium and large spiders sheltering inside; the smaller spiders were simply driven off or dispatched by hand. Noddy attempted, unsuccessfully, to rope and tame one of the smaller specimens using his length of rope — the spider proved unreceptive to his incentives. The party piled the bodies of the larger spiders together as a demonstration of achievement, and Riu took time to sketch the specimens, noting the detail of their joints and anatomy. Discussion turned briefly to whether spider silk might be harvestable from the webs and cocoons — the silk on Noddy's rope was noted to be remarkable material — and to whether the spiders themselves were safe to eat; the consensus was that they were probably both venomous and poisonous, edible at best with the same caution one would give a puffer fish. Before moving on, someone climbed back into the ruined tower for a last look: the interior was scorched down to bare earth and thick with spider gore, and the second floor — its roof torn away by the matriarch herself — held nothing worse, only the wrapped shapes of birds and smaller creatures caught in the webs outside; no human remains turned up anywhere in the village.

As afternoon drew on, the party gathered the great spider's head, strapped to one of its leg segments for carrying, and marched back along the jungle path toward the Islander settlement to the north. Approaching the wall that separated the cleared village from the Islander community, they emerged into open ground to find the wall newly heightened, with dozens of armed Islanders lining the top — spearmen and archers watching the party with open hostility. Leela was visible on the wall but not in a position of welcome.

Mani called out using what Islander vocabulary the party had accumulated — "beeta beeta beeta hintu" — and displayed the giant spider's head as a trophy. It was an extraordinarily persuasive appeal, yet the mass of Islanders remained unmoved; one hurled a spear that landed close enough to rattle him, more a warning shot than an attack. Only Leela came down and out to meet them, climbing over the wall against visible objection from her people.

Leela approached cautiously and unarmed, and the party tried again to convey that the great spider was dead — pointing, repeating "beeta boom," and at one point firing a demonstrative pistol shot into the air. She seemed to grasp that they had killed it, but grew increasingly agitated, evidently fearing her people were being asked to feed the party to something worse, or that some older, larger disaster was connected to this one — Cosimo caught an unfamiliar word that hinted at some far older calamity. Pointing toward the distant south wall to ask whether that older disaster was connected, the party picked up their first word for "wall" — "colo," supplied through Batu Batu — though the exchange never became fully clear. With her people unwilling to let the party through the wall that night, Leela indicated with the word "anto" — later understood to mean something like "the future" — that she would return, then climbed into the trees and made her way back toward the settlement.

Left to fend for themselves overnight, the party withdrew into the abandoned village, leaving the spider's head at the foot of the wall as a parting gesture. They settled into one of the larger buildings already cleared of spiders, which turned out to have its own fire pits and stores of charcoal — evidently once used for some kind of communal work rather than habitation. With time to look around properly, it became clear the village had been abandoned in a hurry rather than packed up and left: possessions lay strewn in the streets, and a child's teddy bear was found half-buried in the rubble. Casual looting turned up a considerable quantity of gold jewellery — discs, chains, and chokers, rough-worked rather than fine — and each member of the party helped themselves to a share, several pounds apiece. The night passed without incident under a rotating watch.

Leela reappeared the next morning with a gift of fruit, which the party accepted along with her continued company. As they set off on the thirty-minute walk south toward the far wall — the one broken months earlier by whatever had come through it — the language lessons shifted direction: rather than teaching Leela their own speech, the party found it more useful to keep learning hers, with Batu Batu's greater fluency in Islander proving invaluable. They picked up words for a panther ("pinta") and some low, ground-crawling creature ("hort hort"), and pieced together gestures for pig. Simple temporal concepts also emerged — "intra" for something like the past and "anto" for the future — though Leela's people seemed to lack any finer division into specific days.

The wall itself was a colossal, pristine structure some eighty feet high, and Leela grew visibly more nervous the closer they came, warning through Batu Batu of dangers that used to come through this very gap before it was sealed. The breach was a twenty-foot-high, twelve-to-fourteen-foot-wide gash near the top, with debris and churned earth spilling down this side; nothing suggested a deliberate excavation or an earthquake, just a mass of rubble slumped from above. Investigating the near side before climbing over, the party found a rusted Northern-make musket half-buried in the mud — Werner's gunsmithing knowledge placed its origin, while its corrosion suggested it had lain there for months rather than years. Tracking checks turned up no boot- or cart-prints, only heavy animal traffic moving in and out of the gap; cross-referenced against the musket's condition and the regrowth over the break, the party judged the wall had come down roughly six months earlier. Pressed for a timeframe of her own — via a stick-count scratched in the dirt and the visible daytime moon — Leela could only confirm it had been a great many days; Batu Batu judged her people lacked any finer reckoning than that, but her answer was at least consistent with the physical evidence. Further searching turned up scattered human remains, including one body still wearing the corded remnants of a ceremonial robe, which Cosimo identified as clerical dress of the Divinity of Two.

Climbing the rubble to look over the crest, the party spotted a ship's cannon on the far side, pointed squarely at the gap, amid the wreckage of a camp — smashed barrels, planks, and scattered supplies. Giant, five-toed footprints and bodies crushed or embedded in the earth showed that whatever had broken the wall had gone on to wreck the camp itself. Crossing over, they found the cannon to be a Northern-standard sixteen-pounder on a wheeled carriage, in poor condition and needing maintenance before it could safely fire, with roughly a dozen cannonballs stacked nearby and a keg of gunpowder that had been left open to the elements. Werner isolated a small quantity of the powder to test it, using his Gunpowder Craft skill — the resulting flash was larger than intended, singeing off part of one eyebrow and sending Leela fleeing back through the wall at the noise.

With Werner's ears still ringing, the party searched the dead for anything of value or informative. The corpses were mostly decomposed, but clothing had survived where flesh had not: plain-dressed sailors alongside officers identifiable by their epaulettes, several bearing a distinctive two-coloured sash worn as a belt or bandolier. By the party's estimate, several score men had died in this vicinity. Reasoning from the cannon, the sashes, and the style of the dead, they concluded that a Divinity of Two expedition — probably the vessel they had spotted near the storm — had reached Spider Island some months before them and come to grief against whatever emerged from the interior. Werner took one of the better-preserved sashes as evidence; Mani raised the possibility that a second Divinity of Two ship might be following, either close behind or already at the island.

Leela returned, and the party tried once more to communicate, pointing to the bodies, to the sashes, and then to the gap in the wall, attempting to convey that the Divinity of Two — not the party — had made the breach. Leela listened and appeared to understand in part, offering the word "dimi," which Batu Batu interpreted as meaning something like "white people" or "more like you."

While this went on, Noddy sent Pocket aloft to keep watch. Through the bird's eyes he spotted a massive creature — a mangani, in Leela's word — lumbering out of the jungle to sniff at the cannon and the patch of scorched earth left by Werner's mishap. It was enormous, easily capable of crushing a man with a single blow. The party moved quietly behind the wall and to one side, clearing the creature's line of sight; Noddy cast Confusion through Pocket, and the mangani continued its erratic sniffing for a time before turning and loping back into the jungle at speed.

Retreating to the tree line with the recovered barrel of gunpowder, the party tried once more to reassure Leela, using Batu Batu's fluency to offer the word "mell" for "friend" alongside gestures meant to convey they had come to help. Cosimo suggested demonstrating their own capabilities — showing that they too possessed power. The discussion was cut short when drums began sounding from the south jungle: many voices, the sound of people advancing. Leela ran toward the noise, then came running back, pulling urgently northward. A mass of Islanders — dozens — emerged from the southern jungle and began advancing across the open ground. Noddy called on Thick Fog and cast it onto the gap in the wall between the two groups, producing a dense, rising mist that swallowed the advancing Islanders in confusion and screams. The party used the cover to follow Leela north into the jungle as fast as they could go.

Moving at pace down the cleared path — evidently cut when the Divinity of Two hauled their cannon inland — the party passed further evidence of past violence: bodies smashed into the earth and against trees, consistent with the mangani. The path was wide and well-made. After roughly thirty minutes of hard movement northward they reached the bank of a substantial river and found an encampment: several tents (some crushed, one intact), equipment in disarray, and — drawn up on the riverbank — two longboats. One had been left with its sail up, which had taken weather damage and partially capsized it. The other was in better condition with sails stored in the locker.

Werner and Salter set to work readying both boats while the rest of the party searched the camp in pairs. The remains of a single body were found at the camp — crushed violently into the ground, wearing robes. In one hand was a broken-hafted axe, its blade carved with stylised suns along one face and moons along the other; in the other, a broken staff, its ornamental head still intact — a depiction of the sun and moon intertwined. Cosimo identified the staff-head immediately as a Diad, a significant holy relic of the Divinity of Two normally kept in the rear of major churches and brought out only for important processions. Its presence here confirmed that a senior cleric — most likely the Censure or a high-ranking cleric of the expedition — had been killed at this camp, presumably by the mangani. There were no papers or records; anything written had been destroyed by weather and time. The party recovered powder horns, spare muskets in varying states of repair, and some additional gunpowder stores.

While sorting out who would ride in which boat, someone recalled that Leela had fought alongside them against the spiders wielding an axe of her own, and wondered whether the recovered axe head — fitted with a new haft — might make a fitting gift for her; the question went unresolved as departure pressed in. Before getting underway, Werner looked over the axe head itself — a fine blade needing maintenance after months in the mud. Cosimo's first attempt to sense anything unusual about it came up empty, but a second, far more successful effort confirmed the axe was enchanted in some way, though its exact nature remained undetermined by the time the boats had to move on. With both boats made serviceable, the group loaded their gear — including the recovered equipment, the two boats' sails, the axe, and the Diad, along with all the gold looted from the village despite the extra weight it added — and set off downstream toward the sea. The river flowed east. Knick Nab and Salter took the second boat; Werner, Batu Batu, Cosimo, and others the lead. Leela came with them, eyeing the larger boat with a mix of curiosity and uncertainty.

Moving downstream through the widening river, the party encountered two mangani on the banks — one on each shore — that had been following them. As the boats came dangerously close to shore, Noddy cast Confusion through Pocket on the smaller of the two; the creature nonetheless swatted at the second boat, knocking Knick Nab down and stunning him in the bottom of the boat. Noddy took over the rudder while Riu moved to cover. Werner fired from the lead boat, scoring a shot to the confused mangani's head that tore off a chunk of ear and stunned it into the shallows. Both boats pushed through, Knick Nab recovering from his stun, and the mangani fell behind as the river widened further.

After roughly two hours of downstream travel the river opened into a sheltered bay and the sea. The boats grounded briefly on silt at the mouth but cleared it with some polling. There was no sign of any other vessel anchored in the bay. Leela grew agitated as they turned toward the shore — she was smelling or sensing mangani nearby — and the party heeded her warning and kept their distance from the beach, abandoning a plan to search the sand there for older signs of a Divinity of Two landing, such as old campfires or tracks, since neither shore seemed safe enough to approach on foot. The group agreed to sail a short distance along the coast to find a hidden cove to spend the night, then return south the following day toward the rendezvous point on the beach where the Amada was expected.

Discussion closed the session: the party debated whether to attempt to return to the Islander village at all, and how to explain — if they could — that the gunpowder explosion near the great outer wall had not been their doing. The consensus was to spend time communicating with Leela at the coast, attempt to learn more of her language, and see whether she could facilitate any renewed contact with her people.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Leela — the Islander woman who had accompanied the party; continued to serve as their only point of contact with the local population; word for giant ape: mangani
  • Batu Batu — the Islander crew member from the Amada, assisting with translation attempts; his greater fluency in Islander proved invaluable during the language lessons on the walk to the south wall
  • Salter — a sailor of the "Amada," formerly of the "Advance"; present throughout, assisting with the boats
  • Mangani — a massive, ape-like creature native to Spider Island's interior; at least two encountered on the riverbanks; responsible for the deaths at both camps; deeply feared by Leela and the Islanders; the word is from the Islander tongue
  • Giant spiders (beeta beeta hintu, beeta beeta beeta hintu) — residual specimens in the village buildings, dispatched methodically during the morning sweep; the enormous matriarch was already dead from the previous session's explosion
  • Two unnamed Divinity of Two clergy — the remains of two robed clerics were found in the expedition's wake: one among the dead near the wall breach, identified by Cosimo from its corded vestments; the other crushed at the river encampment, carrying an axe and the Diad, and possibly the expedition's most senior cleric present

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Spider Island (formerly the Isle of Beasts) — the principal setting throughout; the abandoned village, the two great earthen walls, the interior jungle, and the river system all featured; by the party's own reckoning they were roughly four days' travel into the island's interior with no sign yet of its far side, a measure of just how large the island truly is
  • The abandoned village — cleared of remaining spiders over the course of the morning; the ruined central tower confirmed to be the destroyed nesting site; the party camped here overnight in a large, fire-pitted building, and found evidence of a hasty evacuation (a child's teddy bear among the rubble) along with a cache of gold jewellery; drying racks and a small lake with a well-worn path lay between the village and the south wall
  • The breach in the outer wall (south side) — site of the old Divinity of Two encampment; bodies, a cannon, cannonballs, and degraded gunpowder stores found here, along with a rusted musket and a robed cleric's remains on the near side; as the party fled north under cover of fog, armed figures were briefly glimpsed atop the wall itself, well clear of the breach — evidence of some stair or structure allowing the Islanders to man the wall's crest that the party never located
  • The river encampment (north side) — a campsite on the bank of a large eastward-flowing river; two longboats found here along with crushed tents, supplies, and the robed body bearing the axe and the Diad; both longboats had mounting points for swivel guns, though no guns were aboard to fit them
  • The river — a navigable waterway flowing east from the interior to the sea; used by the Divinity of Two expedition to ferry their cannon inland
  • The bay and open sea — reached after approximately two hours' downstream travel; the mouth of the river opens into a sheltered bay

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• Rebuffed at the Islander wall (afternoon, day one) — Mani's exceptionally persuasive appeal failed to move the assembled spearmen and archers; one threw a spear that landed close by as a warning shot; no one was hurt, and the party retreated to spend the night in the village instead
  • Spider clearance sweep (morning) — the party methodically cleared the village buildings of remaining medium and large spiders using musket fire from doorways and windows; no significant injuries reported; small spiders dispatched by hand
  • Mangani encounter at the wall (midday, day two) — a large mangani emerged from the jungle to investigate the area near the cannon after Werner's accidental gunpowder discharge; the party retreated behind the wall; Noddy cast Confusion through Pocket, which may or may not have influenced the creature's eventual departure; no combat
  • Islander advance (afternoon, day two) — dozens of armed Islanders emerged from the southern jungle and advanced on the party's position; Noddy cast Thick Fog on the gap in the wall, covering the party's withdrawal into the jungle to the north; no direct fighting
  • Mangani on the river (late afternoon) — two mangani followed the party along the riverbanks; Noddy cast Confusion through Pocket on the smaller of the two, which nonetheless swatted at Knick Nab's boat, landing a blow that knocked him out of his seat (stunned for two rounds, knocked down); Werner shot the same confused mangani with a musket ball, tearing off part of its ear and leaving it stunned in the shallows (the bullet grazed its head); the party cleared the encounter and both creatures fell behind; once safely anchored in the bay, Werner properly tended to Knick Nab's bruises and he recovered without lasting injury

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Divinity of Two sent an expedition to Spider Island some months before the party arrived; the expedition included sailors, naval officers, at least one senior cleric (possibly a Censure), and a 16-pounder cannon. Several score men died, most likely in or near the breach in the south wall. A second robed cleric, killed by a mangani at the river camp, was carrying a Diad — indicating very senior ecclesiastical rank
  • The two-coloured sash on the dead soldiers is a Divinity of Two military marking, distinct from standard Northern naval dress; Cosimo recognised the same two colours woven into the corded vestments on both dead clerics, reading them as representing the Mother and the Father
  • The party argued, without resolving it, over whether the Divinity of Two operating on this side of the Maelstrom is the same organisation known back home, or something merely related to it
  • The Diad, identified by Cosimo, is a highly significant holy relic of the Divinity of Two; its normal place is inside major churches; it is only displayed publicly during important processions mounted on a ceremonial staff. Finding one in the possession of a field-expedition cleric suggests the expedition had a formally sanctioned, high-priority religious mission
  • Tracking near the wall breach found no boot- or cart-prints, only heavy animal traffic moving in and out of the gap; cross-referenced with the rusted musket's condition and the regrowth over the break, the party judged the wall had come down roughly six months earlier
  • The Islanders in the village became openly hostile after the gunpowder explosion and the party's inability to communicate that they were not responsible for the breach in the south wall; Leela's word "dimi" appears to mean something like "people who look like you" (i.e. white-skinned outsiders), suggesting she has seen or heard of the Divinity of Two expedition
  • New Islander vocabulary picked up on the walk to the south wall: "pinta" (panther), "hort hort" (a low, ground-crawling creature), a gesture for pig, and the temporal concepts "intra" (something like the past) and "anto" (the future); Leela's people seem to lack finer division into specific days
  • Two more Islander words surfaced earlier in the day: "colo" (wall), offered by Batu Batu while asking Leela whether an older calamity was connected to the south wall, and "mell" (friend), used to reassure her after the first mangani sighting
  • The party estimated roughly 200 Islanders at the village site alone — a number that grew to "hundreds" once the bucket-line workers building the wall were included
  • The black monolith (disc/platform) in the Islander settlement was discussed: the party observed previously that Islanders use it to produce seemingly inexhaustible earth for wall construction; Riu noted that the ability to draw power from such a source is itself the thing of interest, regardless of what the Islanders do with that power; this appears related to why the Medallions drew the party here
  • The cannon left at the south wall is on the wrong side of the wall relative to the Islander settlement and in poor condition; the gunpowder recovered is partly degraded; the party discussed but did not attempt to haul it over the wall
  • Two serviceable longboats with oars and sails were recovered from the river camp; they provide an exit from the island independent of the Amada
  • A decorated hand-axe head was recovered from the river camp, in the same robed corpse's hand as the Diad; it bears sun and moon carvings on its two faces; a first attunement attempt by Cosimo found nothing unusual, but a second, far more successful roll confirmed it is enchanted, though its exact nature remains undetermined; the party briefly discussed giving it to Leela once rehafted, recalling she fought the spiders with an axe of her own, but reached no decision
  • The party levelled to rank 3 at session end (Noddy and Cosimo absent, so level-up deferred for them)
  • Prompted by wondering whether the grenade thrown in the previous session's bomb had actually been consumed, the party clarified with the GM that it had not: Noddy still carries one grenade in addition to his smoke grenade

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• A quantity of gold jewellery (discs, chains, and chokers) looted from the abandoned village, several pounds per person
  • One decorated hand-axe blade (broken haft; sun/moon carvings; possibly magical — result deferred)
  • One Diad — holy relic of the Divinity of Two, recovered from the robed body at the river camp
  • One two-coloured Divinity of Two military sash, taken from the battlefield near the south wall breach
  • Several powder horns recovered from the bodies and the river camp
  • Spare muskets in various states of repair, recovered from the river camp
  • Kegs of gunpowder from the river camp stores
  • Two longboats (with oars and sails), recovered from the river encampment
  • Small quantity of degraded gunpowder from the keg near the south wall (partially salvageable)

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • The keg of gunpowder left behind on the hillside during the withdrawal from the Islanders (abandoned in the confusion)

docs.title: The Diad, the Dimbi, and the Shattering of the Sea
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session opened on the water, with the party sailing in the two recovered longboats and debating the nature of the Diad recovered from the dead cleric at the river encampment. Riu recalled a childhood memory of a Divinity of Two ceremony in his inland town, in which a representative from the capital had arrived specifically to bless a newly dug well — producing a Diad and carrying it in procession to do so. The practice appeared to be standard: the Diad was not merely decorative but an active tool in religious ceremony, never carried casually. Cosimo attempted to attune to the relic; his roll was high and the attunement succeeded. He learned that the Diad functions as a channelling focus — in game terms, it doubles the power available when drawing on the Mother and Father. Riu, recalling that the Diad was always carried in pairs by senior clergy on a ceremonial staff, observed that wandering around with one would draw immediate scrutiny in any civilised Northern port — someone would notice there was only one where there should be two, and the questions would only grow from there. The decision was made to keep it securely aboard.

The talk drifted from strategy into something more personal — an unresolved debate about where the party's own strange abilities actually came from. Pressed on whether he consciously called on the Mother and Father when he worked his healing, or Cosimo his illusions, Riu affirmed his faith but conceded that nothing about the act felt like prayer; it was more an instinct he couldn't name or explain. Someone recalled that both Cosimo and Noddy had been quietly trained by the peculiar figure they'd met at an inn — A'Wood — who had taught them the shape of their power without ever explaining where it came from, "like being shown push-ups without being told what a muscle is." Cosimo raised the strange old woman connected to the party's medallions, and the medallions themselves, neither of which fit any mythology of the Two he had ever encountered, and wondered aloud whether his own gift — plainly the strongest in the party — was somehow shared with the others through whatever bound them together. Riu pointed out that his own abilities, including the levitation he'd used to descend a chasm in Old Port, had shown themselves before the party ever passed through the storm, undercutting any theory that pinned everything on that one event. Nobody had an answer, and the question was set aside once again.

The conversation then ranged more widely across the party's situation. They reviewed what they knew: a Divinity of Two expedition had reached Spider Island some months before them, blown a breach in the great outer wall, suffered heavy losses to the mangani, and apparently withdrawn by sea. A large vessel flying church colours had been spotted some days earlier on a heading for the island. The party reasoned that the ship was likely returning to investigate the fate of its earlier expedition. They agreed that if any such ship appeared, they would hide rather than engage, using Cosimo's illusion capabilities to mask the Amada if necessary.

Turning to the Wazari and to Leela, the party spent a substantial part of the morning conducting an interview through Riu's Islander language and Batu Batu's assistance. Leela's dialect diverged enough from the Islander the two of them knew that real communication meant gesture, sketch, and slow phrasing rather than straightforward translation, and working through even a short list of questions took patience. Leela confirmed that her people's gods took the form of giant animals — beeta, the great creatures of the island. The two magic-users the party had observed atop the black cylinder in the Wazari village, directing earth into the wall, she referred to as hempti and hempto — apparently a male-female pairing; individual magic-workers she called hempa. When Noddy demonstrated his ability to evaporate a bucket of water, Leela named him hempa but showed no great surprise, suggesting that such abilities were not alien to her world. She seemed more astonished by ink and the act of writing than by the conjuring of steam. Asked whether she herself possessed such power, Leela answered with a word new to the party's vocabulary — anto, meaning later or not yet — suggesting she aspired to become hempa herself rather than already being one.

The black cylinder in the Wazari village Leela called Ea Mondo — mondo being her word for black, a term the party already had some confidence in. When Riu drew a second island and suggested a second such cylinder might exist elsewhere, Leela reacted with apparent surprise or disbelief: she indicated that the one in her village was simply the Ea, not one of many she was aware of.

Asked how many times people like the party — dimbi, her word for pale-skinned outsiders — had come to the island, Leela indicated three visits, not counting the current group. Shown the two-coloured sash recovered from the bodies at the south wall, she confirmed that those particular outsiders were not among the three she knew of. This was consistent with the party's estimate that the Divinity of Two expedition had arrived roughly six months ago, while the first outsiders Leela might have encountered were at least two years earlier — around the time of Captain Maynard's voyage. The trail on Maynard, then, was not necessarily cold.

To the east (or perhaps northeast, based on Leela's gestures on Riu's crude sketch), she indicated a second island. The single word she used for it was chba, repeated with evident wariness, and she made clear it was not to be visited — that the people there were dangerous, and that dimbi did not go there. The party added cannibal island to their mental chart.

Riu spent the remainder of the afternoon methodically naming common objects with Leela, building vocabulary. Water, she said, was fto; land was ilant. Through it all, Knick Nab kept the two-boat convoy moving toward the rendezvous, his orders sharp and his handling of the unfamiliar longboats surprisingly assured.

That evening the boats beached on a long stretch of open sand — a clearing chosen for its distance from the treeline, leaving a broad killing ground between the boats and the jungle. No fire was lit. Noddy used his Evaporate Liquid spell to steam clams, mussels, and crab legs gathered at the tideline, producing a decent cold-side meal with no light or noise. The night passed without attack, though the jungle sounded its usual chorus of unsettling noises, and sleep came fitfully.

Come morning, Cosimo levelled his illusionary abilities and demonstrated them by conjuring Handsome Gulliver Gold as a sparring partner for Riu — using the Fantasm 2 spell together with Feel Mirage, which gave his illusions physical substance for the first time. Handsome Gulliver Gold could now be felt as well as seen, appearing dressed as a musketeer and brandishing a rapier. Riu fenced against him for nine minutes, eventually drawing a second weapon to fight two-handed, and still could not land a clean hit; Gulliver Gold taunted him throughout, at one point declining to call him a varlet on the grounds that it "would show you too much respect." The experience was, by Riu's own assessment, deeply instructive and deeply irritating.

Sailing on toward the rendezvous, the party turned to weighing their options. A second raid back over the wall for the small stock of gold statuettes they'd seen in the abandoned huts was considered and set aside — a two-day round trip for a haul smaller than what they already carried didn't seem worth the risk, especially with an unfriendly ship possibly inbound. Someone floated the idea of turning an old tactic back on the newcomers — sending a small boat loaded with explosives at the ship the way a fire ship had once been used against their own vessel — but it went no further than talk, since the party had no evidence the ship meant them harm and no wish to invite a fight they didn't need. Riu put the question of trade to Leela directly: shown a selection of possible goods, she indicated, pointing at a musket, that her people wanted weapons to defend themselves rather than cloth, drink, or trinkets. Asked where the island's gold came from, she gestured vaguely further inland, offering no specific location the party could act on. With no obvious next move on the gold and the ship still a possible threat, the party settled on spending their remaining time harvesting spider silk before departing, reasoning they could always return once the Divinity of Two's business on the island had played out.

Rounding a point of land, they recognised their own ship's masts: the Amada was still anchored where they'd left her. The two longboats signalled and were hailed aboard by Lieutenant Blaque — the Amada's short, bald, moustached second officer — while Captain De Guzman remained below. Before climbing aboard, the party agreed on their story: they would tell the crew everything that had happened to them except for the Diad and Noddy's trick of boiling water. Blaque organised the unloading of the salvaged cargo using the ship's tackle — a barrel of wet gunpowder needing to be dried out, a chest of rifles, and spare sail cloth among it — and on being introduced to Leela, asked bluntly whether she was a slave; told she was a free woman and a friend, he apologised and said she would be treated as such. The party went below to brief De Guzman properly.

Before returning to shore, Riu asked Leela whether she wished to go back to her own people. Her answer centred on wanting to learn magic first; the party understood this to mean she intended to return home eventually, once she had, and resolved to bring her along for now. Riu privately floated the idea of sending powder and shot back with her as a goodwill gift for the Wazari whenever that day came, mindful that the village had not parted from the party on the friendliest terms. The group then went ashore in force to gather resources before departing, using the Amada's own longboat to shuttle silk and supplies back to the ship. Crewmen collected spider silk from the abundant webs throughout the coastal treeline while others watched the perimeter with muskets. As the gathering disturbed the webs, spiders emerged; two beeta hintu specimens — mid-sized by the island's standards — were captured alive in crates the ship's carpenter built for the purpose. The second longboat was dragged up into the jungle edge and hidden, its gear buried in sand beneath it, left as a cached resource in case the party needed to return on foot. Cosimo presented Leela with a carbine — a shorter musket from the Divinity of Two stores, cleaned and polished — and showed her how to fire it. She fired it once, the crack echoing across the beach.

At almost the same moment, the Amada's captain discharged the swivel gun — his signal for urgency. The party looked to the horizon and saw a sail: a large, three-masted vessel bearing down toward the island. The shore party scrambled into the remaining longboat and rowed hard for the ship, taking the boat under tow as the Amada got underway rather than trying to bring it aboard.

Captain De Guzman did not wait. He had the anchor up and the sails filling before the longboat had cleared the surf, then hugged the coast as the party came aboard, using the island's own treeline as visual cover against the approaching vessel. Noddy climbed to the crow's nest with the spyglass and confirmed what they feared: a large three-master, heading toward the island. He could not make out any flag at that distance. Someone raised the idea of cutting the towed longboat loose to gain speed; the party held onto it for now but kept a hand on a hatchet, ready to sever the line at a moment's notice. Cosimo cast Illusion 3 with doubled radius and doubled duration, wrapping the entire hull of the Amada in a static image of jungle shore — enough to blur their outline against the coast for the twelve minutes it held, and cheap enough in power that he judged he could sustain it, recast after recast, for an hour or more if needed. He tried to draw on the Diad to ease the casting, as he had with his other workings, but felt nothing from it this time; whatever the relic's power required, it did not seem to answer him here. The Amada moved west, out along the island's southern coast and then away to sea.

Watching from the crow's nest as the illusion cycled through recasts, Noddy reported that the approaching ship appeared to round the island to the east — toward the river mouth, where the Divinity of Two's earlier camp had been. It did not follow. Once the island itself had dropped away and the illusion no longer needed to match a coastline, Cosimo shifted its image from jungle shore to open ocean, keeping the Amada's outline blurred until they were sure of a clean escape. The Amada sailed clear.

Clear of the coast, Mani noticed something new: alongside the familiar pull he'd carried since they'd reached Spider Island — strong, constant, almost like a voice talking somewhere behind them — he could now make out a second sensation, fainter, more like a whisper, coming from somewhere ahead of them to the west. He had never felt two such pulls at once before.

Two days later, in open water well west of Spider Island, Mani was on deck in the early evening when the sensation he had been carrying since reaching the island — a directional pull, a low hum from somewhere behind them — cut off instantly. No fade. Gone. He described the moment as feeling like a thousand voices screaming out and then silence. He told the others what he had felt. Once again the party turned over the source of these growing, unexplained gifts — Cosimo's illusions, Noddy's command of water and air, Mani's own sense for the buried Totems — without arriving at any answer beyond noting that the feeling had, so far, always led them somewhere important.

Moments later, far on the eastern horizon, there was a flash. Recalling what they already knew of the Great Change — that it began when a Censure of the Divinity of Two consumed a Diad to destroy a Totem of Air — the party immediately suspected the same ritual had just been repeated on the Earth Totem behind them. Cosimo, still holding the party's own recovered Diad, grimly observed that in the right hands it was itself a kind of holy grenade.

Debris began pattering down on the deck: mud, grit, small fragments of rock. Then, all around the ship, the sea began to move wrong. Not waves — something from beneath. Noddy, from high in the rigging, called down that there was land coming. He was right. Spurs of rock and compressed earth erupted from the ocean, bursting upward in lines and fingers that radiated outward from the direction of Spider Island, crossing and re-crossing the ship's wake. Captain De Guzman fought the rudder; crew scrambled to the sails. One mass of rock broke the surface close enough to shudder the hull. The chaos lasted roughly three minutes. When it settled, new islands stood where there had been open water — long, low formations of bare rock, pointing like compass needles back toward Spider Island.

The session closed with every medallion in the party growing hot against the skin.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Leela — the Wazari Islander woman travelling with the party; active participant in the language exchange; received a carbine from Cosimo
  • Batu Batu — the Islander cook aboard the Amada; assisted with translation throughout
  • Captain De Guzman — captain of the Amada; spotted the approaching ship and got the vessel underway without being asked
  • Lieutenant Blaque — a short, bald, moustached officer aboard the Amada; hailed and welcomed the party back aboard, organised the unloading of salvaged cargo, and confirmed Leela's status as a free woman rather than a captive
  • Handsome Gulliver Gold — Cosimo's illusory creation; appeared as a musketeer with a blunted rapier; for the first time possessed physical substance, capable of being touched and of striking back; taunted Riu throughout their nine-minute bout
  • Beeta hintu (giant spiders) — two mid-sized specimens captured alive in crates for transport
  • Mangani — referenced in discussion but not encountered this session; their role in destroying the Divinity of Two expedition was established

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Spider Island (formerly the Isle of Beasts) — primary context for the session's opening discussions; the party departed by sea partway through
  • The open coast (southern beach) — the night camp; a long sandy beach chosen for the clearing between jungle and sea
  • The Amada — the party's ship; primary setting for the second half of the session
  • Open sea, west of Spider Island — two days' sail from the island; location of the Shatters event
  • Chba (cannibal island) — mentioned by Leela as a dangerous island visible to the east/northeast; she advised strongly against going there

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• Evasion of the approaching vessel (Spider Island's coast) — not a combat encounter: a large three-masted ship, presumed Divinity of Two, was sighted bearing toward the island as the shore party finished harvesting silk; Captain De Guzman got the Amada underway immediately and hugged the coastline for visual cover while Cosimo sustained an extended, doubled-radius Illusion 3 disguising the ship's hull as jungle shoreline; the party briefly considered cutting the towed longboat free to gain speed but kept it in tow, ready to cut the line if it became a liability; the vessel was last seen rounding the island toward the eastern river mouth rather than pursuing, and the Amada slipped away without being caught
  • Shatters event (open sea, two days west) — not a combat encounter but a survival scenario: eruptions of rock and earth burst from the ocean around the Amada following the destruction of the Spider Island Earth Totem; Captain De Guzman manoeuvred to avoid the worst of the upwellings; the hull was shaken but took no critical damage; no casualties among crew or party; Knick Nab was braced at the bow and Mani held the mast

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Diad functions as a channelling focus, doubling the power available when calling on the Mother and Father; Cosimo successfully attuned to it; carrying one openly in the North would attract serious scrutiny from the Divinity of Two
  • When Cosimo tried to draw on the Diad while casting the illusion that hid the Amada, it gave him no boost at all, unlike his attunement working — raising the question of whether the relic answers only ordained clergy, or the Two simply object to being invoked by someone outside the church
  • The Wazari are what Leela's people call themselves; their gods take the form of giant animals — beeta, the great creatures
  • Magic-users among Leela's people are called hempa; the two who operated the black cylinder in the Wazari village were referred to as hempti and hempto, a male-female pairing; Leela recognised Noddy as a hempa without hesitation
  • The source of the party's individual gifts remains an open question: several of these abilities are not consciously invoked as prayer to the Two, they were merely shaped (not created) by A'Wood's earlier training, and Riu's own abilities predate the party's storm crossing, ruling out the storm as a sole explanation
  • The party speculated, without confirmation, that Wazari children show no deformities because this island's water has never been blessed by the Two with a Diad — raising an uncomfortable question about what such blessings are actually for back home
  • A separate, unconfirmed theory was raised of a third power distinct from the Mother and Father, based on a symbol of three lines the party has seen elsewhere
  • The black cylinder is called Ea Mondo (mondo = black); Leela appeared unaware of any other such object elsewhere, treating it as singular rather than one of many
  • Pale-skinned outsiders (dimbi) have visited Spider Island at least three times before the current party; the Divinity of Two expedition, whose dead were found at the south wall, does not account for all three of those visits; one or more prior groups predate the church expedition — consistent with Captain Maynard's voyage
  • The two-striped Divinity of Two sash was not recognised by Leela as belonging to any of the three visits she knew of, suggesting the church came a separate, additional time
  • An island to the east/northeast (Chba) is inhabited by people who are dangerous; Leela used the word for cannibal and warned emphatically against going there
  • Leela indicated that the Wazari would want weapons above all else in any trade with the party, rather than cloth, drink, or trinkets; asked where the island's gold came from, she only gestured vaguely further inland
  • Fto = water; ilant = land; mondo = black; hempa = magic-user; anto = later, future, or not yet — used by Leela both when asked if she had magic herself and when asked whether she wished to return home; font, heard when Leela was asked what the Wazari would trade for, remains unclear but seems to mean something like weapons, war, or fight (Islander vocabulary additions)
  • The approaching three-masted vessel appeared to round the island toward the east; it did not follow the Amada west; whether it is the same ship the party had previously observed tracking toward Spider Island remains unconfirmed
  • Once clear of Spider Island's coast, Mani felt a second, fainter pull for the first time — distinct from and much weaker than the familiar sensation behind them, and coming from somewhere ahead of the Amada to the west; he described the two side by side as a whisper against a voice talking
  • Mani's ability to sense the Earth Totem through his Medallion was confirmed again: the sensation was directional (behind them, back toward Spider Island) and cut off instantaneously at the moment of the Shatters — implying the Totem was destroyed in that event
  • Recalling what they had already pieced together about the Great Change — that it began when a Censure consumed a Diad to destroy a Totem of Air — the party suspected the flash on the horizon was the same ritual repeated on the Earth Totem, this time by whoever the Divinity of Two had sent to Spider Island
  • The Shatters produced new land formations radiating in linear patterns outward from Spider Island's direction; some of these rock spurs remain above the waterline; the pattern suggests a violent upwelling of material from deep beneath the seabed
  • All party members' Medallions grew noticeably hot immediately following the Shatters event; what this signifies was not established before the session ended

docs.text:
• Two beeta hintu (mid-sized giant spiders), captured alive in sealed crates
  • Raw spider silk gathered from coastal webs (volume: approximately three hours' work by a shore party; to be processed into rope aboard the Amada)
  • Coconuts and fresh provisions gathered at the coast
  • Water supplies replenished at the river before departure

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text:
• One carbine, given to Leela as a gift
  • One longboat, cached on the island's south coast (hidden in the jungle edge, gear buried beneath it; left as a resource if the party returns)

docs.title: The Shatters and a New Shore
Events and Actions
docs.text:
Two days after fleeing Spider Island and the vessel of the Divinity of Two, Mani's sense of the totem shifted, suddenly detectable only ahead of the ship rather than behind. Moments later the party saw a brilliant flash on the horizon behind them, followed by a distant sound like thousands of voices screaming rolling across the water, and then a wave of land erupted from the sea, speeding towards the Amada like jagged lightning and leaving a treacherous new seascape of rock pinnacles in its wake. As it passed over and through the ship, panic took hold — Captain De Guzman fought to slow the Amada as best he could while everyone clung to whatever was fixed, young Werner among them, wrapped around the mast and crying out until it subsided. In the aftermath, the party discovered their magical medallions had gone hot and each had lost a piece; Noddy found that pressing his own invisible medallion into his palm revealed its new outline, worn away like a coin bitten at the edge.

Fearing the cataclysm might send a tsunami like the one that had destroyed Old Port, the party kept watch from the crow's nest for land to shelter behind, but none of substance was in sight and no wave ever came. Once the danger passed, Noddy teleported onto one of the nearby rock spurs to investigate it directly. The spur ran for about a hundred feet but was barely three feet wide in places, undulating along its length with the odd gap he had to hop across; he found freshly broken, jagged stone and wet sand with small tide pools and a few stranded fish, but no plant life at all, before teleporting back to the ship unseen by the rest of the crew.

They concluded that the Divinity of Two had destroyed the totem, causing a cataclysm similar to the Great Change, an event they now call "The Shatters." Deciding it was too dangerous to turn back, they continued west, navigating slowly through the hazardous new terrain; a long navigation roll by Noddy, cross-checked against Captain De Guzman's own plotting, put them roughly 336 miles from Spider Island, ruling out an ordinary gunpowder explosion as the source of the flash. Before getting properly underway, Randolph the Chronicler pressed the party for more detail on the mangani and giant spiders of Spider Island so he could sketch them for his records, and continued piecing together a map of their travels from what they told him; asked in passing how Old Port had originally fallen, he could only say that the poor of its Cliff Town had likely undermined the cliff face with their tunnelling until it gave way one day, with no single triggering event known to him. To keep the Amada itself out of danger, the party sent the longboat well ahead as a scout, taking soundings and working the sails themselves, so the ship would have room to react if the smaller boat ran into trouble. They spent the better part of a week working free of the rock field this way, sailing at half speed and covering roughly 500 miles in total as the pinnacles grew sparser and more scattered the farther they travelled.

As provisions ran low, Captain De Guzman gathered the party to explain, reluctantly, that he intended to cut rations for the crew's sake unless they could find more food. Noddy sent his familiar, Pocket, ranging far out over the water in response, and the mission paid off when Pocket spotted a giant bird perched on a rock outcrop, dipping into the water for fish and seals. The party closed to firing range and engaged it with grape shot from the Amada's two cannons; the first shot went wide, but the second, fired by Mani, struck the bird's foot and severed a toe. The wounded bird screeched, scattering the smaller birds around it, and took to the air before flying off to the northwest — Cosimo wondered aloud whether it might be intelligent enough to be wary of them now. Leela, asked if she recognized the species, did not; nothing like it lived on Spider Island as far as she knew. With the bird gone, the party moved in on the fish shoal it had been hunting, sharing the water with a couple of unconcerned sharks; Noddy boiled the top layer of the sea with his Evaporate Liquid spell to stun a large catch of bream, sardines, grouper, and other smaller fish for easy collection, while Batu Batu organized drying racks to preserve it. The haul replenished the ship's food stores, though the party remained low on fresh water.

With fresh water running low, the party turned the ship northwest for a day chasing the bird's likely course in search of land, but sighted nothing and turned back onto their original heading. The detour proved useful: successful navigation rolls from Noddy and Werner let them triangulate against the angle to the totem Mani could still sense, suggesting land was only three or four days away. Rationing continued as they pressed on, until Pocket, ranging far ahead and above the ship, spotted haze on the horizon that turned out to be land. They soon made landfall at a wide river delta on a large, sandy landmass that at first looked like nothing but bare, featureless dunes cut by channels of fresh water breaking through to the sea; they spent half a day refilling the ship's water casks before exploring upriver in their longboat.

Before setting off upriver, they swapped anything too obviously military for plainer clothes, mounted a swivel gun on the longboat, and packed a small keg of powder and shot alongside a few days' food and some rum to trade with. They encountered a lone Islander, Fontra, at a small hut on a river island, who mistook them for the southern ship that had visited six months earlier to trade guns; his simple, woven, off-white tunic marked him as more sophisticated in dress than Leela's people, who wore mostly animal skins. Batu Batu was able to communicate with him and learned that a Southerner named Watkin had been left behind to manage the trade. The party decided to pose as a second, unaffiliated merchant ship — borrowing the name Green Gull from a captured southern vessel — and retrieved a crate of muskets and a little powder from the Amada before heading back upriver. Fontra set off on foot to warn Watkin, and though the party's longboat easily overtook him along the way, he caught up with them again, breathless, not long after they arrived. As they travelled upriver, with Leela among them, they passed grazing, horned, ox-like beasts and long-tailed reptilian creatures with wide, tooth-filled mouths basking at the water's edge, along with one distinctive, tall, drooping tree hung with clusters of large yellow flowers that neither Leela nor anyone else in the party could identify, then reached a large, newly built gate spanning the entire river, opened inward by around ten islanders hauling on ropes with the help of one of the ox-like beasts. Beyond the gate the river widened into a broad, fertile valley thick with agriculture, reed-built structures, and canoe traffic — clear signs of a sophisticated Islander settlement far larger than Fontra's lone outpost.

Passing through the gate, the party continued to a small compound within the settlement. There they found Watkin, a large Southerner in fine, poofy-trousered dress and a floppy hat, dozing in a hammock on the porch beside a small table and fan. Riu and Mani introduced themselves, startling him into shouting for help twice before Riu could cast a spell to muffle the sound beyond a ten-foot radius; the warning still carried, and two armed southern soldiers came running to his aid.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Fontra: A young, slightly-built Islander dressed in a simple woven tunic, who lived alone in a hut on a small river island near the delta. He mistook the party for the southern ship that had traded with his people six months earlier, and set off on foot to warn Watkin of their arrival.
  • Watkin: A Southerner left behind on the island to facilitate trade with the Islanders. The party found him dozing in a hammock on the porch of a small compound, dressed in fine, poofy-trousered southern style; he was badly startled by their approach.
  • Southern Soldiers: Two armed men who came running to Watkin's aid when he called out.
  • Giant Bird: A massive bird-like creature found perched on a rock outcrop in The Shatters, feeding on fish and seals. It fled northwest after the party's cannon fire severed one of its toes; Cosimo speculated it might be intelligent enough to be wary of them now.
  • Pocket: Noddy's seagull familiar, sent ranging far ahead of the ship first to search for food and later for signs of land; his sighting of haze on the horizon gave the party their first glimpse of the new landmass.
  • Fred and Wilma: The party's own two giant spiders, taken alive from Spider Island. With that island now destroyed, the party speculated they might be the only giant spiders left anywhere in the world.
  • Randolph the Chronicler: Pressed the party for a fuller description of the mangani and giant spiders of Spider Island so he could sketch them for his records, and continued building a map of the party's travels from their accounts.
  • Creatures: The party observed various new creatures along the river, including large, horned, ox-like beasts — one of which was used by the islanders to help haul open the river gate — aggressive, long-tailed reptilian creatures with wide, tooth-filled mouths that swam and waddled along the banks, and a pair of ordinary-sized sharks that showed no interest in them while they gathered fish.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Shatters: A vast, dangerous new seascape created by the cataclysmic destruction of the totem on Spider Island, characterized by thousands of sharp, freshly-broken rocky pinnacles that erupted from the ocean floor in roughly straight lines, rising nearly sheer from deep water; one spur Noddy explored ran about a hundred feet long but was barely three feet wide in places. The formations grew sparser the farther the party sailed from Spider Island.
  • Isle of Sands: The party's name for the new landmass they discovered. Its coast first appeared as bare, featureless dunes cut by channels of fresh water, but a wide river delta led inland to a fertile valley thick with agriculture, reed-built structures, worked metal tools, and canoe traffic. Past a newly built defensive gate spanning the whole river — manned by some fifty or sixty islanders working construction and dozens more standing armed guard, mostly with bows and clubs and only the rare musket — the party found a large and comparatively sophisticated Islander population.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text: • The party engaged a giant bird found perched on a rock outcrop, hunting fish and seals. They closed to firing range and opened up with grape shot from the Amada's two cannons; the first shot went wide, but the second, fired by Mani, struck the creature's foot and severed a toe, sending it screeching into the air, scattering the smaller birds around it, and off to the northwest rather than pressing an attack.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The party concluded that the Divinity of Two destroyed the totem on Spider Island using a Diad, triggering the cataclysm that formed "The Shatters."
  • The destruction of the totem caused a piece of each of their medallions to break off, diminishing their power.
  • Noddy realized he can sense and manipulate the medallions differently than everyone else — he alone can remove one from another person's neck. Mani recalled that he once did just that to Stick Stab, now aligned with the Divinity of Two, and later placed that medallion on the prisoner Hans; he wondered aloud whether Hans, wherever he is, felt this same change, and whether the enemy could sense it too.
  • Fearing a tsunami like the one that destroyed Old Port might follow the flash, the party kept watch from the crow's nest, but none came.
  • Cosimo revealed he had successfully attuned to the Diad recovered from the dead cleric's boats on Spider Island; along with a boost to his own power, he can now sense that a powerful spell of unknown nature is bound up within it, and hypothesized that this may be the very spell responsible for the cataclysm they had just witnessed.
  • The party theorized that a Diad had been used against a Totem in the same way roughly 40 years earlier, and that this earlier destruction was what caused the Great Change; "The Shatters" appears to be a repeat of that same act, possibly tied to renewed activity by the Church of the Two provoked by the Southern Wind Witches.
  • Rereading the scrap of paper recovered earlier, the party found a line describing the original expedition as unable to return through the Maelstrom "without the aid of the heretic" — a mysterious figure connected to whatever happened forty years ago whom they still cannot identify.
  • Cosimo suspected the black totems are the "bones of the world," conferring special abilities on those who dwell near them, and that a faction within the Church of the Two regards them as a threat — possibly unaware that destroying them is unraveling the world's magic.
  • The party reasoned the first Southern mission to Spider Island had likely run out of priests and Diads fighting through the island's mangani and Islander defenders, making it something of a suicide mission, and concluded that pursuit by the enemy ship was unlikely given how much time and manpower such an assault would have cost it.
  • Debating what to do if the Divinity of Two's ship reappeared, the party weighed fighting it outright — still galled that so powerful a warship stood apart from the war effort — against the reality that it was a triple-decked ship of the line badly outgunning the Amada's four cannons; they settled on staying ahead of it and out of sight rather than risking an engagement.
  • Riu argued that the ship's destruction of Spider Island so soon after the party's own departure was likely coincidence rather than pursuit: the two vessels had simply been converging on the island independently ever since the Amada outran the other ship in the Maelstrom weeks earlier.
  • A limited amount of fresh water can be extracted from fish, from the flesh near the spine and around the eyes, though not enough to meaningfully offset a real shortage.
  • Knick Nab explained that southern ships are typically named with a colour paired with a creature, such as the Green Gull, the Red Robin, or the Blue Lagoon, and that the Amada itself has something of a reputation among southerners — some know it by name, or as "the ghost ship" — which shaped the party's decision to invent an alias rather than sail in under her own.
  • The new landmass is inhabited by a sophisticated Islander society that practices agriculture and is building significant defenses.
  • Southerners have made contact with these Islanders and are trading guns for a "yellow food." A Southerner named Watkin is on the island overseeing this arrangement.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• A large quantity of fish, stunned in bulk with Noddy's Evaporate Liquid spell and dried on racks by Batu Batu, replenishing the ship's food supplies.
  • A full supply of fresh water from the river.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • A piece of each party member's Medallion was lost during the cataclysm, resulting in a tangible weakening of the items' power.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
The party confronted the Southerner, who introduced himself as Mathias Monadero, principal agent for the Southern Federation's trade on the island. Mani took the lead, spinning a cover story — that they were smugglers aboard the "Green Gull," running goods between the Channel Islands, the North, and the South — and lending it credibility with his genuine knowledge of his family's smuggling trade. Asked his name, Mani nearly undid his own ruse, blurting out his real name before catching himself and passing it off as an alias; Monadero thought nothing more of it and simply took to calling him "Manny." Pressed on how they had weathered "The Shatters," they described a flash of light and land bursting from the sea some three weeks past, and mentioned a recent island of hostile giant spiders where they had picked up a new companion, taking care not to mention that Leela had stayed behind aboard the Amada; as proof, they produced a spider's fang and the claw of the giant panther they had killed there. Monadero recalled the actual Green Gull as a three-master rather than the party's sloop, a discrepancy he let pass without comment. Monadero accepted the story, and after he produced a ledger and pressed the party to sign or mark their names as formal conscripts into the Southern Army, they talked their way into a mercenary contract instead, agreeing to help defend the settlement in exchange for supplies and the promise of trade.

Monadero revealed he was awaiting a resupply ship, now several weeks overdue, likely delayed by the cataclysm the party described as "The Shatters." He explained that the local Islanders are peaceful farmers who are periodically extorted for tribute — food, and women — by "Stone Men," desert raiders who ride large, hump-backed animals the party took to calling camels; a raiding band of roughly a dozen had been driven off weeks earlier when Monadero and his two soldiers, Lang and Fritz, opened fire on them, the first resistance the raiders had ever met. In exchange for the party's eight muskets, Monadero set Fritz to arming and training a handful of villagers, while Lang was assigned to guide the party on a tour of the settlement.

A tour of the area revealed a large, agricultural settlement stretching along the river valley, with a central village of huts built on stilts on both banks of the river, joined by a single bridge. Away from that bridge, locals crossed the river routinely in small reed boats poled back and forth without question, a convenience the party made use of themselves. The party's main interest was the "finger fruit" that the Southerners were trading for, which grows on trees violently carnivorous to anything that ventures beneath their canopy; Lang confirmed the orchards were dangerous but claimed not to know why, only that the villagers approached them with fire and smoke. At an isolated tree across the river near the desert's edge, Riu examined the multi-trunked growth — its wood, though plentiful, appeared nowhere in the village's construction — and noted the fruit hung the opposite way up from a normal banana; nearby, scattered bones and the sun-bleached skull of some large, unidentified animal hinted at previous kills. A rock moved telekinetically under the canopy drew no reaction, and a first attempt by Noddy to cast Sleep on the tree beforehand did nothing either, so Knick Nab stepped beneath it himself, shielded by Cosimo's illusion and covered by Riu ready to parry; a bunch of fruit whipped down on its vine like a striking limb, hissing and splitting open to reveal rows of pale, faintly glowing, tooth-lined "fingers," gouging a trench in the earth as it retracted after Knick Nab dodged clear. A second attempt by Noddy to put the tree itself to sleep afterward also failed. Beyond the tree, the party got their first close look at the open desert — a vast, wind-carved expanse of dunes running to the horizon, matching old sailors' tales of a southern hinterland called the Sands, said to hide a great city deep within where trade is struck with some unknown and mysterious people. Riu resolved to keep a small pouch of sand from every new island the party visited from now on, starting here.

The following day, the party watched the Islanders harvest the grove properly. Farmers piled bundles of a small, gnarled root around — never beneath — the canopy, set them alight, and pushed the smoldering bundles under the trees with long-handled tools until thick smoke enveloped the whole grove; only then did harvesters creep in with sharpened sticks to knock down some of the fruit, deliberately leaving the rest of each bunch untouched. Riu recognized the root as very similar to Bitterroot, and Batu Batu's translation confirmed with a farmer that it came from "beyond the wetlands," further upriver, and that the village had none to spare — it was too valuable. Knick Nab, whose old reliance on Bitterroot for pain relief had finally eased over the long weeks since their crossing, was nonetheless keen to gather and dry a supply of this new root for the party's own future use, given its apparent similarity.

Returning to Monadero, the party learned a crucial piece of intelligence: the South's powerful weather-manipulating "Navigators" are Islanders whose homeland was destroyed by the Divinity of Two during The Great Change, 40 years prior, and who now assist the South purely out of a desire for revenge against the North. Monadero seemed genuinely puzzled by the idea that this ability could simply be taught, suggesting it is innate rather than a trained skill, and confirmed the Navigators look like ordinary Islanders — ruling out any connection to the small, pale, hostile people the party had clashed with on the Channel Islands, a group Monadero had never heard of. He also mentioned, unprompted, a grove of enormous trees his ship had once passed growing straight out of the open sea, though it had not been their destination and they had not stopped to investigate. Wanting to keep him talkative, Noddy reached for a subtler working — a second-level charm from his Closed Essence repertoire that left its target believing the caster a good friend — and Monadero grew unaccountably friendly, producing a bottle of Brandy and sharing it from his own proper stemmed glass — one of several personal touches, along with an ornately carved folding camp table and chair, that had plainly travelled with him from the mainland and marked him as considerably more refined than his two soldiers. With that goodwill secured, Pocket flew a survey of the valley for the party, revealing the river — which Monadero's people called the Uron — winding down past extensive cultivated fields and further orchards upriver, before the land gave way entirely to empty desert with no cover for an approaching force. Weighing a mobile response, using the Longboat, the ship's swivel gun, and the elevated stilt-huts as firing positions, against a fixed one, the party settled on trying to lure the raiders into a prepared kill zone with a false offering of fruit, illusions to steer them, and hidden pits, falling back on reacting to wherever the Raiders actually appeared if the ruse failed. They also weighed stripping the removable ramps that gave access to the stilt village from the northern bank, and noted that anyone posted at the desert's edge held higher ground than the settlement below — an advantage that would vanish the moment any attacker crested the rim and dropped down into the valley, out of sight of the huts. Questioning Monadero further, they learned the raiders always announce themselves with a horn and expect an unopposed handover at midday, though whether they could travel and strike at night was unknown.

Before settling in for the night, the party asked Monadero about the fortified gate they had passed through, spanning the river partway downstream of the settlement; he explained he had built it himself from the ship's own supplies purely out of fear of an attack from the sea, well before he knew anything of the Stone Men or their raids. Overnight, the party heard a large gathering of villagers chanting and singing to the moon and stars; asked whether her own people did the same, Leela — travelling with them but still kept out of Monadero's sight — confirmed it, explaining simply that the night is full of danger. Batu Batu questioned one of the few villagers not singing and came away less certain, guessing it was some form of prayer or worship directed at the moon and stars, but nothing else stirred that night, though the party spared a wary thought for the giant bird whose toe they had shot off on a previous island. The next day, after watching the harvest, the party sailed the Longboat back to the Amada to brief Captain De Guzman, bringing a finger fruit for Randolph the Chronicler to sketch and inviting the Chronicler himself into the cabin for the briefing, with Werner posted outside the door to keep it private. They found the crew had kept busy fishing and making repairs, including producing silk rope using the technique Cosimo had taught them before they left. Relaying what they had learned of the Navigators and the overdue resupply ship, the party reasoned that even in ideal conditions a Southern voyage from the mainland would take two to four months, pointing to a closer Southern outpost somewhere nearer at hand.

Warned that a Southern ship might appear at any time, De Guzman had the crew called to readiness with the ship's bell, and admitted he was tempted to attack anything of comparable size that showed itself; the party talked him down, arguing that intelligence on the Navigators mattered more than sinking one ship. De Guzman briefly weighed flying southern colours and papers to pass the Amada off as a second "Green Gull," but judged he couldn't make the ruse convincing enough to risk it. He agreed instead that the Amada would relocate down the coast, leave a hidden marker with a message, and quietly leave someone behind to watch the delta and report back — while the party returned to the Islander settlement to continue their mission and maintain their cover, careful, in the retelling, never to use De Guzman's own name in front of the Southerners. Randolph, delighted by the finger fruit and eager to see more of the island's strange life for himself, was invited to accompany them back.

Before heading back, they arranged an experiment to learn exactly how many person-days of food a single finger fruit represented: the Islanders would log how far one fruit stretched feeding the ship's crew, while Riu set aside a fruit to ration for himself and track how long it sustained him. They were provided with quarters and a small supply of the highly nutritious finger fruit, along with a jug of water.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Mathias Monadero: A "Major Domo" and trade agent for the Southern Federation, stationed on the Isle of Sands. His personal effects — an ornately carved folding camp table and chair, and proper stemmed glassware for his Brandy — had travelled with him from the mainland and marked him as considerably more refined than his two soldiers.
  • Lang and Fritz: Two Southern soldiers serving under Monadero. Lang guided the party's tour of the settlement; Fritz was set to arming and training villagers with the party's muskets.
  • Islanders: The peaceful, agricultural inhabitants of the Isle of Sands, said by Monadero to be led by both a man and a woman, though the party has not yet met either of them.
  • Stone Men: Also called Desert Raiders. A group of hostile Islanders who raid the settlement for tribute. They were discussed but not encountered.
  • Carnivorous "Finger Fruit" Trees: The source of the valuable finger fruit. The trees attack any creature that enters their canopy, striking with a bunch of fruit that splits open to reveal rows of pale, faintly glowing, tooth-lined "fingers"; bones and an unidentified animal's skull found beneath one attest to past kills. They can be safely harvested only after being pacified with the smoke of a root similar to Bitterroot. Despite the trees' plentiful, multi-trunked wood, none of it appeared to be used anywhere in the settlement's construction.
  • Batu Batu: The party's Islander cook, who translated between the party and the Isle of Sands villagers throughout the visit.
  • Captain De Guzman: Captain of the Amada, briefed on the party's findings and the overdue Southern resupply ship; tempted to attack any Southern ship that appeared, he briefly weighed disguising the Amada under southern colours as a second "Green Gull" before deciding the ruse was too risky, and was talked down by the party into agreeing the ship would relocate down the coast, leaving a hidden marker and a watcher behind, rather than risk engaging a Southern warship.
  • Randolph the Chronicler: Aboard the Amada, he pored over the finger fruit the party brought back, filling one notebook with observations and another with sketches, and eagerly accepted the party's invitation to see the island's strange life for himself.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Isle of Sands: The party explored the agricultural settlement along the river Uron's valley, observing the central village of stilted huts spanning both riverbanks — joined by a single bridge — and the dangerous orchards of finger fruit trees. Elsewhere along the river, locals crossed by small reed boats poled back and forth for anyone waiting. The hut given to the party for their stay stood near the settlement's outer wall and entrance, well short of the true village center and the bulk of its cultivated fields, both further upriver. An aerial survey by Pocket showed further fields and orchards upriver before the land gave way to open desert.
  • The Sands: Standing at the edge of the desert beyond the river valley for the first time, the party got a close look at the wind-carved dune country stretching to the horizon — matching old sailors' tales of a southern hinterland by that name, said to conceal, deep within, a great city where trade is struck with some unknown and mysterious people.
  • The Amada: The party briefed Captain De Guzman and Randolph the Chronicler aboard ship before returning to the Isle of Sands.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The party engaged in a tense negotiation with Mathias Monadero, talking their way out of formal conscription into the Southern Army and into a mercenary contract instead.
  • Knick Nab deliberately provoked an attack from an isolated finger fruit tree — after a thrown rock and a first attempt by Noddy to sleep the tree drew no response — and, shielded by Cosimo's illusion and Riu's readiness to parry, dodged clear as a bunch of fruit whipped down and split open to reveal teeth, gouging the earth where he had stood. A second attempt by Noddy to sleep the tree afterward also failed.
  • Aboard the Amada, Captain De Guzman was tempted to attack any Southern ship of comparable size that appeared and briefly weighed disguising his own ship as a second "Green Gull" to avoid suspicion, but the party talked him into holding off outright, arguing that intelligence on the Navigators mattered more than sinking one ship.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
