• The South is trading muskets for "finger fruit," a highly nutritious food that can sustain a person for a full day with just a small slice.
  • A Southern resupply ship is weeks overdue, likely due to The Shatters. Reasoning from their own crossing, the party judged that even a fair-weather Southern voyage from the mainland would take two to four months, suggesting the South keeps a closer outpost somewhere nearer at hand.
  • The finger fruit grows on carnivorous trees, harvested by piling bundles of a root much like Bitterroot around — never under — a grove, burning it, and pushing the smoldering bundles beneath the canopy until heavy smoke subdues the trees enough to approach; even then, harvesters take only some of each bunch. The root itself comes from "beyond the wetlands" further upriver, and the village keeps none to spare. Riu noted that, despite the trees' abundant wood, none of it seemed to be used anywhere in the settlement's construction.
  • The South's "Navigators" (weather mages) are Islanders who hate the North because the Divinity of Two destroyed their homeland during the event known as The Great Change. Monadero seemed genuinely puzzled that an outsider might simply learn the ability, suggesting it is innate rather than trained, and confirmed Navigators look like ordinary Islanders — ruling out any link to the small, pale, hostile people the party had clashed with on the Channel Islands. Monadero also mentioned a grove of immense trees growing straight out of the open sea that his ship had passed but never investigated.
  • The peaceful Islanders are preyed upon by "Stone Men," raiders from the surrounding desert who ride camel-like beasts.
  • Villagers gather at night to sing and chant to the moon and stars; Leela confirmed her own people do the same, calling the night full of danger, though Batu Batu's questioning of a villager suggested it might instead be a form of prayer or worship of the moon and stars.
  • The Amada's crew produced silk rope in the party's absence, using the technique Cosimo had taught them before they left.
  • The stilt village sits lower than the desert's rim, giving anyone posted at the edge the high ground — though attackers would lose that edge, and vanish from the huts' sight, the moment they crested it and dropped into the valley. The party considered stripping the removable ramps that give the stilt huts access from the northern bank, to deny the Raiders an easy approach.
  • The fortified gate the party passed through downstream of the settlement was built by Monadero himself, using the ship's own supplies, purely out of fear of an attack from the sea — well before he knew anything of the Stone Men or their raids.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text: • A bowl containing approximately ten "finger fruits" and a jug of water were provided to the party in their quarters — by the party's own rough reckoning enough to feed their whole crew for roughly six months, pending the results of Riu's more careful rationing experiment.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • Nothing of note was lost.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
With the Southern trade agent's warning in mind, the party spent the following days fortifying the stilted core of the Islander village. One building doubled as a musket nest for Knick Nab and Cosimo's own position, reachable only by a ladder that could be hauled up to deny access from below. Cosimo used his rigging skill to string ropes off the main building in each cardinal direction and out to trees on the far banks, giving anyone up top a fast way to swing or slide down toward whichever bank the raiders approached from; with no pulleys to be found, the party settled on riding the lines down with a musket barrel or another curved handhold rather than bare rope or cloth, reasoning that anything flat would burn through or slip. Knick Nab organized six Islander volunteers, newly drilled on musket use, splitting them between two buildings flanking the central plaza so they could fire out from cover on either side. The ship's boat, mounted with its swivel gun and crewed by Werner, Salter, and Batu Batu, was anchored in the river channel to cover both banks, and Mathias Monadero, the Southern trade agent acting as the village's Major Domo, committed his two soldiers, Fritz and Lang, to the defense under Knick Nab's command.

While the party waited, Leela grew restless and left with a group of Islanders travelling upriver to harvest root near a swampy area three or four days away. Riu spent the same idle days playing amateur chronicler, gathering plant specimens and quietly asking around after mutated children or religious customs that might echo the mother-and-father cult, much as he had on the previous island, though nothing of note turned up. Leela's group had barely begun harvesting when raiders emerged from the desert on strange antlered, camel-like beasts, wrapped head to toe in pale robes and turbans, and crossed toward the party's side of the river; the Islanders scattered and fled. About a week into the party's watch, Leela came sprinting down the north road, breathless and shaken, having run for days to warn that the "Stone Men" had crossed the river and were coming. Riu suggested guarding against fire arrows, and the party had the villagers lay in torches — kept well clear of the tinder-dry finger-fruit trees — a standing bonfire, and buckets of water at the ready, including a bucket on a rope they could lower straight into the river for a quick refill.

Riu spent the following day taking repeated turns levitating a hundred feet into the air to scan the desert, while Knick Nab trekked out to the top of successive dunes on foot and came back convinced the open desert was as flat, featureless, and disorienting as the open ocean, easy to get lost in without landmarks or a compass. Late in the day, near sunset, Riu spotted a distant dust cloud to the southwest. The party settled in for what they assumed would be a night assault, but the night passed without incident.

The attack came the next morning. Pocket, aloft on Noddy's orders, confirmed three approaching groups: raiders coming straight down the river valley, and two more flanking groups cresting the desert ridge on the north and south banks, invisible to anyone below the crest. Faint horn calls passed between the three groups as they closed, confirming a coordinated advance rather than any intent to parley; recognizing that opening a dialogue would only give the flanking riders time to close unchallenged, the party chose to let their muskets answer instead. Knick Nab held the trained Islander riflemen's fire until the lead group of four riders closed to effective range. Their opening volley snapped the lead rider's reins and tore open his hand, and in the same moment Cosimo loosed a blinding flash of light that stunned all four riders and their mounts at once. Mani followed with a shot that opened an artery in a second rider's collarbone, killing him outright, while the other two mounts bolted in confusion, their charge broken before it began.

As the flanking riders reached the village and dismounted, the untrained villagers scattered rather than hold their ground, and the fight turned into a running melee around the huts and stairways. Not every defender held: on one bank, several of Knick Nab's own riflemen broke and dove for the river rather than face the raiders bearing down on them, and two who couldn't get clear in time were cut down where they stood, one gashed across the leg and the other stabbed through the thigh badly enough to leave him barely able to walk. Riu spent much of the battle as Mani's loader, keeping spare muskets primed and swapping them into Mani's hands so he could fire almost every round instead of stopping to reload himself. Cosimo summoned Handsome Gulliver Gold, a phantasmal warrior in a turban with a jeweled feather and a scimitar, who burst from the sand behind two raiders closing on Knick Nab and Leela with a cry of "no one expects Handsome Gulliver Gold," disarmed one with a slash to the wrist, and later vaulted onto a hut roof to flourish his blade at the retreating enemy, a gold stud glinting in his tooth as he grinned. Knick Nab swept an attacker off his feet in melee, leaving him unconscious, while Leela cut a bloody path with her axe, opening a fatal wound in one attacker's thigh, finishing off a second who had already gone down, and shattering the kneecap of a third. When a raider slipped close to Mathias Monadero, Fritz and Lang shot him down at point-blank range.

With most of the raiders dead, unconscious, or scattered, the last rider bolted for the open desert on his camel; Knick Nab lassoed him off the animal with Cosimo's spare rope before he could escape. In the end the party had killed several raiders outright and taken three alive — one relatively unharmed, one with a shattered kneecap, and one with a badly broken hand — along with eight of the raiders' twelve camels, the rest having escaped or scattered too far to bother chasing. Riu used his medicine skill to stabilize the two badly injured prisoners, setting bones that would otherwise have crippled them for life, so all three could be questioned. The party stripped the dead and the captured raiders of their weapons and gear and settled in to plan the interrogation.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Stone Men: The desert raiders who attacked the village, wrapped head to toe in pale robes and turbans and mounted on strange antlered, camel-like beasts. They are named for their reputation as stoneworkers. Armed with spears, scimitars, and bows, they were routed with several killed and three captured.
  • Leela: Left the village to help gather root upriver, was nearly caught when the raiders first crossed the river, and ran for days to warn the village. She fought alongside the party in the battle, cutting down or crippling three raiders with her axe.
  • Camels: The large, four-legged beasts used as mounts by the Stone Men. The party captured eight of the twelve they encountered.
  • Handsome Gulliver Gold: Cosimo's phantasmal warrior, manifested in a turban with a jeweled feather and a scimitar. He burst from the sand announcing himself, disarmed a raider engaging Knick Nab, and later postured triumphantly atop a hut roof.
  • Werner, Salter, and Batu Batu: Crewed the ship's boat and its swivel gun in the river channel throughout the battle, standing ready to fire though the fighting was decided before they were called on.
  • Mathias Monadero: The Southern trade agent acting as the village's Major Domo. He committed his two soldiers, Fritz and Lang, to the defense under Knick Nab's command.
  • Fritz and Lang: Monadero's two Southern soldiers, who fought in the defense of the village and shot down a raider who slipped in close to him.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Islander Village (Isle of Sands): The stilted village where the party organized the defense and fought off the raid.
  • The root-harvesting grounds: A swampy area three or four days upriver where Leela's group was ambushed. Beyond it lies a wilder stretch of river surrounded by untended finger-fruit forest that the Islanders never visit and that the party suspects is the Stone Men's point of origin.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The primary conflict was the large-scale, three-pronged battle against the Stone Men, who approached down the river valley and along both banks of the desert.
  • Reading the raiders' own coordinating horn calls as a sign they meant to fight rather than parley, the party chose to let their muskets speak first rather than risk giving the flanking groups time to close.
  • The party broke the raiders' charge with a coordinated musket volley and a blinding flash of light from Cosimo before the melee even began.
  • Key moments included Mani's fatal collarbone shot, Leela's brutal effectiveness against three separate raiders, Knick Nab's unarmed sweep, and the repeated interventions of "Handsome Gulliver Gold."
  • Fritz and Lang killed a raider who slipped close to Mathias Monadero, and Knick Nab personally lassoed the last fleeing rider off his camel to take him alive.
  • Two of Knick Nab's riflemen broke and fled for the river when raiders closed on them and were wounded before help arrived; Riu treated them, then later stabilized the surviving prisoners' injuries as well.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The party learned more about the local geography and fauna from the villagers, including the existence of a dangerous, wild finger-fruit forest far upriver believed to be the Stone Men's origin, and the nature of the large, domesticated "cow things," which are used mainly for labor and can cross the open desert.
  • They learned that the raiders are called "Stone Men" because they are said to build with stone.
  • The party discovered that the desert is vast, featureless, and navigationally challenging, similar to the open ocean. They also learned that the blowing sand is extremely harsh on firearms, requiring them to be cleaned after exposure.
  • The villagers described their reliance on reed cultivation for construction, a flax-like crop for linen thread, and rice and other grains grown in flood-irrigated fields, along with fishing in both the river and the open ocean, all supplemented by finger fruit when the river runs low. They also make a potent finger-fruit wine, which Cosimo sampled.
  • Asking about "weather witches" turned up no local magic practitioners and no concept of controlling weather; the villagers' entire sense of environmental change centers on the river's rise and fall. The party deliberately avoided asking about the "big black stones" in front of the Southerners, wary of revealing what they know of the old magic.
  • Despite having more material technology than other Islanders the party has met, the villagers keep a notably weak oral tradition — no one could say how long their people had lived in the valley, only that they always had.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• 8 Camels: The party successfully captured eight of the raiders' twelve mounts.
  • Weapons recovered from the dead and captured raiders, including shields, crude but unfamiliar curved scimitars, spears, and composite bows. Knick Nab kept the best of the scimitars — a thick, crudely made blade of an unfamiliar cutlass-like style — meaning to practice with it.
  • Simple twisted-copper rings of no real value, along with the raiders' empty sacks, baskets, and cordage — apparently brought to carry off loot — and a supply of dried fruit provisions.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • Nothing of note was lost.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
Following their successful defense of the Islander village, the party set about interrogating the three captured Stone Men raiders. Unable to tell the identical, wrapped prisoners apart, they settled the matter by "scientific method," choosing whichever one had the most facial hair to question first. Noddy cast Charm Kind on him, and once the spell took hold the prisoner grew cooperative, answering questions through Batu Batu's translation. Early in the questioning, Noddy's own uncanny perception caught something the rest of the party missed entirely: beneath the man's wrappings, his ears were subtly elongated, echoing Knick Nab's own hidden shape. The observation stirred an unbidden, unexplained memory in Noddy — a flash of the deepest ruins of Cliff Town, of places down in the sewers he had never dared explore, though he could not say why they came to mind now.

Through the questioning, the party learned the raiders came from a starving "City of Stone," a twenty-night journey by camel across the desert to the north, traveled only after dark to avoid the worst of the heat. Their homeland's river had dried up many moons past, leaving a people with many workers, leaders, and fighters but no way to grow food; finger fruit and captive laborers were the entire purpose of the raids, taken to feed and build their all-consuming project — a massive stone structure meant to reach and "escape" to the sky, which they worship as the only way to escape death and the desert sands. He described his people's work plainly, cutting stone from cliff and ground with chisel and hammer, and their faith just as plainly: the sky never changes and never goes away, unlike the sands and the river that had betrayed them, so building closer to it was the only escape they could imagine. The prisoner had no knowledge of the black totem stones the party described to him, insisting his people worked only ordinary stone and prized no gold, and could offer nothing beyond crude flint-and-spark fire-making when asked about magic. Doing the math on travel times, the party reckoned that with the first raiding party already some two months overdue delivering food home, any larger, more desperate force the City of Stone might send in response was still fifty to eighty days out.

With this intelligence in hand, the party negotiated with the Southern agent, Mathias Monadero. Acknowledging that his own reinforcements were long overdue and likely lost, Monadero struck a deal: the party would remain to guard the village for two more weeks. If no Southern ship arrived in that time, the party would transport him and his two soldiers, Fritz and Lang, to the nearest Southern port. They also proposed sweeping up and down the river for the one raider who had fled the battle on camelback — a genuine chance to slow any future attack, and a convenient excuse for the trip upriver they were already planning — and Monadero, confident no larger force could arrive for weeks yet, readily agreed it was worth the time. In exchange for the two weeks' protection, Monadero agreed to provision their ship with a substantial supply of finger fruit, offered to keep the three captive raiders guarded and safe with his soldiers while the party was away, and promised to use his influence to arrange introductions that might help them secure a much-needed Navigator, though he was careful to promise nothing beyond the introduction itself. The party further floated chartering their ship for a supply run to the South's nearest outpost, a proposal Monadero welcomed as good business for everyone. He also confirmed that the Southern Federation is a loose alliance of independent, often-rival trading houses that unite only against a common threat, and that unlike the North, the South does not practice slavery.

The party then traveled back to the Amada by longboat to brief Captain De Guzman on the new plan, delivering baskets of finger fruit as promised. De Guzman reported nothing sighted on the horizon; the man he had posted to watch the beach had seen no sign of any ship, Southern or otherwise. The party agreed the crew would present themselves as Southern smugglers, keeping any obviously Northern faces below decks, should Monadero's people ever come aboard — Knick Nab vouched that the ship and crew had worn other guises before and could manage it again — while privately agreeing that if the ruse ever collapsed outright, taking Monadero and his two soldiers prisoner was the fallback. Along the way they passed a handful of giant crocodiles lazing harmlessly on the riverbank, sluggish enough to swim well clear of. They also spoke with the Chronicler, Randolph, who was eager to accompany them inland but agreed to remain behind once the party pointed out that his presence, recognizable to House Ohroh, would compromise their cover; he would take payment instead in notes, trophies, and specimens brought back from the expedition. Randolph mentioned he had already filled several volumes recording the cataclysm the party had described to him weeks earlier, and hoped to find a way to send his account back to the Academy before he ran out of pages — a problem sharpened by the fact that he had left his message pigeons behind and had no way to send word in the meantime. In exchange for their account of the battle, Randolph corrected an old assumption of theirs: his notes on Chronicler Willem's death at Old Port now showed the fatal wound had been a blade strike to the back, not the gunshot to the head they had believed, suggesting the official "plague" record had been deliberately falsified. Pressed on whether the Church had ever moved against a Chronicler for what he knew, Randolph said he was aware of no such case personally, though he pointedly would not say the same of the Academy as a whole; he described his own order's function as simply gathering and conveying information, leaving judgment and analysis of it to the Academy's separate researchers and historians.

Before preparing for their own expedition, the party confirmed their suspicions about the carnivorous finger fruit trees by stripping and feeding one the corpse of a dead raider; the tree slowly dragged the body in over several minutes, the same violent, tooth-lined motion that had nearly caught Knick Nab days before, this time with nothing to fight back. Weighing their options for the trip upriver — sailing, walking, or striking overland through the desert — the party settled on leading their eight captured camels, including one improbably fortunate animal they nicknamed Coins, on foot along the well-worn path Leela described, rather than risk their limited riding skills or leave the boat stranded partway up the river. As night fell, the party pressed the two remaining bound prisoners for practical knowledge of handling and feeding the camels; when one balked at answering, they marched his bound companion toward the same tree as a threat before breaking off to finish planning the journey. The session concluded with the party preparing to use the two-week waiting period to travel upriver, with their captured camels, to locate the totem that Mani could sense.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Stone Man Raider: The eldest of the three captives, questioned first by "scientific method." Charmed into cooperation by Noddy, he revealed his people's origins, desperation, and their goal of building a tower to the sky, along with an unsettling resemblance in his ears to Knick Nab's own.
  • Mathias Monadero: The Southern trade agent from House Ohroh. He negotiated a deal with the party for protection and eventual passage to a Southern port, and confirmed the South's federated structure of rival trading houses.
  • Fritz and Lang: Monadero's two Southern soldiers, who fought alongside the party in the previous battle and stood guard over the prisoners while the party talked amongst themselves.
  • Captain De Guzman: Captain of the Amada, briefed by the party on the new arrangements and the plan to present the ship and crew as Southern smugglers if Monadero's people come aboard. He reported nothing sighted on the horizon from the lookout he had posted on the beach.
  • Randolph the Chronicler: Remained on the ship after acknowledging that his presence would endanger the party's mission, but traded information — including a correction about Chronicler Willem's true cause of death — for the party's continued reports and trophies. He mentioned he had already filled several volumes recording the cataclysm the party witnessed weeks earlier, and was without his message pigeons, having left his rookery behind, leaving him with no way to send word to the Academy for now.
  • Coins: The party's nickname for one of the eight camels taken from the raiders, remembered as improbably fortunate in the previous battle.
  • Giant Crocodiles: A handful of large, sluggish crocodiles seen lazing on the riverbank on the way back to the Amada; harmless enough that the party gave them a wide berth without concern.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Islander Village (Isle of Sands): The site of the interrogation and negotiations.
  • The Amada: The party briefly returned to their ship to deliver supplies and information.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text: • The session's conflicts were social and strategic rather than physical: interrogating a wary prisoner, negotiating delicate terms with Mathias Monadero, and planning a fragile smuggler cover story — one the party quietly agreed to abandon for taking Monadero and his soldiers prisoner if it ever collapsed outright — that would have to hold for weeks. Underlying it all was a genuine rift within the party over where their loyalties lie between North, South, the Church, and the third power tied to their medallions. The session closed on a smaller, sharper edge: a bound prisoner marched toward the finger fruit tree as a threat when he refused to share what he knew of camel handling.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Stone Men come from a large, desperate society a twenty-night journey across the desert, traveling only by night. Their homeland's river dried up long ago, leaving them unable to grow food; their entire society is bent on building a tower to reach the sky they worship as an escape from death, and they showed no knowledge of gold, the totems, or magic beyond simple fire-making.
  • The party held a long debate over where their true loyalties lie. The trigger was that destroying the totems — visibly tied to their own medallions and abilities — seems to tear open the world itself, from tidal waves to land rising from the sea, which felt too violent and too personal to be a neutral act of theology. Weighing evidence that the Church may have silenced witnesses at Old Port and moved against Leela's people, and recalling the secret society opposed to the Church that Major Hubert, Captain Maynard, and Captain Barrows all belonged to — and that Maynard vanished while pursuing this very question — the party concluded they are not necessarily enemies of the North, or even of the two gods themselves, but that the Church of the Divinity of Two must be treated as an active threat — one they will avoid provoking directly, but will not trust if encountered.
  • Randolph revealed that the wound that killed Chronicler Willem at Old Port was a blade strike to the back, not the gunshot to the head recorded in the official account — evidence that his death, and the "plague" explanation given for it, had been covered up.
  • The party learned that the South has at least one established port on this side of the Maelstrom, and that Mathias Monadero belongs to House Ohroh, one of the two largest Southern trading houses — the other, its quartermaster recalled, being House Bax. Unlike the North, the South does not practice slavery.
  • The carnivorous finger fruit trees will consume carrion, not just live prey.
  • Leela informed the party that the path to the area where the root is harvested follows the river's north bank, is used by cart-pulling draft beasts, and is a two-day walk upriver ending in a swampy region where no black stone has been seen.
  • Randolph explained that a Chronicler's function is only to gather and convey information; judging or analyzing it falls to the Academy's separate researchers and historians, and the Chroniclers themselves render no verdicts.
  • Turning over the logistics of the camels, the party recalled that horses in the North are a controlled, almost state-owned resource — carts there are pulled by oxen and donkeys rather than horses — historically the foundation of Northern cavalry dominance, much as the Navigators' skill now anchors the South's unlikely strength at sea.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• The party secured an agreement for a large quantity of finger fruit as provisions for the Amada.
  • They retained the weapons, clothing, and equipment of the defeated raiders, including their small shields, scimitars, spears, bows, and simple twisted-metal rings, along with a full Stone Man outfit and a curved sword that Knick Nab kept for himself, tying its wrapped headscarf into a style of his own.
  • Eight of the raiders' camels remain in the party's hands for the journey upriver.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • Nothing of note was lost.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
Before setting off upriver, the party settled the fate of the three Stone Men held prisoner since the earlier battle for the Islander village: Mathias Monadero, the Southern trade agent acting as the village's Major Domo, agreed to keep them alive and looked after in the party's absence, and the party itself declined to enslave any of them, reasoning that doing so might tip off the southern newcomers to their true origins.

The party continued their journey upriver from the Islander village, weighing the risk of losing the longboat against the risk of losing their camels if things went wrong, and settled on using both: splitting into a group on the longboat and another walking the bank with the captured camels, so either group could fall back on the other. Along the way they passed numerous enormous but harmless lizards sunning on the banks, some reportedly twenty feet long, which showed no interest in the party or their boat. As the river narrowed into a rocky gorge, Noddy sent his familiar Pocket aloft to scout while he and Cosimo climbed to the clifftop above with a spyglass; from there they spotted a large column of people and two longboats approaching the village behind them. A check of religious markings ruled out the colors of the Divinity of Two, and Werner's knowledge of ship construction pointed to a southern force instead, though its size — several dozen at least, perhaps over a hundred — was too large for a simple resupply crew, leaving open whether it was bringing porters or establishing a new base. Sent out further still, Pocket confirmed the newcomers carried muskets. Unwilling to risk finding out more, they pushed on for two more hours into the evening to put distance between themselves and the newcomers; Knick Nab's inspired leadership drove the camel column up and over the clifftop path so briskly that the party broke into an impromptu song — composed on the spot by Noddy — in his honor, dubbing him "Captain of the Ships of the Desert." The next morning, before moving on, Pocket made one last pass over the village and confirmed the newcomers had gone no further than its edge, easing the party's fears of being pursued.

On the afternoon of the second day, as they approached the swampy region at the river's headwaters, they discovered an encampment of "Stone Men" raiders at the very spot where Leela had once fled the same raiders on an earlier journey. Batu Batu attempted to parley with the raiders in their own tongue, first trying to convince them the Islander village lay undefended and open for the taking, but the exchange collapsed once he was pressed on the fate of the village's men and admitted the party had killed most of those who attacked it; the raiders charged. The party's superior firepower and magic proved decisive. Werner opened the fight with a devastating shot from the longboat's swivel gun that killed a camel rider outright, while Mani wounded the enemy leader with a musket shot at extreme range, knocking him from his camel and out of the fight, before later cutting down a second, imposing raider in melee with a "stand and deliver" flourish of rapier and dagger. Cosimo summoned a spectacular illusion of "Handsome Gulliver Gold" riding a Pegasus, which swooped in on a glowing lance to attack and distract the raiders, while Noddy's sleep spells put several opponents down where they stood, leaving three raiders to be taken alive rather than killed. Salter added musket fire of his own, and when the last raider broke and fled, Knick Nab ran him down and Werner finished him off with a reloaded shot from the swivel gun.

During the melee, Leela was seriously wounded in the leg by a raider's scimitar. As the raiders' numbers dwindled, Cosimo channeled a blinding burst of light through Handsome Gulliver Gold's holy symbol that enveloped the nearby combatants while somehow sparing Leela, allowing the party to gain the upper hand. Mani spectacularly leaped across the river to engage the last, large raider, defeating him but stunning himself in the process. After the last of the raiders were killed, captured, or had fled, Riu was able to magically treat Leela's wound, reducing her expected recovery time from a month to less than a week. The party stripped the dead, fed the bodies to the camp's carnivorous finger fruit trees, and searched the raiders' meager belongings, finding little beyond a scavenged catch of fish, frogs, and small lizards from the swamp; Cosimo, an amateur wood-carver, also kept a piece of the dead finger fruit tree's wood to work with later. The session concluded with the party having secured the area, looted the camp, tied up their three sleeping prisoners, and prepared to interrogate them — intending to ask directly whether they knew the whereabouts of the round black stone the party had been seeking.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Mathias Monadero: The Southern trade agent acting as the village's Major Domo. Agreed, before the party set off upriver, to keep the three Stone Men prisoners from the village battle alive and looked after in their absence.
  • Stone Men: A war party of desert raiders encountered upriver, armed only with spears and scimitars rather than firearms. The party defeated them, killing most and capturing three alive who were put to sleep by Noddy's magic.
  • Leela: Guided the party to the site where she had once fled the Stone Men herself, then fought alongside the party and sustained a serious leg wound from a scimitar before Riu treated it.
  • Handsome Gulliver Gold: Cosimo's powerful illusion, which manifested on a Pegasus wielding a glowing lance to attack the raiders, later channeling a blinding burst of light from its holy symbol to shield Leela.
  • Pocket: Noddy's familiar seagull, sent aloft to scout the pursuing force from the clifftop, confirm it was armed with muskets, and check the next morning that nothing was following the party.
  • Salter: Fired his musket alongside the party during the battle.
  • Batu Batu: Attempted to parley with the Stone Men in their own tongue, first trying to convince them the Islander village was undefended before the truth of the earlier fighting slipped out. Once the parley collapsed, he stayed aboard the longboat with his cleaver, ready to repel any raider who tried to board.
  • Camels: The party continued to use their captured camels for transport; one grew inexplicably devoted to Knick Nab after his successful handling of the group.
  • Riverbank Lizards: Numerous enormous but harmless lizards, reportedly as long as twenty feet, seen sunning along the riverbanks; they showed no interest in the party or their boat.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• River Valley (Isle of Sands): The party traveled upriver along the Uron, passing through a narrow rocky gorge — its clifftop path used for scouting — before reaching the swampy region at the river's source, where the channel was expected to widen into a shallow, weed-choked lake of uncertain navigability; Leela, who had reached this point once before on foot, couldn't say whether the longboat would make it through. Aside from the finger fruit trees, the only significant vegetation they saw along the way was reeds, some grown thick and tall enough to resemble trees themselves.
  • Raider Camp: A small encampment established by the Stone Men at the edge of the swamp, on the same spot where Leela had once fled a previous raid, which the party overran. It consisted of a single tent, a felled finger fruit tree the raiders had been harvesting for wood, and several camels.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• Before approaching, the party readied their weapons as a show of force and agreed to concentrate their fire on one side of the river to clear it first if talks failed.
  • Batu Batu's attempt to parley with the raiders and negotiate safe passage collapsed once the party admitted to killing their kin at the Islander village, sparking the battle.
  • The primary conflict was a large battle against a group of Stone Men raiders.
  • The party successfully used a combination of firearms, magic, and melee to overwhelm their opponents.
  • Key moments included Werner's opening cannon shot, Cosimo's flying illusion, Noddy's targeted sleep spells, and a blinding Sunlight spell from Cosimo that protected Leela and incapacitated the enemy.
  • Leela was seriously wounded during the fight.
  • The last raider broke and fled but was run down by Knick Nab and finished off by a reloaded shot from Werner's swivel gun.
  • Three raiders were left alive by Noddy's sleep spells rather than killed, to be tied up, disarmed, and interrogated instead.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The party confirmed the arrival of a large, well-armed Southern force at the Islander village, reinforcing their decision to remain incognito and avoid returning there.
  • A check of religious markings ruled out the colors of the Divinity of Two, and Werner's knowledge of ship construction pointed to a southern origin for the force — though its size, several dozen strong and possibly over a hundred, was too large for a single ship's crew, leaving open whether it was a delayed resupply mission bringing porters or an effort to establish a permanent base.
  • Mani's attunement confirmed the party was heading in the right direction and drawing closer to the totem, though it was still some unknown distance off rather than immediately at hand.
  • The party noted uneasily that, since crossing the Maelstrom, whatever force had been trailing them had consistently stayed three or four days behind, raising the unresolved question of whether it was tracking the totems rather than the party itself.
  • With no other usable timber in the river valley — no coconut or oak trees, only finger fruit trees — the locals cure and braid bundles of reed for firewood.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• An assortment of weapons from the defeated raiders (spears, scimitars, etc.).
  • Three additional camels from the raider camp.
  • A map of the surrounding desert.
  • A supply of wood from a dead finger-fruit tree.
  • A small cache of foraged fish, frogs, and lizards taken from the raiders' camp.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • Nothing of note was lost.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
With the Stone Men's camp secured, Mani took the lead in interrogating the surviving prisoners through Batu Batu's translation. The raiders admitted only that a sandstorm had delayed their arrival. Asked directly about a large black rock, they allowed only that they knew of "powerful carved cut stone" somewhere in the region — vague, but enough to suggest the totem the party sought was real and nearby. More useful was their rough-paper map, crude compared to the skin-bound Gildenhome map but clear enough to show the river, the village, and the raiders' home near a range of hills far to the north — a three-week journey for a people numbering in the hundreds. Mani kept the map for the party's own use. When he demanded payment for further answers, the only "gold" he had to hand was a scavenged jawbone with a gold tooth still lodged in it; the prisoner wanted none of it and asked for information instead. Much of the questioning dwelt on the raiders' uniformly pointed ears, so unlike the Islanders'; a medical inspection found no sign of deliberate mutilation, suggesting the ears were simply an inborn trait of the Stone Men. When Mani held up Knick Nab's own pointed ears for comparison, the prisoner insisted they were wrong somehow — too light, not a proper Stone Man's — leaving open whether Knick Nab shares some deeper kinship with the raiders or merely a passing resemblance. Pressed on what dangers lay in the region, the prisoners described a venomous, long-tailed creature that lived beneath the desert sand near wherever they harvested something they called "the spice," and warned that a bank of mist further upriver would confuse and disorient anyone who entered it — a warning the party would soon test for themselves. With the prisoners offering little else, the party argued at length over their fate — a real split between those pushing to execute the helpless captives and those unwilling to do so — before a vote settled it: release all three unarmed, with a camel apiece, their own gathered food, and a warning never to return to the village.

Before letting them go, Mani made a show of invoking the Mother and Father over the prisoners, having them chant his own name back to him as the first blessing of a faith he was more or less inventing on the spot. As the three departed, Cosimo — under cover of prayer — cast a facade illusion on himself, taking on the terrifying red-skinned, horned, winged shape of a cambion, seized one of the raiders, and warned that he would devour the man's soul should he ever return. The apparition worked: all three fled for the dunes at speed, one glancing back once before disappearing over the horizon.

With camp secured, the party turned to the dead and to the finger-fruit trees nearby. The raiders, it turned out, had been quietly chopping their firewood from a large, long-dead finger-fruit trunk lying at the center of camp rather than risking a living one; a chunk of its wood proved unremarkable under close inspection — flexible but mediocre firewood, with no scream or blood when cut and no notable taste or nutrition — though one softened, rot-spalted piece seemed promising enough that Riu set it aside for a future prosthetic. They stripped enough clothing from the fallen raiders to outfit the whole group, gathered a stock of firewood and root, then turned to a nearby living finger-fruit tree to run their experiment: feeding it all seven raider bodies one at a time showed that a faint chittering sound preceded each strike, that many separate grasping bunches worked independently across the canopy — so the tree could not easily be overfed — and that its fruit carried true seeds, ruling out any thought that it was some deliberately cultivated, seedless strain. Riu experimented with burning root to test its numbing smoke on Leela's wounded leg, finding it a far more potent painkiller than simply chewing the root, while Knick Nab and a couple of others chewed root themselves on the chance it revealed something unusual about the tree, with Werner abstaining as an unaffected control; nothing came of it this time.

Overnight, on watch with Salter, Werner spotted one of the released raiders lingering some two hundred feet from camp near a tethered camel just before dawn. Noddy sent Pocket to confirm it, then stripped, cast an unseen spell on himself, and crept close enough to put the man to sleep, succeeding on his second attempt after his first casting went unnoticed but failed to work. Once captured and roused, the prisoner explained he had lingered out of religious fascination with the party's gods. Rather than kill him, Mani pressed a rifle to his forehead and charged him with becoming the first priest of the Mother and Father — tasked with building a shrine, keeping a candle burning for the moon by day and a large red candle for the sun by night, and awaiting the promised arrival of Cosimo, "blessed of the sun and moon" — before sending him off again. The party debated afterward whether inadvertently founding a religion in territory the Southern navy was moving to occupy might complicate their disguise as ordinary travelers.

The party then judged the ground ahead too boggy for the camels and left them behind, spending a full, miserable day forcing their longboat through the swamp at the river's headwaters, wading waist-deep and picking off leeches as they went. They camped for the night on a small islet further on, marked by an unfamiliar palm-like tree bearing hard wooden nuts, before continuing the next morning past a stretch of river where small hippo-like animals and large, armoured reptiles lounged harmlessly along the banks. There, they spotted three small, pygmy-like figures watching from a distance, better-dressed and seemingly more civilized than the feral pygmies encountered on Bitterroot Isle; hailing them in Islander, Elvish, Common, and the Sand tongue got no response, and the figures retreated into the brush. Ahead, the river gave way to waterlogged ground, with a larger body of water visible beyond it already shrouded in mist; sending Pocket aloft for a look confirmed there was no way around it. The party searched the wet ground for burrows like the ones the pygmies had dug on Bitterroot Isle, found none, and spent a grueling four hours portaging their boat and gear roughly a mile across it. On the far side they reached the lake proper and were confronted by its wall of dense, unnatural mist. There, they spotted more of the small watching figures along its shores and glimpsed one paddling a boat before it vanished into the fog; further hails again went unanswered.

With Mani's senses indicating their objective lay through the mist, the party first spent about an hour tracing the shoreline to look for a way around, catching further glimpses of the small watching figures along the banks, including what looked like a boat slipping away into the fog, but found no gap. Convinced there was no way around it, they warded themselves with a protective spell, lit a lantern against the gloom, and sailed straight in. They immediately experienced its magical, disorienting effects: several of the party lost their bearings entirely despite their usually reliable senses of direction, though Knick Nab held a steady line at the tiller — even as he thought at one point that he glimpsed three boats trailing them through the fog — and one member's detect illusion spell confirmed the mist was no mere trick of the light but some genuine, unnatural phenomenon. After some time, their boat ran aground on the beach of a large, unseen island within the mist, visibility reduced to barely twenty feet in every direction. Knick Nab, whose eyes usually pierce ordinary darkness without trouble, found this fog defeated that gift entirely; he chewed a piece of root hoping it might sharpen his senses against whatever magic was at work, but it made no difference. Another member levitated above the mist with a spyglass to try to get their bearings, but found nothing but fog in every direction before the spell ran out and they had to come back down. Convinced the totem was inland, the party built a fire on the beach as a landmark, lashed themselves together with a rope, and left Leela and Salter behind with the boat — tying Salter to it as well in case the mist's confusion led him to wander off — along with a written note telling them to wait, feed the fire, and stay put. They brought Batu Batu along as translator and ventured into the disorienting fog, sounding off by name every few minutes and logging their steps and turns to keep from losing each other entirely. Even lashed together, Knick Nab and Batu Batu began drifting off in different directions as they walked; the party pushed onward, becoming increasingly confused and lost, until the session ended with them finding themselves surrounded by carnivorous finger-fruit trees.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Stone Men prisoners: Three surviving raiders, interrogated and then released unarmed with a camel and provisions each. One lingered near camp overnight, was recaptured, and was sent off a second time charged with becoming a priest of the Mother and Father awaiting Cosimo's promised arrival.
  • Cosimo's Cambion Illusion: A terrifying red-skinned, horned, winged facade Cosimo cast on himself to threaten a departing prisoner and drive all three raiders into a panicked flight.
  • Batu Batu: Translated during the interrogation of the Stone Men prisoners and later accompanied the party inland as their only means of speaking with anyone they might encounter.
  • Salter: Stood watch with Werner overnight and, along with Leela, remained behind to guard the boat once the party moved inland into the mist.
  • Leela: Still recovering from her leg wound, she was the subject of Riu's root-smoke experiment and later stayed with the boat rather than press on into the mist.
  • Pygmies: Small, elusive figures dressed in earth-toned clothing, first observed watching the party from a distance along the river, then again from the shores of the lake and from a boat. They appeared more civilized than the pygmies encountered previously on Bitterroot Isle and retreated whenever hailed.
  • Creatures: The party observed various creatures in and around the lake, including small hippo-like animals and large, armored reptiles, none of which were aggressive.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Raider Camp: The Stone Men's camp at the swamp's edge, where the party interrogated and released their prisoners and conducted their experiments on the finger-fruit tree before moving on.
  • The Swamp: A difficult, marshy region at the source of the river that took the party a full day to navigate by boat, forcing them to abandon their camels and wade through leech-infested water.
  • The Palm Islet: A small island in the calmer waters beyond the swamp, notable for an unfamiliar palm-like tree bearing hard wooden nuts, where the party made camp for a second night.
  • The Lake of Mist: A large lake reached after a grueling mile-long portage from the swamp, dominated by a wall of thick, magical mist that causes confusion and disorientation. Small pygmy-like figures were spotted watching from its shores and from a boat before vanishing into the fog.
  • The Misty Isle: A large, foliage-rich island located within the mist, where visibility drops to barely twenty feet. The party landed on its shore and began exploring inland.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The party split sharply over the fate of their surviving prisoners, with proposals ranging from outright execution to maiming them (severing Achilles tendons) to prevent pursuit; Werner, a whaler used to killing beasts rather than bound men, refused outright to cut a prisoner's throat himself. A vote ultimately settled on release.
  • The session's conflicts were otherwise primarily environmental and magical. The party contended with the difficult terrain of the swamp — including a leech-infested wade — and the mile-long portage, briefly debated skirting the mist's edge by boat instead of sailing straight through it, and ultimately grappled with the mist's magical disorientation itself.
  • Releasing a captured Stone Man as a self-declared priest of the party's gods raised concerns about complicating their cover in Southern-watched territory.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Stone Men's crude map confirmed their raiding party had come roughly three weeks from a home in the hills to the north, a settlement of hundreds, and that they had been delayed en route by a sandstorm.
  • The Stone Men's uniformly pointed ears appear to be a natural trait rather than the result of mutilation.
  • Burning the numbing root produces a far stronger analgesic smoke than simply chewing it, effective enough to visibly ease Leela's pain; chewing it produced no other unusual effect for anyone who tried, including Knick Nab, who had built up some tolerance to it already.
  • The party recalled that chewing the numbing root had once let them see through the smuggler A'Wood's illusion to his true elven form, and wondered whether it might reveal something similarly hidden about the finger-fruit tree or the mist; it revealed nothing either time.
  • The finger-fruit trees can be fed many bodies without any apparent limit, warn with a chittering sound just before they strike, and bear true seeds — ruling out the idea that they might be some deliberately cultivated, seedless strain.
  • The party recalled that the Church of the Two had once moved against a population of similar pygmies and their native root on a nearby island, deeming them blasphemous, which leaves open how thoroughly that campaign actually succeeded given what they have now found here.
  • The prisoners warned of a venomous, long-tailed creature living beneath the desert sand, near wherever they harvest something they called "the spice" — claws and a stinger were about all the language barrier let them convey.
  • The prisoners also warned that a bank of mist upriver causes confusion and getting lost — a warning that proved accurate once the party reached it themselves.
  • The party reasoned that the Southern Navy's presence at the village is likely tied to trading for the finger fruit as rations, a real advantage for their fleet, while the origin of the mysterious air mages remains unknown — troubling, since their home island is believed to have already been destroyed.
  • The mist is not a natural phenomenon and has a powerful, magical disorienting effect that can overcome even the party's enhanced senses of direction.
  • The party confirmed through Mani's attunement that they are very close to the totem they are seeking.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• The Stone Men's rough-paper map of the desert, taken from the prisoners, marking the river, the village, and the raiders' home to the north.
  • Clothing stripped from the fallen Stone Men, enough to outfit the entire party.
  • A supply of firewood and freshly gathered root.
  • A handful of finger-fruit seeds, collected out of curiosity.
  • A sample of unusually spalted finger-fruit wood, set aside for its potential use in prosthetics.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • The three camels and the weapons captured from the Stone Men raiders in the previous session were returned to the surviving prisoners as a condition of their release.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
Leaving Salter and the still-recovering Leela behind to guard the boat, the party roped themselves together and pushed on into the mist toward its source. The disorientation only worsened as they went, with individual members repeatedly drifting off course despite the rope; Mani took the lead, following an increasingly confident pull from his medallion and singing a sea shanty to keep the others oriented on his position, while — at Knick Nab's suggestion — the group settled on calling out their names in turn so anyone who fell silent could be hauled back into line. Marking a trail proved harder than expected once they left open sand — dragging a branch worked there, but further in they switched to cutting notches into trunks and stacking stones instead. Despite the precautions, Mani wandered directly beneath a finger-fruit tree and was bitten before anyone could react; his armor absorbed most of the blow, and the party fell back to regroup.

Wary of a repeat, Cosimo spent several minutes methodically testing another tree, conjuring an illusory figure he dubbed Handsome Gulliver Gold and sending it to walk, taunt, and even mock-duel beneath the branches while he layered on false taste, smell, and finally the heat of a lit torch, one sense at a time — none of it drew a reaction. Only when a rolled rock struck the base of the tree did one of its fruit bunches visibly flinch, and when Noddy lassoed a fruit with his enchanted rope and hauled on it, the whole bunch fought back before the fruit finally tore free. The party concluded the trees hunt by vibration and touch alone — sight, sound, smell, and taste meant nothing to them — though the effort the tree put into defending its fruit left some of the party uneasy about whether they had just fought over a meal from something that could think.

They pushed on, correcting course again and again — at one point Mani had to shake Werner back to his senses after he drifted off entirely. Voices called from ahead in the mist, and three small figures resolved briefly at the edge of sight before drawing back; Mani hailed them with a boisterous "stand and deliver," and when that drew nothing, Batu Batu tried an Islander greeting of his own, only for a curt rebuff to come back through his translation: "turn about, do not approach." As they pushed on through a denser stand of finger-fruit, Mani broke into an improvised song for the trees themselves — leafy giants with hungry roots, he sang, promising they were just passing through and no one's supper. Further along, cryptic voices called again from deeper in the mist, warning the party to turn back or "three ages await." Batu Batu, translating brokenly, made out only fragments — sorrow, danger, challenge — but the party pressed on regardless.

Following the pull a while longer, the party emerged into a clearing at the heart of the mist: a shallow pool ringed by the last dry ground, a black stone totem rising from its center, and several small rivers issuing from the water around it. On the far side of the pool waited the three pygmy-like figures — "The Three" — who spoke only in short, often contradictory phrases and repeatedly branded the party "bad people" despite their protests. Batu Batu translated as best he could while Mani worked around the pool's edge to close the distance and spoke for the party, and Cosimo conjured an illusory map to explain themselves: the black stone, the mist-shrouded island, their boat's journey up the river, and finally a priest of the Divinity of Two arriving with a diad to threaten the totem. The Three's answers stayed fragmented and evasive, but patterns emerged — they seemed to speak from different vantage points in time, one favoring "not yet," another "been there," and the third undercutting both.

Testing whether the totem could be used for travel, Riu teleported directly onto the stone with a minor leaving spell, then attempted a far larger jump — picturing all the totems as connected, fingers of one buried hand reaching out through the earth, and trying to translate himself along that connection all the way to the totem buried beneath Blackstone Peak on Totem Isle, in the Channel Islands — and failed badly enough that The Three simply told him "no." Mani took a running leap across the pool to join him, landing in an undignified half-dive that left him soaked to the boots, and once there attuned to the stone with both hands pressed against it, confirming the totem's purpose was travel; reaching further out, he sensed the pull of another totem entirely: far across the sea to the east, someplace hot and volcanic, out past the Sands in the region known as The Glasslands. The Three made clear this distant one was not the one under threat — the totem that mattered now was "close," one the enemy had not yet found, though The Three already knew exactly where it was.

Pressed on the medallions, The Three confirmed they were shaped by a convergence of the Divinity of Two and "the old ones" — the elves — under the involvement of what they called "the eight," the first the party had heard of any powers beyond the Two Gods. Knick Nab recounted where he'd found his own medallion — on a body in the deepest dungeon of the Church of the Two, someone he'd taken for a heretic — and The Three confirmed the Church had a hand in placing it there, though "not only" the Church had a hand in making it. Pressed on whether the medallions were a boon or a bane, The Three insisted the answer was neither: a tool, and properly a single item of which each of the party wore a linked copy, "because the enemies are many." Asked whether the Stone Men's own city might hold useful knowledge, one of The Three blurted "sky," as if naming one of the eight outright — confirming that the towering stone structure the Stone Men are building to escape to the sky, the object of their own desperate faith, is bound up with one of the very powers the party's own faith denied. The Three also spoke of "Navigators," sometimes called "wind witches" — people connected to a totem destroyed forty years before, who worked against the Two and could call up storms to travel through them — though none of them knew where such a person could currently be found. Turning the questioning around, Knick Nab pressed The Three on his own murky ancestry; they confirmed only that his lineage ran back beyond the mountains, tangled up with the elves, and that in some sense he had "forgotten" what he once was. Before parting, Mani wrote his name in the sand and had one of The Three sketch its own symbol in return, which he carefully copied into his notebook, intending to have it tattooed later; the two also traded gifts, Mani offering a coin and receiving a pipe in return, though when he reached out to shake hands in farewell he found they had already withdrawn out of reach. Pressed on what an "age" meant, The Three's answers suggested that destroying a totem ends one, and that losing all eight would end the world outright — though the exact reckoning left the party more confused than enlightened. With that, The Three withdrew into the mist, and the party made the return leap across the pool to rejoin the others.

Upon leaving the clearing, the party discovered that significant time had passed. The trail markers they had cut only hours before, by their own reckoning, were now faded and overgrown, barely legible where they could be found at all; when they reunited with Salter and Leela at the boat, they realized they had all physically aged by roughly two years in what felt like a single day — new stubble, a fresh mustache on Mani, tight-fitting clothes, and all. Leela's serious leg wound was completely healed, and Salter and Leela insisted they themselves had waited barely a day. Wary of dragging the boat back through the mist-shrouded swamp at night, the party made camp on the beach outside the mist and set watches until morning.

Traveling back down the now-swollen river, they found the fields where they had gathered root scorched and destroyed, the ground blackened and torn apart with nothing living left in it. Nearing the settlement, Noddy sent Pocket ahead to scout, and the seagull returned with word of stone buildings looming where the village had stood; the party disguised themselves in the same wrapped robes worn by the Stone Men and left their boat behind the cliffs, climbing up on foot rather than announcing themselves. Using a spyglass from the clifftop, they confirmed the Islander village had been replaced by a massive Northern construction project — stone buildings, bridges, and a twin-spired, still-unfinished church of the Divinity of Two built out over the river on pillars. From their vantage, they watched the local Islanders — lightly dressed, without collars or chains, but kept in line by armed minders wielding whips and spears — hauling slabs of quarried stone on rollers down toward the town; the flags and colors visible through the spyglass confirmed the guards as Northern Navy rather than Northern Army.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• The Three: Three pygmy-like figures who guard the Totem of Water. They spoke in a cryptic, often contradictory manner, each seeming to answer from a different vantage in time — past, present, and future — though which was which never stayed consistent. They described themselves only as watchers, refused to give their true names, and possess deep knowledge of the totems, the medallions, and the "eight" powers behind them.
  • Batu Batu: Accompanied the party into the mist as translator, relaying the finger-fruit trees' warnings, the cryptic voices calling the party back, and the entire halting negotiation with The Three.
  • Salter and Leela: Left behind to guard the boat outside the mist. By their own reckoning barely a day had passed when the party returned; Leela's leg wound had fully healed in that time.
  • Pocket: Noddy's familiar seagull, visibly grown from the two years spent in the mist. Sent ahead on the return journey, he was the first to spot the new Northern stone buildings rising where the Islander village had stood.
  • Northern Navy Soldiers: Seen in the distance, whipping and driving the enslaved Islander workforce as they hauled quarried stone toward the settlement; their flags and colors identified them as Northern Navy rather than Northern Army.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Misty Isle (Isle of Sands): An island shrouded in a magical mist that causes disorientation and accelerates the passage of time.
  • Totem of Water: A black stone totem located in a pool at the heart of the Misty Isle. It is the source of both the river and the time-altering mist, and its purpose, confirmed through attunement, is travel.
  • Islander Village (former, Isle of Sands): Now a large Northern settlement and quarry under construction, featuring a twin-spired, still-unfinished church of the Divinity of Two built out over the river on pillars.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The primary conflict was the surreal and disorienting journey through the magical mist and the discovery of its time-altering effects.
  • A finger-fruit tree bit Mani when he wandered beneath it unawares; his armor absorbed most of the damage.
  • A tense and cryptic social encounter with "The Three."

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• Time Dilation: The mist on the island causes time to pass much more rapidly. The party lost approximately two years in a single day.
  • The Totems: There are eight totems in total ("four close, four far"). The party confirmed the existence of a Totem of Water. They were warned that the next totem to be found and threatened by the Divinity of Two is one located "close" to their previous travels, and that The Three already know its location even though the enemy does not yet.
  • A Totem for Walls: In one final, half-answered exchange as the party made ready to leave, Mani asked whether a totem could be used to raise walls of earth. The Three's garbled reply seemed to confirm that one still is — though by whom, and where, was left entirely unclear.
  • A Distant Totem: Through attunement, Mani sensed a totem far across the sea to the east, somewhere hot and volcanic beyond the Sands, in a region called The Glasslands. The Three confirmed this was not the totem currently under threat.
  • The Eight Powers: The party learned for the first time of the existence of "Eight Powers," and that the Two Gods of the Divinity are only two of them. The medallions were created with the involvement of the Two, the elves, and all eight — The Three confirmed the Church of the Two had a hand in placing Knick Nab's medallion where he found it, but said "not only" the Church had a hand in making it. Pressed on whether the medallions were a boon or a bane, The Three called them neither, but a tool — properly a single item, of which each of the party wears a linked copy, "because the enemies are many." Asked whether the Stone Men's city held useful knowledge, one of The Three named "sky" as one of the eight — confirming that the Stone Men's tower, built to escape to the sky they worship, is unknowingly bound up with one of the eight powers.
  • Navigators: The Three spoke of "Navigators," sometimes called "wind witches" — people tied to a totem destroyed forty years ago, who work against the Two and can call up storms to travel through them — but could not say where any might currently be found.
  • Ages: Pressed on what an "age" means, The Three suggested that destroying a totem ends one, and that the destruction of all eight would end the world outright — though their answers left the party more confused than enlightened.
  • Knick Nab's Heritage: The Three confirmed that Knick Nab's murky ancestry runs back beyond the mountains and is tangled up with the elves, though they offered nothing more specific.
  • Northern Invasion: In the two years that passed, the Northern Kingdom has established a major foothold on the Isle of Sands, enslaved the local population, and begun constructing a fortified settlement and church.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text: • A Pipe: Given by one of "The Three" in exchange for a coin Mani offered as a gift.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • Time: The party lost approximately two years.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session begins with the party grappling with the shocking revelation that approximately three years have passed while they were on the mist-shrouded island. Werner uses his navigation and astronomy skills to read the shifted position of the sun and moon against what he remembers, confirming it is the same season they entered the mist in, but roughly three years later. The physical evidence bears this out: their clothes have gone tight and short, faint stubble has appeared, and their voices have begun to change. Looking at their own reflections in the water, and at each other, makes it plain — they have grown into their late teens. Leela, Batu Batu, and Salter have visibly aged as well, and even Noddy's familiar, the seagull Pocket, shows the years, though otherwise seems fine. Oddly, the aging is not complete: none of them carry anywhere near three years' worth of unshaven growth, nor any sign of having gone hungry, and a check of the gear left in the boat turns up nothing unusually worn either — as if the years had been imposed on their bodies without the wear that should have come with them.

Looking down from the cliffs, they observe the massive Northern settlement that has replaced the Islander village, complete with a quarry worked by enslaved Islanders and Stone Men. Before approaching, the party agrees on a cover story: they are northern sailors who were separated from their ship in the Maelstrom while pursuing a Southern vessel, and have been lost in the interior ever since, for a length of time they prefer to keep vague. They agree not to volunteer the Amada's name unless pressed, and to hold Werner's De Rendal name and letter of introduction in reserve. They hide their ship's boat along with its swivel gun, keg of gunpowder, firewood, and a crate of grenades, and split up their remaining store of harvested root to carry on their persons, since they doubt they will ever make it back to retrieve it. Taking stock of what's left to them, they accept that whatever they'd left in their sea chests aboard the missing Amada is gone for good — but each of them had kept a personal store of gold rather than trust it to the crew, so between that and Leela's jewelry they still carry a considerable hoard, their only real resource now. Leela is persuaded, not without difficulty, to conceal that gold jewelry, and both she and Batu Batu are told to present themselves as slaves to avoid drawing suspicion. It stings Batu Batu, a slave of the Navy himself, who struggles to reconcile the request with Leela's status as a free woman among her own people; Leela herself, unfamiliar with slavery as the Northern Empire practices it, only grasps what is being asked of her after a halting, painful conversation, finally summing it up herself as "me slave, me animal, good."

While still on the cliffs, the party pulls out the map taken from the raiders and studies it properly for the first time, matching its markings against what little the raiders had told them. They confirm the Stone Man home is the mountain marked at its centre, and that a nearby pyramid is the "staircase to God" — the tower to the Stone Men's sky god. The map also shows a long-ruined "Old Wall," a caravan route, a possible trading post, a stretch of desert marked with scorpions large enough to be worth avoiding, and an unlabelled body of water where, according to the raiders, "there are no more ships." Both the Old Wall and the Stone Man home appear to lie a couple of weeks' walk away — useful landmarks, though the map answers few of their immediate questions.

They approach the quarry, where islander and Stone Man labourers haul cut stone toward the river under the crack of overseers' whips, and encounter Sergeant Perkins, a Northern NCO. Wary of him at first — and careful to give Werner's family name only as the shortened, noncommittal "Dendle" rather than the full De Rendal — they learn that a Commander Odo is in charge of the settlement before Noddy magically charms the sergeant. Perkins's newfound devotion fixes on Noddy himself — he recalls seeing him in action three years earlier in Zylos, the night a Southern wind witch's fire ship was boarded and stopped in the harbor, and even claims, bafflingly, to have heard that Cosimo died "terribly," a rumor no one in the party can account for. Loosened by the charm, Perkins reveals that Major Hubert is now considered a traitor who was secretly working for the South all along and vanished with the Amada amid the ensuing confusion, that the North has held this settlement for two years by way of a difficult, bitterly cold "Northern Passage" that bypasses the Maelstrom entirely, that construction of the settlement's temple is running months ahead of schedule though the new clergy meant to staff it have not yet arrived, and that most of the Stone Men have been rounded up and brought here as slave labor, with only a handful of holdouts left in their original home to the north. He adds that the truce with the South holds only in the east; out here in the west the two sides remain locked in an unofficial, low-grade fight, and as far as he knows the South still has no way through but the Maelstrom itself, crossed only by their wind witches.

Perkins has a camel-drawn cart brought round and rides the party into the settlement, which they find utterly transformed: a town raised on stone pillars above the water, threaded with causeways, bridges, and small boats, and ringed by fields of rice and grain. At a tavern, the party plies Perkins with a fierce local liquor, and once he is well into his cups he begins talking loudly about a pirate problem — someone, somewhere close by, "hiding in plain sight," preying on shipping in a way no one can explain. Pressed further, he also lets slip that the port at the river delta remains small and poorly organized, with ships simply anchoring wherever the unpredictable depths allow, and that no one has established any shipbuilding on this side of the Maelstrom — nothing like the infrastructure he remembers from Zylos. As his voice rises, Noddy hurriedly casts a spell of silence around the table to keep him from being overheard, but Perkins keeps talking and shouting names and directions within the silenced bubble, so Noddy puts him to sleep with a spell to shut him up. The party carries him out, loads him back onto his cart, and sends him off with his driver, claiming he simply overindulged.

Meanwhile, Knick Nab slips away on his own to gather intelligence. In front of the half-built church, whose plaza is lined with pillars bearing routine notices — hymn schedules, requests for blessings, lost dogs — one posting stops him cold: a declaration of heresy from the Divinity of Two. It names a long list of individuals as heretics: Major Hubert, Captain De Guzman, his lieutenant Blaque, Lieutenant Dardell, the priest Nicolas, and the party members Cosimo, Knick Nab, Mani, Riu, and Werner. Noddy's name is conspicuously absent. Knick Nab tears the notice down and tucks it away before rejoining the others, who by then understand the gravity of their situation: they are fugitives.

They decide their only option is to escape the island. Werner changes out of his midshipman's uniform and back into ordinary sailor's clothes, and the party moves east along the riverbank under cover of night, heading for the river delta to find a ship. Passing through the settlement, they see no cannon, gun slits, or other sign the town is braced for an attack — only routine patrols, as though the surrounding desert is considered defense enough. Their path is blocked by a new and formidable gatehouse and wall spanning the entire river valley — a stone tower complete on the north bank, one under construction on the south, and a barrier running from the gate out to the desert on both sides. Sentries pace the wall's top, visible against the night sky, and a single small boat, its mast unstepped and sail down, sits moored just inside the closed gate. Before they turn to scramble up out of the river valley, someone points out the dark silver lining in it all: since the Navy that owns Batu Batu has just declared the whole party heretics and enemies, its claim on him is worth exactly as much as its goodwill toward them now — which is to say, none. Batu Batu, they agree, has effectively just won his freedom. The session concludes with the party planning a dangerous trek through the desert to come around the wall unseen.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Sergeant Perkins: A Northern NCO overseeing the quarry. Charmed by Noddy, he becomes instantly and utterly devoted to him, recognizing him from a night three years earlier in Zylos and providing key intelligence — about Hubert's disgrace, the temple's construction, the fate of the Stone Men, the state of the war, and rumors of a hidden pirate problem — before the party plies him with drink until he passes out and sends him back to the quarry with his own driver, none the wiser.
  • Commander Odo: Named by Perkins as the officer in command of the settlement. The party does not meet him directly.
  • Northern Soldiers: Seen overseeing the slave labor at the quarry and patrolling the new fortification downriver.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Isle of Sands: The desert landmass and river valley beyond the Maelstrom where the party is now stranded.
  • The new Northern settlement built where the Islander village once stood — stone buildings and pillars raised above the water, linked by causeways, bridges, and small boats, and surrounded by fields of rice and grain. Islanders move through it visibly deferential, though uncollared, alongside ordinary shops going about their business. It encompasses the quarry, a half-built temple to the Divinity of Two, and the tavern where the party interrogated Sergeant Perkins.
  • The fortified river gate and wall: a stone tower complete on the north bank, one under construction on the south, and a patrolled barrier running from the gate to the edge of the desert on both sides, now blocking the river valley entirely. A single small boat sits moored just inside the closed gate.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The primary conflict is the revelation that the party has been declared heretics by the Divinity of Two, making them fugitives within the very Kingdom they serve.
  • A social encounter with Sergeant Perkins is successfully navigated using magic, though plying him with drink until he talks nearly backfires when his voice rises within earshot of the rest of the tavern, forcing Noddy to cast a hasty spell of silence to contain him.
  • Passing Leela and Batu Batu off as slaves for the sake of the cover story causes real strain: Leela only reluctantly accepts, unfamiliar with slavery as her own people practice it, while Batu Batu is asked to perform a role he already lives every day, standing beside a woman he knows to be free.
  • The party's escape is physically blocked by a large, patrolled wall and gatehouse spanning the river valley.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• Approximately three years have passed while the party was in the mist.
  • All party members (Cosimo, Knick Nab, Mani, Riu, and Werner), with the notable exception of Noddy, have been officially declared heretics along with key associates including Major Hubert, Captain De Guzman, Lieutenant Blaque, Lieutenant Dardell, and the priest Nicolas — now defrocked, and named on the notice only by his given name, without the title "Brother" he once held.
