  • One cannonball was used to fell the finger fruit tree.

docs.title: A Familiar Face in a Pirate's Haven
Events and Actions
docs.text:
Guided by Shark Fin, the crew of "The Bull" arrives at the notorious pirate haven known as Drowned Man's Port. Wary of the muskets they can see trained on them from the surrounding high ground, the party approaches under a flag of parlay, dismounts their swivel gun, and leaves the ship's boat visibly on deck to signal they mean no harm. Their entry is halted at Quarantine Island, where they must be vetted by the port authorities, Harbor Master Chretien and his subordinate Engerrand, to prove they are not agents of the Northern or Southern navies. Captain Knick Nab, dressed down from his usual flamboyant garb to something closer to what he wore while serving aboard the Bull's former command, goes ashore to plead their case, and Engerrand notes down the ship's name, its former service with the Northern fleet, and the captain's own name before escorting him to Chretien. After some debate, the party decides to give their true names rather than aliases, reasoning that Knick Nab is already a wanted man and any invented story would not hold up to scrutiny. Chretien demands proof that they can be trusted to keep the port's secrets; when Knick Nab offers Captain De Guzman's name alone, Chretien points out that he has no way to verify a captain who isn't even present, and hands over a paper for a fuller list of names who might vouch for them. The party compiles as thorough a list as they can recall — Captain De Guzman, Captain Barrows, Lieutenant Blaque, Prelate Nicolas, Lieutenant Dardell, Major Hubert, Randolph the Chronicler, Mistress Mary, Lady Clara, Burlyman and his wife, A'Wood, Hans, and Stick Stab — adding what context they can to make the more obscure names meaningful: Hans as a former Southern soldier taken prisoner in the Channel Islands, Stick Stab as a pickpocket the Church took from the capital, and Fritz and Lang as soldiers who had served under Major Domo Mathias Monadero. For good measure they round out the list with Steel Hand of Newport, the deserters Big Red, Tibalt, and Perkin left behind at Old Port's ruined church, and Suzette, a governor's daughter, in case any of the names mean something to the harbor master. Chretien relays the list to the mainland using an elaborate flag-signaling system that takes the rest of the day to complete; watching from a distance, the party catches glimpses of the signalers pausing to double back and correct themselves, a sign of just how intricate the code is. While they wait, the party stows their weapons in their foot lockers as a further gesture of good faith, and Mani whiles away the hours smoking his pipe and playing his lute on the dock. As evening falls, they take shelter in a tent on the island, sharing hammocks, water, rum, and a meal of biscuit and jerky. Before heading to the mainland to deliver the list himself, Shark Fin disarms and formally vouches for the party's character to Engerrand, is granted passage ahead of them, and leaves the party the address of his own lodgings, offering to act as their guide once they reach shore; he also agrees to carry word of Knick Nab's regards to Captain De Guzman and Captain Barrows, should either turn out to be in port. While waiting, the party also spots a large, anchored sloop within view of the harbor mouth that appears entirely deserted, though they cannot identify it at the time.

Their fortunes change the next morning when a boat is spotted approaching with a lady beneath a parasol seated amid its rowers; Mani, guessing at once who it must be, dashes to the dock to meet Mistress Clara, producing a stack of letters he has written her over the years and winning a kiss in their joyful reunion. Having heard of the party's arrival, Clara vouches for them before Engerrand, granting them access to the main port, then comes aboard the Bull herself, greeting the crew warmly and recalling each of the party by name. As they sail in, Clara recounts her harrowing story: she and Mistress Mary were captured and interrogated in the Capitol about the party's medallions after the party fled the city. Clara was pressed into service as ship's surgeon aboard a vessel sent in pursuit of the party — a role she secured only by convincing her captors she remained true to the Two — while Mary was left behind in custody, her fate since unknown. Clara's ship was navigated across the Maelstrom by an ancient Islander named Grantos and given its course by a mysterious red-haired youth; two priests of the Two were also aboard, one of whom went ashore at Spider Island in pursuit of the party and never returned. The ship was wrecked in the cataclysm and left impaled on a spire of rock at the heart of the Shatters, where Clara last saw it still standing before she survived by clinging to wreckage until a passing ship rescued her and brought her here, where she has practiced medicine for the three years since. Piecing together her account, the party suspects the red-haired youth was Stick Stab, though Clara's description of him as bare of any medallion gives them pause, since they know he lost his to Mani long ago.

Before sailing deeper into the harbor, Knick Nab and Werner gather the Bull's crew, backed by De Torres, to warn them that any misbehavior ashore would endanger everyone who had vouched for them; Cosimo lends the moment some theatrical weight, casting illusions that roll the captain's voice like thunder and fill the air with the taste of molasses and rum for encouragement, or bile and death for threat. The party then passes the same deserted sloop they had spotted earlier and, with a sharp eye, makes out its name and figurehead: it is "The Father's Fury," marked by a masterfully carved figurehead of a bearded man gripping a spear, its hold still full of rusting but salvageable cannon. Beyond it, the harbor itself proves well defended and busy, sheltering six or seven vessels including an enormous, heavily armed frigate. Still working their way toward the pier, the party falls into a long-running debate over their larger purpose, torn between the pirate's life the ship and its takings seem to invite and the sense that they are bound to something greater; they ultimately reaffirm that investigating the totems and countering the Divinity of Two remains their true mission, with piracy at most a means to that end. Once ashore, the party finds a sprawling market built from tents and storefronts, spots the Hospital on a hill overlooking the port, and notices the walled-off Shipwright's Yard, identifiable by a single mast rising behind its gates. Before splitting up, they briefly debate whether to spend their coin openly or keep a low profile, concluding that a visible show of prosperity is more likely to attract capable allies than to invite trouble. Some dine privately with Clara, others head for the port's pleasure houses, and the rest gather in the Drowned Man's Tavern's common room. There, a patron named Giles, drawn out with the offer of drinks, reveals that "The Father's Fury" was refitted here after being seized from the North, only to be found twice adrift with no one aboard, and points them toward the Shipwright's Yard for more. The mention of Captain De Guzman's name causes a stir in the tavern, with onlookers eager to hear news of him. A notice board reassures them that no wanted poster names heretics among its postings, though it does confirm "The Father's Fury" is for sale alongside a modest longboat, and lists several open crew positions, including a carpenter and a sailing master, pointing the party toward the Shipwright's Yard as their next step.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Shark Fin: Successfully guides the party to Drowned Man's Port. He vouches for the party's character before Engerrand, disarming himself as a show of good faith, then departs ahead of them for the mainland, leaving them the address of his lodgings and an offer to serve as their guide.
  • Engerrand: A port official on Quarantine Island who handles the initial interaction with the party.
  • Harbor Master Chretien: The official in charge of vetting new arrivals. He requires the party's list of names before he grants entry, and passes their claims to the mainland via signal flags overnight. He ultimately grants the party entry after Mistress Clara vouches for them.
  • Mistress Clara: Now a resident of Drowned Man's Port working as a doctor, she recognizes Mani from her boat and rushes ashore for a joyful reunion, then vouches for the whole party before Engerrand and rides back to the Bull with them. She recounts having been captured and interrogated in the Capitol alongside Mistress Mary, then pressed into service as ship's surgeon aboard a Church vessel hunting the party. She describes two priests and a mysterious red-haired youth aboard that ship, along with the ancient navigator Grantos; the ship wrecked at Spider Island and was left impaled on a spire of rock, and she survived by clinging to wreckage until a passing ship rescued her and brought her to the port, where she has practiced medicine for the three years since.
  • De Torres: The Bull's Master of Sail joins Werner and Knick Nab in addressing the crew before they head into port, backing the captain's warning that misbehavior ashore would endanger everyone who vouched for them.
  • Giles: A patron in The Drowned Man's Tavern who shows great interest in the fate of Captain De Guzman. Bought a round of drinks, he shares what he knows of "The Father's Fury" — that it was refitted here after being seized from the North, only to be found twice adrift and empty — and directs the party to the Shipwright's Yard for more.
  • Grantos (Mentioned): An ancient Islander prisoner who was forced to serve as the navigator for the Divinity of Two's vessel, guiding it through the Maelstrom without difficulty.
  • Red-Haired Youth (Mentioned): A mysterious figure who gave sailing orders on the Church's ship. The party suspects this was Stick Stab, though Clara recalls him as bearing no medallion.
  • Heretical Priest (Mentioned): A "crazy man" in Drowned Man's Port who preaches about "the brothers and the sisters" in addition to The Mother and The Father, suggesting a belief system that deviates from the orthodox Divinity of Two.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Drowned Man's Port: A large, independent pirate haven that was once a Southern naval bastion. Its residents, known colloquially as "the drowned men," are those who have abandoned or been abandoned by their old postings and now claim no allegiance to North or South. It is well-defended and serves as a refuge for pirates, deserters, and smugglers. Its sheltered harbor holds six or seven ships, including an enormous frigate, and its entrance is well covered by shore fortifications.
  • Quarantine Island: A small island at the mouth of the harbor where new ships and crews are held and vetted before being granted access to the main port.
  • The Drowned Man's Tavern: The central social hub of the port where the party gathers information.
  • The Market: A sprawling collection of tents and storefronts inside the port, ranging from stalls selling everyday goods and food to quieter tables dealing in high-value smuggled cargo. There is no visible law enforcement, but the party senses an underlying order all the same, kept by burly, armed men who look very much like hired muscle.
  • The Hospital: Mistress Clara's place of practice, set on a hill overlooking the port. She offers the party a night's lodging there.
  • The Shipwright's Yard: A walled yard behind large harbor gates, identifiable by a single mast rising above them, where a ship is under construction. Pointed to as the place to learn more about "The Father's Fury."

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text: The session's main conflict was social rather than physical. The party had to successfully navigate the vetting process of Drowned Man's Port, proving their independence from the major powers to gain entry, all while aware that a great many armed men watched them from the surrounding high ground and that they were well out of position to flee if the vetting went badly. The party noted no heavy ordnance among the fortifications trained on them, only muskets, though they suspected the port had other means of enforcing compliance without simply sinking a valuable ship outright.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Divinity's Pursuit: The party learned from Mistress Clara that the Church is actively hunting them specifically, rather than having simply stumbled onto a totem — a significant correction to their earlier assumption, though they remained divided over whether the ship's mission was to hunt them alone or to hunt totems in general. A dedicated ship, navigated by the Islander Grantos and given its course by a red-haired youth, carried two priests of the Two in pursuit of the party to Spider Island; one priest went ashore there and never returned. The ship itself was wrecked in the cataclysm and left impaled on a spire of rock, where Clara last saw it still standing.
  • Fate of Mistress Mary: Clara was separated from Mary when Clara was forced onto the Church's ship in the Capitol. Mary's fate since then is unknown.
  • A Heretical Preacher: The party learned from Clara of a "crazy" preacher in the port who speaks of "the brothers and the sisters" alongside the traditional Mother and Father of the Divinity of Two. This suggests the presence of an alternative or heretical belief system within the pirate haven.
  • The Cursed Sloop: The party discovered "The Father's Fury," a powerful sloop-of-war considered cursed after two separate crews vanished from it at sea. It is now for sale, with the Shipwright's Yard identified as the place to inquire further.
  • State of the Wider World: Clara explained that after the Shatters, the North and South settled into an uneasy truce, each preoccupied with concerns more pressing than their old war. Northern ships still reach these waters via the ice road, and Southern ships still cross the Maelstrom with the aid of navigators, but no one who has made either crossing in recent years has returned with word of conditions on the mainland, even though the Shatters reportedly extend as far as it. Giles, who crossed via the ice road and jumped ship about a year ago, added that the route is administered directly by the Northern Kingdom, and that what little trade passes between the port and the mainland is mostly in gold and wealth.
  • The Totems: By measuring the arc missing from their medallions — roughly an eighth of the circle lost for each totem destroyed — the party worked out that there were originally eight totems in the world. With two destroyed, six remain, and they have clues to the locations of four of them: one on Stone Island, one in the Channel Islands, one on the mainland, and one newly sensed by Mani somewhere to the west.
  • The Diad: Discussing the Church's diad, the party noted it is no ordinary symbol but a finely wrought, jeweled artifact of unusual metal, paraded through towns during Church processions and believed capable of enhancing the magical power of whoever is attuned to it. They speculated that diads may be rare and finite in number, and wondered whether this scarcity, and the Church's fear of the medallions, connects back to the desiccated corpse walled into the deepest level of the Capitol's dungeons decades ago.
  • Mission Reaffirmed: After a long debate over whether to pursue piracy or continue their investigation, the group confirmed their primary mission is to investigate the totems and counter the threat posed by the Divinity of Two. Arguments ranged from Cosimo's conviction that they are bound by fate to something larger than themselves, to Knick Nab's more pragmatic worry that an entire nation now seemed willing to devote real resources to hunting them down and that they needed to understand why before it caught up with them. The party agreed they are not alone in this fight and that finding allies among fellow travelers, such as the Islanders, may be part of achieving it, and that the ship, its crew, and their wealth should be treated as tools toward that end rather than distractions from it.
  • Displaying Wealth: Debating how to present themselves in port, the party weighed staying discreet against spending openly, ultimately favoring visible prosperity as a way to attract capable allies and recruits rather than risk looking like easy marks.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• Entry to Drowned Man's Port: The party gained access to a safe harbor, a place to resupply, recruit, and gather information.
  • Shark Fin's Address: The location of Shark Fin's lodgings in the port, along with his offer to act as their guide once they came ashore.
  • Information: Crucial intelligence from Mistress Clara about the Church's pursuit and the existence of "The Father's Fury," along with word from Giles in the tavern of the ship's troubled history, notice-board word of open crew postings for a carpenter and a sailing master, and a modest longboat also listed for sale.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • No significant items were lost during this session.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
In the Drowned Man's Tavern, the party weighed its options for the cursed sloop-of-war "Father's Fury," now that it was known to be up for sale. Discussion turned to the ship's evident needs — even their own vessel, "The Bull," ran short-handed with roughly a dozen crew against the twenty able seamen a ship her size properly required, and a true warship like the Father's Fury would need still more hands, including dedicated gun crews for a full broadside, on top of the difficulty of finding anyone willing to sign aboard a cursed vessel at all. Wary of committing their own ship too readily, they floated the idea of keeping the Bull as a second vessel — a mobile base and cargo hold to ferry supplies and captured animals back to port — rather than selling her outright, and set the thought aside for later. Having pooled what gold they could between them, roughly two hundred fifty gold apiece and some fifteen hundred all told if everyone contributed, the party agreed to inspect the ship before entertaining any purchase, and specifically not to offer up the Bull as part of any deal until they knew more. Someone floated the idea of simply winning the ship's deed at the tavern's card tables instead of buying it outright, but a quick round of self-assessment found nobody skilled enough at gambling to pull it off fairly, and the notion was dropped. That settled, they made their way to the shipwright's yard, drawing enough attention along the way — Cosimo's conspicuous hat chief among the reasons — that Knick Nab dropped back to watch for anyone following; he found only a knot of local boys eyeing them with idle curiosity, nothing more organized. There they found Master Borin, the peg-legged owner, presiding over a hive of construction: a dry dock nearing completion, and, separately, a ship drawn up on the beach to be careened and cleaned. Borin, checking his books, confirmed the Father's Fury had drawn no reasonable offers yet and quoted the going rate for an ordinary, uncursed sloop-of-war in the low thousands of gold, though he could not say what a seized, unmaintained, and cursed vessel like this one might fetch by comparison. He arranged for a reluctant laborer named Johan to row them out and note their questions, on the condition that he not board the ship himself.

During the row out, Johan recounted the ship's cursed history: long before it was a pirate vessel, the Father's Fury had been a captured northern ship, brought here to be refitted, and only afterward passed through two doomed pirate crews, led by captains "The Skull" and "Wolf," both of whom vanished without a trace after taking her to sea. He also mentioned that when the ship was first captured, its cargo hold held nothing but large barrels of what was said to be water, all of which had been found broken open. Climbing a thrown grapple line, the party scrambled aboard between two large skull-carved posts flanking the boarding point and found the rest of the ship similarly adorned, which Johan confirmed had been added at the Skull's order by the master carver Old Man Rayhar. In contrast, they noted that the figurehead — an exquisite carving of a furious, bearded man, worked from a single piece of oak — was original to the ship, carefully built into its front spar as one integrated piece rather than bolted on like the skulls; its quality struck them as reason enough why, superstition notwithstanding, no one had ever renamed the ship despite its curse. Asked whether the shipyard would still take on rigging and refitting a cursed vessel, Johan allowed that everything has its price. The vessel appeared to have been abandoned in a hurry, still equipped with four cannons, cannonballs, gunpowder, and the personal effects of its former crew.

Before setting foot near the bow, Noddy cast a spell of presence and sensed a sapient being nearby — something with intelligence well beyond an animal's — centred close to the figurehead. Once the party reached the forecastle, Noddy also cast detect magic on the figurehead and confirmed it was enchanted, before Riu attuned himself to it directly, sensing first that it was alive and aware; when he greeted it aloud in hope of a reply, it gave no response at all, but pressing deeper with a second attempt he discovered it was a sentient, magical entity imbued with the power of The Father, and that a third, unknown magic — neither The Father's nor The Mother's — permeated the entire ship, not just the carving. In the captain's cabin, the party recovered the log of Captain Wolf: he had taken the ship after buying it from the Skull, fitted it out with four guns and a bare-bones crew, and sailed uneventfully until a final entry recorded sighting an unnamed northern sloop, which he set off to pursue with all haste — the log ending abruptly there. Before beginning any ritual, Noddy quietly put Johan to sleep so the laborer would not witness what came next.

While Cosimo prepared his ritual, a search of the hold — prompted by a passing thought of where a smuggler might hide something worth taking — turned up nothing; it was entirely bare, without so much as a rat's carcass, an absence the party found unsettling for a ship abandoned in such haste and resolved to look into later. Reaching out toward the ship's magic a second time to aid the ritual, Riu felt his own connection to his medallion abruptly sever; he did not understand what had been lost, only that it took real effort — and a stroke of luck — to grab hold of it again and restore the connection before the ritual went ahead. Cosimo then wove a magical ritual around a simple sound illusion spell, channeling it through Riu's ongoing attunement and praying to The Father throughout, in an attempt to give the ship's presence an actual voice. After a tense wait, the figurehead responded: it animated, pulling itself free of the bow to confront the party as a towering, jerkily-moving wooden golem gripping a wooden trident, seeming to swell larger still as it drew itself upright. The sight struck the entire party with a paralyzing fear that rooted them to the spot; only Knick Nab and Noddy broke free of it, Knick Nab shouting for a retreat and leaping overboard to swim for shore while Noddy vanished under an invisibility spell. The being, identifying itself as The Father, rose denouncing Cosimo as "blasphemous heresy" and commanding him to be gone from its ship; when Mani protested that Cosimo had only ever given it glory, The Father dismissed him just as coldly — "he has done and brought me nothing... I do not know him" — and hurled its trident at Cosimo; only his helmet kept the blow from caving in his skull, deflecting it into his cheek instead. Mani, invoking the power of the medallions against the creature as he shot it — landing a solid, bleeding wound — felt nothing come of the invocation itself, learning that whatever fear or protection the medallions hold over the Church meant nothing to The Father. In the midst of the fight, the party also came to suspect that The Father was a being distinct from the ship itself, raising hope that destroying it might free the vessel rather than doom it.

As the party fell back toward the boats, an earlier spell of Noddy's meant to trip the creature failed outright, and his follow-up water bolt did almost nothing — the creature seemed to shrug off water as though it were part of its own being. Werner's javelins fared better: his prized enchanted +10 javelin, thrown first, punched clean through the creature's chest, and his two remaining javelins followed, one tearing off a finger and the other pinning a foot to the deck, while gunfire and Cosimo's own spellfire, his eyes crackling with lightning as he loosed a bolt, chipped away at it further and set it alight. Standing his ground nearest the creature to cover the others' retreat, Mani twice met its swings with a full parry and a practiced riposte, landing counterattacks that did little more than bounce his rapier off the wood — though one of the creature's own missed blows smashed clean through a section of the ship's carved skull railing instead. Riu broke off from the fight to stem Cosimo's bleeding with a string of healing spells while the others covered the retreat. Mani, the last to leave the ship, tried to swing down on a rope to snatch away the creature's fallen trident and deny it a ranged weapon, but found it pinned under The Father's own feet and had to abandon the attempt, diving into the sea instead as the burning, heavily damaged creature leapt in after him.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Master Borin: The peg-legged owner of the shipwright's yard who wants to sell the "Father's Fury." He confirmed the ship had drawn no reasonable offers yet and quoted the going rate for an ordinary, uncursed sloop-of-war in the low thousands of gold.
  • Johan: A laborer from the shipyard who rowed the party to the cursed ship. Put to sleep by Noddy so he would not witness the party's ritual, he wasn't woken until the fleeing Knick Nab was thrown into the boat with him — at which point he saw The Father and screamed in terror, rooted to the bottom of the boat.
  • The Father: The animated, sentient figurehead of the "Father's Fury," a large wooden golem that embodies the wrath of The Father.
  • "The Skull" (Mentioned): The first pirate captain of the "Father's Fury," a brash young upstart who took the moniker to inspire terror. After capturing the ship, he commissioned the master carver Old Man Rayhar to add its many skull carvings, then took her to sea laden with swords and muskets, and vanished with his crew without a trace.
  • "Wolf" (Mentioned): The second pirate captain of the "Father's Fury," a seasoned southern captain who bought the ship from the Skull, fitted it out with a bare-bones crew, and also vanished with his crew after logging a final sighting of an unnamed northern sloop he set off to chase.
  • Old Man Rayhar (Mentioned): The master carver of Drowned Man's Port, an elderly Islander of exquisite skill, commissioned by the Skull to carve the "Father's Fury"'s many skull decorations from oak staves.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Drowned Man's Port: The party explored more of the pirate haven.
  • The Drowned Man's Tavern: Where the party debated the merits of the cursed ship against their own before setting out.
  • The Shipwright's Yard: A large, active yard under Master Borin, with a dry dock nearing completion and, separately, a ship drawn up on the beach to be careened and cleaned.
  • The Father's Fury: A cursed sloop-of-war anchored outside the port, originally a captured northern vessel before it was ever refitted as a pirate ship. The party explored its deck, gun deck, and captain's cabin before being attacked; its gun deck was fitted with ports for eight cannons, though only four were actually mounted, run in and untouched for months.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The party confronted the animated figurehead of the "Father's Fury."
  • Upon animating, the creature struck the entire party with a paralyzing fear, rooting them to the spot; only Knick Nab and Noddy broke free of it immediately.
  • The creature, "The Father," attacked the party, focusing its wrath on Cosimo.
  • Cosimo was struck in the face by the creature's thrown trident, but his helmet saved him from a more grievous injury.
  • Mani invoked the power of the medallions against the creature as he shot it, but the gesture had no apparent effect.
  • The party fought a running battle while retreating from the ship, inflicting significant damage on the creature: setting it alight, driving Werner's enchanted javelin through its chest, shooting off part of an ear, and burning a bolt across its forearm, though Noddy's water bolt and a spell meant to trip it both failed to do much.
  • Mani twice parried the creature's blows and countered with a riposte, though his rapier barely scratched the wood; one of its missed swings instead smashed through a section of the ship's own carved railing.
  • Mani's attempt to swing down on a rope and steal the creature's fallen trident before retreating failed when he found it pinned beneath its own feet.
  • The conflict ended with the creature, ablaze and badly damaged, leaping into the sea in pursuit of Mani.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The party learned the detailed history of the "Father's Fury," including that it began as a captured northern vessel before its two vanished pirate crews, and that its original cargo was said to have been many barrels of water, all of which were found broken open.
  • They confirmed the ship is cursed, with the source being its sentient figurehead.
  • Riu's attunement revealed three distinct sensations from the figurehead: 1) it is sentient, 2) it has been blessed by The Father, and 3) a third, unknown magic (not of The Mother) permeates both the figurehead and the entire ship.
  • Reaching for the ship's magic a second time to aid Cosimo's ritual, Riu felt his own connection to his medallion abruptly sever; he managed to reforge it only with real effort and a stroke of luck, though its meaning remains unclear to him.
  • A search of the hold, prompted by wondering where a smuggler might hide something worth taking, found it entirely bare — not even a rat's carcass — an absence the party found unsettling for a ship abandoned in such haste, and one they resolved to look into later.
  • The medallions' power, or whatever fear they inspire in the Church, seemed to mean nothing to The Father: invoking them while attacking it had no discernible effect.
  • The party came to suspect The Father is a being distinct from the ship itself, raising hope that destroying it might free the vessel without harming it.
  • A ship the size of the Bull needs roughly twenty able seamen to be properly crewed, well beyond the party's current complement of about a dozen; a true warship like the Father's Fury would need still more hands on top of that, including dedicated gun crews for a full broadside.
  • Johan confirmed the shipwright's yard would still take on rigging and refitting a cursed ship, provided the price was right.
  • With its trident lost to the deck, the creature was left without a ranged attack for the rest of the fight, a small tactical relief as the party fell back.
  • The creature declared Cosimo a blasphemer, stating, "He has done and brought me nothing. He is no one. I do not know him."
  • Before being interrupted, the creature declared, "All power is mine and hers."

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• The party recovered navigation maps from the captain's cabin of the "Father's Fury."
  • Master Borin confirmed no reasonable offers had yet been made for the ship, and quoted an uncursed sloop-of-war's worth in the low thousands of gold; the Father's Fury, seized, unmaintained, and cursed, may go for considerably less. It remains equipped with four cannons, cannonballs, gunpowder, and the personal effects of its former crew, all ready for whoever takes it.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: • Werner used all three of his javelins, including his prized +10 enchanted javelin thrown first, embedding them in the creature — one driven clean through its chest, one tearing off a finger, and one pinning a foot to the deck.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session began with the party scattered after the animated figurehead, the "Father's Fury," fell burning into the water. Moments earlier, Mani and Werner had pelted it with javelins and harpoons while it drove them back to the stern; Werner leapt off first, then Mani, and the figurehead plunged into the sea right after them. Riu and Cosimo waited in a small boat with the unconscious sailor, Johan, while Mani and Werner made for the boat as well. Knick Nab swam for the shore, and Noddy climbed onto the deck of the ship. Cosimo was carrying a severe, near-fatal wound from the earlier fight; Riu spent much of the coming battle keeping him stable with Flow Stop and Cut Repair spells, though the wound left Cosimo unable to move — or be moved — without risking the bleeding starting again.

As the party regrouped on and around the ship, a cold fog rolled out of the sea itself, swallowing visibility down to fifty feet, and the figurehead rose on a column of water to attack. A chaotic battle ensued as the party fought the creature while simultaneously working to gain control of the ship and sail it away. Partway through the fight, Johan panicked and abandoned the boat to swim for shore; the figurehead answered by churning the water around him into a vortex that nearly dragged him under. Noddy's familiar, Pocket, spotted him struggling, and Noddy teleported him safely onto the ship's deck with a Lofty Bridge spell cast through the bird.

Cosimo pressed the attack with repeated Shock Bolt spells, invoking the Mother to strike the figurehead down; one solid hit shattered its ankle and hampered its advance across the water. On a later casting attempt, the figurehead countered with a Cancel Essence spell of its own, dissipating Cosimo's incoming lightning and declaring, "It is you, creature, who falsely calls upon the mother. The mother rejects you, as do I." It answered with a bolt of water of its own, which Cosimo split harmlessly in two with a shouted "Shield me," and later turned the trick back on the figurehead, casting Cancel Essence himself to deflect a second bolt aside. Noddy tried to frighten the creature away with a Fear spell, but it seemed wholly unaffected, leading the party to suspect it was a golem or otherwise immune to mind-affecting magic; he had far more success collapsing the water column it stood on with repeated Vacuum spells, sending it crashing back down to the surface again and again, and later pinned it in place with a Staying spell, exerting 125 pounds of telekinetic counterforce that forced it to visibly strain against the resistance and bought the party several crucial rounds. When the figurehead conjured a churning wall of water across the deck to blind the party to the ship's wheel, Noddy burned it away again with an Evaporate Liquid spell. Mani, convinced the figurehead was merely an avatar of something else being controlled, repeatedly demanded to know who commanded it; the figurehead only replied that "the Father listens only to the true believers," offering no further explanation, and gave much the same non-answer when Mani pressed the question again later in the fight. He also twice searched the ship's countless skull carvings for some distinguishing mark that might explain how to control it, hoping the party might tame the figurehead rather than destroy it, but found nothing that stood out from the rest. Mani hurled chain shot and bolas at the creature — most throws going wide, though one chain-shot wrenched its already-shattered ankle and left it limping on both legs — while, with help from an illusory "Handsome Gulliver Gold" summoned by Cosimo, the rest of the party worked to raise the anchor and unfurl the sails. The forward anchor's chain couldn't be cut, so Knick Nab worked the capstan across several rounds to haul it free before climbing the rigging himself to help drop sail; the stern anchor's rope was thick enough to give even Noddy trouble, but he hacked through it in one blow that sent one end splashing into the water and the other slithering across the deck. Gulliver Gold tied off one critical line that gave the rigging effort a significant boost, but in a later round threw himself between Cosimo and an incoming water bolt meant for his summoner, losing his sense of touch and, with it, his ability to keep helping with the sails. Werner initially helped fend the ship off the nearby rocks with a pole before taking the helm and later firing one of the ship's cannons.

During the fight, Riu made an early attempt to attune to the ship and, later, to command it to sail away on its own; the command worked, but as he gave it, every skull carving on the hull seemed to turn and look at him, an omen unsettling enough to nearly cost him his composure. His attunement also confirmed the ship possessed genuine sentience of its own, distinct from the figurehead, whose presence he could not detect within it. Later, as the figurehead closed on the fleeing ship, Noddy tried to attune to it again to make sense of what they were facing; the attempt itself failed at that range, but it pulled him into a trance regardless, and he emerged moments later with a complete vision of the ship's history — that it was the Father's Fury, a vessel saturated with holy water whose figurehead animates and seeks vengeance whenever priests of the Divinity of Two are slain aboard it.

The party finally managed to get the ship under sail and began to pull away, but the figurehead refused to give up the chase, wading doggedly after them across the water even as it took hit after hit. Once they broke clear of the fog with it still several hundred feet behind, an argument broke out over what to do next: Cosimo argued strongly against firing the ship's cannons, warning that the shore battery overlooking the harbor might mistake it for an attack and sink them for it, while Mani and others countered that no one watching from the fort would think twice about cannon fire aimed at a walking, animated tree. Part of the party pushed instead to find a way to tame the figurehead rather than destroy it outright, while others balked at giving any outside priest that kind of leverage over their new ship, but the debate went unresolved. Riu, still puzzling over why the figurehead had singled them out when none of them had killed a priest aboard, tried to commune with it directly as it closed the distance, but got no answer. The party kept the guns loading while they argued; when the figurehead finally came within range, Werner fired one of the ship's cannons and scored a direct hit, destroying the creature completely in a spray of splinters and water.

With the figurehead destroyed, the party dropped anchor, and Riu made one more attempt to attune to the ship; he concluded it hadn't been formally enchanted so much as simply saturated through and through with whatever power the holy water carried, and resolved to try again after a night's rest. Mani, holding one of Riu's Diads in one hand and his own Medallion in the other while touching the ship, attempted his own attunement and felt a personal connection to both the ship and his Medallion, though notably not to the borrowed Diad. Rowing back toward shore, the party debated what to do about Johan, who had no memory of anything past hitting his head; Cosimo initially tried to convince him the whole ordeal was a bump and a bad dream, but the others opted to tell him the truth instead, and a jubilant Mani began rehearsing how the party — freshly settled on the name "The Faded" after briefly considering and rejecting "the Heretic Six" — would be remembered as legends. Back at the Shipwright's Yard, Master Borin met them with visible unease; Mani, backed by Johan's account of the fight, offered 1,000 gold for the ship and invoked the party's reputation, including their past defense of the Port of Zylos and their standing as declared heretics, while Borin — noting this would be the third time he had sold this particular ship, and that its true value might run closer to 3,000 gold, if anyone actually wanted it — said the situation was too strange for him to decide alone and that he needed to consult his council.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• The Father's Fury: The animated figurehead of the ship. It demonstrated powerful water-based magic, including walking on water, creating a water wall, firing bolts of water, and countering one of Cosimo's spells with its own Cancel Essence. It proved unaffected by Noddy's Fear spell and spoke twice during the fight, declaring itself loyal only to "true believers" and rejecting the party's invocations of the Mother. It was ultimately destroyed by a cannonball.
  • Johan: The sailor who rowed the party to the ship. He was knocked unconscious, thrown in the boat, and later panicked and jumped overboard during the fight, nearly drowning in the figurehead's churning water before Noddy teleported him to safety. Afterward, Cosimo tried to convince him he had simply struck his head and imagined everything, though the party ultimately told him the truth instead; a delighted Mani recruited him to back up their story with Master Borin and to help spread word of the party's exploits.
  • Master Borin: The master shipwright at the port. The party began negotiations with him to purchase the ship, offering 1,000 gold; he noted its estimated value might run closer to 3,000 gold if there were any real demand for a cursed vessel, remarked that this would be the third time he had sold this particular ship, and said the situation was too strange for him to decide alone, needing to consult his council before naming a price.
  • Handsome Gulliver Gold: An illusion with physical form summoned by Cosimo to assist with sailing the ship. He helped haul rigging and later took a water bolt meant for Cosimo, losing his sense of touch in the process.
  • Pocket: Noddy's familiar, who located Johan struggling in the water and helped guide Noddy's rescue spell to him.
  • The Skull: The pirate captain who first purchased the Father's Fury after it was saturated with holy water, refitted it with cannons, and commissioned Old Man Rayhar's skull carvings; his own crew was later wiped out by the figurehead's first vengeful massacre after they killed two captive priests, learned from Noddy's vision of the ship's history.
  • Wolf: A Southern pirate captain who later acquired the Father's Fury; his crew forced two captive priests to walk the plank, triggering the figurehead's second massacre, learned from Noddy's vision of the ship's history.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Father's Fury: The primary location of the session. A ship of Northern Navy origin, commandeered by the Divinity of Two, and later used by pirates. It is covered in skull carvings and its figurehead is prone to animating.
  • The waters outside the harbor: The battle took place here, near a rocky shoreline.
  • The Fort: The harbor's shore battery, visible above the water where the battle took place; the party held their fire until clear of its line of sight for fear of provoking it.
  • The Shipwright's Yard: The party returned here at the end of the session to speak with Master Borin.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The party engaged in a prolonged battle against the animated figurehead, the Father's Fury, while Cosimo fought the entire encounter with a severe, near-fatal wound from the earlier fight, requiring ongoing field treatment from Riu.
  • The figurehead attacked with powerful water magic and demonstrated notable magical resistance, shrugging off a Fear spell and countering one of Cosimo's attacks with its own Cancel Essence spell.
  • No significant new injuries were sustained by the PCs during this session's combat.
  • The figurehead was hit with numerous spells and projectiles before being destroyed by a cannon shot from Werner.
  • Once the ship broke clear of the fog with the figurehead still in pursuit, Cosimo and Mani clashed over whether to fire the ship's cannons at it, Cosimo fearing it would draw retaliatory fire from the fort guarding the harbor; the party loaded the guns anyway and fired once the figurehead came within range.
  • Mani repeatedly demanded to know who commanded the figurehead, but got only the same non-answer about "true believers" each time; Riu's separate attempt to commune with it and learn why it had singled out the party went unanswered.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• As the figurehead closed on the ship, Noddy's attunement attempt failed outright at that range, but it pulled him into a trance regardless, and he emerged with the ship's complete history:
    • It is the Father's Fury, sister ship to the Mother's Sorrow. Both were originally standard Northern Navy vessels, blessed in the name of the Father, before the church commandeered them near the end of the war.
    • The two ships were purpose-built to carry casks of holy water to the New World to bless it, and were hauled across the ice bridge by slave labor before sailing south to their separate destinations.
    • It was commandeered by the Divinity of Two and filled with barrels of holy water.
    • A priest broke the barrels, saturating the ship's wood with holy water.
    • The figurehead animates to seek vengeance whenever priests of the Divinity of Two are killed aboard the ship. This has happened at least twice, leading to the death or disappearance of two separate pirate crews.
    • The ship was bought and refit by a pirate captain known as "The Skull," who commissioned the extensive skull carvings from an islander named "Old Man Rayhar." The first massacre occurred under his command, after his crew killed two captive priests taken from a prize ship.
    • The second massacre occurred years later under a pirate captain named "Wolf," who bought the ship after it was found abandoned following the first massacre, after his crew forced two captive priests to walk the plank.
  • Riu's early attempt to attune to and command the ship confirmed it possesses genuine sentience of its own, separate from the figurehead — his attunement detected no trace of the father's presence within the ship itself.
  • Mani theorized aloud that three distinct magics were at play: whatever power the ship itself was imbued with, the ship's sentience, and the figurehead's connection to "the father" — a connection Riu's attunement suggested had been severed, which Mani took as a sign the figurehead itself might one day be tamed or controlled rather than simply destroyed.
  • Amid the debate over what to do with the pursuing figurehead, someone raised the idea of consulting Nicolas — the mad hermit-preacher of the hills above Drowned Man's Port, who preaches of "brothers and sisters" — to see if he could help control it, though others were wary of giving any priest that kind of leverage over their new ship.
  • Riu's attunement attempt after the battle suggested the ship had not been formally enchanted, but was simply saturated through and through with whatever power the holy water carried; he could not say more without trying again after a night's rest.
  • Mani, holding a borrowed Diad and his own Medallion while touching the ship, felt a personal, magical connection to both the ship and his Medallion, but not to the Diad.
  • The party settled on a group name — "The Faded" — after briefly floating and rejecting "the Heretic Six."
  • The party began negotiations to buy the ship, offering Master Borin 1,000 gold. Mani invoked the party's reputation — including their past defense of the Port of Zylos and their standing as declared heretics — to press for a sale, though Borin said he needed to consult his council first.

docs.text:
• The party has taken effective control of the ship, the Father's Fury.
  • Mani collected a finger bone from the destroyed figurehead.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text:

  • Mani used all three rounds of chain shot he had found.

docs.title: A Tale of Spies and Statues
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The party wraps up its opening haggle with Shipwright Master Borin over The Father's Fury, having opened at 1,000 gold and argued that only they can manage the ship's curse, making it worthless to anyone else; Borin says he must consult others before he can commit to a price and excuses himself. A soldier then comes running into the shipyard, badly winded, asking whether anyone saw what happened out in the harbor — he's been sent to find and report on whoever was responsible. When the party admits it was them, he panics, trips over some baskets scrambling to get away, and bolts off towards the fort regardless. The party decides to seek out the local "crazy priest" before dealing with the authorities, reasoning that if the fort's business really concerns them, it will come looking regardless. They learn from the sailor Johan that the priest lives in the hills but sometimes preaches in the market. Before leaving, Mani turns his charm on Johan directly, pitching him a berth aboard their future ship with the promise that facing one's fears means living dangerously at sea; Johan, having just watched them face down the ship's curse, is won over and agrees to consider sailing with them — and to see who else he can bring.

In the marketplace, they find the soldier telling a confused, disjointed story about the battle with the ship's figurehead to a gathering crowd. Before Knick Nab takes over — bareheaded, having left off his usual headband for the performance — the party quickly agrees on how to frame themselves: the ship's animated figurehead as a monstrous antagonist and their own role as its slayers, with the fog and the stranger magic left deliberately vague. Knick Nab steps up, gently eases the soldier off his soapbox, and retells the tale with far more drama and coherence, subtly enhanced by Cosimo's illusions — a touch of extra volume and a nimbus of light rather than anything overt. During his tale, he attributes the fight's stranger effects to "the three," implying powers beyond the Mother and Father worshipped by the Two, and the crowd's chatter about wind gods, water gods, and family analogies eventually settles into a connection between his description of a flying golden man and a pre-existing figure in their beliefs known as "the brother." While Knick Nab performs, the rest of the party quietly watches the crowd for anyone reacting badly or suspiciously; they find only fascination, disbelief, and a few people insisting they'd seen it with their own eyes — no sign of hostility.

Their performance is interrupted when a mountain of a man shoulders through the crowd carrying an oversized boat hook — Captain Garth 'The Gaff' Morgan, enforcer of the town's ruling body, who "invites" them to speak with the council. Mani, Knick Nab, Werner, and Cosimo go with him, while Noddy and Riu stay behind; Noddy uses attunement to keep a general sense of the others' direction and follows at a discreet distance, while Riu rows out into the bay to salvage debris from the shattered figurehead, confirming with a quick casting that the wood no longer carries any trace of the magic that once animated it. The other four are led to a cluster of tents and driftwood buildings — the council's meeting hall, built around a large, ramshackle round table of driftwood and carved timber — and brought before "The Drowned Council," five pirate captains who govern the town: Captain Silas 'Blackheart' Kane, Isla 'The Weaver' Vargo, Garth 'The Gaff' Morgan, 'Rattlebone' Jones, and Corbin 'Turncoat' Vance. Kane presses them on their origins; the party recounts sailing first under Captain Barrows and later Captain De Guzman, being put ashore to investigate the "Stone Isle," and losing their rendezvous with the ship. Kane recognizes both names "from the war" but has no news of either captain's whereabouts, and Isla Vargo — the council's information broker — admits she doesn't know either, though she recalls a Major Hubert may be among those the Church has executed as heretics. Werner introduces himself in full, as the third son of Kasimir De Rendal, Duke of the North, and Kane recognizes the family name at once; Mani, more guarded, gives the council a name that isn't his own, and receives no such courtesy. The conversation turns tense when the council notices Knick Nab's ears, uncovered since his performance in the market, and brands him a "misborn" — a term he bristles at, nearly demanding satisfaction before the rest of the party talks the moment down. Kane rises and circles him afterward on a peg leg of curved, pale bone — whale, perhaps, or something larger — studying him from both sides, and offers only a cryptic "I think I know you" before returning to business. Satisfied, the council offers a deal: they will help the party acquire The Father's Fury and grant them safe harbor if the party investigates potential spies watching the town from the nearby hills.

The party agrees to the terms, framing it as a chance to earn a permanent home for the whole crew, not just themselves. They settle the outline of the ship exchange — the Bull, sound but for a cracked spar from an old cannon shot, fully restocked and outfitted apart from a crew, for the cursed ship repaired to a comparable standard — with Rattlebone doing a bone-casting to seal the arrangement and facilitate it with Master Borin; they deliberately hold off on commissioning a new figurehead until they're sure the old one won't animate again. Kane confirms there are no regular patrols into the hills, no known threat from the local islanders (several of whom live and work peacefully in the port), and that the sense of being watched is recent and strongest during the day. The council also notes, when asked, that the port has no slave market and no slavery of its own — a point of pride, in contrast to some other ports the party has seen. Before they leave, Vance provides a note granting the party access to the fort's battlements and a second letter authorizing townsfolk to render them aid.

The party regroups and heads to the fort — built into the cliff overlooking the harbor and still under construction — to survey the surrounding hills. From the ramparts, Noddy spots a strangely shaped, artificial-looking hill in the distance, and the party also makes out wisps of smoke rising along the coast to the north, hinting at another settlement further up the shore. Werner also feels a disturbing sense that the cursed ship in the harbor is watching him — not for the first time, he recalls, since the skulls carved into its hull turned to watch him once before, when he first tried to sense the ship's magic.

That evening, the party returns to the hospital, where Mistress Clara allows them one more night's lodging. They ask to speak with the islander who works there and question her about the third hill and the wildlife of the interior; she describes deer, goats, and dangerous bears and wolves, but nothing resembling pygmies or witch doctors, and confirms that the priest's shrine lies close by, in the ravine. Down in the town's lower quarter, Knick Nab buys a pair of grenades and finds the tavern crowd already talking of nothing but the harbor commotion; a few recognize him from his performance and buy him drinks, and word is quietly spreading that the cursed ship's crew might soon be looking for hands. Mani, for his part, tries his charm on Mistress Clara directly, falling just short — a near miss rather than a disaster — before climbing up to leave a flower and a signed haiku on her windowsill: "Island beauty comes / Healer of my heart and soul / Lost and now returned." It seems to have little apparent effect.

Werner spends that night cleaning and re-oiling his firearms, as is his habit before heading into the field. The following morning, the party provisions heavily — several days of food and water, rope, and an away-team kit of torches and oil — but opts for a tarp over a proper tent to keep moving quickly. They set out, with Leela and Batu Batu in tow and Salter left behind both to mind the ship and to keep their personal gear off the books before the trade with the council goes through, along the path into the ravine where the priest is said to live, bandying about possible names for their still-unofficial crew along the way ("the fated" and "the blessed men" among the contenders) without settling on one. Partway in they come across a life-size wooden carving of Handsome Gulliver Gold standing in a niche in the rock, painted and exquisitely detailed — though this one, unlike earlier sightings, has no wings. It faces a second, matching niche cut into the rock across the passage, clearly prepared but left empty. Cosimo swears the carving isn't one of his illusions, and Werner's examination of the wood — expert work in a single piece, at most a year or two old — turns up an odd, unbidden association with the individually carved and tapered skulls on the Father's Fury. Deeper in, the ravine opens into a small clearing tidied into a rough shrine: log seating, a hewn table, and a second carving of Handsome Gulliver Gold, sword drawn, built up from many joined pieces rather than one, facing another empty space clearly left for a third. A door of rough-hewn timber seals a cave at the back of the clearing; the party knocks and calls out, but gets no answer beyond the sound of someone sleeping deeply within, and the door resists both force and magic. They leave word that they'll return, and press on into the hills.

The trek to the strange hill Noddy spotted takes a full two days, foraging as they go — Werner manages only a single rabbit with his harpoon, while Leela and Batu Batu bring in several more by the campfire — before they reach its base and confirm, with a careful climb and a wide perimeter check, that it is in fact a large, man-made pyramid of fitted, man-portable local stone, roughly thirty feet on a side and thirty feet high. The stonework shows real skill but no exotic materials or tools, and its style tells them nothing — though Noddy recalls tales from his childhood in the Highlands of similar stacks of stone out in the wastelands beyond the hills to the east. The capstone, they determine, was recently replaced; lifting it and the layer beneath turns up nothing but more stone, no chamber, no markings, and no trace of magic anywhere on the structure — nor any sign of a path leading to or from it, leaving no clue how its builders reached the summit. An item feel spell reveals its purpose as "calm and familial success" — a phrase that echoes the kind of blessing the Church of the Two might offer — but who built the pyramid, and why, remains a mystery.

• There were no physical conflicts in this session.
  • The primary conflict was the tense negotiation with The Drowned Council, where the party's future in the port was decided.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The town is governed by a council of five pirate captains known as The Drowned Council. They are concerned about being spied upon and have tasked the party with investigating. The party learned the following about its members:
    • Captain Silas 'Blackheart' Kane: The apparent leader, who has a bone peg leg. He is deeply concerned about spies watching the port from the hills. Though no one has seen them, he suspects their presence based on a persistent feeling and observing unusual animal behavior (goats, birds, a bear). He wants to know who the spies report to. He recognized Werner's noble family name on sight, and studied Knick Nab with unsettling familiarity after the council challenged his hidden nature.
    • Isla 'The Weaver' Vargo: The sole female member, she is an information broker whose business is "knowing where people are." She had no current knowledge of Captain Barrows or Captain De Guzman's whereabouts, though she recalled that a Major Hubert may be among those the Church has executed as heretics.
    • Garth 'The Gaff' Morgan: A massive man who acts as the council's enforcer, wielding a giant boat hook (a gaff).
    • 'Rattlebone' Jones: A gaunt, superstitious man who uses bone-casting for divination and agreed to facilitate the party's acquisition of the ship after a reading.
    • Corbin 'Turncoat' Vance: A disgraced former Northern Navy officer who still wears his uniform and provided the party with written permission to access the fort, along with a separate letter authorizing townsfolk to render them aid.
  • The "crazy priest" is almost certainly Nicolas, the former priest from the "Advance," who now worships Handsome Gulliver Gold as "the brother." He has established a shrine in a cave.
  • The people of the port seem to have a pre-existing belief in "the brother," which aligns with Cosimo's illusions of Handsome Gulliver Gold.
  • Werner learns that the skulls on the Father's Fury have an unsettling awareness of him, having turned to watch him on a previous occasion.
  • Examining the shrine's carving of Handsome Gulliver Gold, Werner found himself recalling — without knowing why — that the individual skulls on the Father's Fury were each tapered pieces of expertly joined white oak. The unbidden memory suggests some connection between the ship's carver and whoever carved the shrine's statues, though neither its meaning nor its source is clear.
  • There is a large, man-made stone pyramid on a hilltop, built within the last 40 years. Its purpose is unknown but seems to be related to "familial success." Noddy associates it with similar structures rumored to exist in the eastern wastelands.
  • While debating whether the port's watchers might be using animals as spies, the party confirms the limits of Noddy's bond with Pocket: it lets him sense the presence of other sentient, thinking beings, not ordinary animals — an actual bird or mouse wouldn't register as anything unusual. Cosimo, for his part, insists there's no such thing as "animal magic" in the eyes of the Two.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
The party camps for the night at the base of the large stone pyramid they discovered, under a clear, moonless, starry sky with a warm breeze blowing in from inland. Someone floats the idea of testing whether the deer and goats they'd seen watching them are being magically controlled, but casting a working capable of detecting it would mean investing two hours in a ritual for only a 50-50 chance of even managing to cast it, and the herd has already wandered off by the time anyone could attempt it.

During the night, while Cosimo and Noddy are keeping watch, they hear a distant, muffled, irregular thumping echoing up from the valley below — like a slow drumbeat, with no flash of light to match it. Pressing an ear to the ground brings no clearer sense of it. Werner is woken to listen, and drawing on his family's knowledge of naval ordnance, identifies it as cannon fire, though the rate of fire is far too fast for any real gun crew — either an implausibly large number of guns or an unnaturally fast gunner. Pocket flies to the top of the pyramid to look but sees nothing. Werner then tries to triangulate the source with a compass and dead reckoning, walking some distance along the ridge and lining up stones to mark the bearing, but the sound stops before he can get a fix, leaving the mystery for morning.

Morning turns up no smoke, no fire, and no other trace of whatever made the noise, and breakfast is a simple meal of beans Batu Batu had left soaking overnight. The party then descends a meandering game trail — clearly never maintained for human travel — down into the valley. At the bottom, Leela finds boot prints in the meadow: one or two days old, and possibly belonging to a single person who passed through twice, though she can't be certain which. The party follows the trail across the open, lightly wooded meadow toward the far side of the valley.

They come upon a man calling himself Arnum: a sailor-turned-homesteader splitting wood beside a crude log-and-leaf hut, with an unlit fire pit nearby. He claims to live here alone, visiting town only now and then in an unsuccessful search for a wife. He's curt and denies noticing anything odd about the local wildlife.

Noddy approaches Arnum alone and casts Charm Kind on him, feeling something try to interfere with the spell before it takes hold anyway. A charmed and suddenly friendly Arnum offers him a ladle of water, invites him closer, and advises him to head back to town. Watching from above, Pocket notices that the hut looks unnaturally shallow for its apparent depth — a facade — and relays the impression to Noddy, who returns to the group and casts Detect Illusion, confirming the hut isn't real.

Back with the group, growing wary, Arnum seems to concentrate on something and edges around to the far side of the woodpile, leaving his axe behind but keeping hold of his musket. Cosimo casts his own Detect Illusion directly at Arnum, but the spell is forcibly and deliberately blocked — the first time any of them have felt magic actively resisted like that. Around the same moment, Knick Nab hears a voice in his head — "I wasn't expecting relief for another year" — and, alarmed, calls for the group to seize him. Weapons are drawn and the standoff turns tense, but Noddy talks the group down, pointing out that people with pointed ears have done them a good turn before (recalling the Elf A'Wood, who once taught Noddy and Cosimo the fundamentals of their magic), and the group stands down.

Chewing on his Bitterroot, Noddy alone can now see that "Arnum" has unmistakably pointed ears, and that the hut has resolved into stacked piles of stone, atop one of which sits a second, naked Elf holding a rolled sheet of paper. A third Elf, Hortaf, then walks out unarmed and sits down to negotiate, introducing the other two as Abedneith and Coralon — visible to everyone now, since he wears no glamour of his own. To let the rest of the party see what only he can, Noddy shares a piece of his Bitterroot around; Riu chews some and notices the same faint numbness and sharpened focus it's given him before. The illusion over Abedneith and the hut persists for the rest of the party until, near the end of the conversation, Hortaf lets it drop.

Hortaf confirms they are the "spies" the council is concerned about. He explains they have a secret arrangement with Isla 'The Weaver' Vargo: they feed her up-to-date intelligence from the mainland in exchange for being allowed to watch the port, an arrangement the rest of the Drowned Council does not appear to know about. Pressed on their origins, he says only that his people come from a land beyond the mountains, in the Highlands, and that his group's relief isn't due from the west for about another year.

Amid the exchange, the party shows Hortaf an old map bearing a reference to "Gildenhome." He recognizes it as the name of an ancient city but knows nothing more, and offers to try to learn more, though it will take time. Asked about the black obsidian totems the party has encountered, he describes them only in the vaguest terms — buried pillars of great power — and claims no deeper knowledge, deflecting further questions. He's equally dismissive of the Pygmy people, saying his kind pays them no attention.

Going around the group for questions, Cosimo asks whether Hortaf's people built the stone pyramid the party camped beside the night before. Hortaf confirms it: raised many generations ago by a single family or group of his kind as a deeply personal place, used to perform certain acts of magic at its peak. That family is long gone, and beyond that he claims to know nothing of their history. Pressed further, he confirms that Elves are a true, distinct people — not, as Church doctrine holds, mere abominations born to parents who failed to honor the Two — and his talk of Elven legend touches on "the old crone," one of three revered elders and a symbol of fate, luck, and happenstance, echoing the unease A'Wood once showed on learning the party's Bitterroot came from an old woman.

Questioned about her own people, Leela explains that her mother and father served as shaman-like figures who bless every newborn by bathing it in mud drawn from their totem; she has never known a child to skip the ceremony. Asked whether her people worship the same gods as the party, she says no — just the earth itself.

The conversation circles back more than once to the party's anxieties about their standing with the church. Riu recalls a specific childhood memory: two clerics of the Divinity of Two once blessed a choice of breeding horses on his family's ranch, and it's that same unmistakable sense of divine presence he recognized in the animated figurehead of the Father's Fury — a figurehead that, tellingly, turned and pointed at Cosimo specifically when it named him a heretic, not at anyone else nearby. Pressed by Knick Nab about an earlier incident aboard a rice boat, when the skies opened in apparent blessing after his prayers, Cosimo admits he "made it happen" himself through prayer — and is visibly shaken by the thought that what he takes for illusion could be mistaken for divine favor, or the reverse. The party also weighs a harder question: none of the outlying communities they've visited practice anything resembling the church's birth-blessing rites, yet none of them suffer for it with a higher rate of abominations either.

Hortaf, for his part, admits he'd have preferred the party say nothing of the encounter at all, and settles for their proposal to simply tell the council that Isla Vargo already knows the whole situation. Mani then sums up their situation for Hortaf: three years lost and entangled in events tied to the Divinity of Two, the Shatters, the Maelstrom, and the Three, and the party is willing to share what they've learned in exchange for anything he can tell them of his people and the totems. A deal is struck: the party will share what they know of the Shatters, the Divinity of Two, and how the diad works, withholding only the matter of the medallions, and in return the Elves will use their resources to learn what they can about Captain De Guzman and the ship "Advance" first, then Captain Barrows, then Captain Maynard. The party agrees to return in one week to exchange this information.
