docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
The party debated their long-term mission goals and how to report their findings about the Elven spies to the Drowned Council. They agreed to be largely truthful while omitting the "elf" detail, and settled that Riu would speak for the group before the council so they would not contradict one another. Along the way, they puzzled over talk in town of Handsome Gulliver Gold as "the brother" — with hints of a "sister" besides — and concluded their old shipmate Nicolas, last seen as a disgraced priest of the "Advance," was almost certainly behind it.

Their journey back to Drowned Man's Port took them down a narrow ravine where a weathered wooden carving of "Handsome Gulliver Gold" stood in a niche in the rock — old enough, by Cosimo's woodcraft, that it hadn't been made in the last few months — facing an empty twin niche on the opposite wall, as if awaiting a second occupant. Further along, the ravine opened onto the cave shrine of Nicolas, the former junior priest of the "Advance." They found him kneeling before a crude table and a second, even more finely carved statue of "Handsome Gulliver Gold," dishevelled, reeking of drink, and so overjoyed to see Cosimo that he collapsed at his feet, weeping. Questioned, Nicolas explained he had been sustained since his arrival by a small flock of townsfolk, including Sven and Mistress Clara, and that he had been carried to Drowned Man's Port aboard a ship brought by Corbin "Turncoat" Vance. Both statues, he said, had been carved to his descriptions by Old Man Rayhar — not himself a believer, but drawn by the challenge of the work — and he admitted he had written and prayed for another priest to join him, as his faith required a partner, but no one had ever answered. Emboldened, he attempted to bless Knick Nab; the blessing went wrong and seared Knick Nab's ears, and Knick Nab answered by punching the priest to the ground.

Despite the outburst, the party pressed on, weighing whether to quietly cultivate Nicolas as a foothold in the Church of the Two — even floating the idea of one day using his growing following as bait to lure a ship of the Church here so they could kidnap and interrogate real priests about the totems and the wind witches. They ultimately judged the risk too great: one Church ship drawn to Drowned Man's Port would become three, then thirty, and endanger the whole secret harbour. They set the bait plan aside for some other port, someday, resolving instead to nurture Nicolas quietly and keep him in reserve as the only ordained cleric they could stomach bringing aboard the "Father's Fury," should one ever prove necessary.

Cosimo then asked to pray with Nicolas alone. Through a ritual-cast illusion, he summoned Handsome Gulliver Gold descending in a beam of light from the statue, commanding Nicolas to abandon drink, clean himself and his temple, build a larger ministry among the port's faithful, groom a successor so that he might one day serve as "first" among them, and await the party's support when they returned — after they had gone out to find "the sister." Overjoyed, Nicolas flung his bottle and rags aside and wandered off naked toward Mistress Clara's care, vowing to do everything asked of him.

At the Council Tent, the party was told to return in an hour and used the time to visit the market, where each acquired a minor item. Ushered back into a chamber arranged around a long, gently curved table seating the council's five members, Riu introduced himself and recounted their encounter with the "homesteaders," carefully omitting that they were elves, and pinpointed the location for Isla when she pressed for it: a cairn-marked hilltop with a trail leading down into the valley clearing. Captain Kane raised his own impression that animals had been watching the town; Isla demanded proof, and Riu admitted he could not speak conclusively, only that the homesteaders did keep animals nearby. She also brought up Major Hubert, one of the missing captains, prompting Riu to resolve to follow up with her on it later. Corbin Vance suggested sending someone out to speak with the homesteaders directly. Satisfied — and swayed in part by Mistress Clara's word on the party's trustworthiness — Captain Kane granted the party leave to buy a new ship and depart port; pressed by Riu on how long the port's secrecy could realistically hold, he allowed that he hoped it was decades away, though he warned that if the port were ever found, he would find someone to blame — "maybe everyone." Mani, hand tucked into his new belt, pledged that the party would defend the port's secrecy with their lives if it ever came to that.

The party then approached the shipwright, Master Borin, about buying the "Father's Fury" outright. He opened at 3,000 gold; the party pushed back that with no other buyers interested in a decaying, cursed hull nobody had even come to view, he might as well pay them 30 gold to take it off his hands, and after a long haggle backed by a strong trading roll, pushed him down toward roughly 1,000 gold all in — enough to buy the hull and see it fully fitted out — while noting they would also trade in their old ship, the "Bull." They specified what they wanted from the refit: a full complement of seven cannons plus a single massive bow-chaser on the prow, as much sail as the hull could bear for speed, and the keel and hull careened, scraped, and made sound. Borin estimated the refit alone could run into the thousands depending on how far they went, and warned that fully arming and crewing the ship for all of it would take a crew of about a hundred — though a smaller crew could still sail her, just with fewer guns manned at once. The party agreed to see the ship itself again before committing to numbers, and floated trading the "Bull" to Borin outright in exchange for the full refit rather than paying for both separately, though they left the specifics for later.

They also debated how to crew her. Hiring pirates would mean paying in shares of plunder rather than wages — split far more evenly than a navy's prize money, where officers took the lion's share and ordinary sailors got next to nothing beyond room, board, and clothing — but it also meant compensation if a hand lost a limb or their life, and pirates expecting a steady score every month or two to keep from growing restless: a feast-or-famine arrangement likely to see much of the crew replaced after every big payout, once a flush crew went ashore to spend it. Hiring on sailors instead meant modest, steady wages and a more stable crew, though still with the promise of shares should they take a prize. The party leaned toward paying sailors generously and keeping the promise of adventure and opportunity alive, rather than committing to piracy as a way of life, but left the final decision for later.

Before setting out, Werner drew his cousin De Torres aside to ask if he would serve as sailing master on the new vessel; unwilling to return to the Navy himself, De Torres said the idea interested him in principle but he'd need to know the terms and his share before committing, and the party agreed to bring him a formal offer.

Finally, the party rowed out to the "Father's Fury" in two boats, boarding in order — Knick Nab first, then Mani, Riu, Noddy, and Cosimo last — while Salter held one boat off in reserve and De Torres came along in the second boat for his own look at the ship. The ship was still missing its figurehead and remained covered bow to stern in carved skulls, which Cosimo learned had been commissioned generations ago by a pirate captain remembered only as "the Skull," carved by the master carver Old Man Rayhar. Cosimo re-attuned to the vessel, confirming it was still sentient and still soaked through with old magic, though the presence of the Father was gone entirely. An attempt to make the ship levitate through its own power failed, but a second ritual to give the ship a voice succeeded. Before the party had even agreed on a system, the ship's own alarm bell began ringing unprompted at the mainmast — recognized by ear as a standard danger signal and taken as proof it could answer them — and from there they settled on one bell for yes and two for no, then extended the code so specific outward-facing skulls could ring out compass bearings. Through careful questioning they learned the ship could detect other vessels or threats out to ten nautical miles and could sense that someone was aboard, though not tell individual presences apart, but confirmed it could not help sail itself, breathe fire, spit water, fire its own cannons, bite intruders, cast spells, or learn new ones, and that removing a skull or replacing other rotting timber elsewhere would not harm it. Asked plainly, it confirmed through its bell that it wanted a new figurehead. Satisfied, each party member made a personal pledge to the ship — Mani cut his own thumb at the mainmast and swore to protect it — and it welcomed them all as crew. Riu also gave De Torres the ship's history — built as one of a pair with her sister ship, the "Mother's Sorrow," the power that had soaked into her timbers when her holy cargo was destroyed, and the carved skulls that gave that power its voice — and, pressed on whether the crew could truly master such a strange vessel, reminded him of the party's own record: crossing the Maelstrom, surviving three years, saving the port of Zylos, taking this very ship from her vanished crew, fighting off a Kraken, and now speaking with her directly. De Torres set aside his doubts and agreed in principle to sign on as Master of Sail once the party worked out formal terms — the party privately leaning toward a full two shares for the role, among the best-paid positions short of captain.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Nicolas: The mad priest, now a zealous preacher of "Brother Gold." Sustained by a small flock of townsfolk including Sven and Mistress Clara, he was carried to Drowned Man's Port by Corbin "Turncoat" Vance. Chastened and redirected by an illusion of Gulliver Gold, he vowed to reform, build a larger ministry, and find a successor.
  • Mistress Clara: Has been quietly caring for Nicolas since his arrival and agreed to help him recover further; her account of the party's past help to her also helped convince Captain Kane of their trustworthiness.
  • Old Man Rayhar: The master carver of Drowned Man's Port. He carved the "Father's Fury"'s hundreds of skulls generations ago, commissioned by the pirate captain remembered only as "the Skull," and more recently carved Nicolas's shrine statues to the priest's own descriptions — not, by Nicolas's account, out of belief, but simply for the challenge of the work.
  • The Drowned Council:
    • Captain Silas 'Blackheart' Kane: Satisfied by Riu's report, he granted the party leave to buy a ship and depart port, but warned that if the secret port were ever found, he would find someone to blame — "maybe everyone."
    • Isla 'The Weaver' Vargo: Pressed for the homesteaders' exact location and demanded proof of Captain Kane's suspicion that animals had been watching the town; also mentioned Major Hubert, one of the missing captains, during the debrief.
    • Garth 'The Gaff' Morgan
    • 'Rattlebone' Jones: Offered to help arrange the sale of the party's old ship, the "Bull," and asked them to meet him aboard his own ship later that day.
    • Corbin 'Turncoat' Vance: Suggested sending someone to speak with the homesteaders directly.
  • Master Borin: The shipwright at Drowned Man's Port, who negotiated the sale and refit of the "Father's Fury."
  • "Father's Fury": The sentient, cursed ship, now accepted the party as its crew and confirmed, bell by bell, that it wants a new figurehead.
  • De Torres: Werner De Rendal's cousin and a skilled sailing master, unwilling to return to the Navy himself. Approached about serving as Master of Sail on the new ship, he wanted to know the terms before committing; hearing the ship's history and the party's own record of feats, he set aside his doubts and agreed in principle, pending a formal offer of a full two shares — among the best-paid positions short of captain.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Drowned Man's Port:
    • Nicolas's Cave Shrine: A cave in the hills reached down a narrow ravine, filled with carvings of Handsome Gulliver Gold. Partway down the ravine, an older carved statue of Handsome Gulliver Gold sits in a niche in the rock, facing an empty twin niche as if awaiting a counterpart; a second, finer statue stands within the shrine itself, before the crude table where Nicolas prays.
    • The Council Tent: The meeting place of the Drowned Council, arranged around a long, gently curved table with seats for its five members.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• Knick Nab punched Nicolas after a botched blessing from the priest burned his ears.
  • The party debated whether to use Nicolas as bait to lure and interrogate real priests of the Church of the Two, ultimately judging it too dangerous to attempt from their own secret port.
  • The party debated at length whether to confront Isla Vargo privately over her prior knowledge of the homesteaders watching the port, or simply report their findings to the council and let the matter lie; wary of making an enemy of a council member, they chose not to name her before her colleagues, planning to raise it with her directly later instead.
  • The party engaged in several lengthy debates regarding their primary mission, how to deal with the council, and whether to hire a crew as pirates (paid in shares) or as sailors (paid in wages).

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The party codified their primary mission objectives: investigate the disappearances of Captains Maynard, Barrows, De Guzman, and Major Hubert; investigate the Wind Witches/navigators and their source of power; understand the link to the Totems; and uncover why the Church of the Two fears these powers. They also set aside a running list of secondary mysteries not to be lost in the shuffle — Gildenhome, the Diads, and why the totems react to their medallions — agreeing to keep these four objectives as the main thread while staying alert for anything relevant along the way.
  • There is no formal treaty with the Wind Witches, only an uneasy ceasefire.
  • The "Father's Fury" is no longer imbued with the divine power of The Father, but its hull and many skull carvings remain sentient and steeped in the older magic.
  • The ship's skulls were carved by Old Man Rayhar, commissioned by a former pirate captain known only as "the Skull."
  • The ship can communicate via a system of bell rings — one for yes, two for no — and specific outward-facing skulls can be used to ring out compass bearings.
  • The ship will accept the party as its crew and can detect other vessels or threats up to ten nautical miles away and sense that someone is aboard, though it cannot tell individuals apart, and cannot help sail itself, fight, cast spells, or learn new ones.
  • The ship wants a new figurehead, though it offered no opinion on its design or on being given a new name.
  • Removing one of the ship's skulls, or replacing other rotting timber elsewhere on the hull, would not harm its sentience.
  • The party discussed the significant costs of refitting the "Father's Fury" — likely in the thousands of gold, with a full crew of around a hundred needed to work every cannon and sail at once — and weighed the moral and practical implications of recruiting a pirate crew, paid in shares and prone to restlessness between scores, against hiring on sailors for steady wages.

docs.title: A New Crew and a New Commission
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The party finalized their decision to operate as "spicy adventurers" rather than pirates — free to fight and plunder when it served them, but never bound to piracy as a trade, so a restless crew couldn't force their hand — and moved to secure their new vessel and crew. Knick Nab took charge of piloting the Father's Fury back into the sheltered harbor, directing the skeleton crew — including Master of Sail De Torres — to weigh anchor and thread her into the channel a safe distance off the cliff face, then moored her near the shipyard. They then successfully negotiated a deal with the shipwright: the "Bull" traded in exchange for the Father's Fury, fully refitted to their specifications. Deciding the ship's armament meant weighing speed against firepower — a ship laden with guns would be slower, but one with no stern-facing guns would be defenseless while fleeing. They settled on keeping the ship's four existing 12-pounder long guns, adding two salvaged 24-pounder carronades (mismatched enough between themselves to need separately-sized shot until a matching pair could be found) and a mortar for close, devastating broadsides, and mounting four swivel guns for flexibility, arranged three guns per side with none mounted fore or aft. They also agreed to stock a proper arsenal of pistols, rifles, and other small arms for the crew at large, planned for a dedicated powder room deep in the hull — lined with wet leather and ringed with water buckets against a stray spark — and confirmed the captain's cabin would double as the officers' mess. Only two small private berths stood beside it, one of them doubling as the ship's surgery, with the rest of the crew sleeping in hammocks slung between the guns on the gun deck.

Before heading to recruit, Mani presented Mistress Clara with a fine hat as thanks for her hospitality, which she accepted warmly despite it clashing with her hospital robes. Following her advice, the party then went to "The Sunken Keg" tavern, secured six private rooms and board there for a two-week stay, and made a grand entrance by buying a round for the entire house. They arranged with the tavern's quiet proprietor, Gobin, for a formal recruitment drive the next day at high noon in the tavern's back room, and settled on a standard cover story for every prospective recruit: that the ship's curse had resided in the figurehead's animated spirit, which they had destroyed, with the ship's now-empty bow and widely circulated eyewitness accounts as proof. That evening, the party settled into the tavern's hospitality — Knick Nab fiddled while Cosimo backed him on mandolin, cards ran late, and Riu enjoyed a hot bath — before turning in with their usual precautions against trouble. During a training session in the tavern's yard the next morning, Knick Nab — with no real swordsmanship to speak of — beat Mani in a sparring match through sheer, uncanny luck, leaving Mani determined to train twice as hard afterward.

Before the interviews began, the party tallied the specialist roles they already had covered — Mani as captain, De Torres as Master of Sail, Cosimo as master rigger, Riu as ship's doctor, Salter as carpenter, and Batu Batu as cook — and confirmed that roughly eight hands from their old crews, including the senior sailor Beck and the marine Stanley, were willing to stay on, a headcount that shaped how many new hires they'd need. At high noon, they interviewed dozens of applicants and hired 66 new hands, bringing their total crew complement, including returning crew and themselves, to 80 — well above the bare minimum of 60 they judged sufficient for a lean, speed-focused ship, but a buffer they wanted against future casualties. They settled on a flat share structure — three shares for the party and other senior commanders, two for officers and specialists, one for common hands — paired with a flat signing bonus of five silver per recruit, paid on reporting to the ship rather than at the moment of signing, to keep new recruits from drinking the money away before showing up. Key recruits included a retired Northern Navy Sergeant-at-Arms (Tyler), who satisfied Mani that his retirement settled any awkwardness with the party's own strained standing with that service; a former Southern merchant captain who talked his way into the Quartermaster's post once others present vouched for his grasp of ship's supplies (Leopold); a one-eyed surgeon's mate referred by Clara (Jeffrey), taken on with the understanding he'd pitch in on other shipboard duties between patients and that his credentials would be confirmed with Clara; a big, powerfully built ship's carpenter aptly named Carpenter; an Islander pilot and senior sailor (Gam); two more experienced senior sailors (Old Salter, Perkin); an Islander cook's assistant with practical shipboard cooking experience, hired despite a language barrier with Batu Batu (Edith); and a handful of able seamen and deckhands with more varied backgrounds, including a former whaler, a pressed hunter, a conscripted fisherman, a runaway blacksmith's apprentice, and a poacher pressed into naval service. Riu also insisted on casting a poison and disease relief spell over the new hires as they came aboard, quietly ensuring the crew joined the ship clean, and weighed whether Cosimo could help supply the power such a large-scale casting would demand.

With their crew largely secured, the party turned to the ship's identity, weighing names like "Sister Seeker" and "the Audacity" before settling on "The Medallion" — fitting, they agreed, since every one of them already wore one. They then visited the workshop of the master carver, Old Man Rayhar, to commission a new figurehead. Rayhar was initially indignant that they had destroyed his previous "masterwork," but grew intrigued once he understood the figurehead itself had come to life and attacked the crew, and agreed to take the commission — though he turned down an invitation to join the crew outright, insisting his craft needed the stability of his own workshop rather than a ship underway. His crowded workshop was full of gleaming tools, a single spectacular central workbench, and dozens of small clay figures of his own making — some lifelike, some fantastical creatures. The party proposed carving the new figurehead in Mistress Clara's likeness, but Rayhar, a self-described purist, refused to combine a real person's face with a fantastical body, insisting a subject must be either wholly real or wholly imagined. During their conversation, he revealed that he had not carved the ship's original figurehead but had merely "corrected" its crude design, and that all 156 of the skulls carved across the ship had been made from oak staves the former captain supplied him — with only 27 boards of that oak left over in his yard, strongly implying the rest came from the barrels of holy water. He also mentioned he had never seen the rare "finger fruit" wood the party had heard of, and grew visibly interested on learning they owned four boards of it.

While at the workshop, Cosimo detected a magical aura, at first suspecting it came from Rayhar's carved figures before tracing it instead to a stack of leftover oak planks stored in a lean-to out in the yard — the last of the wood used for the ship's skull carvings. Rayhar, prizing the rare material, refused to sell the planks at any price, insisting he would only use them if they proved to be the right material for the right work. The party agreed to return with a final figurehead design. Rayhar also recounted a story of a pair of Islander hempti and hempto pulling earth from a stone the size of a table to raise an entire wall — a feat he could not otherwise explain, though he wondered aloud whether "hempti" and "hempto" simply meant "mother" and "father" in the Islander tongue. Knick Nab recognized the story as connected to the magic-users who operate the totems. During the day's events, he also received a telepathic message from the Elves, reminding him of their agreement to exchange information; the party chose to hold to their original timeline of about a week rather than rush to meet sooner.

docs.title: Of Figureheads, Faith, and Future Voyages
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The party settled on the operating philosophy for their crew: they would present themselves as explorers and "spicy adventurers" rather than declared pirates, adopting a pirate-style share structure for pay — three shares for the most senior officers and party members, two for other officers and senior hands, one for everyone else — well above standard naval pay, alongside a generous signing bonus for new hands.

The session began in the workshop of the master carver, Old Man Rayhar, sorting out what to do with his shop full of rare, magical oak barrel staves—remnants of the holy water barrels recovered from the Father's Fury and confirmed magical by a prior detect magic. Rayhar, a local Islander, had never handled a strain of oak like it before; none grows on the island at all, so the wood could only have been carried across from the mainland aboard ship. His 27 remaining staves were each only about four feet long and fairly narrow, but no less prized for it. Rayhar explained that he had never carved the ship's original figurehead; it came with the vessel, and all he had done was carve the skulls that adorn her hull and "correct" the crude original figurehead into something finer. The party weighed several notions for the leftover staves—a gun stock, tentacles that might let the ship grapple enemy vessels, even a face to let the ship communicate—but reached no consensus and left the wood to Rayhar's discretion.

After a lengthy discussion, the party decided to commission a new figurehead in the likeness of Mistress Clara for their ship, now called The Medallion. Riu asked Rayhar to carve a life-sized relief of himself from the magical wood, giving his true name—Infurious Montesigna the Third—and even levitating before the old carver to prove he was no common man, but he could not adequately explain the source of his power, and Rayhar deferred judgment—agreeing he would gladly carve an ordinary likeness of Riu, but not from the precious staves, until Riu understood himself better. Later in the session, after an impassioned speech from Mani recounting his history with Mistress Clara—complete with poems he had written for her (he recited one in full: "Island beauty comes, healer of my heart and soul, lost and now return"), letters recounting his adventures addressed to her, and his cherished main gauche dagger, which he calls "Mr. Stone" and keeps in his off hand to defend his heart, calling it the first gift he received since the adventure began—Rayhar agreed to use the special wood to carve a small, personal figurine of her for him to keep.

Returning to their ship, the party began moving their most trusted people—Leela and De Torres among them—over from their previous ship, the Bull, to help ready The Medallion for the crew's arrival the next day. Their newly hired quartermaster, Leopold, was waiting for them at the gangplank with a gift of fine rum to toast his new post. He presented them with a draft of ship's articles for governing the crew, requested a 10-silver advance to purchase initial supplies—logging it as the first entry in a new ledger the moment it changed hands—and pressed the party to settle on a command structure before the crew arrived, noting that subordinate roles such as carpenter's mate, or whether Tyler would serve as Mani's mate in the master-at-arms role, remained undecided. Knick Nab separately asked Leopold to find out where on the island gold could be exchanged for coin. The party also searched the captain's cabin for charts, finding a locked cubby (its key missing) full of maps covering the waters to the north and the mainland coasts, with little reliable detail on The Shatters and only sparse, sketchy hints of the seas farther west. Riu, meanwhile, resolved to give every new hand a physical once they returned from the Elves, quietly intending to work a minor curative spell into each examination over the following weeks. The party then planned their next moves, deciding to visit Nicolas before heading to their scheduled meeting with the local Elves.

At his cave shrine—its statue of Handsome Gulliver Gold freshly cleaned and repainted for the occasion—they found Nicolas sober but in a state of religious mania, preaching to a small congregation of two townsfolk, including their own new hand, Robin, a former poacher. Pressed on doctrine, Nicolas insisted the church itself is not the Mother and Father but merely the conduit by which the faithful reach them, and admitted that this very distinction, together with his growing conviction that the church's teachings were incomplete, was enough to see him branded a heretic if he preached it in the Capitol. The party questioned him on the nature of holy water, learning only that it originates from the basement of the main cathedral in the Capitol, produced by priests trained to that specific purpose from a young age; Nicolas himself had instead been chosen young for service aboard naval ships, and so could offer nothing more on how it was actually made. He did recall having seen church clergy work lesser wonders—turning carved wood into a flexing, grasping arm among them—and had heard old tales of pillars of light called down against the church's enemies, though never witnessed such a thing himself. Nicolas confessed he had no way to grow his following, since the sailors and townsfolk who might carry useful tales gathered in the taverns and inns he no longer dared enter, having sworn off drink at Gulliver Gold's own command; when pressed to send one of his two congregants there in his stead, the man refused, unconvinced. To aid their own intelligence-gathering efforts, Cosimo performed a powerful ritual, creating a waiting illusion of Handsome Gulliver Gold designed to appear before Nicolas's congregation within a day and, at a spoken command phrase, charge them to gather more of their fellows and carry word of a coming mission—planting the seed of a following that might, in time, surface useful information about the church and its powers on the party's behalf.

Mani challenged Knick Nab to a friendly sparring match—first with swords, then bare-fisted—and was soundly beaten both times, enough to leave him asking to be taught swordsmanship in earnest. Afterward, the party met with Mistress Clara to formally ask her permission for the figurehead, which she happily granted once Knick Nab explained that the ship's new name honored the medallion that had first bound the party together—a symbol, as he put it, of their destiny and their opposition to the tyranny of the two. The visit continued with a round of introductions in which each of the party settled on a shipboard role for her benefit: Mani as leader of the vanguard, Riu as ship's surgeon, and Cosimo, to everyone's confusion, as "master of fog." Mani then escorted her on a walk, which included the visit to Rayhar and culminated in a successful romantic encounter.

Finally, the party journeyed to the Elven homestead, with Leela accompanying them. Abedneith greeted them by speaking directly into Knick Nab's mind, an intrusion so unpleasant that Knick Nab objected; Abedneith apologized and promised restraint in the future. The meeting proved fruitful, as the groups exchanged vital information, with the party letting the Elves speak first and deliberately holding back Mistress Clara's eyewitness account of the Shatters as a card to play later if needed. The party revealed the true cause of The Shatters: the destruction of a Totem of Earth on Spider Island by the Divinity of Two, including the giant spiders and gorillas that apparently doomed the church's first expedition there before it returned in greater force—a revelation that led the party to debate, without reaching a conclusion, whether whoever destroyed the totem had known the mission would cost their own lives, recalling that previously recovered church writings had spoken of an "imperative" to destroy such totems regardless of the cost. In return, the Elves disclosed the existence of a secret society called "The Triad," marked by a sigil of three lines, which opposed the Divinity and counted Major Hubert, Captain Maynard, and Captain Barrows among its members; the Elves stressed that the society was so guarded that even its own members knew little of one another, communicating so circumspectly that they could not always be sure their messages had gotten through. They also provided the last known location of Captain Barrows' ship, the "Advance"—it was sighted arriving at a remote and dangerous location called Birdcrown Isle two years prior and never seen leaving—and revealed that a small band of their own kin, marooned on a smaller island nearby, keep a distant watch on Birdcrown Isle and might, in time, be worth rescuing. Furnished with coordinates, the party weighed a voyage to Birdcrown Isle, months away, against a return to the ruins of Spider Island at the heart of The Shatters, only a few weeks' sail and within the expertise of their newly hired pilot Gam, and weighed the prospect of recoverable treasure aboard the wrecked Divine Rite against the risk that the Shatters had become a breeding ground for kraken. Riu argued for making directly for Birdcrown Isle and Barrows, but the party ultimately voted, by majority, to investigate Spider Island first.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Drowned Man's Port: The primary location for the first half of the session.
    • Old Man Rayhar's Workshop: Also holds a table of the carver's smaller studies and personal pieces, not carved from wood but from some other material—among them a hulking, one-eyed, horned creature, a winged four-legged beast with a birdlike head, and a mermaid seated upon a rock with flowing hair.
    • The Docks, where The Medallion is moored.
    • The Medallion's Captain's Cabin: Contains a wall of lockable cubbies, its key missing, holding a chart collection of clearly mixed origin—northern, southern, and hand-drawn—reasonably detailed for the waters north and along the mainland coasts, but sparse and contradictory on The Shatters and offering only sketchy, unreliable hints of the seas farther west.
    • The Hospital, where Mistress Clara works.
  • Nicolas's Cave Shrine: A cave in the hills above the port, centered on a statue of Handsome Gulliver Gold—freshly cleaned and repainted for the occasion—with log benches for a small congregation.
  • The Elven Homestead: A secluded dwelling in the hills.
  • Mentioned:
    • Birdcrown Isle: A mysterious, uncharted island far to the southwest and the last known location of the "Advance." The Elves' distant watchers describe it as roughly circular, ringed by sheer cliffs with jagged, tooth-like peaks that look almost like a deliberate palisade, and home to enormous birds — some apparently ridden by the native islanders.
    • The Elves' Marooned Outpost: A small, unnamed island near Birdcrown Isle where a handful of Elves are marooned and keep a distant watch on it.
    • Spider Island: Now known as The Shatters, the location of the destroyed Totem of Earth.
    • Port of Zylos: Where Major Hubert died.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• Riu attempted to convince Old Man Rayhar that he was a worthy subject for a carving from the magical wood, even levitating before him as proof of his exceptional nature. Rayhar, who claimed to have known others who commanded the wind, pressed him on whether that was the source of his gift; Riu could only say the power came from within his own mind, and the carver remained unconvinced without a clearer account of where it truly originated.
  • Mani challenged Knick Nab to a sparring match, first with swords and then bare-fisted, and was decisively beaten both times—so thoroughly with fists that Knick Nab could knock him down, set him back on his feet, and knock him down again—enough to leave him asking to be taught swordsmanship.
  • Nicolas pressed one of his two congregants to venture into the taverns and inns on his behalf to gather word of the church and other powers; the man refused, unconvinced by the priest's pleas.
  • Abedneith greeted the party by speaking directly into Knick Nab's mind; the sudden intrusion left him deeply unsettled, and Abedneith apologized, promising restraint in the future.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• Crew Identity and Shares: The party decided their crew would operate as explorers and "spicy adventurers" rather than declared pirates, while leaving the door open to opportunistic piracy. Pay follows a pirate-style share system — three shares for the most senior officers and party members, two for other officers and senior hands, one for everyone else — rather than a stricter naval scale.
  • Ship's Articles: Leopold presented a draft set of articles for the crew to formally adopt, covering command and governance, division of spoils, discipline, duties and responsibilities, conduct in battle, matters of faith, treatment of outsiders, and the ship's stance on slavery — each with multiple traditions to choose between, from strict naval hierarchy to full pirate democracy. Sample clauses included settling any quarrel between shipmates before the quartermaster and fighting it out ashore rather than aboard, a lashing or forfeited share for sleeping on watch, and a ban on smoking or striking sparks in the hold. Leopold, as Quartermaster, will manage supplies and act as the crew's representative and go-between.
  • Command Structure: Leopold pressed the party to formalize roles beyond the officer titles they had already claimed, flagging subordinate positions — such as who would serve as carpenter's mate, or whether Tyler would act as Mani's mate in the master-at-arms role — that remained undecided and would need to be settled before the crew arrived.
  • Magical Wood: Rayhar's 27 remaining oak barrel staves, recovered from the Father's Fury itself, are each roughly four feet long and fairly narrow, but an unfamiliar strain of white oak exceptionally suited for fine carving — detail his blade can always find more of, no matter how sharp. No oak of any kind grows on the island, so the wood can only have come from the mainland. Rayhar agreed to use a piece of it for a small figure of Mistress Clara for Mani, though he left the fate of the remaining boards to his own judgment.
  • Wind Witches: Rayhar recalled once carving a memorial figurine, at a wind witch's request, depicting a woman the witch had loved and lost when her home island was destroyed; the witch had at one point been employed by one of the pirate captains of the council, possibly 'Rattlebone' Jones.
  • The Triad: The party learned of a secret society within the Northern Kingdom, marked by a sigil of three lines, that questions the authority of the Divinity of Two. Major Hubert, Captain Maynard, and Captain Barrows were all members or believers. The Elves described it as extraordinarily guarded — its members reportedly know little of one another and communicate so circumspectly that they cannot always be sure their messages have gotten through.
  • The "Advance": The party was given the last known location of Captain Barrows' ship: Birdcrown Isle, a remote island to the southwest which the ship reached two years ago and never left. The Elves could offer a precise latitude but only a rough longitude, and were confident the ship had not slipped away unseen. A small band of the Elves' own kin are marooned on a smaller island nearby and keep a distant watch on Birdcrown Isle; the Elves suggested they might, in time, be worth rescuing.
  • Fate of Key Figures: The party learned that Major Hubert died a year prior in Zylos under suspicious circumstances and that Captain De Guzman (Duzman) has completely disappeared. They noted a puzzling gap in the timeline: the heretic bounty naming the party was issued roughly three years ago, yet Hubert remained easily found in Zylos until his death only a year ago.
  • The Ship That Attacked Them: Mistress Clara further identified the vessel that destroyed the Totem of Earth as a three-masted frigate originally called the King's Right, seized from the King's Navy and rechristened the Divine Rite by the Divinity of Two. Aboard were at least two clergy and a navigator named Grantos, who guided the ship through the Maelstrom.
  • A Suicide Mission?: Recalling the wording of previously recovered church writings on the "imperative" to destroy such totems regardless of cost, the party debated whether whoever destroyed the Totem of Earth had known the mission would kill them. Some argued the church's agents were most likely zealots willing to accept that price, but the group reached no firm conclusion.
  • Holy Water: Nicolas confirmed that holy water comes from the basement of the Capitol's cathedral, produced by priests trained to that specific purpose from a young age; he himself was instead chosen young for naval service, and so remains ignorant of the actual process of its creation. He also insisted the church itself is not the Mother and Father but only the conduit by which the faithful reach them, and recalled having witnessed clergy work minor wonders — including turning carved wood into a flexing, grasping arm — along with old tales of pillars of light called down against the church's enemies.
  • Next Destination: Weighing a voyage to Birdcrown Isle, months away, against a return to the epicenter of The Shatters (the former Spider Island), only a few weeks' sail and well within the expertise of their newly hired pilot Gam, the party also weighed whether the wrecked Divine Rite might still hold recoverable treasure there against the risk that the Shatters had become a breeding ground for kraken. Riu argued for heading directly to Birdcrown Isle, but the party voted by majority to make for The Shatters first, keeping Birdcrown Isle as a longer-term goal.

docs.title: Articles of Agreement and Preparations for the Shatters
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The senior officers turned to finalizing the articles for their ship, The Medallion, working from Leopold's draft and amendments Riu had proposed in the interim. They agreed on a command structure of eight senior officers — quartermaster, captain, master at arms (Mani), master of fog (Cosimo), master lookout (Noddy), master surgeon (Riu), master gunner (Werner), and master of sail (De Torres) — who hold a vote on all matters of moment, with the captain's word absolute only in times of chase or battle and the quartermaster acting as magistrate, mediating disputes and speaking for the ordinary crew. Because eight officers meant a tie was possible, the party debated at length how to break one — proposals ranged from letting whichever officer's specialty was most relevant to the dispute decide, to a captain's tiebreak, to leaving deadlocks to be settled by violence — before settling on "the most appropriate senior leader decides," with outright violence acknowledged as the fallback should that fail. On the division of spoils, common seamen would draw one share, junior officers and specialists two, and senior officers three, with an extra half-share available at the officers' discretion for acts of uncommon valor; the ship herself would also be allotted a number of shares toward her own upkeep, a figure Leopold offered to work out and propose later. Leopold's suggested compensation for grievous wounds — scaled from 600 pieces of eight for a lost right arm down to 100 for an eye or a finger, drawn from his experience aboard true pirate ships living on plunder — was negotiated down by a full order of magnitude to a flat five gold per injury regardless of the wound, with the door left open to award more in cases of unusual bravery.

On discipline, quarrels between crew would go first to the quartermaster for mediation and only then to the captain; personal disputes that could not be reconciled were to be settled ashore by duel, while formal offenses carried fixed penalties — theft meant the lash and forfeiture of the next prize share, drunkenness meant irons for seamen or a tenth-share forfeiture for officers, and sleeping on watch or otherwise neglecting one's station meant a lashing or forfeited share at the company's discretion. Every man was further bound to keep his weapons clean and fit for service. Deserting one's post in battle was punishable by death or marooning, as was defrauding the company by keeping plunder back from the common share; good quarter would be given to any who asked for it unless the captain declared "no quarter" before a battle began. Every man and woman aboard was guaranteed an equal share of food and drink regardless of rank, and no smoking or gunfire would be allowed in the powder hold. No one could speak of quitting the company's service until they had earned 500 silver apiece, talked down from Leopold's opening figure of 1,000 silver. After a heated debate over slavery, weighing its acceptance in the North against the party's wish to distinguish themselves from other Northern crews, the officers voted, effectively unanimously, that the ship and her company would take no part whatsoever in the trade of human souls; valuable prisoners could still be ransomed, and the rest set ashore or otherwise released rather than sold. The articles closed with guarantees of freedom of worship, a rule barring passengers without the captain's express consent (with any passenger bound by the same articles), a berth set aside for the sick and wounded including prisoners, a standing duty to detect and punish any aboard — prisoners included — who violated the ship's good order, and a clause condemning to death anyone who forced themselves upon another crew member without their consent, extended in the final wording to cover men and boys as well as women. Since women would now serve aboard for the first time on a ship of this kind, the officers briefly weighed whether to legislate personal relations among crew directly, but declined to add anything beyond the consent protections already agreed, leaving such matters to individual discretion. In the midst of that discussion, Cosimo made a private admission to his fellow officers: though his illusion powers were awakened through his devotion to the Two, and he owes his early training in them to that faith, he has come to believe over recent months that the Two are not actually the true source of his power. Every article would be put in writing and signed by the entire company, senior officers included, with no exceptions, and could only be amended by a majority vote of the senior officers; Leopold further insisted that anyone who objected to the finished articles and could not in good conscience put their mark to them be released from service despite having already been paid, a condition the officers accepted. Before moving on, the party also held a formal vote on Nicolas and turned him down four to one, with one abstention — Cosimo's waiting illusion of Handsome Gulliver Gold would nonetheless return to appear before Nicolas's congregation a second time, reinforcing its call to build an intelligence network in port, once the party had actually left. They also weighed asking the Elves to reach out again about a second missing ship, the "Mother's Sorrow," but never followed through on it before turning to other business.

With the articles settled, focus shifted to preparing for the journey to Spider Island (referred to by the party as Leela's Island). The party consulted Gam, the ship's pilot, showing him their existing charts — including one marked with a well-traveled north-south route maintained by beacons of the Northern Navy, and a scatter of "K" markings left by the explorer Colchester noting kraken sightings. Gam warned them off that charted route as one likely to bring them into contact with Northern fleets, and estimated the epicenter of the Shatters lay to the north and west of their current position, cautioning that the charts themselves could not be fully trusted since the reefs and shoals were still shifting. His central warning concerned the krakens: since the Shatters' creation disturbed the seafloor, the creatures have moved into the newly shallow waters in search of easier hunting, so the party should take frequent soundings and keep to deep water wherever possible. This led to a long brainstorming session on anti-kraken tactics: Riu, drawing on what he knew from his pet squid, warned that krakens do not fear ships at all — to them, a ship is simply prey — and judged the creatures hunt by sight and smell rather than sound, which ruled out noise as a reliable deterrent or lure; the party instead discussed painting eyes on the hull, having Cosimo mask the ship's silhouette and sound with illusion, rigging illusioned decoy barrels to smell like prey or a rival kraken, stocking oil for burning the water, and weighing harpoons and an anchor-and-rope tactic against simply relying on cannon and swivel guns. They settled on a shopping list of a field gun carriage, extra swivel guns, large harpoons, a crate of grenades, rifles and rifle muskets, oil, long spears and boarding axes for repelling tentacles that came aboard, and a few goats to sacrifice as chum if needed.

To fund that list, the officers decided to sell some of their raw gold. They first met with Captain Corbin Vance, who opened with a lowball offer before a round of haggling settled on 10 lbs of gold for 300 gold coins, on the condition that they take his 14-year-old stepson, Tolly, aboard as crew; Riu drew up a formal receipt for the exchange. Weighing and appraising each chunk confirmed the party was sitting on a genuine fortune in raw gold. Needing still more to cover Leopold's itemized total of 398 gold, 6 silver — 99 gold for ordnance and powder, 45 gold for three months of ship's stores, 120 gold for three months of provisions for a crew of eighty, and 102 gold for a small-arms locker of muskets, pistols, cutlasses, and boarding axes — they returned and sold another 5 lbs of gold to Vance for 145 gold, setting aside 20 gold for Leopold to cover the extra kraken-preparation shopping list and splitting the remainder among themselves for personal purchases.

During the downtime, Mani purchased a pair of exquisite dueling pistols from a gunsmith recommended in town; after haggling down from an opening price of 40 gold and having them test-fired and gunsmith-appraised, they proved to be enchanted, granting a much larger bonus when the pair is used against each other in a formal duel, and Mani closed the deal at 25 gold. He also picked up a plain rifle for 2 gold, along with the collected works of Raphael Sabatini and several books by the author Sebastian de Castell, whose definition of swashbuckling — "solving an unsolvable problem with a preposterous level of daring" — Mani adopted as his new personal credo, along with a resolution to have a kraken tattooed across his shoulder. Riu made a second attempt to commission a carving from Old Man Rayhar, who again insisted on understanding the "truth" and source of Riu's power before he would begin work on Riu's own likeness, though his figurehead carving of Mistress Clara was well underway and unmistakably lifelike. On his way in, Riu crossed paths with Clara herself, leaving her own sitting; a subsequent conversation with her reinforced her belief that their powers originate from The Two, though Riu remained privately unconvinced. With the ship's refit — held up mainly by the figurehead work — expected to take about two weeks under Master Borin's schedule, the officers laid out their plans for the downtime: Werner would drill the gun crews on loading and handling, short of live fire since the ship remained in port; Noddy would identify the crew's best fighters and shooters and drill defense against boarding tentacles; Mani would practice swordsmanship daily with his new blades; Cosimo would apprentice under De Torres to learn the specific rigging of their own ship; and Riu would conduct physicals on all eighty crew members, senior officers included. They also commissioned a new ship's flag in blue and gold.

docs.text:

docs.text:

  • During the articles debate, Cosimo privately admitted to his fellow officers that although his illusion powers were awakened through his devotion to the Two, and he owes his early training in them to that faith, he has come to believe over recent months that the Two are not actually the true source of his power.
  • Cosimo confirmed the ship can currently answer only yes-or-no questions through its bell, and only after a multi-minute ritual to channel it; a faster or more convenient way to communicate with the ship remains an open problem, though Cosimo floated layering a waiting effect atop the ritual so any crew member could trigger a question within a day of it being cast. The party intends to test the ship's sense for danger — such as nearby kraken — once they are underway.

docs.title: Events and Actions
docs.text:
In their final fortnight ashore, the officers each kept sharpening their own trade: Werner drilled with the gun crew, Mani trained with the weapons instructors, Cosimo continued his apprenticeship under De Torres in the ship's rigging, and Riu worked alongside the surgeon's mate, Jeffrey, while Knick Nab spent his nights ashore talking up the ship and its mission, drawing a trickle of fresh recruits to the docks. With preparations nearly complete, Leopold, the quartermaster, presented the completed ship's articles and crew roster, noting that Riu had already rejected a handful of prospective recruits as unfit for duty during the refit, and that the crew still lacked a cooper and an armorer. Reviewing the roster, the officers realized they had no mates to run the watches, leaving that burden to fall on themselves; Knick Nab, De Torres, Werner, and Cosimo settled on taking turns as the four watch leaders, with De Torres offering to formally serve as first mate. Leela's role was likewise settled: she joined the marines alongside Mani and Tyler, meaning she would now stand a regular watch rather than live as an idler, and — finding gunfire too loud for her liking — asked to be armed with a bow rather than a crossbow or firearm. The ship's boy, Tolly, was assigned to work simply as a deckhand rather than rotate through each officer's department as first planned. Old Salter, the bosun, then laid out the watch schedule the crew would now live by: four hours on and four off around the clock, broken twice a day by a pair of shorter two-hour dog watches so that no one stood the same hours every day.

With preparations complete, Old Man Rayhar arrived at the docks with the finished figurehead of Mistress Clara, shrouded in sailcloth and hauled down to the ship on a pair of trolleys. Hoisting it into place with the shipyard's cranes, the foremast, and a yardarm took most of the day; Cosimo, unable to stand by and watch the crew fumble with the ropes and blocks, waded in to correct their rigging himself, putting his fortnight of training under De Torres to use, and at one point the figurehead's sword arm snapped off under the strain, though Rayhar had it mended and back in place within minutes. Once mounted at the bow, its joinery was so intricate in places that it seemed impossible it had been carved from a single piece of wood. Rayhar also presented a set of gilded letters spelling out the ship's name for the stern, a parting gift arranged by Mistress Clara, along with a spare flag identical to their medallion colors but bearing a skull, to be run up as piracy colors if ever the need arose. The ship was officially christened when a bottle of exquisite red clarity was broken across the figurehead's face, then set sail from Drowned Man's Port, heading north towards the Shatters.

The first week at sea was dedicated to a shakedown cruise. At the urging of De Torres and the sergeant-at-arms, Tyler, the crew ran extensive drills for sailing, gunnery, and boarding actions, including firing the ballista and harpoons at floating targets. During this period, two notable crew-related incidents occurred. Arnum, an able seaman, came to Riu in the night for treatment of a puncture wound clean through his hand. He claimed it was a whittling accident, but the wound looked more like a blade thrust; when pressed, he offered no attacker's name, a tossed object meant to reveal his dominant hand was caught with both, and his own knife, when inspected, showed no trace of blood. Jeffrey, assisting, privately agreed the whittling story sounded unlikely for a blade driven clean through a man's palm, and was equally startled at how quickly Riu's spellwork closed a wound that should by rights have been life-threatening — though he was told to keep both observations to himself for now. Riu brought the matter to Knick Nab, who summoned Leopold and Old Salter to his cabin before Arnum was brought in, hoping the presence of the ship's senior authorities might unsettle a confession out of him; it didn't. Leopold offered the counterpoint that if there had in fact been a quarrel, Arnum might be the wronged party rather than the guilty one. Lacking firm evidence either way, the officers chose to monitor Arnum rather than press further, and Mani later arranged a friendly sparring match with him, wooden swords in hand, as a discreet way of keeping a closer watch. The officers also agreed to start meeting briefly twice daily, at the change of the morning and evening watches, to keep one another informed of anything unusual aboard. Shortly after, several officers separately noticed odd movement in the rigger Jacopa, and on being questioned directly, Jacopa admitted to serving in disguise as a man. In a private interview, she told them she was an islander who had worked trading skiffs in the Channel Islands before years of enslavement, escaping five years past; her family remained somewhere beyond the maelstrom, and she asked to be allowed to seek them out if the ship ever passed that way again. Satisfied the rest of her story held true, the officers granted her request and assured her she could continue serving openly with no special treatment. Also during the shakedown, a large bird bearing a rider was spotted flying north ahead of the ship, well out of range of the swivel guns and rifle hastily readied at the bow; some aboard recalled sighting a similar creature in these same waters three years before, shortly before the ship was marooned for two years, raising suspicion it might still be watching them. Tracked by bearing until it vanished into the sun's glare, the rider was moving faster than the ship could match. Riu argued for changing course to avoid being tracked into a fight, but Gam counselled holding the charted route: it was well known and mapped, if more likely watched by the Northern Navy, while any detour would carry them into waters just as dangerous and far less certain. The officers chose to hold their course.

Upon entering the Shatters, the crew found little but bare rock jutting from the sea, some patched with scrub and nesting birds, having passed the island of the Stone Men from an earlier voyage along the way in. They slowed to a crawl, taking constant soundings — sixteen fathoms, then ten, over a sandy bottom — and doubling their watch as Gam had advised. One night, stopped and drifting, they heard a distant cry carry across the water; Noddy sent his bird into the darkness to investigate, and it returned to report a light far ahead, hundreds of feet off.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The officers found themselves noticeably more capable than before, having each honed new skills since their last outing.
  • The command structure and daily life aboard the ship were formalized through the ship's articles and watch assignments. With no mates aboard, the officers learned the burden of leading the watches would fall to themselves; Knick Nab, De Torres, Werner, and Cosimo were settled on as the four watch leaders, and De Torres offered to formally take on the role of first mate. The watch schedule itself — four hours on, four off, broken twice daily by shorter dog watches — was explained as an arduous but standard rhythm of shipboard life, one none of the officers, least of all the captain, would be exempt from.
  • The shipboard articles were reaffirmed as the framework for handling disputes: quarrels are to be brought before the quartermaster to mediate, escalating to a duel of sword or pistol to first blood if reconciliation fails; meddling with another without consent is punishable by death, theft by the lash, and drunkenness by the irons.
  • The officers agreed to hold brief meetings twice daily, at the change of the morning and evening watches, to share anything unusual observed by the crew.
  • It was discovered that Jacopa, a rigger, was a woman in disguise. The officers interviewed her, confirmed the rest of her story was true — including her history as an escaped slave from the Channel Islands with family somewhere beyond the maelstrom — and assured her that she could serve openly without issue, noting she would be the third woman aboard alongside Leela and the cook's assistant, Edith, and that the ship's existing rule against meddling with a shipmate without consent — punishable by death — would protect her like any other member of the crew.
  • The sighting of a bird-rider sparked discussion about its origin (possibly Birdcrown Isle, where Captain Barrows is believed to be) and intent, with some recalling a similar sighting in the same waters three years prior. Weighing Riu's concern about being tracked into a fight against Gam's point that an unplanned detour would be no less dangerous than the known route, the officers decided to stick to their planned, charted course into the Shatters rather than divert into less certain waters.

docs.title: Serpents, Survivors, and a Sudden Stillness
Events and Actions
docs.text:
While sailing cautiously through The Shatters at night, the party hears a distant hail, spots a flickering light, and moves to investigate. As they draw near, Wat, at the wheel, calls out a string of shrinking soundings — twelve fathoms, then ten, then eight, then six — and Captain Nab presses on until the ship is finally brought to anchor just short of the shallows. No sooner has the anchor caught than the ship finds itself surrounded by a massive swarm of aggressive sharks, and Cosimo answers the alarm with two light spells at once: a brilliant burst covering fifty feet in every direction, layered over a softer, more intimate glow pooling across the main deck, revealing the full extent of the danger to the unnerved crew.

An away team (Knick Nab, Mani, Riu, Werner, and Salter) takes a boat to investigate the light's source. They navigate the shark-infested waters and discover a small, rocky island populated by giant sea tortoises, one of which Knick Nab flips onto its back to clear a path ashore. Rather than row the boat around a still-larger specimen blocking their way, Knick Nab instead vaults it outright — clearing the tortoise but landing squarely on a smaller one, which snaps and claws at him for his trouble. On the island, they find a lone survivor sheltering behind the shell of a butchered giant tortoise with a small, guttering fire at his side: a sailor named Keyes, ragged and bedraggled with a few days' beard growth, armed with only a knife and a pistol, who claims he was swept overboard and his longboat crushed when a massive sea serpent attacked his ship, the "Fortnum," four or five days prior, and that he does not know what became of the ship or its crew. Brought back to the "Medallion" and examined by Riu, Keyes proves consistent with his story — battered and scraped from days of exposure, subsisting on raw tortoise, with only a mild ailment that Riu's healing quickly clears. Mani takes it upon himself to shadow Keyes for the rest of the night, and the quartermaster formally signs him onto the ship's articles before dawn, assigning him to the captain's watch under the eyes of Tyler and Old Salter.

The next morning, with the sharks mysteriously gone and only two young tortoises left on the rocks, an away team returns to the island. The team discovers a box containing a single bullet and powder charge, along with an empty grog keg — evidence suggesting Keyes was not shipwrecked but deliberately marooned. Confronted with this, Keyes confesses the truth: the "Fortnum," a Northern ship of war out of New Sardinia, had been pressing deeper into The Shatters for reasons even Keyes did not know, when a sea serpent surfaced without warning during a gunnery drill. Keyes fled his post at a swivel gun rather than fire on it, and for this act of cowardice his captain, Mason, marooned him on the island. The "Fortnum," though damaged, survived the encounter and, at the priests' insistence, continued its mission deeper into The Shatters. The officers make clear to Keyes that the crew takes an equally dim view of abandoning one's post in battle, but confirm he has a place aboard regardless. Poring over the charts with him afterward, the party realizes New Sardinia, the "Fortnum's" home port, is the same Northern settlement they already knew as the island of the Stone Men. Consulting his own journal, Mani finds a further record placing a ship named the "Fortnum" among the frigates that had been in port when the party made their escape from that same island years before. The two young tortoises are brought aboard as well, named Creep and Creep Too, and given into Batu Batu's care as ship's mascots. In response to this new threat, the officers establish a new set of battle-ready procedures for responding to sea monster attacks.

The party later encounters two more sea serpents — smaller than the one Keyes described, but still far larger than any of the crew — racing alongside the ship beyond a long rocky spit, faster than the "Medallion" itself. Only Noddy, watching from the rigging, and Knick Nab, who climbs up to join him, can actually see the creatures, so Werner has to fire the mortar blind, walking his shots onto target on their shouted corrections; two ranging rounds barely graze a serpent, but spending two Coins of Fate on a third shot, he lands a solid hit that sends it into a squealing dive, its companion fleeing with it. Moments later, the "Medallion" demonstrates its own magical nature, lifting itself on a great wave to pass safely over a rocky reef that would have otherwise destroyed it. Doubling back afterward to search the water, the party finds no corpse, no blood, and no oil slick, leaving the serpent's fate unconfirmed.

After several more weeks of travel, the ship is suddenly becalmed by a powerful, unnatural stillness in the air. The crew spends the windless first day on routine maintenance and fishing, netting enough to supplement the ship's stores for a hot fish stew that evening, but the calm holds through the night. The next morning, Noddy sends his familiar, Pocket, high into the air to scout ahead, and the bird spots distant peaks in the direction they had been heading. Unable to sail, the crew, including the officers, takes on the arduous task of towing the ship with its longboats, rowing in relays of about four hours each through a full day and night while Batu Batu keeps them fed with hot meals brought out through the day rather than saved for its end. They sight two massive island spires in the distance. One bears the wreckage of a ship perched atop it, while on the other a mysterious lone figure is spotted, who then uses a large sail to leap from the taller spire to the lower one before disappearing from sight.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Keyes: An able seaman from the Northern naval vessel "The Fortnum," rescued by the party after being marooned for fleeing his post during a sea serpent attack. He has joined the crew of "The Medallion," assigned to the captain's watch where Tyler and Old Salter keep an eye on him.
  • Captain Mason: The captain of "The Fortnum" who marooned Keyes for cowardice.
  • Jacopa: A crewmember on "The Medallion" who explained the Northern Navy's informal practice of marooning to the party.
  • Wat: A former whaler serving as an Able Seaman aboard "The Medallion." Manning the wheel through the night, he calls out the night's shrinking soundings as the ship creeps toward the light, and is later assigned to the harpoon gun under the new serpent orders.
  • Naymes: A large, physically imposing able seaman placed in charge of a four-man team of axemen under the new serpent orders.
  • Arnum: A Medallion crewman put in charge of a four-man team of spearmen under the new serpent orders.
  • Tyler: The Medallion's Sergeant-at-Arms. Alongside Old Salter, he is charged with keeping an eye on the newly recruited Keyes, and stands among Mani's marines under the new serpent orders.
  • Gus: A Medallion able seaman assigned musket duty under the new serpent orders, tasked with aiming for the eyes of any serpent that attacks.
  • Sharks: A large swarm of various dangerous sharks, including hammerheads and tiger sharks, that surrounds the ship at night and drives the local tortoises ashore.
  • Giant Tortoises: A large population of sea tortoises, some of immense size, inhabiting a small rocky island in The Shatters; two young ones are adopted as ship's mascots and named Creep and Creep Too.
  • Sea Serpents: Two sea serpents, smaller than the one described by Keyes but still enormous, were encountered and driven off by Werner's mortar fire. A much larger one was described by Keyes as having attacked the "Fortnum," crushing part of its foredeck with a head the size of a horse.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Shatters: The party continues their slow, cautious journey through this treacherous region of rock spires.
  • Tortoise Rock: The party's name for a small, rocky island pinnacle inhabited by a large number of giant sea tortoises, where they found the marooned sailor, Keyes.
  • The Twin Spires: Two massive rock spires sighted at the end of the becalmed night's rowing. One bears the wreckage of a ship perched atop it; on the other, the party glimpses a lone figure who leaps between the two spires using a large sail before vanishing from sight.
  • New Sardinia: The "Fortnum's" home port, marked on the party's own charts. Consulting those charts with Keyes, the party realizes it is the same Northern settlement they already knew as the island of the Stone Men.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text: • Sea Serpent Encounter: The party engaged two sea serpents from a distance as the creatures raced alongside the ship beyond a rocky spit, faster than the "Medallion" could match. Only Noddy and Knick Nab, aloft in the rigging, could actually see the serpents past the intervening spit of rock, forcing Werner to fire the mortar blind on their shouted, ill-measured corrections; with an indirect weapon lobbing shots at a moving target he couldn't see, the first two ranging rounds only grazed a serpent before Werner, spending two Coins of Fate, scored a solid hit that sent it into a squealing dive, its companion fleeing with it.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The party rescued a sailor, Keyes, who initially claimed to be a shipwreck survivor but was later revealed to have been marooned for deserting his post during a sea serpent attack on his ship, the "Fortnum."
  • Brought aboard, Keyes was awestruck by the "Medallion's" unexplained glow, immediately assuming the ship must belong to the Two — evidently the default explanation for any inexplicable display of power. The officers, amused, briefly weighed letting the assumption stand and passing themselves off as carrying a prophet of the Two, though nothing came of the idea.
  • Keyes's account provides the party with their first second-hand description of a sea serpent: a single, massive, snake-like body with a head the size of a horse and coils stretching far into the distance, which surfaced without warning during a gunnery drill and crushed part of the foredeck. He also confirmed the "Fortnum" was damaged but survived and, at the priests' insistence, continued its mission deeper into the Shatters. The party notes with unease that the attack came while the "Fortnum's" guns were being drilled, raising the question of whether gunfire itself might draw the creatures.
  • The party learned from Jacopa that marooning, while not a traditional Northern Navy punishment, has been informally adopted by some captains for capital offenses — such as desertion in battle — now that ships can no longer return to the mainland; it is considered less cruel than a court martial since the condemned is left a small store of supplies.
  • The officers developed a detailed set of "serpent orders," a new standard operating procedure for how the crew should react to a sea monster attack: all four swivel guns permanently manned, Wat posted at the harpoon gun, a dedicated mortar crew, incendiaries kept ready, and two four-man melee teams — spearmen under Arnum and axemen under Naymes — standing by for boarders. Mani's own marine detachment — himself, Tyler, Gus, and Leela — was assigned to repel boarders directly, with Gus posted for aimed musket fire and Leela wielding her prized monster-slaying axe. The party also discussed weighting a large net with cannonballs as a possible means of entangling a serpent, though nothing came of the idea this session.
  • The party witnessed a powerful magical act from their own ship, "The Medallion," which lifted itself on a wave to avoid running aground on a rocky reef. Combined with the ship's bell ringing of its own accord earlier in the session, this further convinces the party that the ship itself is sentient and protective.
  • When the ship was becalmed, Cosimo and Noddy determined the cause was an active, large-scale magical effect they identified as "Still Air," sensing only that, in Cosimo's words, "a foul voice on the wind sets its will against us."
  • During the cautious transit through the Shatters, Noddy repeatedly used a water vision spell to see up to 100 feet into the water ahead, watching the seafloor for the shoaling that warns of hidden rocks.
  • The party discussed tactics for a future encounter with an enemy ship. Cosimo described an illusion that could cloak the "Medallion" inside a stationary false image roughly 160 feet across — not proof against close inspection, but effective at a distance or by night — which he could sustain for up to seven hours a day without depleting his reserves, or longer in a pinch at the cost of days to recover. Noddy's portal spell, capable of tearing a temporary hole through a ship's hull below the waterline, was floated as a devastating, if risky, option if the party could get a swimmer close enough; short of that, they discussed swimming a sealed, weighted keg of gunpowder up to an enemy hull to be set off by hand, ideally against the powder store, or aiming for a fire on the enemy's gun deck instead.

  • Two small, live tortoises, adopted as ship's mascots and named Creep and Creep Too.
  • The shell of a large, butchered tortoise, kept as a souvenir and for collecting rainwater.
