docs.title: The Prisoner of the Shatters and the Sunken Wreck
Events and Actions
docs.text:
Musing over the mysterious figure they had watched glide between the spires the night before, the party fell into a broader debate about the true nature of magic — noting that the priests' powers, Riu's healing gift (which even Mistress Clara says comes from the two), and Noddy's own hybrid essence-and-mentalism magic all seemed to work differently, despite the church's insistence that all power flows from the two gods alone.

The party, becalmed in The Shatters, continued their approach via rowboats toward two prominent rock spires, one of which held the wreckage of a large ship. They were confronted by an old Islander who had positioned a large cannon menacingly. Rather than fly a national flag or colors of convenience, the party ran up their own banner — the Medallion's circular device — and used semaphore to warn him that firing his loose, unbraced gun would send it recoiling back through his own shelter as much as it would endanger them. When he demanded to know who they represented, the party toyed with him through the flags, claiming allegiance to "the three" rather than the two and describing their quest as a search for "power beyond the two," testing his reaction before revealing anything more concrete. After this exchange, Riu teleported directly onto the spire to parlay; his sudden appearance so alarmed Mani that he nearly opened fire, believing Riu had been dragged there by hostile magic, until Noddy talked him down.

The man revealed himself to be Grantos, the legendary wind mage who was captured during the voyage of the "Kingship" 44 years ago. Riu, drawing on evidence the party had gathered at an old ruined port in the Channel Islands — graves of the "Kingship"'s dead, some seemingly by plague and some by violence, and hints in a ruined church that a navigator had survived and returned north — guessed correctly who he was, even venturing the name "De Rendal" as someone Grantos might have sailed with, a guess Grantos did not deny. When the rest of the party rowed over to join him, Mani suggested leaving weapons in the boat as a show of good faith; Leela flatly refused and kept her axe. As introductions were made, Grantos recognized Werner at once by his family's resemblance — and by the harpoons slung across his back — and confirmed he knew of the De Rendal line, leaving unspoken the question of whether Werner's own long-vanished grandfather, commissioned to lead a westward expedition before the Great Change, might have sailed with Grantos aboard that same doomed "Kingship." Riu, in a rare moment of candor, gave his true family name, Infurious Montesigna, alongside the name he now goes by, while Knick Nab stayed guarded and offered only an alias, "Nemo." Grantos explained that he has been a prisoner of the Divinity of Two ever since and is now magically bound to protect the wreck of the "Divine Rite," the very ship impaled on the spire. His magical binding is tied to a Diad that was lost in the surrounding waters when the ship was destroyed. He also confirmed he knew Mistress Clara, Riu's mentor and a fellow prisoner of the church — a claim he only fully accepted once shown the "Medallion" through a spyglass and recognized Clara's likeness carved into the ship's own figurehead — which helped settle any remaining suspicion between the two parties. Kneeling at the water's edge, Riu attempted to attune himself to the bound Diad and succeeded; through it he sensed an immense and alien power, one capable of channeling the full destructive wrath of the two gods — clearly not the same magic as his own healing gift, nor, as far as he could tell, the same as the priests' more mundane divine magic.

Leela and Grantos shared a conversation in their native tongue, grieving the destruction of their respective homelands by the Divinity. Moved by Leela's sorrow, Mani gripped his necklace and silently vowed that the party would stop the Divinity's destructive actions — the realization that the church could annihilate an entire island turning what had felt like an adventure into something far graver. At the party's request, Grantos summoned a wind to allow "The Medallion" to anchor safely nearby.

The party then began preparations for an underwater expedition to find the lost Diad. Noddy's initial dive was cut short when the cold and the disorientation of breathing water for the first time left him nauseous and panicked; he had to cancel the spell and vomit up the water before he could breathe air again. Before risking anyone else, Cosimo dropped a globe of illusory light down onto the wreck to scout it from the surface; the sudden glow drove the resident giant octopus into hiding but drew swarms of fish and several sharks toward the area, confirming both the wreck's location and the dangers waiting below. Werner, relying on his natural talents for cold resistance and breath-holding, then successfully completed a harrowing 100-foot dive to secure a guide rope to the sunken portion of the wreck, though he was menaced by a shark on the way back up. Riu followed down the same rope, using water breathing, water vision, and underwater movement magic to explore the wreck and surrounding seabed; he drove off the skittish giant octopus with a light spell of his own, spotted the spilled treasure chest and a giant clam, and confirmed the seabed was far too vast to search by hand, before repelling two more curious sharks with a telekinetic push on his way back up. To narrow down the search area, Cosimo performed a four-hour ritual to cast a long-range "Detect Magic" spell, which successfully located several magical sources on the seafloor. As night fell over the search, Mani offered the crew a silver piece for every shark they could haul out of the water, and hands set to work with drag nets and gill nets to help clear the area for the dives still to come.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Grantos: An ancient and powerful Islander wind mage. He was the sole occupant of the rock spire, magically bound to protect the wreck of the "Divine Rite." He has survived alone for three years by carefully rationing collected water and eating the giant tortoises that visit the spire.
  • Leela: She had an emotional conversation with Grantos about the loss of her home, Spider Island, and refused Mani's request that she leave her axe in the boat before boarding.
  • Prelate Jacque: Named by Grantos as one of two "Divine Rite" crew members he overheard discussing the party — the same prelate who once tried to have Cosimo confined as a heretic aboard the "Advance." He and an unnamed Censure spoke of Cosimo as having "corrupted the powers of the two."
  • Giant Octopus: A large octopus was seen near the wreck on the seafloor. It fled repeatedly, first from Cosimo's scouting light and later from Riu's, each time appearing agitated by the sudden glow.
  • Sharks: Numerous sharks were attracted to the area by magical light and menaced the party members during their dives.
  • Giant Sea Tortoises: Several large tortoises were seen in the area.
  • Giant Clam: A massive clam was observed on the seafloor near the wreck. It closed abruptly at one point, prompting speculation about what might be sheltering inside.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Shatters: The session took place entirely within this treacherous region of shattered rock spires, the former site of Spider Island. The party's focus was a pair of rock pinnacles, one of which holds the aft section of the "Divine Rite."
  • The Sunken Wreck of the "Divine Rite": The forward section of the holy vessel rests on the seabed 100 feet below the surface. The area is littered with debris, a spilled treasure chest, and is home to various sea creatures.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The initial encounter with Grantos was tense, as he had a cannon aimed at the party's boat. The situation was de-escalated through conversation.
  • Mani nearly fired on Grantos the instant Riu teleported onto the spire, mistaking the sudden appearance for an attack, before Noddy convinced him Riu had done it under his own power.
  • Werner De Rendal was menaced by a shark during his ascent. Riu was also followed and threatened by two sharks, which he pushed away with a telekinetic spell before returning to the surface unharmed.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The party confirmed the man on the spire is Grantos. He has been a prisoner of the Divinity of Two for 44 years, since being captured on the "Kingship" expedition.
  • Grantos was forced to guide the "Divine Rite" on its mission to destroy the Totem of Earth on Spider Island. He is magically bound by a Diad, wielded by a cleric on that ship, to fulfill his last given order: "protect the ship." He cannot leave the immediate vicinity of the wreckage.
  • The party learned there was more than one Diad on the original "Kingship" voyage. Censure Bayar consumed one to destroy the Totem of Air, while the ship's cleric, Abiyard, used a second one to enslave Grantos. Grantos revealed that Abiyard survived the disastrous return journey and has since risen to become one of the Twin Eminences, the highest authority in the Divinity of Two.
  • Grantos offered his own explanation for why the church destroys what it cannot control: he believes the two gods, and their priests, cannot accept that any power exists beyond their own — that admitting as much would mean admitting there are other gods.
  • Grantos overheard crew members of the "Divine Rite" — Prelate Jacque and an unnamed Censure — discussing the party. They spoke of Cosimo as an "evil one" who had "corrupted the powers of the two," suggesting Jacque's suspicions of Cosimo followed him well beyond his time aboard the "Advance."
  • Attuning to the Diad, Riu sensed it holds an immensely powerful and destructive spell, one capable of amplifying a wielder's magic manyfold — a plausible explanation for how it can unleash a cataclysm on the scale of the ones that consumed the Totem of Air and, more recently, Spider Island's Totem of Earth.
  • Deep-sea diving at 100 feet is incredibly dangerous due to the intense cold and water pressure, which causes severe pain and discomfort. Ordinary tricks for clearing painful ear pressure don't work when the lungs are full of water, though working water through the nasal passages offers some relief. These environmental hazards pose a significant obstacle, even for characters with magical assistance.
  • Weighing how to make future dives safer, the party discussed several options: an improvised diving bell made from an upturned, weighted boat (rejected as impractical — keeping such a thing balanced and airtight while descending was judged too great a risk), securing ropes to the wreck and its cannon to ease movement up and down, and chumming the water some distance away to draw sharks off from the dive site. Cosimo also revealed that his ritual magic can draw bonus power from any crew members willing to participate, hinting at a larger, ship-wide ceremony to come.
  • Using a long-range "Detect Magic" spell, Cosimo located multiple magical sources on the seabed: one in the prow of the wreck, another in a spilled treasure chest, a third inside a giant clam, and a fourth within a cave beneath a giant tortoise.

docs.title: Nets, Clams, and the Scourge of the Heretic
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session opened with the party still anchored near the wreck of "The Divine Rite" in The Shatters, finalising preparations for their underwater recovery operation. Drawing on his own earlier test dive, Riu shared with Noddy the trick for equalising the ear pressure of a fast descent — knowledge Noddy would soon put to use. Noddy then tested the destructive potential of his vacuum spell by casting it at a shark directly from the jolly boat; the shark went limp and began to bleed, and the party was fairly confident they had killed it. The party rowed ashore to consult with Grantos. He confirmed that while he could keep the seas perfectly calm for their work, his powers did not extend to commanding sea creatures, the wind and air being his sole domain. Asked about the giant sea tortoises occasionally seen nearby, he explained they were normally docile — though they might bite defensively if crowded — and had long been a source of food that helped sustain him through his captivity. Grantos agreed to maintain calm waters and, when informed that Captain Mason's "The Fortnum" had been mapping The Shatters and might eventually find its way to the site, resolved to remain vigilant for approaching ships; he noted grimly that a Northern Navy vessel finding him would, at best, simply strand him here again and, at worst, re-enslave him.

Back aboard, the party briefly weighed more ambitious schemes — hauling the entire prow of the wreck to the surface, or dredging the debris field wholesale — before concluding both were impractical given the wreck's size and the ship's limited rigging. With the plan finalised, Cosimo constructed a net cage approximately eight feet on a side from the ship's cargo nets, framed with spare spars and weighted with cannonballs at the base, with a four-point harness rigged at the top and reinforced with a strength-enhancing spell. The netting was left open at the bottom so its flexible walls could drape and seal around whatever uneven terrain it settled on, whether bare seafloor or a wrecked ship's deck. The crew rigged the ship's yard arm and capstan as a crane to raise and lower the cage, with Cosimo directing as the ship's rigger, and a barrel on a separate line was prepared to receive recovered goods. Cosimo also cast smell-obscuring illusions on the divers to reduce their chances of attracting sharks.

After a full night's rest to restore their magical reserves, the operation began the following morning, targeting the debris field of the spilled treasure chest. Noddy directed the cage from the surface using his underwater vision while Cosimo worked the crane. The cage landed slightly off target, but Riu dove down and, using his supernatural freedom of movement underwater, pushed the cage directly over the pile of scattered coins and valuables. Werner De Rendal then made a spectacular diving entry, harpoons and all, and joined Riu inside the cage, helping muscle it fully into position over the pile. Werner then grabbed a single shiny coin off the top and swam straight back to the surface with it — a decision that earned him some ribbing once it turned out he'd been sitting on a magic item the whole time. Riu remained below and set about methodically gathering coins, gems, and jewellery from the seafloor into the barrel. Noddy swam down to join him, taking a minor concussion hit as he brushed past one of the sharks on the way and discovering firsthand that shark hide is rough and scratchy rather than smooth — the startled shark seemed equally unsure what to make of him. He then kept it and its circling companions at bay from inside the cage, poking out at them through the netting with his magic rope. Before signalling to surface, Riu checked the broken treasure chest itself for a false bottom or hidden compartment; finding nothing, and with the chest too large to fit in the barrel regardless, he left it behind in the debris field. After roughly ten minutes of collection, Riu untied the barrel and gave its rope several sharp tugs; up on deck, Cosimo read the subtle, rhythmic strain of a hundred feet of hemp cordage as only an experienced rigger could, recognised the signal to haul away, and had the sailors bring the barrel up heavy with recovered treasure.

Rather than ascending immediately, Riu and Noddy set about moving the cage over to the giant clam nearby. Shifting it proved far harder while it sat on the seabed than it had while still being lowered, so Noddy used his ventriloquism spell to call up to Cosimo to raise it a few feet off the bottom; freed of the ground, Riu was then able to muscle the cage into position directly above the clam. Peering inside, Riu could see something tangled within the clam's interior—a looped cord or pendant of some kind—beside an enormous pearl, larger than a man's head and oddly patterned as though painted, though it drew less interest than the stranger prize. His attempt to teleport the object out failed, as though the item resisted the magic. Noddy then threaded his spider silk magic rope into the clam's opening and looped it around the object. The clam snapped shut on the rope. They tied the other end of the rope to the cage and signalled the crew to raise it. As the cage was winched upward, it dragged the enormous clam off the seafloor. Under the tremendous strain, the clam eventually released the rope—and the object within—before slowly sinking back to the bottom, spitting a jet of water at them as parting commentary. Three sharks followed the cage up as it ascended but did not attack.

Back on deck, both Riu and Noddy coughed up considerable quantities of water. Noddy, in high spirits, enthusiastically dropped several red-hot cannonballs into the sea until the officers put a stop to the waste of ammunition. The treasure tipped from the barrel onto the deck amounted to approximately 464 gold pieces' worth of mixed coins, gems, and jewellery. The single coin Werner had grabbed from the pile turned out to be the Twin-Faced Doubloon—a holy relic of the Divinity of Two, made of combined gold and silver, bearing a sun face on one side and a moon face on the other. Werner determined that wearing it sun-side out grants a substantial bonus (+20) to projecting authority, while the moon side fosters trust. He noted that priests of the Divinity are commonly seen wearing similar medallions in exactly this fashion, switching sides depending on the occasion. The object from the clam was the Scourge of the Heretic: a two-tailed whip with a finely crafted wooden handle and silver pommel, one cord ending in a silver sunburst and the other in a silver crescent moon. The sunburst lash inflicts burning pain well beyond what a physical whip should; the moon lash has a strangely soothing quality. A hook near the pommel lets one lash be clipped back so only the other trails free. Noddy struck himself with it once to test the claim, and confirmed the pain was far sharper than the whip's size would suggest. When both are used together they create a cycle of torment and restoration that prevents death but makes survival unbearable. The senior officers, impressed by the haul, proposed that Riu, Werner, and Noddy each receive an extra share of the loot for their uncommon feats of valour — a decision left for the full body of senior officers to formalise later. The whole crew cheered as the loot was revealed, clapping the divers on the back.

That evening the party brought Grantos food and rum—his finest meal in perhaps forty years—and shared what they had found. Grantos recognised the Scourge of the Heretic at once, confirming it had been used on him and others throughout his captivity, and that it was a unique item passed among the clergy as needed. It had been brought aboard "The Divine Rite" specifically for his punishment and motivation. The party also recalled that the other priest who had survived the original voyage with Grantos—the one who did not perish alongside the Diad—was named Abiyard, now risen to become one of the Divinity of Two's Twin Eminences. Mani, deeply moved, vowed the scourge would never touch Grantos again. The party also discussed whether the Diad they already possessed could be used to break Grantos's magical binding; the answer appeared to be no. Asked to describe the Diad that bound him, Grantos could only offer a hazy image—something spherical and ringed, like a small world—unable to recall more after so many years. All recovered items were placed with the Quartermaster under lock and key, with the Scourge of the Heretic retained by Noddy pending a formal share allocation among the senior officers. Cosimo, meanwhile, entertained the crew with a dramatic account of the dive, accompanied by musical accompaniment on the fiddle.

The following morning the party turned their attention to the second magical location identified by Cosimo's earlier ritual: the prow of the sunken "Divine Rite." Noddy prepared a barrier spell capable of conjuring a pocket of dense, breathable air anchored to the seabed, but held it in reserve as an emergency measure rather than commit to maintaining it throughout the dive. Cosimo's crane work landed the cage squarely on the prow on the first attempt. Riu went down first, weighting himself with a cannonball for a faster descent rather than swimming down slowly as before; the rapid drop built painful pressure in his ears that he only barely managed to relieve before reaching bottom. His projected light then drove the octopus sheltering there away into the wreck. Finding little of note on the exposed deck, he opened a hatch and descended into the hold to search inside. Noddy followed soon after, riding a cannonball he had heated to a glowing 500°F and adjusting to the fast descent without trouble this time; he remained on the prow beneath the net, harrying the water with his magic rope. Outside, however, three sharks closed in more aggressively than before. Noddy brandished the cannonball and then unleashed his vacuum spell on the nearest attacker—a devastating hit that sent a plume of water geysering up to the surface, visible from the deck. The blast churned up such a thick cloud of bubbles and silt that Werner, swimming down to help, found himself completely blind and had to turn back before reaching bottom. Seeing the attack from inside the hold, Riu cast a shock bolt upward at the sharks. The electricity arced through the seawater, striking the sharks but also propagating back through the water to shock both Riu and Noddy painfully. Riu was knocked down with burns and Noddy was stunned and thrown to the seafloor. Recovering, Noddy cast another vacuum spell at a second shark, again suffering concussive feedback. The combination of lightning and collapsing vacuums proved too much for the sharks, and all three scattered and fled. The session ended with the sharks driven off and Riu inside the sunken hold of the "Divine Rite," the Diad still not yet recovered.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Grantos: The ancient Islander wind mage bound to the wreck of "The Divine Rite." He kept the seas calm for the party's diving operations and identified the Scourge of the Heretic, confirming it had been used on him throughout his 40-year captivity.
  • Giant Sea Tortoises ("Kota"): Enormous tortoises that inhabit the waters around Grantos's wreck. Normally docile, they may bite defensively if crowded. Grantos identified them as a food source that has helped sustain him through his long captivity.
  • Giant Clam: A massive clam on the seafloor near the treasure chest debris, found to contain the Scourge of the Heretic tangled within it alongside an enormous, oddly patterned pearl.
  • Sharks: Multiple sharks circled the cage and menaced the divers during both dives. Three attacked aggressively during the second dive at the prow before being driven off by Noddy's vacuum spells and Riu's shock bolt.
  • Giant Octopus: Present at the prow of the sunken "Divine Rite." It was driven away from its position by Riu's projected light and retreated into the wreck.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Shatters: The entire session took place within this treacherous field of shattered rock spires, the former site of Spider Island. The party remained anchored near the towering spire from which the wreck of "The Divine Rite" is suspended.
  • The wreck of "The Divine Rite": Two areas of the submerged forward section were worked this session. The first was the debris field around the spilled treasure chest on the seafloor, roughly 100 feet down. The second was the prow of the sunken ship itself, which sits on the seabed and includes an accessible hatch leading into the forward hold. Cosimo's earlier ritual had identified four sites of magical interest within the wreck in total; with these two now searched, two more remain unexplored.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• At the very start of the session, Noddy tested his vacuum spell on a shark directly from the jolly boat; the shark went limp and began to bleed, leaving the party fairly confident they had killed it.
  • During the second dive, three sharks attacked aggressively outside the cage at the prow. Noddy's Total Cavitational Collapse spell severely injured the first shark, but the spell's own shockwaves knocked Noddy down and stunned him. Riu's shock bolt struck the second shark but propagated through the seawater, knocking Riu down with burns and a minus-15 injury to activity. Noddy's second vacuum spell badly injured a third shark, again with concussive feedback. Even sheltered inside the wreck's hold, Riu felt both of Noddy's blasts and was knocked down in turn each time. All three sharks then fled the area. Neither Riu nor Noddy sustained permanent injury beyond their temporary wounds.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Twin-Faced Doubloon is a holy relic of the Divinity of Two. Worn with the sun face outward, it grants a substantial bonus (+20) to projecting authority. Worn with the moon face outward, it fosters trust in those the wearer addresses. Priests of the Divinity are routinely seen using it in exactly this way—sun out for sermons and pronouncements, moon out for private counsel.
  • The Scourge of the Heretic is a unique item passed among the Divinity of Two's clergy as required, not assigned to any one priest; it was specifically brought aboard "The Divine Rite" to punish and motivate Grantos, and has been used on him and many others throughout the church's history. The sun lash inflicts burning pain beyond its physical impact; the moon lash has a soothing quality. Used together, sun and moon create a cycle of torment and restoration that keeps a victim conscious and suffering indefinitely.
  • The other priest who survived the original voyage alongside Grantos was named Abiyard, who has since risen to become one of the Divinity of Two's Twin Eminences.
  • The Diad already in the party's possession does not appear to have the power to break another person's magical binding. Grantos will not be freed simply by recovering a different Diad—the specific Diad that binds him must be found. Grantos's own memory of that Diad is hazy, but he described it as spherical and ringed, like a small world. He also revealed he once tried to leave the wreck under his own power; the attempt nearly killed him, underscoring how lethal the binding truly is.
  • Electricity propagates through seawater in all directions. Casting a shock bolt underwater affects everyone nearby, not only the intended target.
  • Noddy's vacuum spell (referred to as "Total Cavitational Collapse" by the party) generates powerful concussive shockwaves that injure nearby party members in addition to the target.
  • Spellcasting underwater is possible for those breathing water, but noticeably harder than on the surface; a caster must recast their water-breathing spell before it lapses or risk being caught without air mid-dive.
  • Cosimo can, with three to seven minutes of ritual preparation, roughly triple the duration of another caster's spell, at something like a 75–80% chance of success — a capability he offered up for future dives but which went untested this session.
  • Captain Mason's "The Fortnum" has been mapping The Shatters extensively and may eventually reach the site of the wreck. Grantos was advised to watch for it—the Northern Navy would not leave him at liberty; best case, they would simply strand him here again, worst case, they would re-enslave him.
  • The giant sea tortoises around Grantos's wreck are normally docile and have long been a food source for him, though they may bite defensively if crowded.
  • Power points recover slowly—only 40% of a caster's total can be restored in a single night's sleep of eight hours—meaning successive days of heavy magical work will gradually deplete the spellcasters.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• Approximately 464 gold pieces' worth of mixed coins, gems, and jewellery (recovered from the spilled treasure chest debris field).
  • Twin-Faced Doubloon: A combined gold-and-silver holy medallion of the Divinity of Two bearing a sun face on one side and a moon face on the other, with two small holes near the edge for wearing on a cord. Currently held in the ship's strongroom pending share allocation.
  • Scourge of the Heretic: A two-tailed whip with a finely crafted wooden handle, silver pommel with an affixing hook, one cord ending in a silver sunburst and the other in a silver crescent moon. Currently held by Noddy pending share allocation.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text:
• Several cannonballs (used as descent weights and heated as shark deterrents, including a number dropped into the sea by Noddy before being stopped).
  • The treasure chest itself: checked for a false bottom or hidden compartment and found to hold nothing further; too large to fit in the barrel, it was left behind in the debris field.
  • A pearl larger than a man's head, seen inside the giant clam alongside the Scourge of the Heretic but not recovered before the clam sank back to the bottom.

docs.title: Ink, Fear, and a Favorable Wind
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session resumed with the party still anchored in The Shatters at the wreck of "The Divine Rite." Riu remained inside the forward hold of the sunken ship, searching in near-darkness, while Noddy waited outside the dive cage after the sharks from the previous session had dispersed.

Not long after, the corpse of one of the sharks Noddy had fatally wounded in the previous dive drifted into view near the cage — confirmation that at least one casualty of that earlier fight hadn't survived. The giant octopus, having earlier retreated deeper into the wreck, came slithering back over the coral toward it; when Noddy prodded at it with his rope, it settled on the dead shark instead, a beak disproportionately large for its body tearing into the carcass just yards from him. Unsettled by the sight, he pulled his rope back and let it feed.

A large lobster then emerged from the gloom beyond the cage and advanced steadily through the water; nearby clams sensed it coming and skittered out of its path, giving it a wide berth as though they knew something Noddy didn't. As its claws began probing through the air wall, Noddy cast Fear on it. The lobster retreated at a speed that was, in his words, disturbingly fast, and the fear spell's area of effect spread underwater in all directions, sending smaller nearby sea life scattering as well.

Shortly after, the giant octopus that had retreated in earlier dives returned, one tentacle probing through the mesh of the cage toward Noddy. He cast Fear on it as well. The octopus shot backward and released a vast cloud of black ink that blotted out the surrounding water entirely. Noddy's knowledge of cephalopods told him this was a flight reflex, not an attack — the ink a smokescreen for escape — but it left him temporarily blind in a dark cloud that his water-sight could not penetrate. He used his clear desalinate liquid spell — its effect confined to roughly a cubic foot — to scrub the worst of the ink from the water around his face, then dropped his existing air wall and cast a fresh one inside the cage.

While the commotion above continued, Riu pressed on with his methodical search of the hold. He recovered a small flat box — roughly the dimensions of a pistol case, apparently sealed — and placed it in his sack without opening it, uncertain whether breaking the seal might compromise its watertight integrity. He continued searching and ultimately found, buried under a layer of silt and debris, an object he recognised on sight as a Diad — not because it was one of a kind, but because he had seen others like it displayed at church ceremonies in his former life. He put it in his sack. With the sack now heavy and unwieldy, his air running low, and no way to speak to Noddy underwater beyond taps on the dive rope, he thumped on the hatch. Noddy heard the knocking and relayed the signal to the surface, and the crew began turning the capstan.

Above, the captain, Knick Nab, had been keeping watch from the crow's nest. As the cage was being winched up, he spotted the tip of a mast on the horizon — a large ship, sails furled, being slowly towed or pulled through the calm. He sent for the ship's boy, Tolly, who brought up the sextant; with the mast just cresting the horizon on flat, calm seas, the geometry gave a fixed and reliable range, and the captain called it out: six caliber-cams. He ordered all hands to bring the boats and cage aboard at speed and called for Cosimo. Cosimo, who had been preparing for exactly this possibility, cast a large-scale illusion — the ocean background behind the ship, covering a radius far wider than "The Medallion" herself — effectively making the ship invisible to any observer from that direction for as long as the spell held.

The divers were pulled to the surface and extracted from the cage and jolly boats. Sharks had returned to circle during the ascent but did not attack. As the crew worked, the ship's bell rang of its own accord: "Danger."

With both divers safely aboard, Riu took the Diad and attempted to attune to it in the jolly boat on the short row to Grantos's island. He succeeded. The Diad is a holy relic of the Divinity of Two — among the most powerful the party has encountered — and what it allows its wielder to do is unmistakable: it enables the direct imposition of a divine geas upon another person, backed not by priestly authority but by the literal will of the Two gods themselves. A task so commanded cannot be resisted, and any failure to obey invites the wrath of the gods directly. Riu also felt, with certainty, that he himself could not use it. Since being declared a heretic by an avatar of the Father in an earlier encounter, he is cut off from any direct conduit to the Two.

The party landed on the rock and climbed to where Grantos kept his post among the remains of "The Divine Rite." When shown the Diad, Grantos confirmed it was the relic — and that despite the party now holding it, he still felt no change in his compulsion. He remained bound to guard the wreck. Having the Diad in hand was not sufficient to free him; the binding would only end if a qualified follower of the Two used the Diad to issue a new command releasing him.

The party returned to "The Medallion." Mani, mindful that magic has never taken hold of him the way it does others, wondered aloud whether simply holding the Diad might weaken or negate its hold over Grantos where attunement could not — no one could say for certain, so he decided to find out directly. He held the Diad and attempted to attune to it. He gained a sense of its nature broadly consistent with what Riu had described — immense power, a direct link to the Two — but he too could not operate it. His resistance to magic proved no help here; using the Diad requires full commitment to the Two, not merely proximity to its power, and Mani had never committed himself fully as a follower of the Two. The Diad made that plainly felt.

The captain had meanwhile rowed out past the edge of Cosimo's illusion in the jolly boat, spyglass in hand, to observe the ship on the horizon. Its sails remained furled; it was definitely being towed. He assessed it as days away, not hours. On returning to the ship, Keyes — the able seaman the party had rescued from Tortoise Rock, formerly of "The Fortnum" — confirmed what many already suspected: the ship was "The Fortnum" herself, under Captain Mason. Keyes knew the ship well. She carried at least two priests.

What followed was a long and heated deliberation about whether to run, hide, or fight. Cosimo's illusion, cast at full strength, could mask "The Medallion" for roughly an hour at a time and cover far more than enough radius to hide the whole ship, but sustaining it through daylight hours would cost him twice what he could recover overnight — nowhere near enough to hide the ship for the days it would take "The Fortnum" to arrive. Grantos could provide favorable wind, create fog, and make the passage difficult for any pursuing ship, but he could not guarantee "The Fortnum" carried no wind mage of her own to contest him. The party could not free Grantos without a qualified priest of the Two to wield the Diad, and Nicolas, the priest from "The Advance" who might have served this purpose, had not been brought on this voyage.

One proposal was to fight: with at least two priests known to be aboard, capture one and either persuade or compel them into using the Diad to free Grantos. Suggestions ranged from talking the priest around to using magic to sway them to duping them under a false pretext. The idea was set aside — "The Fortnum" was reckoned a three-decked frigate carrying some two hundred men, far beyond what the party believed it could take and hold cleanly, and handing the Diad to any priest, willing or not, risked losing it to the enemy outright.

Cosimo proposed spending an hour or two attempting a ritual to break Grantos's binding directly, channelling the crew's faith through himself to petition the Two. The idea foundered on the same problem as attuning the Diad: whoever performed the ritual would still be the one asking, and none of them believed themselves a clean enough vessel for it. Cosimo admitted he did not believe strongly enough to serve as a conduit himself — gathering the crew's faith through him would not change whose intention the gods were judging. Mani, pressed on whether he was willing to fully commit himself as a follower of the Two, admitted he was not, unwilling to give up his other loyalties. Riu suggested Noddy might have the standing to try, since he had not been declared a heretic, but Noddy — no ardent follower of the Two himself — declined the charge. Without anyone both able and willing to serve as a true conduit to the Two, the ritual was abandoned in favor of the plan to return for Nicolas.

The party visited Grantos a final time to ask directly what he needed. He confirmed that being forced from the island against his geas — whether by the party rescuing him or by "The Fortnum" capturing him — would itself risk the wrath of the gods, so neither side could simply carry him off. He judged that if "The Fortnum" did take him, he would likely not survive; his captors would have little reason to keep him alive once the Diad was beyond their reach. He told the party: give him wind, and they could escape. He would keep "The Fortnum" at bay with storms and unfavorable currents as long as he could. He acknowledged that if they fled with the Diad, the worst that could happen — the enemy seizing the Diad and giving him a new, hostile command — was prevented. He urged them to leave.

The vote was unanimous. They would run.

Cosimo offered Grantos a cake of rum and a loaded pistol with shot and powder — a gesture Grantos accepted with the wry observation that he had not had rum in thirty years. The party promised to return with a means to free him. Grantos told them to make their course and tell him what he needed to do.

They chose to sail southwest, reasoning that "The Medallion" was the faster ship and would have a head start regardless of the route "The Fortnum" took. Grantos warned there was still a chance "The Fortnum" could tack and give chase in the same direction, but agreed the head start would be theirs regardless. He sent a strong west wind ahead of them, carrying "The Medallion" out from The Shatters in the opposite direction from "The Fortnum." Cosimo created a vast cloud bank to cover their departure, obscuring the ship's movement from any observer looking toward The Shatters. "The Medallion" slipped away under full sail into the open sea.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Grantos: The ancient Islander wind mage bound to the wreck of "The Divine Rite." He confirmed that possessing the Diad is not sufficient to break his binding — a new command must be issued through it by a qualified follower of the Two — and warned that forcing him from the island against his geas, by either side, would itself invite the wrath of the gods. He believed he would not survive if "The Fortnum" captured him. He provided strong westerly winds to cover the party's escape and accepted their promise to return. He was left behind, still bound, but no longer at risk of the Diad falling into enemy hands.
  • Giant Octopus: The same octopus that had been lurking at the dive site in previous sessions. It first returned to feed on the corpse of a shark Noddy had killed in the previous dive, then later advanced on the cage and began probing it with a tentacle before being driven off by Noddy's Fear spell. It released a large cloud of black ink as it fled.
  • Giant Lobster: A very large crustacean that emerged from the gloom and advanced steadily on the cage until its claws came through the air wall. It was repelled by Noddy's Fear spell and retreated at speed.
  • Keyes: Able seaman aboard "The Medallion," formerly of "The Fortnum." He identified the ship on the horizon as his old vessel, confirmed Captain Mason's command, and noted she carried at least two priests.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• The Shatters: The entire session took place within this field of shattered rock, the former site of Spider Island. The party remained anchored near the rock spire at its centre throughout.
  • The wreck of "The Divine Rite": The forward hold of the sunken ship, approximately 100 feet below the surface, was the site of Riu's final search. The Diad was found here.
  • Grantos's post: The remains of "The Divine Rite" perched atop the central rock spire, where Grantos keeps watch. The party visited twice this session.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
• The giant octopus was repelled by Noddy's Fear spell. It inked the surrounding water before fleeing, temporarily blinding Noddy to anything outside the air wall.
  • The giant lobster was repelled by Noddy's Fear spell. It retreated rapidly without making contact.
  • No combat with sharks occurred. They circled during the ascent but did not attack.
  • A plan to capture a priest from "The Fortnum" and compel or dupe them into using the Diad to free Grantos was proposed and rejected, on the grounds that the frigate's crew was too large to take and hold safely, and that surrendering the Diad to anyone aboard risked losing it to the enemy.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Diad recovered from the hold of "The Divine Rite" is the holy relic that created and sustains Grantos's binding. It allows its wielder to impose a divine geas upon another person, backed by the direct power of the Two gods. The compelled individual has no choice but to obey, and any defiance would invite the wrath of the gods themselves.
  • Holding the Diad does not break an existing binding. The binding will only end when a qualified follower of the Two uses the Diad to issue a new command superseding the old one. Grantos's compulsion remains in force until this is done.
  • Riu is unable to use the Diad. His declaration as a heretic by an avatar of the Father has cut him off from any direct conduit to the Two. He felt this directly when he attuned to the relic.
  • Mani also cannot use the Diad in its present form. Using it requires full commitment to the Two, not merely acknowledgment of their existence. Cosimo and Noddy, pressed on the same question, likewise proved unwilling or unable to serve as a true conduit to the Two.
  • Nicolas — the priest of the Two known to the party — was not brought on this voyage. His absence is the critical obstacle to freeing Grantos.
  • Grantos can provide favorable winds and create weather adverse to other ships, but he cannot guarantee he would prevail against another wind mage. He did not know whether "The Fortnum" carried one, though he noted that her furled sails and slow, towed approach through dead-calm water suggested no such contest was underway yet — either she had no wind mage aboard, or one was being held in reserve.
  • Wind witches are native to the south, where Grantos believes they serve the church as willing partners. The north has none of its own — Grantos, taken captive decades ago, is the exception, held prisoner rather than serving as a partner.
  • "The Fortnum" under Captain Mason carries at least two priests of the Divinity of Two, and is a three-decked frigate with an estimated crew of some two hundred men — too large a force for the party to fight and control cleanly.
  • "The Medallion" is assumed to be the faster ship, giving the party a head start once they broke away from The Shatters.
  • A fourth magic item remains uncollected in a cave beneath a giant tortoise near the seafloor. It was not retrieved this session. While keeping watch, the captain turned the divers' reports over in his mind — the octopus, the lobster — and grew increasingly convinced that whatever lurked in that heat-vented cave was a giant sea serpent. Half tempted to dive down and see for himself, he was pulled back to his duties only when the ship on the horizon was sighted.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text:
• The Diad: The holy relic of the Divinity of Two recovered from the hold of the sunken "Divine Rite." This is the specific Diad used to bind Grantos. It allows its wielder to impose a divine geas on another person. Currently held by the party.
  • A sealed flat box: A low, flat box roughly the dimensions of a pistol case, recovered from the hold of the "Divine Rite." Its contents are unknown. It may be watertight.
  • A small collection of pouches recovered from the hold, including one of wax-sealed leather that had somehow kept the water out despite years submerged. Contents and value not yet assessed.

  • A loaded pistol with shot and powder (given to Grantos).

docs.title: Barnacles, Bonfires, and a Three-Master to Windward
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session began mid-narrative, with earlier events summarized before recording commenced. The Medallion had departed the Shatters heading southwest toward Drowned Man's Port, sending a decoy off in the opposite direction using Cosimo's illusion magic to throw off any pursuit, when the crew discovered her hull was encrusted with giant barnacles — dinner-plate sized and still growing — from the Totem-infused waters near the site of Spider Island. The ship's speed had dropped to almost nothing. Before settling on careening, the party had tried removing the growth directly — sending swimmers over the side to pry barnacles off by hand and trying shock bolts against them — but neither method made a real dent in growth this size.

The party theorized that the barnacles had attached while the Medallion was becalmed near the Shatters, then grew to extraordinary size from the concentrated Essence in those waters. Two possibilities were debated: that these were a distinct species native to the Totem island waters, or that ordinary barnacles had been transformed by the same forces that made everything on Spider Island grow large. They noted that The Fortnum — still somewhere behind them — had been in the same waters and likely faced the same problem, potentially slowing its pursuit.

Leela was consulted about the growth patterns of her island. She confirmed that large growth was simply normal there, that big animals were kept outside the great wall, and could offer no clear explanation for why it occurred. Asked separately about trade with neighboring islanders, she said the closest ones were not good people — hungry enough, by her account, to eat each other, let alone strangers. The course of action was decided: rather than limping toward Drowned Man's Port in this state, the party would return to the Isle of Sands and careen the ship on a remote beach well clear of New Sardinia and the rest of the Northern presence on the island's eastern coast.

Word of the destination spread among the crew — many recognized New Sardinia by name and reputation, and some recalled that the settlement had originally been a Southern outpost before the North seized it, confirming what the party already suspected from the terms of the truce. After about a week's sailing, Noddy, on watch, made out a wide, dark landmass on the horizon at sunset: the island. The approach was made carefully, creeping through the Shatters in darkness and rounding the island's southern coast by daylight. Night travel meant crawling along, taking constant soundings and repeatedly redirecting around obstacles in the Shatters' unpredictable waters. The party knew from their charts of a river mouth near the island's northern delta, with two old ships known to be further upriver, but ruled it out as a landing site — it lay too close to New Sardinia and the well-travelled northern shipping lane — in favor of the emptier, better-covered waters to the south. The western coast proved suitable — an open beach with a sandy bottom, trees large enough to anchor ropes to, and no visible shipping traffic. The party sent boats ahead to inspect the bottom, confirmed it clean, and brought the Medallion in on a high tide.

The careening operation took the better part of two days. Everything came off the ship: all cannons, powder and shot, stores, and livestock. With the ship lightened, she was pulled over by ropes run to the shore trees and anchors set further out in the water. For a crew normally confined aboard ship, the chance to work ashore lifted spirits despite the labor involved. The exposed hull was dense with barnacles, but the growth proved fresh — it had not yet bored deep into the wood, and stripping it clean was straightforward once underway. Cannon were repositioned on shore to cover the sea approaches, one facing inland, one each way along the beach. Mani organized the Marines into watches and defensive positions throughout the operation. Search parties sent up and down the coast found no fresh water; the land became inhospitable desert almost immediately beyond the shoreline scrub. Noddy and the lookout Jacopa split the exhausting watch from the ship's increasingly tilted mast, with Noddy's bird ranging the skies around the beach to extend the lookout further.

While the scraping was underway, Riu arranged a makeshift field station in a natural rock hollow nearby — books, instruments, and his octopus in its jar among the belongings moved ashore, with a broad flat rock serving as an operating table and a scooped-out hollow in the stone to sit and read in comfort. He noticed a faint hum or vibration, initially dismissed as background noise, coming from somewhere among his possessions. Casting Detect Essence over the area turned up no trace of active magic, but taking inventory of his belongings, he found the Diad felt unusually warm. He concluded, on reasonable grounds, that someone had used magic to probe for or detect the Diad's location just before he noticed the hum. He placed it immediately on a cord around his neck under his shirt, and reported his suspicion to Knick Nab. The captain acknowledged the warning, chose not to curtail the crew's coming celebration, and ordered quiet defensive preparations maintained.

Batu Batu studied the material being scraped from the hull and identified the giant barnacles as edible — comparable to goose barnacles, a delicacy in parts of the world prized for a flavor described as somewhere between lobster and clam, prepared by boiling briefly in seawater and peeling back the tough skin of the stalk for the meat inside. He noted that ordinary ship's barnacles were usually too small to bother eating, but goose barnacles of any real size fetched high prices precisely because they had to be hand-harvested from dangerous, wave-battered rocks, and that barnacles on this scale were used to make a rich seafood stew in some distant lands. He also cautioned that barnacles, like all filter feeders, absorb whatever is in the water around them, so a batch grown in fouled water could be dangerous to eat — though nothing suggested that was a concern here. Mani, initially skeptical, conceded the point. Batu Batu prepared barnacle chowder for the crew over the course of the operation.

The flooding tide refloated the Medallion to a cheer from the crew. That evening the party allowed a full celebration: bonfires on the beach, a roast pig, barnacle chowder, generous grog rations, and music. Knick Nab attempted a performance on his mandolin, singing along with some enthusiasm if limited success. A weather check that evening suggested the fair skies wouldn't hold — the glass was dropping, hinting at a storm by morning. Mani kept his Marines from the revelry; though a little disappointed, they accepted that they'd had an easier few days than the rest of the crew during the careening, and took him at his word that their own turn would come. He coordinated with Werner to keep the guns sighted out to sea through the night. The bonfires blazed visibly for miles in every direction.

The following morning, with the last cannon still being swung back aboard from the yard arm, the lookout Jacopa called from the crow's nest: a sail to the west. Knick Nab scrambled up to look. Through the spyglass — visibility reduced by the onset of rain — a three-masted frigate could be made out, making good speed on the westerly wind. Jacopa confirmed what the captain had already suspected: it was The Fortnum, Captain Mason's ship. A 24-gun frigate.

The party made sail at once, heading south — the most favorable point of sail given the prevailing westerly wind and the direction furthest from the Northern port. Cosimo raised a broad illusion to conceal the Medallion from visual observation. The tactical situation was recognized as difficult: The Fortnum had the weather gauge, meaning she was upwind and controlling the engagement. She could choose when to attack, and on her current course was traveling faster than the Medallion.

The Diad's warmth the previous day suggested The Fortnum had been tracking the party's position by magical means, making Cosimo's illusion of limited use against that particular advantage. Nevertheless it offered concealment from conventional observation, and the Medallion's freshly cleaned hull gave her speed she had not had since leaving the Shatters.

After a tense period of maneuvering in rain and poor visibility — the crow's nest calling down the Fortnum's bearing as she adjusted course — the party weighed their options. Simply holding their course risked being run down outright, since The Fortnum was faster on her present heading; angling away to run parallel might let them slip past unseen, but any turn would cost speed at the moment it was needed most, and a wrong guess would leave the Medallion caught flat-footed. Rather than accept that The Fortnum would dictate the engagement either way — and unwilling to be remembered as a captain who ran from a fight a second time — Knick Nab made a bold decision: hard starboard, turning the Medallion directly toward the Fortnum's path. It was the least expected move — coming about to cross ahead of the larger ship, trading the safety of distance for the possibility of gaining the wind. The maneuver cost speed through the turn but, if successful, would put the Medallion in a superior position.

As the ships closed, the crew stripped the Medallion for action: the bulkheads throughout the ship were struck down and stowed, turning her interior into one open space beneath the guns. Buckets of sand and water were set out across the deck for damage control, and more sand was scattered for traction, to keep footing sure once blood began to flow. The gun ports on the side facing the Fortnum were opened and the cannon loaded and run out — short-handed from the careening, the crew had enough hands to fully work only one side at a time. Swivel guns were shifted to the same side, and Mani sent his best shot up to the fighting tops for the range advantage, aware it was also the most exposed and unsteady post on the ship. He also lined up the Marines' muskets with orders to concentrate fire on the Fortnum's priests, reasoning from past experience that their divine protection could turn aside a few shots but not survive sustained fire, and armed himself with grenades and a lit slow match. Riu's assistant Jeffrey took up his post in the infirmary to await casualties. Passing the ship's figurehead on his way to the quarterdeck, Mani laid a hand on it and quietly asked the Three to keep her safe, promising to spill blood in her defense. With the gun crews unable to see through Cosimo's illusion well enough to aim, the party dropped it in the same moment they opened their gun ports, trading concealment for the ability to fight back. The session ended as the first shots of the engagement lit the rain — muzzle flashes from The Fortnum's bow chasers, a pause, and the sound of cannon.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Leela: Consulted about the unusual growth patterns of Spider Island. She confirmed large growth was simply normal there, that big animals were kept outside the great wall, and offered no explanation for its cause. Asked about trade with neighboring islanders, she described the closest ones as dangerous and hungry enough to eat their own kind, let alone strangers.
  • Batu Batu: Identified the giant barnacles as edible and prepared barnacle meals for the crew throughout the careening operation.
  • Jacopa: A crew member of the Medallion serving as lookout in the crow's nest. She spotted The Fortnum on the western horizon and identified it to the captain.
  • Jeffrey: Riu's surgeon's mate. He took up his post in the infirmary, ready for casualties, as the Medallion prepared for battle with The Fortnum.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Isle of Sands (western coast): The large landmass the party previously escaped from, whose Northern settlement, New Sardinia, sits on the river delta elsewhere on the island. New Sardinia was originally a Southern settlement before the North seized it, as some of the crew confirmed — a detail that matched what the party already suspected from the terms of the truce. The party careened the Medallion on a remote beach on the island's western side, well clear of New Sardinia and any other Northern activity. The interior of the island is described as flat and inhospitable desert beginning just past the shoreline scrub.
  • The Shatters: The site of Spider Island's destruction and the wreck of The Divine Rite. The barnacles encrusting the Medallion's hull are attributed to exposure to the Totem-infused waters of this area.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text: No combat occurred this session, though the crew spent the morning stripping the Medallion for battle. The engagement with The Fortnum commenced as the session ended, with The Fortnum's bow chasers firing on the Medallion as she completed her turn.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• Giant barnacles grew on the Medallion's hull from exposure to the Totem-infused waters of the Shatters. The party debated whether these were a distinct species, ordinary barnacles transformed by concentrated Essence, or the product of some interaction with the Medallion's own magical nature; the question remains open. They agreed that if The Fortnum is ever sunk, diving on her hull before she goes under would be worth doing, to check whether she grew the same barnacles. Careening removed them entirely with no lasting damage to the hull.
  • The Fortnum was likely affected by the same barnacle growth and is presumed slower than normal — but she still had the weather gauge when encountered.
  • The Diad may have been detected by a magical scrying attempt while the ship was careened. Riu heard a faint hum and found the Diad unusually warm afterward; a Detect Essence spell cast on the spot found no trace of active magic, consistent with a probe that had already finished by the time he noticed it. The Diad has been moved to Riu's person and is now worn against his body at all times.
  • The Fortnum's ability to locate the Medallion despite Cosimo's illusion implies she is tracking by magical means, not visual.
  • Giant barnacles of the size found on the Medallion are considered a delicacy in some parts of the world, unlike the small ship's barnacles usually not worth harvesting. Batu Batu confirmed this and demonstrated it with the careening harvest, while cautioning that barnacles grown in fouled water can be dangerous to eat.
  • The Medallion's hull, now clean, is significantly faster than before.
  • The Medallion's cannon sit exposed on the open deck rather than behind a proper gun deck like the Fortnum's, leaving her powder and matches exposed to the weather — a disadvantage noted as the rain set in ahead of the engagement.
  • Cosimo's concealing illusion also blocks the view of those inside it: the gun crews could not aim through it, forcing the party to drop it before they could return fire.
  • The Stone Men have a city somewhere on the Isle of Sands that the party has not yet visited.

docs.title: Items Gained
docs.text: • Approximately 20 finger fruit, gathered from trees on the careening beach — somewhat more were picked, but part of the haul was eaten by the crew before it could be stored.

docs.title: Items Lost
docs.text: (none)

docs.title: Smoke, Sleep, and the Apparition of Gulliver Gold
Events and Actions
docs.text:
The session picked up directly from the end of Session 6. The Fortnum's bow chasers had just fired, and both shots went high — shearing a line and tearing a ragged hole through a topsail near Noddy's position in the crow's nest, but hurting no one. Cosimo, who had maintained a broad illusion concealing the Medallion throughout the approach, dropped it so the guns could bear.

Battle stations were already set: Knick Nab commanded from the quarter deck, Werner managed the gun crews on whichever broadside bore, Mani stood at the rail with his rifle and spyglass, Noddy held the crow's nest, Riu was on deck with a box of grenades and a lit match, and Cosimo readied his spellwork. As was his habit before any fight, Noddy had already cast Resilient Invisibility on himself, reasoning that nobody could shoot a lookout they couldn't see. Keyes, the former Fortnum seaman now sailing with the party, was noted as a potential source of intelligence on the enemy's armament and layout.

Before the guns opened up again, the party talked through their priorities: with The Fortnum tracking them no matter what illusion or evasion they tried, killing or crippling her priests took precedence over sinking the ship outright, and Riu — the only capable healer aboard — was reminded to weigh any offensive move against the cost of being out of position if someone went down.

Cosimo made the first decisive move. After quickly casting Lesser Ranging to extend his reach, he raised a dense illusion of black powder smoke that blanketed The Fortnum's entire gun deck from bow to stern, covering every port on both sides of the hull. Ten guns fired blind on that broadside and every shot went into the sea.

Under that cover the Medallion struck hard. Riu used a Leave Object spell to plant a lit grenade directly on The Fortnum's fore deck, where it detonated among the crew. Mani swept his spyglass across The Fortnum's quarter deck and fixed on a cluster of three officers. His shot found one — the man's clavicle and shoulder joint were shattered, his arm rendered useless on the spot. Werner fired the long gun as The Fortnum came straight on, sending a shot raking the length of the ship at deck height; the ball punched through every lower sail from the flying jibs to the mizzen. Two more of the Medallion's guns scored solid hits: one shell landed somewhere near the mechanisms connecting wheel to rudder, another punched a hole in the hull above the waterline.

The Fortnum's marines — an estimated twenty to thirty strong — assembled along the port rail for a coordinated volley. Noddy called it down from the crow's nest. Mani directed the Medallion's three marines to reply, and the swivel guns were swung to bear. The enemy volley was disciplined but the range was not in their favour; one Medallion sailor took a ball to the clavicle. Riu crossed the deck to attend him. Mani then put a shot into the helmsman's foot, shattering several small bones and leaving him struggling to hold the wheel.

Noddy cast Sleep 10 into The Fortnum's rigging. One man dropped immediately, bouncing off spars and landing on the deck below. Two others resisted. Around the same time, Riu lit and lobbed a second grenade into the marines still massed at the rail: the shrapnel tore into one man's shoulder, ripping the stripes from his uniform, and mangled another's musket-holding hand. Cosimo placed a tear cloud on the forward end of The Fortnum's main deck, timing it so the wind would carry the gas across the full length of the ship. The cloud caught the marines, the deck crew, and the off-duty watch together — roughly four-fifths of the main deck was left staggered and blinded, useless for the remainder of that exchange. Only the captain on the quarter deck and the gunners sealed below it remained effective.

Noddy, watching from the crow's nest, had already spotted the female priest standing at the base of the main mast and called her position down. With the main deck now suppressed, Mani directed all three of the Medallion's marines to fire on her in sequence before taking his own shot, hoping the volume of fire would overwhelm any magical deflection she might invoke. The tactic worked, and worked better than expected: still reeling from the tear cloud, she never got the chance to turn the shot aside. A musket ball passed through her gut and lodged in her spine. She fell paralyzed.

The Fortnum broke off and ran. Noddy cast Sleep 10 into the rigging again during the pursuit; three more sailors fell, one dragging a fourth down as he went. Riu sent a grenade onto the quarter deck, wounding three of the crew there. The helmsman — already limping from the shot to his foot — took the worst of it, his elbow shattered and his arm left useless. Captain Mason and a nearby officer were caught by the same blast; the captain's hip was fractured. Battered and propped against the rail, he continued barking orders regardless.

Around this time, Noddy spotted something stranger: a soft aura of light welled up from the middle of The Fortnum and spread across the whole ship. Mani tried a Spell Lore to identify it but learned only that it was magical in nature — its source and purpose remained a mystery. The paralyzed priest was seen wiping tears from her eyes, but she still could not stand.

Werner repositioned the mortar to the bow for forward fire. While it was being moved into place, The Fortnum's stern chasers found the Medallion twice — punching a hole above the waterline and tearing a huge rip through a top-gallant sail. As the shell was loaded, Mani marked it with three lines and murmured a quiet prayer to the Three, certain this was the moment the fight would turn. Mortars fire wild until ranged in, so Werner held off firing the prepared shell on the first attempt — which fumbled anyway, a ramrod left in the barrel putting the mortar out of action for three turns. Once it was back in service, an ordinary ranging shot tore an upper sail; the next shot, carrying Cosimo's prepared shell, plunged into a pile of replacement canvas the crew had hauled up on deck to repair the sails already lost to the fighting. The cloth caught immediately, and flames began spreading along the deck railings. Before the crew could bring buckets, Cosimo's waiting fantasm triggered. From the fire rose Handsome Gulliver Gold — the illusionary figure Cosimo had conjured many times before — dressed this time in white robes with gold accents, the symbol of the Two prominent on his chest, levitating above the impact site. He addressed the ship: "Your priests on board have offended the Two. They are heretics. Cast them into the sea behind you and you and my acolytes shall spare you and let you go." Then he spun in place and vanished. The effect was immediate and visible to the crow's nest: the Fortnum's crew, already stunned and burning, now faced divine judgment arriving from inside their own damaged deck. Noddy watched the disorder spread from above — sailors near the rail cradling a shipmate who had fallen asleep and dropped from the rigging, some of the crew turning their anger on the priests they blamed for it. Noddy's take: the surprise that had carried the fight this far wouldn't work twice, so the advantage was worth pressing while it held.

The Fortnum's stern chasers continued firing during the chase, though poorly served while shooting blind — one gun crew lost coordination entirely, its gun rolling back over its own loaders and sitting idle for four turns. Cosimo tried to compound their trouble with a fantasm making the Medallion appear to veer fifteen degrees off her true course, but the stern chasers kept firing true regardless — further proof The Fortnum's priests were tracking something other than sight. The shots that did land found the Medallion twice: the topsail was ripped and the ratlines severed; a spar near the captain's head was shot away. Werner's mortar fire damaged The Fortnum's steering and later destroyed her ship's boat. The gap between the ships held roughly constant; The Fortnum's crew were fighting hard to hold what speed they had. With The Fortnum reeling but still afloat, the party weighed calling off the attack against pressing on to board her; the vote went to press the advantage.

Then Noddy called something down from the crow's nest. The female priest — who had been paralyzed and should not have been walking — was on the move. A second figure was being brought up to join her. The captain was drawing his sword; the crew was arguing visibly. Then both priests went to the rail. They took cannonballs and jumped. Noddy was clear: the crew had not thrown them overboard. They had jumped themselves.

Knick Nab ordered the Medallion brought to and the search begun. The decision to stop was not unanimous — some argued for pressing on at speed in case the priests intended something offensive rather than an escape — but the vote went to searching. Riu and Noddy readied to go into the water, a boat was made ready to lower, and a dive line was rigged. Wary that the same trick the party had used to breach hulls underwater could be turned against them, Knick Nab posted extra hands in the bilge; Old Salter, the ship's bosun, suggested doubling the crew on the pumps as well, and the order was given. The Fortnum continued running and eventually disappeared over the horizon; Noddy, no longer able to see her from the crow's nest, came down, leaving Jacopa on watch above. Soundings found the water over one hundred fathoms deep. A scan of the surface and what little could be seen in the water column below showed nothing. Keyes was questioned: the two priests were named Margot and Arnim. He knew of no diving equipment aboard The Fortnum, though both priests had been young and healthy and might have been strong swimmers. The party debated whether the jump meant suicide to prevent capture, an attempt to reach the Diad from below, or a decoy to cover something else entirely. The session ended as Cosimo began preparations for a ritual to communicate with the Medallion itself, hoping the ship might be able to sense whether the priests were somewhere beneath them.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Keyes: Able seaman aboard the Medallion, formerly of The Fortnum. Rescued earlier from a small island where he had been marooned; he claimed to have gone overboard when The Fortnum fought a sea serpent, though the party had already deduced he was actually marooned by Captain Mason for lacking vigor during that fight. Provided the names of the two priests and confirmed he had seen no obvious underwater equipment aboard The Fortnum.
  • Margot: A female priest of the Divinity of Two assigned to The Fortnum. Shot through the gut during the battle, with the ball lodging in her spine and paralyzing her. Despite the wound, she later rose, walked to the rail with a cannonball, and jumped overboard together with Arnim.
  • Arnim: A male priest of the Divinity of Two assigned to The Fortnum. Jumped overboard with a cannonball alongside Margot.
  • Captain Mason: Commander of The Fortnum. Wounded early in the battle, then caught by Riu's grenade on the quarter deck, which fractured his hip. Seen propped against the rail, continuing to issue orders even as his crew argued and the ship fled.
  • Handsome Gulliver Gold: Illusionary apparition conjured by Cosimo using a waiting fantasm placed on the mortar shell before firing. Appeared in white robes bearing the symbol of the Two, rising from the fire on The Fortnum's deck to demand the crew cast their priests overboard.
  • Jacopa: Medallion lookout. Held the crow's nest observation after Noddy descended during the search phase.
  • Old Salter: The Medallion's bosun. Suggested doubling the crew on the pumps once Knick Nab set extra hands watching the bilge during the search for the priests.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text: • Open water north of New Sardinia: The engagement and subsequent search for the priests took place here, in open ocean with land barely in sight and water too deep for soundings to find bottom at over one hundred fathoms.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
Naval engagement with The Fortnum, continuing into a pursuit:

Medallion casualties: one sailor wounded in the clavicle by musket fire (tended by Riu).

Medallion damage: a hole punched above the waterline, a top-gallant sail badly torn, topsail ripped, ratlines severed, a spar shot away near the captain, minor hull and rigging damage throughout, own mortar crew fumbled its first ranging shot when a ramrod left in the barrel put it out of action for three turns.

The Fortnum losses: one officer's shoulder destroyed, a marine's shoulder torn by grenade shrapnel with the stripes ripped from his uniform, another marine's musket-holding hand mangled by the same blast, helmsman shot in the foot and later his elbow shattered by grenade shrapnel, Captain Mason's hip fractured by the same blast along with a nearby officer, Margot shot through gut and spine, multiple sailors put to sleep and fallen from the rigging, the main deck crew widely stunned by tear cloud, main deck fire started, cargo hold breached with half her fresh water stores ruined, steering damaged, ship's boat destroyed, one gun crew put out of action after losing coordination while firing blind, sail damage across the entire ship including a hole through every lower sail and a missing spar.

Recovery time for the Medallion's wounded sailor: not established.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
• The Fortnum carries 24 guns — ten to a broadside, two bow chasers, two stern chasers.
  • The Medallion herself carries two 24-pounders (one per broadside), four 12-pounders split between the sides for three guns a broadside, a mortar aft, at least four swivel guns, and an arbalest capable of throwing a harpoon-sized bolt.
  • On paper, The Fortnum outclasses the Medallion — she has an actual gun deck, more guns, and a much larger crew that would matter in a boarding fight — though the Medallion can point closer to the wind than the bigger ship regardless of direction.
  • The Fortnum was tracking the Medallion by magical means and could do so regardless of Cosimo's concealment illusion — even a fantasm making the ship appear to veer off course fooled no one aboard The Fortnum, whose gunners kept firing true. The party believes the Diad that Riu carries is the likely focus of this tracking.
  • The two Divinity of Two priests aboard The Fortnum were named Margot and Arnim. Both jumped overboard with cannonballs during the pursuit. Their fate is unknown.
  • The priests may have been tracking the Diad rather than the Medallion itself — suggesting they were prepared for some form of underwater action, potentially related to recovering the Diad from the sea.
  • A priest's gift for magically deflecting incoming shots seems to fail while she is stunned or otherwise incapacitated — Margot's paralyzing wound only landed because Cosimo's tear cloud had already staggered her.
  • Waiting fantasm can be placed on a projectile and triggered on impact, allowing illusionary apparitions to be delivered at range into a target.
  • At over one hundred fathoms depth, the search area is beyond conventional recovery of any objects or persons that went to the bottom.
