docs.title: Fourteen Sources of Power and a Melted Diad
Events and Actions
docs.text:
Weeks had passed since the escape from the Fortnum before the session picked back up, and Randolph opened it by reading aloud from a reconstructed account he had pieced together from his recovered three-year casebook and a fortnight of frank conversation aboard the Medallion — his older, more detailed folio having been left behind at the Academy and out of reach. His account filled in the gap in brief: as agreed, the party had made a short stop at the pirate enclave near Drowned Man's Port, collected Brother Nicolas, and got underway west again, pausing along the way to visit Mistress Clara, who tearfully declined an invitation to join the crew. Nicolas came aboard on his own terms: passage for his two most fervent converts — Sven, previously one of Mistress Clara's helpers looking after him, among them — his carved statue of Handsome Gulliver Gold, standing permission to preach daily from the forecastle, and a promise, honored once the ship was properly underway, that he would be shown the Diad.

Randolph's written account carried the bulk of what he had learned since his rescue. The war between the two nations had not ended but stalled — the Shatters had thrown up a barrier neither fleet had found a way around, and both sides had turned their spent energy toward other ends, the Kingdom pouring resources into a crossing meant to carry it around the Maelstrom entirely, toward the New World — a race he understood the southern houses to be reading the same way, as the next arena for an old rivalry now that the old one had gone quiet. On the heresy declaration, Randolph's notes recorded only unease rather than an answer: the church's public bounty had been issued with unusual speed and certainty for a group of unproven youths, and he had a name in mind for the hand behind it, though he refused to commit it to paper. Drawing on his own long-standing interest in the Advance and her captain, he confirmed that the ship had been tracked two years past to an island the islanders and elves both called Birdcrown Isle and had not been seen or heard from since, without ever being struck from a Navy list or formally reported lost — a silence he found stranger than he could yet justify with evidence, fitting a pattern he did not like: this was the second man of Barrows's fellowship to go quiet on that same stretch of water. On the Totems, he confirmed that the light said to rise from a totem's destruction was not unique to Spider Island — it matched an independently recorded account some forty years old — and that a totem's power does not vanish when it breaks but is loosed all at once, ungoverned, with the aftermath scaling to whatever the totem was worth destroying; he noted, carefully, that more such sites are known to people he trusts than the two the world has already mourned. On the Fortnum's two priests, he confirmed from her own crew that both Margot and Arnim were missing, presumed drowned, and that neither held any rank above ordinary cleric. He laid out the church's full hierarchy for the party's benefit — the Twin Eminences at its head, then Archons, High Clerics and Canons, Vicars, Clerics, Curates, Prelates, Deacons, and Acolytes — and one further office sitting entirely outside that ladder: the Censure, drawn from the ranks of Cleric or High Cleric and given special authority to hunt down and destroy whatever the church has already judged heretical. Neither Margot nor Arnim, he confirmed, had held that office, nor was either a "summoner" — a rank he assured the party does not exist anywhere in the church's structure, despite the word one of them had used in front of him.

Randolph also gave an honest accounting of his own conduct: he had gone looking for the Fortnum in person rather than by correspondence once he learned she'd been reassigned from convoy duty to hunting, and had been confined by Captain Mason once his prying became obvious — though Mason, whom Randolph judged an honorable man doing an ugly job, kept his writings safe rather than destroying them and extracted only Randolph's word not to escape while he held them, a bargain Randolph considered voided the moment the party carried the writing case off the ship. He confirmed he had likely called the sea serpent that broke the Fortnum in two using a rare Academy talent for calling birds and beasts, extended past its normal scale by the desperation of the moment, and admitted he still could not explain an earlier incident where a smaller summoning of his was answered by an unclaimed burst of mortar fire. Finally, at secondhand from crew gossip during his confinement, he related what had become of the Advance's second voyage under Captain Barrows: she sailed west under a quieter, more deliberate Barrows with the senior priest Jacque aboard, bound for the same waters where Maynard had vanished, with no port of call between the mainlands and Port Sardinia; a junior priest named Philip had not sailed with her a second time, for reasons no one aboard would discuss, and whatever split Jacque from the ship at Port Sardinia was, in Nicolas's account, as much a falling-out with the priest who ordained him as anything else.

Once the reading was done, the party pressed Randolph further over an elaborate dinner attended by Quartermaster Leopold and De Torres, the Master of Sail — Batu Batu serving fresh meat and good claret, an extravagance the ship could still afford so soon after leaving port. Randolph confirmed that a chronicler's abduction was entirely unprecedented, that the church's neutrality had been thrown into question by the act, and that the Academy possessed capabilities of its own that could seriously damage the church's standing if it chose to retaliate — though what the Academy would actually do, he could not say. Pressed on what chroniclers actually do with what they gather, he described a strict neutrality: information such as fleet movements is recorded and passed on to the Academy's own researchers, never used to hand one side an advantage over the other, though he admitted that interpreting and acting on it falls to others back at the Academy, not to him. Pressed on the Triad, he acknowledged his own membership for the first time, describing a loosely organized fellowship that communicates through dead drops and identifies itself with a private mark — three lines, drawn to see whether another party recognizes them — whose members mostly do not know each other's identities. He confirmed that Major Hubert had definitely been a member, that Maynard had joined deliberately while Barrows had been drawn in only after his court-martial and rescue — likely without fully realizing it, and, Randolph suspected, with the Triad's own unseen hand behind both his surprising promotion and his return to a ship the church had never wanted him to command — and that the society itself does not know what its own "third way" beyond the Two actually is, only that it must exist. The party laid out everything they knew or suspected of other sources of power in the world in an effort to help answer that question, and Randolph, delighted, began keeping a running list.

The party also worked through why the church had focused so intensely on them: Randolph judged it was less their youthful heresy-adjacent conversations years ago than the overt displays of power they had since shown, combined with the Medallions specifically, which he believed frightened the church for reasons even it did not fully understand. Pressed for a count, the party confirmed seven medallions known between them — six carried among the party itself, and a seventh taken years before from Stick Stab, not presently in their keeping. Asked why Knick Nab alone had been left off the wanted poster, Randolph reasoned it came down to visibility — the others carried renowned family names, noble school connections, or a public position that put them in the church's eye, while Knick Nab, arriving from nowhere and never formally recorded anywhere, simply left no name behind to write down — though the party noted one wrinkle in that theory: Knick Nab had signed a ship's registry once, marking it with an X for lack of letters, proof he wasn't entirely invisible to the written record even if it evidently hadn't been enough to put a name to his face. During the same conversation, Randolph produced a folded letter found among Captain Mason's personal effects — addressed to "my dearest Herod" from his wife, Eleanor, revealing Mason's own given name and announcing the birth of their son, whom she had named Herod after his father and taken to calling "little Herod" to keep the two straight — along with the other valuables taken off the Fortnum: a pouch of 49 silver, a large diamond and matching pearl necklace and bracelet, a matched pair of fine sabers, and a stack of charts confirming a route west but with no island marked "Birdcrown."

With dinner concluded, the party formally presented the Diad to Nicolas, who took it into his care as agreed — reduced from constant possession to daytime use once Werner raised the risk of it being tracked. Wary of what an unstable priest might do with it, the party kept someone with him at all times and had the quartermaster cut off his rum; Mani went further, making a point of befriending Nicolas in earnest rather than merely tolerating him — attending his sermons and treating him with real respect, partly from a long-held instinct to bring people together and partly so that, if Nicolas's temper ever did turn dangerous, it would not fall on a stranger first. When Nicolas asked whether he might bind Grantos to some new task rather than simply free him, he was told flatly that the deal already struck with Grantos was not his to renegotiate. The party sailed on to Grantos's wreck, becalmed within sight of it and forced to row the last distance by boat, a hardship the crew endured well enough since they knew their destination this time. Reunited with Grantos, the party brought Nicolas ashore to attempt the binding's reversal. Nicolas listened as Grantos described, in increasingly strange terms, the effort of endlessly managing the air and pressure around the wreck to keep it safe — then, apparently on inspiration, struck Grantos with the Diad itself. A sudden violent inrush of wind swept the area, briefly endangering the Medallion at anchor until her crew got a second anchor down, and when it settled Grantos declared himself free, shaking Nicolas's hand as the priest who had finally released him.

Grantos immediately demanded the Diad be destroyed, unwilling to risk anyone using it to imprison him — or anyone else — again. When Nicolas balked, protesting that he had sensed truth and even glimpsed Handsome Gulliver Gold through the Diad and could not give it up, Mani talked him down, arguing that the item was only a tool — the true culprit for Grantos's decades of imprisonment was the priest of the Two who had wielded it against him, not the Diad itself. The party debated at length whether to destroy it, cast it into the deep sea, or keep it secretly, weighing the sole known example of undoing a Diad's compulsion (this very item, on this very effect) against the risk of the church tracking it. With votes split and Nicolas pleading to keep it, the party settled on a middle path: try to destroy it, using a forge rigged from the ship's oven. Asked whether his mastery of wind could part the murky water for a dive, Grantos confirmed his power was limited to air and pressure and could not touch the water itself, so the party turned to swimming instead. Heating and hammering alone would not melt the Diad, so the party turned to the sea: Knick Nab made a first attempt alone, swimming the hundred feet down before the murk defeated him and he surfaced empty-handed, and it was Riu and Knick Nab together, working a net down on a second attempt, who recovered a strange, eternally warm lump of black material from an underwater cavern near the wreck — a lump that caused the Diad to deform and melt the moment it was added to the fire. The molten material was worked into six pieces of shot for Riu's pistol, a set of knuckle dusters, and a small blank ingot; Riu attuned to the remnant and found it still magical but purposeless, its original power gone. The gemstones pried from the Diad beforehand were handed over to the quartermaster as ship's loot.

With his side of the bargain honored, Grantos packed his few belongings, accepted a bath, clothes, and a haircut, and formally joined the crew; the party left a small carved marker at the wreck commemorating his decades of imprisonment and release. Asked about Birdcrown Isle, he said the name meant nothing to him specifically, though he recalled people who rode giant birds visiting his home island more than fifty years earlier and had seen none since his imprisonment began — nor ever in the old world, doubting more than a few northerners even know such riders exist. With Grantos aboard, the party briefly weighed leaving Nicolas behind now that his mission was accomplished, worried he might talk carelessly about Grantos or the party to outsiders, before voting to keep him with them regardless — Mani arguing they had made him what he now was and owed him the follow-through of setting him right. The Medallion got underway at full speed toward Birdcrown Isle.

docs.title: NPCs & Creatures
docs.text:
• Randolph the Chronicler — read aloud a reconstructed journal covering the gap since the party's rescue of him: the stalled war, the unresolved reason for the heresy declaration, confirmation that totem destructions release ungoverned power scaling to the totem's worth, the fates of Margot and Arnim, and secondhand news of the Advance's second voyage under Barrows. Confirmed his own Triad membership for the first time and his belief that the Medallions specifically unsettle the church. Produced a letter from Captain Mason's personal effects. With Riu and Cosimo's permission, examined both of the party's Diads side by side, finding them worked metal, nearly identical, and impossible to distinguish by any power beyond what was already known, though he confirmed such pieces are normally kept within the church's private spaces and shown publicly only during certain processions on holy days.
  • Nicolas — reunited with the party as agreed, appearing sober and focused; given custody of the Diad by day, used it in his shipboard sermons, and confided privately to Cosimo — judged the most sympathetic of the crew — a growing conviction that the Two themselves, not just their church, were evil and needed to be defeated, going so far as to embrace being a heretic against evil gods. Recalled having touched a diad only once before, during his own ordination. Ultimately freed Grantos from his binding by striking him with the Diad after listening to his account of the wind, then dropped to his knees to embrace Cosimo's legs and hail him as a prophet after Cosimo conjured a fleeting illusory apparition of Handsome Gulliver Gold over his shoulder. Argued to keep the Diad rather than destroy it; the party voted to bring him along toward Birdcrown Isle.
  • Grantos — freed from his decades-long binding to the wreck of the Divine Rite when Nicolas struck him with the Diad; immediately demanded the item's destruction, confirmed his wind mastery could not extend to water when asked to help clear the murk for the recovery dive, joined the crew afterward, and confirmed no specific knowledge of "Birdcrown Isle" by that name, though he recalled giant-bird riders visiting his home island over fifty years ago.
  • Mistress Clara — visited off-page during the time-skip; tearfully declined the party's invitation to join the crew.
  • Captain Mason — referenced via his recovered personal effects: a letter addressed to him as "Herod" from his wife, Eleanor, revealing his own given name and announcing the birth of their son "little Herod," alongside valuables and charts taken from the Fortnum.
  • Margot and Arnim — the two priests of the Fortnum; confirmed by Randolph, via her surviving crew, to be missing and presumed drowned, and neither of any special rank ("summoner" or otherwise) within the church hierarchy — Margot the more fervent and senior of the pair, Arnim junior and very much under her thumb, both by Randolph's judgment expendable rather than powerful. The party's own working theory, unconfirmed, was that the two carried cannonballs into the water deliberately, drowning themselves and their own Diad rather than let either fall into anyone else's hands.
  • Batu Batu — served the party's dinner and rigged the ship's oven into a working forge for the attempt to destroy the Diad.
  • Leopold and De Torres — the quartermaster and Master of Sail, invited to the private dinner with Randolph as senior command staff.
  • Sven — named by Randolph as one of Nicolas's converts, previously helping look after Nicolas alongside Mistress Clara; a second named convert was mentioned but the name was not recovered this session.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Grantos's Wreck — the wreck of "The Divine Rite," ringed by sharks and the occasional giant lobster, where the party freed Grantos from his binding and where an underwater cavern nearby yielded the eternally warm black lump used to melt the Diad.
  • Aboard the Medallion — site of the private dinner with Randolph, Nicolas, Leopold, and De Torres, and later the improvised forge built from the ship's oven.
  • Drowned Man's Port pirate enclave — visited off-page during the time-skip to collect Nicolas as previously agreed.

docs.text: None.

docs.title: Learnings and Discussions
docs.text:
Randolph's reading covered the state of the world during the party's three-year absence and since: the war between the two nations stalled rather than resolved, both sides investing instead in expansion elsewhere; the heresy declaration's cause still not fully explained, though Randolph suspects a specific hand behind it he declined to name; confirmation that totem destructions release raw, ungoverned power scaling with the totem's own worth, and that more totem sites exist than the two already lost; and the fates of Margot and Arnim, neither of whom held any special rank in the church. Pressed on why the two had thrown themselves into the sea rather than be taken, the party settled on its own working theory, unconfirmed by Randolph: that they carried cannonballs into the water deliberately, drowning themselves and their own Diad rather than let it — and whatever means it may have given them to track the party — fall into anyone else's hands.

Over dinner, Randolph confirmed his own Triad membership and explained the society's core uncertainty: even its members do not know what the "third way" beyond the Two actually is, only that the evidence of other power in the world — which the party has demonstrated repeatedly — makes its existence undeniable. He also floated the theory that the Divinity of Two might be an active, not merely passive, cause of the deformities suffered by unblessed births in the north, since the same effect does not seem to occur in the south or wherever the church's control is weaker. Riu, occupied elsewhere at the time and relayed secondhand through Randolph, reiterated an old theory of his own that the deformities trace back to the church's holy water specifically; unresolved alongside it, the party noted they still do not know what became of the water carried aboard the Mother's Sorrow — sister ship to the Medallion itself — unlike their own vessel's well-known cargo. The party catalogued as many as fourteen suspected sources of power for Randolph's notes: the Two, the Totems, the Elves, the pygmies of the Three (kept distinct from the hostile pygmies of Totem Isle), the three PCs' own individually distinct abilities, Leela's people, Grantos, the southern wind witches, the Medallions, the southern fire cult, and — added later — Mistress Clara, with general agreement that several of these likely trace back to a common, unidentified root. Randolph himself was tallied as the fourteenth, once he admitted his own bird- and beast-calling talent answered to no god he could name.

The debate sharpened when Nicolas, freshly trusted with the Diad, confided to Cosimo that he had come to believe the Two themselves were evil and needed to be defeated, not merely their church — a position the party did not fully share. Wary of throwing out centuries of northern faith on a hunch, the party held that everything witnessed so far, the deforming of unblessed births chief among it, could still be laid at the feet of a corrupt clergy rather than the gods themselves, especially since the same deformities do not occur in the south or in places outside the church's direct control; some wondered aloud whether that same clerical hand might explain supposedly separate peoples, such as the elves and the enslaved pygmies of the south, being something other than what they seemed. Werner, still unwilling to call the Two themselves evil, prayed sincerely to them that night for a sign that they had not been corrupted by their own church, and received nothing beyond the same ordinary silence he had always gotten.

Randolph confirmed a chronicler's abduction is entirely unprecedented and that it has placed the Academy's neutrality in question, though he could not say how the Academy would respond. Asked why Knick Nab was absent from the church's original wanted poster, Randolph reasoned it was simply that Knick Nab had no name on any public record, unlike the others.

The party also revisited, without resolving, the old mystery of who else might have been unable to see them during their original medallion-acquiring incident years earlier — they recalled that during that first phase they could see the effects of each other's actions, such as rats someone else had already killed, without being able to see one another directly, and that a bartender at the time had seemed to react to other people who were not visible to the party at all. They also turned up an odd detail from that same night: a red-haired child who had stood on the dock alongside one of the priests, watching them, and to whom only Knick Nab had sensed any connection at the time. Whatever ended that separation, they believed, happened at the same moment they returned wearing the medallions themselves. Given that Stick Stab apparently acquired his medallion at a different time and was never one of the invisible-to-each-other group, they tabled the question of who else might have shared it for later rather than press it further. A related question went unresolved alongside it: whether Stick Stab was ever subject to the same compulsion that keeps the rest of the party from straying too far from one another, since he spent many months away from them without apparent ill effect — though the party allowed he could simply have stayed close to someone else carrying a medallion the whole time.

The decision to destroy rather than keep the recovered Diad was reached by group vote after extended debate, weighing the one known example of undoing a Diad's compulsion against the risk of the church tracking it indefinitely; the eternally warm black lump recovered from the underwater cavern proved to be the key to melting it down, deforming the Diad the moment it was placed in the same fire.

docs.title: Interlude 1
docs.text:
True to his word, Major Hubert, commander of the Fort of Port of Sardinia, allows the party to, for the most part, recover from their ordeal with the fire ship. Or rather, allows Werner De Rendall proper time for his burns to heal, which takes the better part of a month. Having taken up residence in the gambling den and rooming house The Treasure Hunt, De Rendall is provided regular visits by the army surgeons, who, while perhaps not so pleasant in appearance, or treatment, as the lovely ladies above The Crow’s Nest, do seem to know what to do; and with further administration by Riu, De Rendall is soon put to rights. It is only the loss of his third harpoon which sours his mood. Northern harpoons are hard to come by this far south.

The Treasure Hunt turns out to be an ideal, although somewhat pricey, place for all the party (save Nick Nab) to spend their days. Entertainment abounds, and while at some times the youth of the group is questioned, never is their silver; food, drink, and games are a’plenty, and the rooms, as compared to berth aboard ship, are well appointed. The party has arranged for their own, personal (albeit small) rooms, rather than the more communal and familiar hammocks hung beneath canvases on the back yard. Riu manages to introduce Noddy to the mysteries of “the bath”, which at first glance seems to Noddy to be a horrible practice, but after some prodding takes to as well as the next.

Company is never difficult as well, as the common and games rooms are always full of sailors just come ashore, and so up-to-date information on the state of war, accurate or not, is always available. Company of other sorts, rough and tumble in a different way, is also available for a price, as ladies of the night (or day) are aplenty in The Treasure Hunt.

While there is the occasional disagreement, brawling and the like is kept quite in check. Overseeing the establishment is the Lady Rees, a stout woman who during the day can be seen flitting in and out of her offices on the second floor, overlooking the games room. Lady Rees employs many burley men to act as muscle, and her word seems to command quite a measure of respect. Or at least actions of her in-house bouncers do. She does not interact with her patrons, although upon occasion she makes announcement from the balcony and corridor which perches about the dice.

It is not just the common sailor who comes to The Treasure Hunt. Some smaller rooms and tables are put aside for officers and more well off locals, and there is a regular coming and going by those that are clearly of the more established class of the Port. It becomes clear enough as well that some amount of money lending business is underway here as well, which Lady Rees seems to attend to, privately and personally. It is not overt, but also from available chatter a well known function of this place. Money is available. For a price it seems.

Once he establishes the lay of the land, Cosimo finds himself quite at home here, and tries his luck on many occasions at the dice tables. In the end he finds himself neither ahead nor behind, but the young man, after some initial reluctance from the staff, finds that he is accepted without much question in the more pedestrian back rooms of the house. Less accepted is his attempts to bring with him to the tables the young Suzette, daughter of Governor Francisco. But, in the end, he manages to entice her away from a more fancy gathering of pretty young things and accompany him to dance and place some dice. And any more play he may desire.

While Cosimo finds himself often late at night at the tables, Mani finds himself often early in morning at the training yard, brandishing sword and dagger, being beaten and bested by The Chronicler. Nonetheless, progress is being made.

--

Nick “Hob” Nab, on the other hand, enjoys none of these relative comforts and relaxations. He has disappeared on the cutter “Amada”, which left without warning the night before the Governor’s party. Indeed some of the first rumours and tales heard around the dice tables were of this ship, and its Captain, one Otto “Cut Close” De Guzman. De Guzman is known to be from the cold regions north of the capital, and expert navigator and sailor, and many accolades are told of his accomplishments in recent times. He seems to have hand-picked his crew from across much of the navy, all of whom keep close their ship, and their mouths, closed as to what they are doing.

For his part, Nick Nab is miserable for this first month. Soon after departing the Port, the discomforts began. First it was simple fatigue, with the most simple of tasks taking more and more effort, and more demanding tasks such as climbing the rigging being the worst. But then as the days wore on this became more than just tiredness, and transitioned to proper pain. Pain in the feet, legs, arms and hands, reaching into the very depths of his chest as well. He presented it to his shipmates and Captain as mere seasickness, and it was treated as such; a simple young landlubber not yet accustomed to the rise and fall of the Seas. While looked at as a weakness by his fellow sailors, they also saw determination in the young, frail and weak looking Nick.

Then, as strangely as the onset of this condition arrived, after that first month it began to subside. Not all at once, but slowly Nick seemed to become accustomed to, well, whatever this was. By the end of the second month, he felt as normal, and could better assume his duties.

--

With De Rendal recovered, those left back at port were finally assigned temporary positions on a supply ship, destined as it turned out to be bringing necessities to the island where the Southerners had set up a watch over the Channel Isles. Knowing of their interest in returning to this place, Major Hubert arranged for the youth to go as crew, but afforded some independence to them during unloading, so that they could make their own investigations regarding the cypher sought out by Riu. Sadly, no such writings could be found, and indeed by this time the site of the Southern encampment had been thoroughly scoured, and occupied, by the North, as it had been decided to use the hidden watch as a means to stand sentry above the channels for the safety of the North.

The party then wanted to go and revisit the mysterious black stone peak, but in this they were denied; it seemed that passage to and from the watch point was highly regulated. Not to be denied, the party went anyways at nighttime, slipping up the stone pathways to retrace their steps to the hidden perch. While they were able to reach it without being discovered or challenged, nothing new about the strange material was discovered. I was clear that the diggings they has made to reveal the surface and side of the strange rock had been covered over so as to hide it from view. Watchers remained on the peak itself, and discretion prevented further re-exploration there.

--

Upon return to the Port, the party’s hope to visit The Academy seemed to have to be put on hold. New orders had arrived from the Admiralty. The Northern Navy was to cease excursions towards the south, or west, and instead concentrate their fleet to barricade and isolate the Channel Islands and Northern Coast from the marauding ships of the south. What was spoken of in some whispers among the men of the Navy was now proving to be quite true; the South was in command of the Seas, and the value of the more powerful and bigger ships of the North was in a defensive role to protect the Northern shores and resources. En masse they could defend against the nimbler South, but to reach out too far from the safety and supply of known friendly ports was a losing strategy. Already too many ships of the line had been lost to ambush, and even some coastal towns had seen some bombardment from Southern ships.

Irrespective of complaint from The Chronicler, these tightened rules of engagement were quickly adhered to by the Captains of the Northern fleet, and under the direction of Major Hubert the forces in his port were relegated to picket duty along the southern edge of the Channel Islands, and also to ensure safe passage of goods to and from the Mainland. As such, the party was assigned to various ships and various duties, under the command of various Captains, as needs seemed fit. True to his word, the Major kept the party together in these assignments, and while there was some action to be seen against the Southern Fleet on occasions, none of these resulted in any significant prize or outcome. Most were probing attacks by the South, and the strict orders of the Northern Captains was to intercept and intercede, but not pursue.

So, while many shipboard skills and experience were gained by all, no fortunes or glory were earned.

The one exception to this rather busy but unproductive time aboard ship was an opportunity to accompany a ship carrying a cargo of slaves and dried peas to the Capital. While under strict orders to remain aboard, the party nonetheless slipped ashore during the nighttime, and using the secret smuggling passageway made their way up to the basement of The Crow’s Nest. This travel proved uneventful; there seemed to have been no disturbance of the passageway since they used it last (although Noddy was pretty sure it had been used since, as the position of the carts had been moved). Upon arriving, they were greeted with some amazement and surprise by Barleyman, who upon seeing them was happy his passageway remained a secret.

His news was not, however, not happy. Soon after their departure, his steady customer Randolph had packed up and left, and while he was on occasion able to rent out the side room for gatherings it was not the steady income to which he had become accustomed. Worse, however, was that priests of The Divinity had shown up soon thereafter, demanding to see the boys who were known to be working and staying at the tavern. Upon finding the party to be gone the priests became angered, and began to search the entirety of the tavern.

At this point, Mistress Mary and Mistress Clara made themselves known, and demanded to know why the tavern was being turned upside down. A great argument erupted between the ladies and the priests, and while there was no actual conflict the end result was that the two healers were marched off by the priests and some soldiers, accompanied by a young red-headed man. Neither Mary nor Clara have since returned.

--

While this lack of serious adventure befell all others in the party, Nick Nab’s experience was quite the opposite. The “Amada” was kept apart from these more banal duties (whether on purpose or due to the judgment of Captain De Guzman) and continued to make excursions deep into the South, and on occasion on the extreme western edge of the Channel Islands. Engagements in the Islands were not so dangerous; there were other Northern ships about and the excellent skills of the crew of the “Amada” allowed for it to retreat into the narrow channel to escape if needed. But those few excursions south were perilous, indeed some good fortune was needed for escape on occasion. But De Guzman's recklessness was, regardless, unsuccessful. He had made it clear that his goal was to capture one of these so-called “Wind Lords”, those mysterious figures seen aboard some ships of the South. Or to discover where they came from. In both tasks he was unsuccessful.

De Guzman took the slight and weak Nick Nab under his wing, and in his dubious role as “Captain’s Mate” Nick was taught, and observed, all sorts of naval tactics and navigation. For his part, Nick seemed for once to be at ease. Of note, the “Amada” did not count among its complement any member of the Divinity. Nick didn’t know why, nor did he ask.

The “Amada”, as much as possible, avoided going to port. Being small and nimble, resupply was often done ashore, on a quiet beach or even river mouth. At more than one point De Guzeman ordered his ship to be careened in some out of the way place, removing all manner of barnacles and shipworm from its hull to maintain its speed.

--

In total, a full two years of time has passed since the party arrived in the Port of Sardinia. Other than the above, most of the rest of the time was spent aboard ship, literally “learning the ropes”.

On a final note, Prelate Nicholas, true to his word, has been preaching most mornings on the beach at the Port. On many days, however, he continues to overly take to drink. Nevertheless, when sober, he is a fiery speaker, and has a great many admirers among the more pious of the sailors when ashore. What supports him you do not know, as surely his share of the prize money has long since been pissed away.

docs.title: Interlude 5
docs.text:
There is a place that is not a place. Shore without sea, under stars without sky. There is a moment of silence, stillness at turn of tide, between final ebb of world and first surge of next. Upon this shore of non-existence, three figures appear in timeless triangle, hunched and eternal, each before a great stone bowl, tethered to the ground by the chains of reality.

The first has skin like cracked riverbed, hands gnarled as ancient roots. Her gaze is heavy; where it falls, mist in her bowl thickens and slows, possibilities coalescing like dew on spider's web. The second figure’s eyes are chips of flint, sharp, penetrating. Her hands are never still, twitching as she makes sharp, sudden movements. With a violent flick of her wrist above the bowl, she tears at the vapours without contact, sending chaotic ripples through the whole. The third is creature of shadow and suggestion, her face a pattern the eye cannot hold. She never touches the mist, but hums low, dissonant tune, and vibrations cause patterns in her bowl to dance and reform, weaving and unweaving themselves in time with the sound.

From within each dark, unadorned bowl, pearlescent mist coils and writhes, living vapour that holds echoes of worlds. It is possibility itself, swirling with potential of every choice made and unmade. The mist shimmers with faint colour of souls and deep light of raw power, a chaotic soup of destiny being served.

Their work is constant, silent conversation. Sharp stir from the second is softened by heavy gaze of the first. Chaotic ripples are given structure by humming of the third. They act not in sequence, but in concert—a system of perfect, inscrutable balance. One ripple spreads, image flares into focus across all three bowls at once, fleeting window into world of wind, and salt, and sail.

But the concert is not always gentle melody; it is often cacophony of competing wills. The second will plunge her hands deep, twisting mist into maelstrom that threatens to shred delicate thread of fate—a ship, perhaps, caught in sudden squall. In response, the third’s hum will rise in pitch, a sharp, cutting note that attempts to weave safe channel through chaos. The first will then fix her heavy gaze upon the thread itself, lending it impossible weight and resilience, forcing it to hold fast against tearing winds.

This is their eternal game, contest of wills played out in vapour and light. No single impulse ever allowed complete triumph. Chaos met with order, intention with inertia, every possibility tested, strained, and contested before becoming single truth. They are adversaries as much as partners, each ensuring the others do not pull tapestry of reality too far in any one direction.

And now, their collective attention fixes. Within swirling mists of all three bowls, the same scene unfolds. Vapours bleed with colour, pools of raw power vying for dominance: blinding white and velvet black; smouldering crimson and deep sapphire; rich umber and stormy grey; luminous violet and vibrant emerald. And scattered among these warring hues, eight small lights have appeared upon the waters. Insignificant sparks in grand design, yet they pull at threads of destiny with force far greater than size would suggest.

For something has begun to unravel. A great thread from within, woven with power of gods and poison of certainty, seeks to unmake world's design. It pulls and tears at the balance, threatening to bleach all colour from the mist, leaving only stark white and bottomless black. And so the three, for the first time in an age, find shared purpose, if not shared path. Two gaze upon six, nurturing them as world's best hope; one watches two, for in chaos hides opportunity. They nudge and guide their chosen sparks, granting impossible luck, steering with unseen currents, for in these tiny, flickering flames, they have placed the world's hope to remain unfinished and the game played on.

docs.title: Interlude 6
docs.text:
First clear night since we sailed, and the first time in a fortnight I've trusted my hand enough to write plainly. I keep this now less as a Chronicler's record than as my own — a habit older than the Academy ever gave me, of not trusting a thing to be true until I've seen it hold still on a page.

My working case came back into my hands only this past week — pulled, intact, from a locked chest in a dead man's cabin, three years of my own shorthand no worse for the crossing than I am myself. It should be a comfort, and in its way it is; but shorthand wants leisure to unpick properly, and leisure is the one thing this fortnight has not given me. The older folio, the one I kept at the Crow's Nest before I ever left the Capitol, is further out of reach still — I have had no word of it since, and no way to ask. What follows leans on neither: it is reconstructed from memory, and from a fortnight of unusually frank conversation aboard a ship I do not command, with a crew whose full particulars I am still assembling. I have made it a habit, these many years, never to consider a picture finished until it is complete. That habit does not serve me tonight. Better an incomplete page than none, and some of what I have learned will not keep quietly in my head until I can set it down whole.

--

Begin with the plainest matter, since it is the one I am most sure of. The war I grew up hearing about is not being fought. It has stalled, not ended — the Shatters threw up a barrier between the fleets that neither side has found a way around, and both nations have spent on their own recovery what they might once have spent on each other. I should not mistake that for peace, and I remind myself of it as I write: nothing has been negotiated, the two sides have simply been unable to reach one another, and the Kingdom has used the lull to look west rather than stand down, pouring what it can spare into a crossing meant to carry it around the Maelstrom entirely. I am told, though I have not verified it myself, that the Southern Houses read the New World the same way — the next arena for the old rivalry, now that the old one has gone quiet. What I can attest to more confidently is the shape of the gap itself: a ship carries news across the Maelstrom in weeks at best, and what survives the crossing is whatever a captain or a trading house has chosen to repeat. I spent three years assuming my own information was current and have spent this last fortnight discovering how much of it was not. Let that stand as a caution to myself, set down where I will have to see it again: whatever I believe I know of the other side of that water right now, I should treat as provisional.

There is a harder matter, and one that touches the young people I've fallen in with too closely for me to write about with any pretense of distance. They were declared heretics of the Church some years past, over a matter I have reason to believe I understand better than most — I will not detail it here, save to say it concerns an object, and a doctrine, and is not itself in question. What troubles me is the manner of the declaration: a public bounty, issued with a speed and a certainty that is not how the Church ordinarily moves against a handful of unproven youths. My own old notes, written before I understood any of this, already recorded alarm at the Church's sudden interest in them — I did not know, at the time, that I was watching the opening move of something already decided. I have a name in mind for the hand that decided it. I have turned it over enough now that I am no longer troubled by how well it fits, only by how much I would prefer to be wrong. I will not write it here, or anywhere. Not because I distrust this page particularly — I distrust any page, including the ones I mean only for myself, more than I trust my own memory to hold a thing until I can lay it across a table instead, in front of the people who need to hear it.

--

My old interest in the "Advance" and in Barrows, her captain, goes back further than anything else in this page — he belongs to a small and careful fellowship whose name I have never once committed to paper, and will not start now. I can confirm, from these young people's own report, what I had only suspected: the "Advance" was tracked two years past to an island the Islanders and the Elves both call Birdcrown, and has not been seen or heard from since. She has not been struck from any Navy list I am aware of, nor formally reported lost, which I find as strange as anything else in this account — a missing warship, on a mission that mattered to people who do not forget such things easily, going unremarked in the official record is either an oversight or a silence someone has chosen to keep. I do not know which. I will say plainly, because there is no one here to soften it for, that I am uneasy in a way I cannot yet justify with evidence, only with pattern: this is the second man of that fellowship to go quiet on that same stretch of water, on business the fellowship itself sanctioned, and I do not like patterns I cannot explain.

On the Shatters themselves, and what caused them, I know rather more now than I did when I left the Capitol. The light said to rise from a Totem in the instant of its destruction is not, I am now confident, a detail specific to what happened at Spider Island — it matches, closely enough that I no longer credit it to coincidence, an account already forty years old and independently recorded. My own circle's working belief is that a Totem's power does not simply vanish when the pillar breaks; it is loosed all at once, ungoverned, which is why the aftermath scales with whatever the Totem itself was worth destroying. One thing more, and I mean to treat it as carefully in my own thinking as I do on this page: there are more such sites, known to people I trust, than the two the world already has cause to mourn. I do not know how many. I do not know where. I set it down only so that I do not, myself, mistake two incidents for the whole of a pattern.

--

A smaller, tidier matter, if only because questions of Church structure are the one part of this page I can answer without hedging. I had cause recently to confirm, from a captured vessel's own crew, the fates of two priests aboard her — a senior woman, Margot, trusted with a relic and formidable in her own right, and a junior man, Arnim, neither talented nor especially unlucky, simply posted where the Church needed a warm body willing to go. Both are missing, presumed drowned, and I do not expect that to change. Worth recording for my own reference is the question that was put to me afterward: whether either of them held some rank above the ordinary — a "summoner," in the word used to me, as though the Church kept some office for commanding power beyond a cleric's reach. It does not. I can say this with the flat certainty of a man who has spent a decade cataloguing that hierarchy: Twin Eminences, Archons, High Clerics and Canons, Vicars, Clerics, Curates, Prelates, Deacons, Acolytes, and one office outside that ladder entirely, the Censure — sent when the Church expects to find and destroy something it has already judged heretical, and equipped accordingly. Neither Margot nor Arnim was a Censure. I write the distinction here as plainly as I can, if only so I remember it myself the next time I am tempted to treat a difficult priest and a genuine one as the same order of danger.

I owe myself, if no one else, an honest accounting of my own conduct here, if only to understand why I am this late getting anywhere at all. I went looking for a ship called the Fortnum in person rather than by correspondence, once I learned she had been reassigned from ordinary convoy work to something closer to hunting — the particulars of what, I will not set down here, save that it touches the same doctrine as the matter above. That was my own choice, not an assignment, and I do not regret making it. I learned, aboard her, rather more than a Chronicler's ordinary remit allows, and rather less discreetly than I intended — enough that her captain, a man named Mason, had every reasonable cause to treat me as something closer to a spy than a guest. I will not pretend otherwise, least of all to myself. He did not treat it as a hanging matter. He confined me, took my writings into his own keeping for safety rather than destroying them, and asked only my word that I would not attempt escape while he held them — a bargain he kept in full, and one I broke only once the writings themselves were no longer his to hold, at which point I told him so to his face and considered the matter closed between us. He accepted that without argument, which I have not stopped turning over since. He was, by every measure I could take of him in the time I had, an honourable man doing an ugly job competently, and I do not enjoy that his death sits at the end of my own rescue.

--

The last matter I set down here I still do not entirely understand, and I will let this account end in a shrug rather than a conclusion, because that is the honest shape of it. Chroniclers are taught to call and steady message birds over long distances; a very few of us are taught that the same faculty, cautiously and rarely used, extends further, toward creatures larger and less biddable than any bird — not command, properly understood, so much as an urgent suggestion laid across an animal's own instincts, which it is free to answer or ignore as it chooses. I had used this, in small and careful measure, more than once during my confinement aboard the Fortnum, to harry her with lesser creatures and buy myself what openings I could. In the last extremity of my escape from her, with the outcome very much in doubt, I called again, with rather more need behind it than I had ever risked before, and something answered that was larger than anything I had thought myself capable of reaching — large enough to break the ship in two. I do not know why that attempt succeeded where my earlier, smaller ones only startled a watch. My best guess, and it is no more than that, is that the size of the need shapes the size of the answer, but I have no way to test it, and no wish to test it again if I can help it. Nor can I explain a stranger detail from earlier in that same voyage: on one occasion, a lesser summoning of mine was answered not only by a serpent but by a burst of mortar fire from a source no one aboard, on either side of the fighting, ever claimed. I have turned over every ordinary explanation I can think of and settled on none of them. I set it down here only because a loose thread left unrecorded is one I will not be able to pull on later, should I ever need to.

--

There is one more thread from these weeks, and I have it only at second hand, since I was not there to see any of it myself — kept below decks the whole while we lay at anchor, by the party's own vote, so that nothing of where we'd called would find its way into these pages even by accident. What follows is reconstructed from what a fortnight of conversation since has let slip, not from anything I witnessed, and I set it down with that caveat attached and no other. Among the old company of the "Advance" was a junior priest, Nicolas, whom I gather has gone thoroughly to seed in the years since — preaching, by all report, a private gospel of his own devising to a "Brother (Handsome) Gulliver Gold" he holds to be some manner of divine kin to the god he was ordained under. He has made real converts of it, a modest handful of local sailors taken hard enough by his preaching that he would not leave without two of the most fervent among them, nor at all without the freedom to preach daily from the forecastle to whoever cared to listen, and his carved statue of Brother Gold carried along with him. He is, I am told, unchanged in every other particular — touched, possibly deranged, in a way none of them could quite agree was worsening or simply constant. What moved him in the end, more than anything else tried, was the promise that the voyage itself might turn up some trace of a "Sister Silver" he believes must exist somewhere to match his Brother. He has already asked to see the object I am not to name even here; he was told, truthfully as far as I can judge, that he will, once we are properly underway. I record the promise only because I mean to hold the ones who made it to it.

--

Once we were properly underway and Nicolas had settled into the ship's routine, I made a point of sitting with him myself, rather than leaving the whole of him to what others had gathered secondhand. My own old interest in Barrows and the "Advance" is a thing I have already set down here, and it seemed a poor use of the opportunity to let it pass unquestioned. He was willing enough to talk, more so, I think, once he understood I asked as a man who keeps a page rather than as anyone likely to repeat him to a superior.

He served on the second voyage of the "Advance," this time under the command of the newly captained Barrows, the senior priest, Jacque, set over him. He described a captain much changed from the one I gather the party knew — quieter, more deliberate, a man who had been given his ship back once and did not mean to lose it a second time to a mistake of temperament. Of the ship's heading he could tell me only what a junior priest is ever told: west, and further west, into the same waters where Maynard had gone missing, with no port of call he could name between the mainland and Port Sardina, where he himself came off her partway through the crossing. He does not know, and was careful to say he does not know, what waited for her past that point — only that Barrows meant to sail on, and did. Of the "Advance"'s first, ill-fated voyage under Maynard he was no part, nor was Jacque; of it he knew only a single name, the one junior priest who came home again — Philip. Why Philip did not sail a second time under Barrows, Nicolas could not tell me, only that the name went unspoken aboard ship, and that he had learned early not to ask why.

Of Jacque himself he would say little, and what he did say came slowly, and touched only the end of it: that whatever finally split him from the ship in Port Sardina was as much a falling-out with the priest who had ordained him as it was anything else pressing on him by then, and that the fault, such as it was, sat more with him than with Jacque. He did not want to say more of that, and I did not press him — a man does not owe a stranger the whole of a falling-out with the priest who ordained him, and I have my own reasons for knowing better than to demand it. Of what came after Port Sardina, though, he was almost eager to talk, as though the telling cost him less than the parts that came before it. He does not remember those weeks kindly — a passage south worked rather than paid for, aboard a hold whose name he never learned, captained by men content to leave a defrocked priest's questions unasked so long as he pulled his share, and more of the crossing lost to drink than he cared to number. He fetched up in Drowned Man's Port for no better reason than that it was as far as that ship went and no ship going further would have him, and he has stayed ever since less from any decision than from never finding cause to leave. What carried him the distance, he said, was that Gulliver Gold had followed him aboard every hull since the "Advance," and that a carver in the port's shipwright's yard, once shown what Nicolas meant by the name, proved willing to give it a face. He did not call that meeting a beginning. He called it, if I understood him rightly, the first time since the "Advance" that anyone had taken him seriously enough to argue with.

--

I began this page meaning only to steady my own hand, and I find, having written it, that I am less troubled by the gaps in it than I expected to be. The old folio I kept at the Crow's Nest, before ever I left the Capitol, was the most densely annotated document I had ever kept on these young people, and still the least finished — wherever it sits now, I doubt that has changed. The case I carry in its place, three years' worth and still growing, will have to do the same work from here; I have watched them long enough now to trust that it, too, will stay unfinished for some time yet. I mark this page in the corner as I always do, for reasons that are mine alone to know.

docs.title: Letter from Eleanor Mason
docs.text:
Among the personal effects looted from Captain Mason's sea chest during the escape from the Fortnum was a small, oilskin-wrapped keepsake pouch: a plain gold ring and a handful of folded letters in a woman's hand. This is the one letter from that packet worth reading in full.

The Capitol, KC 8

My dearest Herod,

I pray this finds you well, and that the seas have been kinder to you than the winter has been to us here. I have news that I could not bear to entrust to anyone's pen but my own, though I have started this letter three times now and blotted the first two with foolish tears.

You have a son.

He came two nights ago, loud and furious about it, with your temper already plain in him if nothing else of you is yet visible in his face. He is small but sound, the midwife tells me, and feeds well, and I am mending faster than I did the first time, whatever that is worth to you from so far away. I have named him Herod, after his father, though I confess I already call him "little Herod" to keep us straight, and I suspect the house will call him that long after he has outgrown the need for it.

I wish you could see him. I wish that more than I have wished for anything since you last sailed. He has your stubbornness already — he would not settle until I gave up and let him have his own way of it, which I am told is no way to raise a child and which I intend to do anyway, at least until you are home to tell me otherwise.

The house is quiet without you in it, quieter still now that there are two of us waiting instead of one. I do not ask when you will be back — I have learned better than to ask, and I know you would tell me if you could — but I will say that I count the days regardless, and that your son will know your face from the miniature on the mantel long before he knows it from the man himself, unless the Two are kinder to us than they have been.

Come home safe, Herod. Come home soon, if you can manage it, but safe above all. We will be here.

Your loving wife, Eleanor

docs.title: Final Account of Abiyard, Cleric of the Kingship
docs.text:
This document contains the final, fragmented writings of a cleric aboard the Kingship.

…final thoughts. Scarce remains now o’ person and place, nae do aye expect t’endure ‘til Mother’s Morn; indeed aye doubt tha’ aye will. Nae, aye know it, for blood does boil w’the fever, and the bursting continues…

…set adrift, but t’was not enough. The I’Hand’s affliction was already felt amongs’t crew, and those fellows began t’fall t’it as well. T’was him that guarded o’er our captive, an’so t’was him first t’succumb. The native, for h’self, strangely, d’nae seem…

…summary o’ our return journey, as aye am nae certain my foregoin’ missives will ha’ reached to t’Temple. The Maelstorm which we hae passed was, w’out th’aid o’ th’ Heratic, impossible to return athwart. DiRendal’s fo’cast proved correct in this regard, but fortunately th’other did as well. While we lost more wi’th crossing, the cold could nae…

…can nae let his journals be returned, these matters…

…at Sebastian’s insistence we were forced t’accept him. But nae matter, Baynar and aye decided he would prove nae match f’the pair o’us, given he were alone save his stew…

…overed i’scratches. As each one struck the Totem, whisps o’this same light were drawn up and sent…

…sacrifice o’Baynar to achieve this end. What other choice c’be considered? It was just as Grantos ha’described, and as we feared. Such heresy could nae be left unchecked, nae unpunished…

…must surely ha’perished, close as they were. E’en this far a’sea, we were near o’ercome by the effect. Baynar was right t’insist on bringing the Dyad, and aye maintain its loss will o’a surety prove…

docs.title: The Articles of Agreement of The Medallion
docs.text: Herein be the Articles of Agreement for the company of this vessel. Let every man read and set his mark to these laws ere we venture forth upon the seas.

docs.title: I. Command and Governance
docs.text:
1. The Senior Officers shall comprise of the Quartermaster, the Captain, the Master at Arms, the Master of Fog, the Master Lookout, the Master Surgeon, The Master Gunner, and the Master of Sail.
  2. Senior Officers shall have a vote in affairs of moment, whether it be the charting of our course or the choosing of a prize to be taken.
  3. The Captain's word is law in time of chase or battle. In all other matters, his authority shall be guided by the will of the Senior Officers, as determined by a majority vote. In the event of a tied vote, the Senior Officer whose area of expertise is most relevant to the matter shall cast the deciding vote.
  4. The Quartermaster shall be the magistrate of the company, charged with settling all disputes and ensuring the voice of the crew is heard.

docs.title: II. The Division of Spoils
docs.text:
1. All prize and treasure shall be allotted into shares. A common seaman shall be granted one share. A man of special skill or a junior officer, such as a Surgeon's assistant or Mid-shipman, shall be granted two shares. The Senior leaders of the vessel shall be granted three shares.
  2. An act of uncommon valour or singular skill in the heat of battle may be rewarded with an extra half-share, should the Senior leaders vote it so.
  3. Any person who should lose a limb or be grievously wounded in the service of the ship shall have compensation from the common stock ere the prize is divided. For the loss of a right arm, sixty silver pieces; for a left arm, fifty silver pieces; for a right leg, fifty silver pieces; for a left leg, forty silver pieces; for an eye or a finger, ten silver pieces. This sum may be increased by a vote of the Senior Officers in recognition of uncommon valour.
  4. A portion of shares from every prize shall be set aside for the upkeep of the ship, the amount to be determined by the Quartermaster with the consent of the Senior Officers.

docs.title: III. Onboard Discipline
docs.text:
1. Let no person presume to strike their shipmate. All quarrels shall be brought before the Quartermaster, who shall mediate the dispute. If he cannot bring the parties to reconciliation, the matter shall be ended on shore, by duel of sword and pistol to first blood, with the Quartermaster presiding.
  2. Any person who offers to meddle with another without their consent shall suffer present death.
  3. He that is found guilty of theft from a shipmate shall feel the lash and forfeit his share of the next prize taken.
  4. He who is guilty of drunkenness, if a seaman, shall be put in irons until he is sober. If an officer, he shall forfeit one-tenth of his next share for his lack of discipline.

docs.title: IV. Duties and Responsibilities
docs.text:
1. Every person to keep their piece, pistols, and cutlass clean and fit for service.
  2. He that shall sleep upon his watch, or neglect his duty, or forsake his station, shall suffer a lashing or forfeit his share, as the company shall see fit.
  3. No person shall give or dispose of the ship's provisions, but every one shall have their equal share of fresh victuals and strong liquors.
  4. No snapping of guns or smoking of tobacco in the hold.

docs.title: V. Conduct in Battle
docs.text:
1. To desert the ship or one's quarters in battle is punished with death or marooning.
  2. Good quarter to be given when craved.
  3. If any person shall defraud the company to the value of a single silver piece in plate, jewels, or money, marooning shall be their punishment.
  4. No person to talk of breaking up their way of living, till each had shared five hundred silver.

docs.title: VI. On Matters of Faith
docs.text:
1. Every person may worship as they see fit, or not at all, so long as their practices do not endanger the ship or her company.
  2. No person shall be compelled to attend any religious service, nor shall any person be scorned for their private beliefs.

docs.title: VII. Treatment of Outsiders
docs.text:
1. No passenger shall be taken aboard this vessel without the Captain's express consent. All who sail with us shall be subject to these articles.
  2. A fit place shall be set apart for the sick and hurt, prisoners included, where they may be tended to by the surgeon.
  3. The Commanders shall use their utmost endeavours to detect, apprehend, and bring to punishment all offenders, prisoners among them, who do violate the good order of the ship.

docs.title: VIII. On the Matter of Slavery
docs.text: 1. This ship and her company shall take no part in the trade of human souls. No man, woman, or child shall be held in bondage aboard this vessel, whether as cargo or chattel. Any found engaged in such trafficking shall forfeit his share and be cast from the company.

docs.title: IX. The Articles Themselves
docs.text:
1. These articles shall be put in writing, by way of bond or obligation, and every person who joins the company shall set their hand to it, and be bound by its laws.
  2. He who offends against these articles shall be punished as they prescribe. All other faults and misdemeanors not herein mentioned shall be punished according to the laws and customs used at sea.
  3. These articles may be amended only by a majority vote of the Senior Officers.

docs.title: The Medallion - Watch Assignments
docs.text: This document outlines the standard watch assignments for the crew of "The Medallion".

docs.title: The Seven Watches of the Day
docs.text:
A typical watch system on a sailing ship divided the 24-hour day into shifts. The period from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. was divided into two shorter, two-hour "dog watches" to ensure the watch teams rotated their duty times each day.

Watch Name Time Period Description Middle Watch Midnight – 4:00 AM The "Graveyard Watch." Extremely cold and dark. Morning Watch 4:00 AM – 8:00 AM Included the sunrise and the "washing of the decks." Forenoon Watch 8:00 AM – Noon The main period for heavy maintenance and drills. Afternoon Watch Noon – 4:00 PM Often the hottest part of the day; drills continued. First Dog Watch 4:00 PM – 6:00 PM A short, 2-hour watch. Last Dog Watch 6:00 PM – 8:00 PM The second 2-hour "half" watch. First Watch 8:00 PM – Midnight The first watch of the "night cycle."
